nuggets.title: Diversity of life and the need to name it
lines: The number of species that are known and described ranges between 1.7–1.8 million.
This number and types of organisms present on earth is what we call biodiversity.
Local (vernacular) names vary from place to place, so organisms need standardised names that are known the world over; this process is nomenclature.
Nomenclature is possible only when the organism is described correctly and we know what it is: this is identification.
Plant names follow the ICBN (International Code for Botanical Nomenclature); animal names follow the ICZN (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature).
Scientific names ensure each organism has only one name and that the name is not used for any other known organism.
nuggets.tip: Identification comes first; naming is impossible until you know what the organism is.

questions.why: 1.7–1.8 million species are known and described (NCERT). The other ranges are not NCERT figures.
NCERT defines biodiversity as the number and types of organisms present on earth, not just in a country, state or region.
Naming is possible only after the organism is correctly described and we know what it is. This step is identification, which comes before nomenclature.
ICBN = International Code for Botanical Nomenclature, which gives the rules for naming plants. It is an international code, not an Indian one.
A is right: a scientific name gives each organism only one name. B is wrong: vernacular names vary by place, and only scientific names guarantee the name is not used for another organism.

nuggets.title: Binomial nomenclature: the rules
lines: Binomial nomenclature was provided by Carolus Linnaeus: each name has a generic name and a specific epithet.
In Mangifera indica, Mangifera is the genus and indica is the specific epithet.
Biological names are generally in Latin and written in italics; they are Latinised or derived from Latin irrespective of their origin.
Printed names are in italics to indicate their Latin origin; handwritten names have both words underlined separately.
The genus starts with a capital letter; the specific epithet starts with a small letter.
The author's name appears after the specific epithet in abbreviated form, e.g. Mangifera indica Linn.
nuggets.tip: Italics show Latin origin, not non-Latin origin. NEET 2025 tested exactly this twist.

questions.why: Names are in Latin or Latinised, so 'any language' breaks the rules. Genus first + specific epithet, italics, and separate underlining when handwritten are all correct rules.
NCERT: names are printed in italics to indicate their Latin origin, not their non-Latin origin. The other three statements are the correct rules.
The correct form is Mangifera indica Linn.: the author's abbreviated name comes after the specific epithet. Capital 'I' in Indica or a 'Car.' prefix is wrong.
In Mangifera indica Linn., indica is the specific epithet, Mangifera is the genus and Linn. is the author.
Both the genus and the specific epithet are printed in italics. Only the genus starts with a capital letter, and the genus is always written first.

nuggets.title: Classification, taxonomy and systematics
lines: Classification is the process by which anything is grouped into convenient categories based on some easily observable characters.
The scientific term for these categories is taxa (e.g. plants, animals, mammals, dogs are all taxa at different levels).
Characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature are the processes basic to taxonomy.
Modern taxonomic studies use external and internal structure, cell structure, development process and ecological information.
The word systematics comes from the Latin systema (systematic arrangement); Linnaeus titled his book Systema Naturae.
Systematics studies the kinds and diversity of organisms and their relationships, including evolutionary relationships.

questions.why: NCERT's definition: grouping into convenient categories based on easily observable characters is classification. Nomenclature is naming.
All four (characterisation, identification, classification, nomenclature) are the basic processes of taxonomy.
Modern taxonomy uses external and internal structure, cell structure, development and ecological information, so 'all of the above' is right.
Both are correct: systematics comes from Latin systema (systematic arrangement), and Linnaeus titled his publication Systema Naturae.
Systematics studies the different kinds of organisms, their diversity and the relationships among them. It is not about organ systems or habitats.

nuggets.title: Taxonomic categories, taxon and hierarchy
lines: Classification is not a single-step process; it involves a hierarchy of steps where each step is a rank or category.
Each category, a unit of classification, represents a rank and is called a taxon (plural: taxa).
A taxon can be of any rank: insects are a taxon, and so are species, genus or order.
The obligate categories in ascending order: species → genus → family → order → class → phylum/division → kingdom.
This arrangement of categories in ascending or descending order is the taxonomic hierarchy.
nuggets.tip: Taxon is singular, taxa is plural. 'Category' is the rank; 'taxon' is the actual group placed at that rank.

questions.why: Taxon is the term for a taxonomic group of any rank. Class, order and species each name one specific rank.
A taxon is a taxonomic group of any rank, not only a group of species or families.
Both are NCERT lines: the categories are called taxa, and characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature are basic to taxonomy.
Taxa arranged in ascending or descending order of rank form a hierarchy. A key is a tool for identification, not an arrangement.
Ascending order: species → genus → family → order → class → phylum → kingdom. Skipping levels still keeps species → order → phylum → kingdom in the right order.

nuggets.title: Species and genus
lines: A species is a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities; it is the lowest taxonomic category.
In Mangifera indica, Solanum tuberosum (potato) and Panthera leo (lion), indica, tuberosum and leo are specific epithets.
A genus is a group of related species that have more characters in common than species of other genera.
Potato (tuberosum), brinjal (melongena) and nigrum are species of genus Solanum.
Lion (leo), leopard (pardus) and tiger (tigris) are species of genus Panthera, which differs from genus Felis (cats).

questions.why: Tiger is Panthera tigris, so tigris is its species name. Mollusca is a phylum, Primata is an order and Musca is a genus.
tuberosum (potato), melongena (brinjal) and nigrum are all species of the genus Solanum.
A genus is a group of related species with more characters in common than species of other genera. It is not a random collection.
Solanum and Mangifera are both genera (generic names). tuberosum and indica would be species epithets.
Potato, tomato and brinjal belong to Solanum. Onion (Allium) belongs to another genus and family.

nuggets.title: Family and order
lines: A family is a group of related genera with still fewer similarities than genus and species.
Plant families are characterised on vegetative and reproductive features: Solanum, Petunia and Datura are in Solanaceae.
Genus Panthera and genus Felis are in family Felidae; cats and dogs are in separate families, Felidae and Canidae.
An order is an assemblage of families with a few similar characters, fewer than among the genera of a family.
Plant order Polymoniales includes Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae, mainly on floral characters.
Animal order Carnivora includes families Felidae and Canidae.
nuggets.tip: Carnivora is an ORDER, not a class or family; Felidae and Canidae are FAMILIES, not genera.

questions.why: Carnivora is an order. Muscidae is a family, Insecta is a class and Panthera is a genus.
A is wrong: Allium (onion) is not in Solanaceae; NCERT lists Solanum, Petunia, Datura. B is wrong: Felidae and Canidae are families, not genera.
Order Polymoniales includes Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae, grouped mainly on floral characters.
A group of related families with a few common characters forms an order. A group of related genera would be a family.
X = order, an assemblage of families with a few similar characters. These similar characters are fewer than among the genera of one family.

nuggets.title: Class, phylum, kingdom and the trend of characters
lines: A class includes related orders: order Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and order Carnivora (tiger, cat, dog) are both in class Mammalia.
Classes of animals (fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) are grouped into phylum Chordata because they have a notochord and a dorsal hollow neural system.
In plants, classes with a few similar characters are assigned to a higher category called Division, the plant equivalent of phylum.
All animals form kingdom Animalia; all plants form kingdom Plantae.
As we go from species to kingdom, the number of common characteristics decreases; the lower the taxon, the more characters its members share.
nuggets.tip: Higher taxon = more organisms, fewer shared characters. Species shares the most, kingdom the least.

questions.why: A is wrong: Carnivora is an order, not a class. B is right: order Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) is in class Mammalia.
In plant classification, Division is used in place of the animal category Phylum.
Going up from species to kingdom, members share fewer characters, so common characteristics decrease.
Class Mammalia includes order Primata and order Carnivora. Primata is an order, not a class.
Two genera in the same family must share every higher rank (order, class, phylum). Being different genera, their species must differ.

nuggets.title: Organisms with their taxonomic categories (Table 1.1)
lines: Man: Homo sapiens, family Hominidae, order Primata, class Mammalia, phylum Chordata.
Housefly: Musca domestica, family Muscidae, order Diptera, class Insecta, phylum Arthropoda.
Mango: Mangifera indica, family Anacardiaceae, order Sapindales, class Dicotyledonae, division Angiospermae.
Wheat: Triticum aestivum, family Poaceae, order Poales, class Monocotyledonae, division Angiospermae.
Mango and wheat are in different classes, orders and families but the same division (Angiospermae).
nuggets.tip: Endings help: plant family -aceae, plant order -ales, animal family -idae.

questions.why: House fly (Musca domestica) belongs to family Muscidae (order Diptera).
Wheat: genus Triticum, family Poaceae, order Poales, class Monocotyledonae. Sapindales and Anacardiaceae belong to mango.
Mango is a dicot (Sapindales, Anacardiaceae) and wheat is a monocot (Poales, Poaceae). They share only division Angiospermae.
Dicotyledonae is a class. Man's class is Mammalia; Chordata is a phylum and Primata an order.
Mango (Mangifera indica) belongs to family Anacardiaceae. Poaceae is wheat, Hominidae is man, Muscidae is housefly.

nuggets.title: From Aristotle to Whittaker's five kingdoms
lines: Aristotle was the earliest to attempt a scientific basis: plants into trees, shrubs and herbs; animals by presence or absence of red blood.
Linnaeus gave the Two Kingdom system: Plantae and Animalia.
Two kingdoms did not distinguish eukaryotes from prokaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, or photosynthetic (green algae) from non-photosynthetic (fungi) organisms.
R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed the Five Kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Whittaker's main criteria: cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.
nuggets.tip: Whittaker's year is 1969 (not 1996). Reproduction IS one of his criteria.

questions.why: R.H. Whittaker proposed the five kingdom classification in 1969. 1996 is a common decoy.
Aristotle classified plants by simple morphological characters into trees, shrubs and herbs.
The two-kingdom system lumped prokaryotes with eukaryotes, unicellular with multicellular, and green algae with fungi, so it distinguished none of these.
The criteria are cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships (i–v). Mitochondria and plain morphology were not separate criteria.
Whittaker used phylogeny, reproduction and nutrition, but not embryological characters.

nuggets.title: What the five kingdoms changed
lines: All prokaryotes were grouped under kingdom Monera; unicellular eukaryotes were placed in kingdom Protista.
Protista brought together Chlamydomonas and Chlorella (with cell walls, earlier in Plantae) and Paramoecium and Amoeba (without cell walls, earlier in Animalia).
Eukaryotic organisms are spread over four kingdoms: Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Fungi got a separate kingdom because of their heterotrophic nutrition and cell wall of chitin.
A three-domain system has also been proposed that divides kingdom Monera into two domains, leaving the eukaryotes in a third.
nuggets.tip: Three-domain system: Monera is split into TWO domains (Archaea and Bacteria); eukaryotes form the third.

questions.why: In Whittaker's system, unicellular eukaryotes like Chlamydomonas and Chlorella are in Protista, not Plantae or Monera.
Both true: Protista brought together Chlorella (earlier a plant) and Paramoecium (earlier an animal), because different systems use different criteria.
The three-domain system divides kingdom Monera into two domains; eukaryotic kingdoms make up the third domain.
I is false: Paramecium and Amoeba lack cell walls. II, III and IV are NCERT lines: Chlorella/Chlamydomonas have walls, prokaryotes are Monera, unicellular eukaryotes are Protista.
Eukaryotes are in four kingdoms (Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia); only Monera is prokaryotic.

nuggets.title: Kingdom Monera: bacteria in general
lines: Bacteria are the sole members of Monera and the most abundant micro-organisms; hundreds live in a handful of soil.
By shape there are four groups: spherical coccus, rod-shaped bacillus, comma-shaped vibrium and spiral spirillum.
Bacterial structure is very simple, but they are very complex in behaviour.
As a group they show the most extensive metabolic diversity.
Some bacteria are autotrophic (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic); the vast majority are heterotrophs.

questions.why: Rhodospirillum is spiral (spirillum), Staphylococci spherical (coccus), E. coli rod (bacillus) and the cholera organism comma-shaped (vibrio).
Bacteria (Monera) show the most extensive metabolic/nutritional diversity: photo- and chemoautotrophs, saprophytes, parasites.
NCERT: bacteria are the most abundant micro-organisms, found almost everywhere.
A is wrong: the shapes are swapped (coccus is spherical, bacillus is rod-shaped). B is right: some bacteria are autotrophic and most are heterotrophic.
All three are true: bacteria are simple in structure but complex in behaviour; autotrophs can be photo- or chemosynthetic; heterotrophs are parasites or saprophytes.

nuggets.title: Archaebacteria: life in extreme habitats
lines: Archaebacteria live in harsh habitats: extreme salty areas (halophiles), hot springs (thermoacidophiles) and marshy areas (methanogens).
They differ from other bacteria in having a different cell wall structure, which is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions.
Methanogens are present in the gut of several ruminant animals such as cows and buffaloes.
Methanogens are responsible for producing methane (biogas) from the dung of these animals.
nuggets.tip: Archaebacteria differ in their CELL WALL; methanogens live in the gut of RUMINANTS (cows, buffaloes).

questions.why: Organisms in extreme saline conditions are halophiles, a type of archaebacteria.
Methanogens are archaebacteria found in marshy areas and the ruminant gut, where they produce methane.
Marshy area = methanogens, hot spring = thermoacidophiles, salty area = halophiles.
NCERT: archaebacteria differ from other bacteria in having a different cell wall structure, which lets them survive extreme conditions.
Methanogens in the gut of ruminants (cows, buffaloes) produce methane (biogas) from dung. Their cell wall differs from other bacteria, and they are not halophiles.

nuggets.title: Eubacteria: cyanobacteria and chemosynthetic autotrophs
lines: Eubacteria (true bacteria) have a rigid cell wall and, if motile, a flagellum.
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) have chlorophyll a like green plants and are photosynthetic autotrophs.
Cyanobacteria are unicellular, colonial or filamentous, freshwater/marine or terrestrial; colonies have a gelatinous sheath and often form blooms in polluted water.
Some, like Nostoc and Anabaena, fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called heterocysts.
Chemosynthetic autotrophs oxidise inorganic substances (nitrates, nitrites, ammonia) and use the released energy for ATP production.
They play a great role in recycling nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur.
nuggets.tip: Cyanobacteria have chlorophyll a (no chlorophyll b). Chemosynthetic bacteria recycle N, P, Fe and S.

questions.why: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic autotrophs in Monera. Bacteria are not all heterotrophic, slime moulds are protists, and Mycoplasma has no cell wall.
A is the NCERT line. B is wrong: chemosynthetic bacteria recycle nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur, not potassium and selenium.
Nostoc and Anabaena fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called heterocysts.
A is true: cyanobacteria are photosynthetic autotrophs. R is false: they have chlorophyll a only, not a and b like green plants.
Both correct: chemosynthetic autotrophs oxidise inorganic substances (nitrates, nitrites, ammonia) to make ATP, and the bloom-forming cyanobacteria of polluted water are photosynthetic autotrophs.

nuggets.title: Heterotrophic bacteria, reproduction and Mycoplasma
lines: Heterotrophic bacteria are the most abundant; many are decomposers, help make curd from milk, produce antibiotics and fix N2 in legume roots.
Some are pathogens: cholera, typhoid, tetanus in humans and citrus canker in plants.
Bacteria reproduce mainly by fission; under unfavourable conditions they produce spores.
They also show a primitive sexual reproduction by transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another.
Mycoplasma lack a cell wall; they are the smallest living cells known and can survive without oxygen.
Many Mycoplasma are pathogenic in animals and plants.

questions.why: Heterotrophic bacteria are the most abundant prokaryotes and are used for making curd and producing antibiotics.
Citrus canker is a bacterial plant disease. Cholera and typhoid are human diseases; potato spindle tuber is caused by a viroid.
Both correct: bacteria reproduce mainly by binary fission and form spores under unfavourable conditions.
Mycoplasma: smallest living cells, no cell wall, survive without oxygen, pathogenic to plants and animals.
A is right: Mycoplasma, the smallest living cells, pass through filters finer than 1 µm. B is wrong: they lack a cell wall.

nuggets.title: Kingdom Protista: general features
lines: All single-celled eukaryotes are placed under Protista, but the kingdom's boundaries are not well defined.
Members are primarily aquatic.
Protista forms a link between Monera and the kingdoms of plants, animals and fungi.
The protistan cell has a well-defined nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles; some have flagella or cilia.
They reproduce asexually, and sexually by cell fusion and zygote formation.
Protista includes Chrysophytes, Dinoflagellates, Euglenoids, Slime moulds and Protozoans.
nuggets.tip: What is 'a photosynthetic protistan' to one biologist may be 'a plant' to another, which is why the boundaries are not well defined.

questions.why: Chrysophytes, euglenoids, dinoflagellates and slime moulds (plus protozoans) are all in kingdom Protista.
A is true: all protists are eukaryotes. R is false: protists have a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
A (aquatic), C (well-defined nucleus) and D (flagella/cilia) are true. B is false: Protista's boundaries are not well defined, so three are correct.
The boundaries are unclear because what one biologist calls a photosynthetic protistan another may call a plant.
1 and 2 are NCERT lines: Protista links Monera with plants, animals and fungi, and reproduces by cell fusion and zygote. 3 is wrong: protists are eukaryotic.

nuggets.title: Chrysophytes: diatoms and golden algae
lines: Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae (desmids), found in fresh water and marine environments.
They are microscopic and float passively in water currents (plankton); most are photosynthetic.
In diatoms the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells that fit together as in a soap box.
The walls are embedded with silica, so they are indestructible; their wall deposits over billions of years form diatomaceous earth.
Being gritty, diatomaceous earth is used in polishing and in filtration of oils and syrups.
Diatoms are the chief 'producers' in the oceans.
nuggets.tip: Diatom walls: silica, indestructible, soap-box halves. Dinoflagellate walls: stiff cellulose plates.

questions.why: Diatoms (chrysophytes) are the chief producers in the oceans.
Diatom walls are embedded with silica and are indestructible, so 'easily destructible' is wrong. The other three are NCERT lines.
In chrysophytes (diatoms) the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells that fit together like a soap box.
Gritty diatomaceous earth is used in polishing and in filtration of oils and syrups, so all options apply.
Both are NCERT lines: chrysophytes are microscopic plankton, and the group includes diatoms and golden algae (desmids).

nuggets.title: Dinoflagellates
lines: Dinoflagellates are mostly marine and photosynthetic.
They appear yellow, green, brown, blue or red depending on the main pigments in their cells.
The cell wall has stiff cellulose plates on the outer surface.
Most have two flagella: one lies longitudinally and the other transversely in a furrow between the wall plates.
Red dinoflagellates (e.g. Gonyaulax) multiply rapidly and make the sea appear red (red tides); their toxins may even kill fish.

questions.why: Dinoflagellates have two flagella: one longitudinal and one transverse, lying in a furrow between the wall plates.
Red dinoflagellates like Gonyaulax release toxins that may even kill fish and other marine animals.
Both are NCERT lines: dinoflagellates have stiff cellulose plates on the outer wall, and toxins from their large numbers can kill fish.
Rapid multiplication of red dinoflagellates such as Gonyaulax makes the sea look red: the red tide.
Varied colours, stiff cellulose plates, one longitudinal and one transverse flagellum, and photosynthesis describe the dinoflagellate Gonyaulax.

nuggets.title: Euglenoids and slime moulds
lines: Euglenoids (e.g. Euglena) are mostly freshwater organisms of stagnant water.
Instead of a cell wall they have a protein-rich pellicle that makes the body flexible; they have two flagella, a short and a long one.
They are photosynthetic in sunlight but, when deprived of sunlight, behave like heterotrophs by predating on smaller organisms; their pigments are identical to those of higher plants.
Slime moulds are saprophytic protists; the body moves along decaying twigs and leaves, engulfing organic material.
Under suitable conditions they form an aggregation called plasmodium; under unfavourable conditions it forms fruiting bodies bearing spores at their tips.
The spores have true walls, are extremely resistant, survive for many years and are dispersed by air currents.
nuggets.tip: Euglena pellicle is PROTEIN-rich (not cellulose). Slime mould spores travel by AIR, not water.

questions.why: Both are NCERT lines: euglenoid pigments are identical to those of higher plants, and the body is covered by a protein-rich pellicle.
Euglenoids have two flagella of unequal length (one short, one long), so 'two equal flagella' is the exception.
Euglenoids photosynthesise in light, but when deprived of sunlight they behave as heterotrophs by predating on smaller organisms.
Slime moulds are saprophytic, the plasmodium has no wall, and the spores have true walls.
i and ii are NCERT lines (true walls; resistant for years). iii is wrong: slime mould spores are dispersed by air currents.

nuggets.title: Protozoans
lines: All protozoans are heterotrophs, living as predators or parasites; they are believed to be primitive relatives of animals.
Amoeboid protozoans live in fresh water, sea water or moist soil; they capture prey with pseudopodia; marine forms have silica shells; some, like Entamoeba, are parasites.
Flagellated protozoans are free-living or parasitic; parasites such as Trypanosoma cause sleeping sickness.
Ciliated protozoans (e.g. Paramoecium) are aquatic, actively moving with thousands of cilia, and have a cavity (gullet) opening to the outside.
Sporozoans have an infectious spore-like stage; Plasmodium causes malaria.

questions.why: Pseudopodia are the locomotory and feeding organs of amoeboid protozoans, not sporozoans, so that statement is wrong.
Plasmodium is a sporozoan, amoeboid = Entamoeba, ciliated = Paramecium, flagellated = Trypanosoma.
Paramoecium (a ciliate) has a cavity, the gullet, that opens to the outside of the cell surface.
Sleeping sickness is caused by the flagellated parasitic protozoan Trypanosoma.
Protozoans are all heterotrophs (so i is wrong); they are predators or parasites, are protists, and are thought to be primitive relatives of animals.

nuggets.title: Kingdom Fungi: body and nutrition
lines: Fungi are a unique kingdom of heterotrophic organisms, e.g. Puccinia (wheat rust), white spots on mustard (a parasitic fungus), Penicillium (antibiotic).
Except yeasts (unicellular, used to make bread and beer), fungi are filamentous with thread-like hyphae forming a network called mycelium.
Some hyphae are continuous tubes with multinucleated cytoplasm: coenocytic hyphae; others have septae.
Fungal cell walls are composed of chitin and polysaccharides.
Most fungi are saprophytes on dead substrates; some are parasites; some are symbionts in lichens (with algae) and mycorrhiza (with roots).
Fungi prefer to grow in warm and humid places, which is why food is refrigerated.
nuggets.tip: Fungal wall = chitin, not cellulose. Coenocytic = no septa + many nuclei.

questions.why: The fungal cell wall is made mainly of chitin (with polysaccharides). Peptidoglycan is bacterial and cellulose is plant.
Fungal walls contain chitin, not pure cellulose, so that statement is wrong. Fungi are heterotrophic, eukaryotic, and unicellular or multicellular.
Saprophyte = decomposes dead matter, parasite = lives on living hosts, lichen = alga + fungus, mycorrhiza = fungus + plant roots.
Coenocytic hyphae are continuous tubes, without septa, filled with multinucleated cytoplasm.
Yeast, a unicellular fungus, is used in making bread and beer. Nostoc/Anabaena are Monera; lichens are alga + fungus; Paramecium is a protist.

nuggets.title: Reproduction in fungi
lines: Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation, fission and budding.
Asexual spores are conidia, sporangiospores or zoospores; sexual spores are oospores, ascospores and basidiospores, produced in fruiting bodies.
The sexual cycle has three steps: plasmogamy (fusion of protoplasms), karyogamy (fusion of two nuclei) and meiosis in the zygote.
In ascomycetes and basidiomycetes an intervening dikaryotic stage (n + n, two nuclei per cell) occurs; this is the dikaryophase.
Fungi are divided into classes based on morphology of mycelium, mode of spore formation and fruiting bodies.
nuggets.tip: Order: plasmogamy, then karyogamy, then meiosis. Dikaryon only in Asco- and Basidiomycetes.

questions.why: Plasmogamy is fusion of protoplasms between two motile or non-motile gametes. Karyogamy is fusion of nuclei; saprophytes feed on dead matter; N2 fixation is in heterocysts.
The fungal sexual cycle runs plasmogamy → karyogamy → meiosis in the zygote, giving haploid spores.
The dikaryotic (n + n) stage and dikaryophase occur in Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes.
Fungal classes are based on mycelium morphology, mode of spore formation and fruiting bodies. Mode of nutrition is not a criterion.
Vegetative means in fungi are fragmentation, fission and budding. Sporulation produces spores, which is asexual reproduction.

nuggets.title: Phycomycetes
lines: Phycomycetes are found in aquatic habitats, on decaying wood in moist and damp places, or as obligate parasites on plants.
The mycelium is aseptate and coenocytic.
Asexual reproduction is by motile zoospores or non-motile aplanospores, produced endogenously in a sporangium.
A zygospore forms by fusion of two gametes, which may be isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous.
Examples: Mucor, Rhizopus (the bread mould) and Albugo (parasitic fungus on mustard).
nuggets.tip: Albugo = white rust of mustard; Rhizopus = bread mould. Do not swap them.

questions.why: White spots on mustard leaves are caused by Albugo, not Rhizopus (the bread mould). The other three are true for phycomycetes.
Non-motile asexual spores of phycomycetes such as Rhizopus are aplanospores; motile ones are zoospores.
Albugo is the parasitic phycomycete on mustard.
Both false: ascomycetes (not phycomycetes) are the sac fungi, and ascospores in asci are ascomycete features.
Phycomycete mycelium is aseptate, coenocytic and multinucleate.

nuggets.title: Ascomycetes: the sac fungi
lines: Ascomycetes (sac fungi) are mostly multicellular (e.g. Penicillium) or rarely unicellular (e.g. yeast).
They are saprophytic, decomposers, parasitic or coprophilous (growing on dung); the mycelium is branched and septate.
Asexual spores are conidia, produced exogenously on special mycelium called conidiophores.
Sexual spores are ascospores, produced endogenously in sac-like asci, arranged inside fruiting bodies called ascocarps.
Examples: Aspergillus, Claviceps and Neurospora (used extensively in biochemical and genetic work).
Many are edible delicacies, e.g. morels and truffles.
nuggets.tip: Ascomycetes: conidia EXOgenous, ascospores ENDOgenous.

questions.why: Yeasts are unicellular, so 'filamentous bodies with long hyphae' is wrong. Morels and truffles are edible, Claviceps yields alkaloids/LSD, and the spore positions are correct.
In ascomycetes, conidia are produced exogenously on special mycelium called conidiophores.
Neurospora (an ascomycete) is used extensively in biochemical and genetic work.
Morels and truffles are edible ascomycetes. Mushrooms, Agaricus and puffballs are basidiomycetes.
Ascomycete mycelium is branched and septate; coenocytic aseptate mycelium belongs to phycomycetes. The other options are NCERT lines.

nuggets.title: Basidiomycetes: the club fungi
lines: Common basidiomycetes are mushrooms, bracket fungi and puffballs; they grow in soil, on logs and tree stumps, and in living plants as parasites (rusts and smuts).
The mycelium is branched and septate; asexual spores are generally not found, but vegetative reproduction by fragmentation is common.
Sex organs are absent; plasmogamy occurs by fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains, giving a dikaryotic structure.
This gives rise to the basidium, where karyogamy and meiosis produce four basidiospores.
Basidiospores are produced exogenously on the basidium, which is arranged in fruiting bodies called basidiocarps.
Examples: Agaricus (mushroom), Ustilago (smut) and Puccinia (rust).
nuggets.tip: Puccinia = rust, Ustilago = smut. Basidiospores are four, exogenous.

questions.why: In Agaricus (a basidiomycete), karyogamy and meiosis in the basidium give four exogenous basidiospores. Neurospora/Saccharomyces make endogenous ascospores.
No sex organs, plasmogamy by fusion of somatic cells, and asexual spores generally absent are features of Basidiomycetes.
Karyogamy and meiosis in the basidium produce four basidiospores.
Rhizopus = bread mould, Ustilago = smut, Puccinia = rust, Agaricus = mushroom.
Basidiomycetes have no sex organs or gametes; plasmogamy happens by fusion of two somatic cells.

nuggets.title: Deuteromycetes: the imperfect fungi
lines: Deuteromycetes are called imperfect fungi because only their asexual or vegetative phases are known.
When their perfect (sexual) stages were discovered, members were often moved to Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes.
They reproduce only by asexual spores called conidia; the mycelium is septate and branched.
Some are saprophytes or parasites, but many are decomposers of litter and help in mineral cycling.
Examples: Alternaria, Colletotrichum and Trichoderma.
nuggets.tip: Class nicknames: phyco = algal fungi, asco = sac fungi, basidio = club fungi, deutero = fungi imperfecti.

questions.why: The imperfect fungi that decompose litter and help mineral cycling are the Deuteromycetes.
Alternaria is a deuteromycete, with no known sexual stage. Mucor is a phycomycete, Agaricus is not a parasite, and Phytophthora is not a basidiomycete.
Alternaria, Colletotrichum and Trichoderma are deuteromycetes. Ustilago (smut) is a basidiomycete, so it is the odd one.
Deuteromycetes are 'fungi imperfecti' because only their asexual/vegetative phase is known, so the Reason explains the Assertion.
Phycomycetes = algal fungi, Basidiomycetes = club fungi, Deuteromycetes = fungi imperfecti, Ascomycetes = sac fungi.

nuggets.title: Kingdoms Plantae and Animalia
lines: Plantae includes all eukaryotic chlorophyll-containing organisms: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
A few are partially heterotrophic: insectivorous plants (bladderwort, Venus fly trap) and parasites like Cuscuta.
Plant cells have chloroplasts and a cellulose cell wall; the life cycle shows alternation of generation between diploid sporophytic and haploid gametophytic phases.
Animalia are heterotrophic eukaryotes that are multicellular and lack cell walls; their nutrition is holozoic.
Animals store food as glycogen or fat, follow a definite growth pattern, and most are capable of locomotion.
nuggets.tip: Venus fly trap and bladderwort are INSECTIVOROUS; Cuscuta is a PARASITE.

questions.why: Both wrong: bladderwort and Venus fly trap are insectivorous plants, and Cuscuta is a parasite, not insectivorous.
Insectivorous plants photosynthesise but also take nutrients from insects, so they are partially heterotrophic.
Plants alternate between a diploid sporophytic phase and a haploid gametophytic phase.
Animals are heterotrophic (holozoic), lack cell walls and have a definite growth pattern, so autotrophism is not their feature.
Animals store reserve food as glycogen or fat. Starch and cellulose are plant materials.

nuggets.title: Viruses: discovery and nature
lines: Viruses are not truly 'living' and are left out of Whittaker's five kingdoms; they are inert crystalline structures outside the living cell.
Once they infect a cell they take over its machinery to replicate, killing the host; so they are obligate parasites.
Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892) recognised certain microbes as the cause of the mosaic disease of tobacco; they could pass through bacteria-proof filters.
M.W. Beijerinck (1898) called the infectious fluid from infected tobacco 'Contagium vivum fluidum' (infectious living fluid).
W.M. Stanley (1935) showed viruses could be crystallised, and the crystals consist largely of proteins.
nuggets.tip: Years in order: Ivanowsky 1892, Beijerinck 1898, Stanley 1935, Diener 1971 (viroids).

questions.why: Viroids were discovered by T.O. Diener (1971), not Ivanowsky, who identified the tobacco mosaic agent in 1892. The other three are correct.
Beijerinck = 1898, Ivanowsky = 1892, Stanley = 1935, Diener = 1971.
All known viruses are obligate parasites. They have no cellular structure and no metabolism of their own, and are not facultative.
NCERT: viruses are inert crystalline structures outside the living cell, becoming active only after infecting a host.
Stanley showed virus crystals consist largely of proteins.

nuggets.title: Viruses: structure, genetic material and diseases
lines: Besides protein, viruses contain genetic material that may be RNA or DNA, never both; a virus is a nucleoprotein, and its genetic material is infectious.
Plant viruses generally have single-stranded RNA; animal viruses have single- or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA.
Bacterial viruses (bacteriophages) usually have double-stranded DNA.
The protein coat, capsid, is made of subunits called capsomeres, arranged in helical or polyhedral forms, and protects the nucleic acid.
Viral diseases: mumps, small pox, herpes, influenza, AIDS; in plants: mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing, vein clearing, dwarfing, stunted growth.
nuggets.tip: The infectious part of a virus is its nucleic acid, not its protein coat.

questions.why: In viruses the genetic material (RNA or DNA) is infectious, not the protein coat. Viroids lack a coat, viruses are obligate parasites, and prions are misfolded proteins.
Plant viruses generally have single-stranded RNA.
I is the NCERT line. II is wrong: bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA, not ssRNA.
Capsomeres of the capsid are arranged in helical or polyhedral geometric forms.
Virus-infected plants show mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing, dwarfing and stunted growth: all of these.

nuggets.title: Viroids and prions
lines: In 1971 T.O. Diener discovered viroids, infectious agents smaller than viruses that cause potato spindle tuber disease.
A viroid is a free RNA that lacks the protein coat found in viruses.
The RNA of a viroid is of low molecular weight.
Prions are infectious agents made of abnormally folded protein, similar in size to viruses.
Prions cause bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease, in cattle and its analogue Cr–Jacob disease (CJD) in humans.
nuggets.tip: Viroid = naked low-molecular-weight RNA. Prion = misfolded protein, no nucleic acid.

questions.why: Viroids are free RNA without a protein coat; viruses have a protein coat around RNA or DNA.
Viroid RNA is of low molecular weight, so 'high molecular weight' is wrong. They are smaller than viruses, infectious, and lack a coat.
BSE (mad cow disease) is caused by prions, abnormally folded proteins.
NCERT: prions are infectious agents of abnormally folded protein, similar in size to viruses. Viroids are smaller.
A is right: Diener (1971) found an agent smaller than viruses. B is wrong: potato spindle tuber disease is caused by a viroid, not a virus.

nuggets.title: Lichens
lines: Lichens are symbiotic associations, i.e. mutually useful associations, between algae and fungi.
The algal component is the phycobiont and the fungal component is the mycobiont; they are autotrophic and heterotrophic respectively.
Algae prepare food for the fungi; the fungi provide shelter and absorb mineral nutrients and water for their partner.
Their association is so close that a lichen looks like a single organism.
Lichens are very good pollution indicators: they do not grow in polluted areas.
nuggets.tip: Phyco = alga (food); myco = fungus (shelter, water, minerals).

questions.why: Both are NCERT lines: lichens are symbiotic associations of algae and fungi, and they do not grow in polluted areas.
In lichens the algal component is the phycobiont and the fungal component is the mycobiont.
The fungus absorbs minerals and water; the alga provides food. So 'algae provide mineral nutrition' is wrong.
Both false: the fungus (mycobiont) is the dominant partner, and it is the alga that provides food while the fungus gives shelter.

nuggets.title: Artificial and natural systems of classification
lines: The earliest systems used only gross superficial morphological characters such as habit, colour, number and shape of leaves.
Linnaeus gave an artificial system based mainly on vegetative characters or on the androecium structure.
Artificial systems gave equal weightage to vegetative and sexual characters; this is unacceptable because vegetative characters are more easily affected by environment.
Natural systems were based on natural affinities among organisms and considered both external and internal features.
Internal features used include ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry; George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker gave such a classification for flowering plants.
nuggets.tip: Artificial = Linnaeus, androecium. Natural = Bentham & Hooker, external + internal features.

questions.why: Linnaeus' artificial system was based mainly on vegetative characters or on the androecium structure.
The natural classification for flowering plants was given by George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker.
A is the NCERT line. B is wrong: vegetative characters are more easily affected by environment, which is why equal weightage was unacceptable.
Both wrong: natural systems consider both external and internal features, not only internal ones, and they do not rely mainly on vegetative characters.
Artificial systems gave equal weightage to vegetative and sexual characters.

nuggets.title: Phylogenetic system and newer taxonomies
lines: Phylogenetic classification is based on evolutionary relationships; it assumes organisms in the same taxon have a common ancestor.
Where no supporting fossil evidence exists, taxonomists use information from other sources to resolve difficulties in classification.
Numerical taxonomy uses computers and is based on all observable characteristics; characters are given numbers and codes.
In numerical taxonomy each character gets equal importance, and hundreds of characters can be considered at a time.
Cytotaxonomy uses cytological information such as chromosome number, structure and behaviour; chemotaxonomy uses chemical constituents of the plant.

questions.why: Classification based on evolutionary history (relationships) is phylogenetic classification.
In numerical taxonomy, characters are assigned numbers and codes and processed by computers.
Numerical taxonomy is based on all observable characteristics, each given equal importance.
Chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of plants. Chromosome data belongs to cytotaxonomy.
Classification using chromosome number, structure and behaviour is cytotaxonomy.

nuggets.title: Algae: general features and reproduction
lines: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and largely aquatic (fresh and marine) organisms.
They also occur on moist stones, soils and wood; some live with fungi (lichen) and with animals (e.g. on sloth bear).
Form and size vary: colonial (Volvox), filamentous (Ulothrix, Spirogyra), and massive marine kelps.
Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation; each fragment develops into a thallus.
Asexual reproduction is by spores, most commonly zoospores, which are flagellated (motile) and germinate into new plants.

questions.why: Chlorophyll-bearing, thalloid, simple, autotrophic, largely aquatic organisms: the NCERT definition of algae.
Volvox is NCERT's example of a colonial alga; Ulothrix and Spirogyra are filamentous, Chlorella unicellular.
The most common asexual spores in algae are flagellated zoospores.
Vegetative reproduction in algae is by fragmentation.

nuggets.title: Algae: isogamy, anisogamy and oogamy
lines: Isogamous fusion is between gametes similar in size; they may be flagellated (Chlamydomonas) or non-flagellated (Spirogyra).
Anisogamous fusion is between two gametes dissimilar in size, as in some species of Chlamydomonas.
Oogamous fusion is between one large, non-motile (static) female gamete and a smaller, motile male gamete.
Oogamy is seen in Volvox and Fucus.
nuggets.tip: Spirogyra is the NEET favourite: isogamous with NON-flagellated gametes.

questions.why: Spirogyra shows isogamy with non-flagellated gametes. Volvox and Fucus are oogamous.
Oogamy is fusion of one large (non-motile) female gamete with a smaller motile male gamete.
Fusion of two gametes dissimilar in size is anisogamy; oogamy specifically has a large non-motile egg.
A small motile male gamete with a large non-motile female gamete is oogamy, seen in both Fucus and Volvox.
I (oogamy) and IV (Chlorophyceae: chl a, b; starch) are correct. Similar-sized gametes are isogamous, and red algae store floridean starch, not mannitol.

nuggets.title: Usefulness of algae
lines: At least half of the total CO2 fixation on earth is by algae through photosynthesis; they also increase dissolved oxygen in their immediate environment.
Algae are primary producers and the basis of the food cycles of all aquatic animals.
About 70 species of marine algae are used as food, e.g. Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum.
Marine brown and red algae produce hydrocolloids: algin (brown) and carrageen (red).
Agar, from Gelidium and Gracilaria, is used to grow microbes and in ice-creams and jellies.
Chlorella, a unicellular alga rich in proteins, is used as a food supplement even by space travellers.
nuggets.tip: Algin = brown; carrageen = red; agar = red (Gelidium, Gracilaria).

questions.why: Marine algae used as food include Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum. Gracilaria is an agar source, not a food example.
Carrageen is obtained from red algae (Rhodophyceae) only; algin is from brown algae.
Agar comes from Gelidium and Gracilaria, which are red algae.
Chlorella is a protein-rich unicellular alga used as a food supplement even by space travellers.

nuggets.title: Chlorophyceae: green algae
lines: Chlorophyceae (green algae) may be unicellular, colonial or filamentous; they are grass green due to chlorophyll a and b.
Chloroplasts may be discoid, plate-like, reticulate, cup-shaped, spiral or ribbon-shaped.
Most have one or more pyrenoids in chloroplasts that store protein besides starch; some store food as oil droplets.
The rigid cell wall has an inner layer of cellulose and an outer layer of pectose.
Asexual reproduction is by flagellated zoospores produced in zoosporangia; sexual reproduction may be isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous.
Examples: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra and Chara.

questions.why: Green algae are grass green because chlorophyll a and b dominate. Chl a, c is brown algae; chl a, d is red algae.
Green algal cell wall: inner layer of cellulose and outer layer of pectose.
Pyrenoids in green algal chloroplasts store protein besides starch.
A is wrong: only some algae store food as oil droplets. B is right: the green algal wall has inner cellulose and outer pectose.
Green algae in the list: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara = 5. Nostoc is a cyanobacterium, Ectocarpus brown, Porphyra red.

nuggets.title: Phaeophyceae: brown algae
lines: Phaeophyceae (brown algae) are found primarily in marine habitats, from simple branched filamentous forms (Ectocarpus) to profusely branched kelps up to 100 m.
They have chlorophyll a, c, carotenoids and xanthophylls; colour varies from olive green to brown depending on fucoxanthin.
Food is stored as complex carbohydrates: laminarin or mannitol.
Vegetative cells have a cellulosic wall, usually covered on the outside by a gelatinous coating of algin.
The body is attached by a holdfast, with a stalk (stipe) and a leaf-like photosynthetic organ (frond).
Asexual reproduction is by biflagellate pear-shaped zoospores with two unequal, laterally attached flagella; sexual reproduction is iso-, aniso- or oogamous.
nuggets.tip: Brown algae: fucoxanthin, mannitol/laminarin, algin, holdfast-stipe-frond, two unequal LATERAL flagella.

questions.why: Mannitol (or laminarin) is the reserve food of brown algae, e.g. Ectocarpus. Gracilaria is red; Volvox and Ulothrix are green (starch).
Holdfast, stipe and frond describe the brown algal body, e.g. Laminaria.
I, III, IV, V are NCERT lines. II is wrong: brown algal sexual reproduction may be isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous, not only oogamous.
Brown algae range from olive green to brown depending on the amount of fucoxanthin (a xanthophyll) present.
Vegetative cells have an inner cellulosic wall covered on the outside by a gelatinous coating of algin.

nuggets.title: Rhodophyceae: red algae
lines: Red algae (Rhodophyceae) owe their colour to the predominance of the red pigment r-phycoerythrin.
Most are marine, with greater concentrations in warmer areas; they occur in well-lighted surface waters and also at great depths with relatively little light.
Most red algae are multicellular, some with complex body organisation.
Food is stored as floridean starch, very similar to amylopectin and glycogen in structure.
Asexual reproduction is by non-motile spores; sexual reproduction is by non-motile gametes, oogamous, with complex post-fertilisation developments.
Examples: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria and Gelidium.
nuggets.tip: Red algae have NO flagellated stages: spores and gametes are both non-motile.

questions.why: Phycoerythrin (pigment) and floridean starch (food) are the hallmarks of red algae.
Red algae live in well-lighted surface waters and at great depths with relatively little light.
Floridean starch is very similar to amylopectin and glycogen in structure.
A is wrong: red algae show complex post-fertilisation developments, not pre-fertilisation. B is right: Porphyra, Polysiphonia, Gracilaria are red algae.
Red algae in the list: Gelidium, Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria = 4. Spirogyra is green; Laminaria and Fucus are brown.

nuggets.title: Comparing the three algal classes (Table 3.1)
lines: Pigments: green = chl a, b; brown = chl a, c, fucoxanthin; red = chl a, d, phycoerythrin.
Stored food: green = starch; brown = mannitol, laminarin; red = floridean starch.
Cell wall: green = cellulose; brown = cellulose and algin; red = cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters.
Flagella: green = 2–8, equal, apical; brown = 2, unequal, lateral; red = absent.
nuggets.tip: Chlorophyll c = brown; chlorophyll d = red; chlorophyll b = green.

questions.why: Ulothrix is a green alga storing starch, so 'Ulothrix – mannitol' is the mismatch. Mannitol is a brown algal reserve.
Chl a, b = Chlorophyceae; chl a, c = Phaeophyceae; chl a, d = Rhodophyceae.
Chlorophyll b gives green, fucoxanthin gives brown and phycoerythrin gives red: green, brown, red.
Phaeophyceae have chlorophyll a and c, not a and b, so II is the wrong match.
Green = 2–8 equal apical flagella; brown = 2 unequal lateral flagella; red = no flagella; mosses = multicellular branched rhizoids.

nuggets.title: Bryophytes: the amphibians of the plant kingdom
lines: Bryophytes (liverworts and mosses) usually grow in moist, shaded areas in the hills.
They are called amphibians of the plant kingdom: they live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction.
The plant body is more differentiated than algae: thallus-like, prostrate or erect, attached by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids.
They lack true roots, stem or leaves but may have root-like, leaf-like or stem-like structures.
The main plant body is haploid and produces gametes, so it is a gametophyte.

questions.why: Bryophytes live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction, hence 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'.
Like algae, bryophytes have a thallus-like body, no vascular tissue and autotrophic nutrition. They have no true roots.
The bryophyte body attaches to the substratum by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids.
Bryophyte antherozoids are biflagellate, so 'uniflagellated sperms' is wrong. The other options are NCERT features.

nuggets.title: Bryophytes: sex organs, zygote and sporophyte
lines: Sex organs are multicellular: the male antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids.
The female archegonium is flask-shaped and produces a single egg.
Antherozoids are released into water, reach the archegonium and fuse with the egg to form a zygote.
The zygote does not undergo reduction division immediately; it forms a multicellular sporophyte.
The sporophyte is not free-living; it is attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and derives nourishment from it.
Some sporophyte cells undergo meiosis to produce haploid spores, which germinate into gametophytes.
nuggets.tip: In bryophytes the sporophyte is a dependent 'guest' on the dominant gametophyte.

questions.why: The moss sporophyte is attached to the gametophyte and draws nourishment from it, so it is partially parasitic on the gametophyte.
The bryophyte archegonium is flask-shaped and produces a single egg.
Gametophyte attached to substratum (B) → antherozoids released into water (E) → fusion with egg (A) → sporophyte forms (D) → meiosis gives spores (C).
B is the NCERT line. A is wrong: spores form by reduction division (meiosis), not mitosis.
Antherozoids of bryophytes and pteridophytes reach the archegonium only through water.

nuggets.title: Economic and ecological importance of bryophytes
lines: Some mosses provide food for herbaceous mammals, birds and other animals.
Species of Sphagnum, a moss, provide peat, long used as fuel.
Because of its capacity to hold water, peat is used as packing material for trans-shipment of living material.
Mosses, along with lichens, are the first organisms to colonise rocks; they decompose rocks, making the substrate suitable for higher plants.
Mosses form dense mats on soil, reducing the impact of falling rain and preventing soil erosion.
nuggets.tip: Mosses + lichens = pioneers on bare rock (ecological importance).

questions.why: Peat is formed from the moss Sphagnum.
Peat holds water well (it is hygroscopic), so it keeps flowers and live plants moist during shipping.
II and III are right: mosses decompose rocks and form dense mats. They are among the first (not last) to colonise rocks and reduce rain impact and erosion.
A is wrong: NCERT calls mosses with lichens of great ecological importance (pioneers on rocks). B is right: mosses prevent soil erosion.
Mosses along with lichens are the first organisms to colonise bare rocks.

nuggets.title: Liverworts
lines: Liverworts grow in moist, shady habitats such as banks of streams, marshy ground, damp soil, bark of trees and deep in the woods.
The plant body is thalloid, e.g. Marchantia; the thallus is dorsiventral and closely appressed to the substrate.
Leafy members have tiny leaf-like appendages in two rows on stem-like structures.
Asexual reproduction is by fragmentation or by gemmae: green, multicellular, asexual buds that develop in small receptacles called gemma cups on the thalli.
Gemmae detach and germinate into new individuals; the sporophyte has foot, seta and capsule, and spores form in the capsule after meiosis.
nuggets.tip: Gemmae = MULTIcellular ASEXUAL buds of liverworts (not mosses).

questions.why: Gemmae are found in some liverworts (e.g. Marchantia), developing in gemma cups.
A is wrong: gemmae are multicellular, asexual buds. B is right: the moss protonema develops directly from a spore.
Gemmae detach from the parent and grow into new plants: asexual reproduction.
Marchantia (a liverwort) has a thalloid body; Sphagnum and Funaria are leafy mosses and Salvinia is a fern.
The liverwort thallus is dorsiventral and closely appressed to the substrate.

nuggets.title: Mosses
lines: The predominant stage of a moss is the gametophyte, with two stages: the protonema and the leafy stage.
The protonema develops directly from a spore; it is a creeping, green, branched and frequently filamentous stage.
The leafy stage develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud; it has upright slender axes with spirally arranged leaves and multicellular, branched rhizoids.
Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation and budding in the secondary protonema; sex organs develop at the apex of leafy shoots.
The moss sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) is more elaborate than in liverworts; mosses have an elaborate mechanism of spore dispersal.
Examples: Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum.

questions.why: The protonema is the first gametophyte stage because it develops directly from the spores made in the capsule, so R explains A.
The leafy stage arises from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud.
Vegetative reproduction in mosses is by fragmentation and budding in the secondary protonema.
In mosses, antheridia and archegonia are produced at the apex of the leafy shoots.
Mosses have an elaborate mechanism of spore dispersal, and their sporophyte is more elaborate than in liverworts.

nuggets.title: Pteridophytes: the first vascular land plants
lines: Pteridophytes include horsetails and ferns; they are used for medicinal purposes, as soil-binders and as ornamentals.
Evolutionarily they are the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues, xylem and phloem.
They are found in cool, damp, shady places, though some flourish in sandy-soil conditions.
The main plant body is a sporophyte with true root, stem and leaves; leaves are small (microphylls, as in Selaginella) or large (macrophylls, as in ferns).
Sporangia are borne on leaf-like sporophylls; in some (Selaginella, Equisetum) sporophylls form compact strobili or cones.
Spore mother cells in the sporangia undergo meiosis to produce spores.
nuggets.tip: Microphylls = Selaginella; macrophylls = ferns; cones = Selaginella and Equisetum.

questions.why: Pteridophytes are evolutionarily the first terrestrial plants with vascular tissues (xylem and phloem).
Small leaves (microphylls) are found in Selaginella; ferns like Dryopteris have large macrophylls.
Sporophylls form compact strobili or cones in Selaginella and Equisetum.
Pteridophytes are used medicinally, as soil-binders and are frequently grown as ornamentals.
Pteridophytes are vascular cryptogams: seedless plants that have both xylem and phloem.

nuggets.title: Pteridophytes: prothallus and fertilisation
lines: Spores germinate into inconspicuous, small but multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophytes called prothallus.
The gametophytes need cool, damp, shady places; this need, plus water for fertilisation, restricts the spread of living pteridophytes to narrow geographical regions.
The gametophyte bears male antheridia and female archegonia.
Water is required to transfer antherozoids (male gametes released from antheridia) to the mouth of the archegonium.
Fusion of male gamete and egg in the archegonium gives a zygote, which produces a multicellular, well-differentiated sporophyte.
nuggets.tip: Prothallus = pteridophyte GAMETOPHYTE; protonema = moss gametophyte stage.

questions.why: A prothallus is the free-living gametophyte of pteridophytes, formed from a spore, not a sporophyte or post-fertilisation structure.
The pteridophyte gametophyte (prothallus) is inconspicuous, small but multicellular.
Meiosis in spore mother cells (B) → prothallus (A) → sex organs (D) → antherozoids reach archegonia in water (E) → fertilisation (C).
Antheridia bear male gametes and archegonia bear female gametes; the statement reverses them. The other options are correct.
A is wrong: the prothallus is inconspicuous. B is right: the spread of living pteridophytes is limited by their need for water.

nuggets.title: Heterospory, seed habit and the four classes
lines: Most pteridophytes are homosporous: all spores are of similar kind.
Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous: they produce large (macro/mega) and small (micro) spores.
Megaspores and microspores germinate into female and male gametophytes; the female gametophytes are retained on the parent sporophyte for variable periods.
The zygote develops into a young embryo within the female gametophyte, an event that is a precursor to the seed habit.
Classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).
nuggets.tip: Heterosporous pair to remember: Selaginella and Salvinia (not Salvia, which is an angiosperm).

questions.why: Selaginella and Salvinia are the NCERT heterosporous pteridophytes; Lycopodium, Psilotum and Equisetum are homosporous.
In Selaginella/Salvinia the embryo develops inside a female gametophyte retained on the parent sporophyte, a precursor to the seed habit.
Retention of the female gametophyte with a developing embryo on the parent sporophyte is first seen in heterosporous pteridophytes.
Ferns belong to Pteropsida; Sphenopsida is Equisetum. The other pairs are correct.
Psilopsida = Psilotum, Lycopsida = Selaginella, Sphenopsida = Equisetum, Pteropsida = Dryopteris.

nuggets.title: Gymnosperms: naked seeds and vegetative features
lines: In gymnosperms (gymnos: naked, sperma: seeds) the ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and stay exposed before and after fertilisation; seeds are naked.
They include medium-sized or tall trees and shrubs; the giant redwood Sequoia is one of the tallest tree species.
Roots are generally tap roots; Cycas has coralloid roots associated with N2-fixing cyanobacteria; Pinus roots have fungal mycorrhiza.
Stems are unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus); the pinnate leaves of Cycas persist for a few years.
Leaves are adapted to extremes of temperature, humidity and wind; conifer leaves are needle-like with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata to reduce water loss.
nuggets.tip: Cycas: coralloid roots (cyanobacteria), unbranched, pinnate leaves. Pinus: mycorrhiza, branched, needles.

questions.why: Gymnosperm ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall. Horsetails are pteridophytes, Salvinia is heterosporous, and Cedrus is branched.
Sequoia (giant redwood) is one of the tallest trees. Gymnosperms are only heterosporous, Salvinia is a fern, and gymnosperm leaves resist extremes.
Conifer leaves have a thick cuticle, needle shape and sunken stomata to tolerate extreme conditions.
A is right: coralloid roots of Cycas harbour N2-fixing cyanobacteria. B is wrong: Cycas pinnate leaves persist for a few years, not days.
All wrong: the Cycas stem is unbranched, its leaves are pinnate (not palmate), and its coralloid roots host cyanobacteria, not fungi.

nuggets.title: Gymnosperms: cones and the male side
lines: Gymnosperms are heterosporous: they produce haploid microspores and megaspores in sporangia borne on sporophylls.
Sporophylls are arranged spirally along an axis to form lax or compact strobili or cones.
Male strobili (microsporangiate) bear microsporophylls with microsporangia; the microspores develop into a highly reduced male gametophyte, the pollen grain.
Female strobili (megasporangiate) bear megasporophylls with ovules.
Male and female cones may be on the same tree (Pinus) or on different trees (Cycas).
In gymnosperms the male and female gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence.
nuggets.tip: Pinus = monoecious; Cycas = dioecious.

questions.why: Pinus bears male and female cones on the same tree, so it is monoecious. Cycas and papaya are dioecious.
Pinus is monoecious, so 'Pinus – dioecious' is the mismatch. Cycas dioecious, Salvinia heterosporous, Equisetum homosporous are correct.
The gymnosperm male gametophyte is highly reduced and confined to a limited number of cells (the pollen grain).
Sporophylls are arranged spirally along an axis to form lax or compact strobili or cones.
In gymnosperms like Cedrus the gametophytes stay within sporangia on the sporophyte; Polytrichum, Pteris and Funaria have free-living gametophytes.

nuggets.title: Gymnosperms: ovule, female gametophyte and seed
lines: The megaspore mother cell differentiates from one cell of the nucellus; the nucellus protected by envelopes is the ovule.
The megaspore mother cell divides meiotically to form four megaspores.
One megaspore develops into a multicellular female gametophyte bearing two or more archegonia, retained within the megasporangium.
Pollen grains, released from the microsporangium, are carried by air currents to the opening of the ovules.
The pollen tube carrying male gametes grows towards the archegonia and discharges its contents near their mouth.
After fertilisation the zygote develops into an embryo and the ovules into seeds, which are not covered.
nuggets.tip: In gymnosperms a pollen tube IS formed; it carries male gametes to the archegonia.

questions.why: The megaspore mother cell divides meiotically to give four megaspores.
The megaspore mother cell differentiates from one of the cells of the nucellus.
The nucellus protected by envelopes is the ovule; gymnosperms have no ovary.
II (multicellular female gametophyte retained in the megasporangium) and III (heterosporous) are right. I is wrong: gametophytes are not independent.
A is true: pollen is carried by air currents. R is false: pollen reaches the ovule opening, and a pollen tube carries male gametes to the archegonia.

nuggets.title: Levels of organisation, digestive and circulatory patterns
lines: In sponges (Porifera) cells are arranged as loose cell aggregates: the cellular level of organisation, with some division of labour among cells.
In coelenterates cells performing the same function form tissues: the tissue level of organisation.
Organ level is shown by Platyhelminthes and higher phyla; organ system level is seen in annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates.
An incomplete digestive system has a single opening serving as both mouth and anus (e.g. Platyhelminthes); a complete one has two openings, mouth and anus.
In an open circulatory system blood is pumped out of the heart and directly bathes cells and tissues; in a closed system blood flows through vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries).
nuggets.tip: Platyhelminthes = organ level; organ-system level begins higher up. Don't call flatworms 'cellular' or 'tissue' level.

questions.why: A-Q, B-P, C-R: sponges are cellular level (loose aggregates), coelenterates tissue level, and Platyhelminthes show organ level where tissues group into organs.
Organ level: NCERT places Platyhelminthes at organ level (tissues grouped into organs); organ-system level is seen in annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates.
All of these: chordates, echinoderms and arthropods (along with annelids and molluscs) all have organ systems for specific physiological functions.
Only one opening serving as mouth and anus makes the digestive system incomplete in flatworms; a complete system has separate mouth and anus.
I false, II true: molluscs are at organ-system level, not cellular; arthropods have an open circulatory system where blood (haemolymph) directly bathes tissues and organs.

nuggets.title: Symmetry: asymmetry, radial and bilateral
lines: Sponges are mostly asymmetrical: no plane through the centre divides them into equal halves.
In radial symmetry any plane passing through the central axis divides the body into two identical halves, e.g. coelenterates, ctenophores and adult echinoderms.
In bilateral symmetry the body can be divided into identical left and right halves in only one plane, e.g. annelids and arthropods.
Echinoderms are a key exception: adults are radially symmetrical but their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
nuggets.tip: Echinoderm symmetry flips with age: bilateral larva, radial (pentamerous) adult.

questions.why: A-Q, B-R, C-P: sponges are asymmetrical, adult echinoderms are radial, and echinoderm larvae are bilateral.
Both 2 and 3: bilateral symmetry means identical left and right halves in only one plane, as in annelids and arthropods. Option 1 describes radial symmetry.
All of these: ctenophores, coelenterates and adult echinoderms are all radially symmetrical.
Echinodermata: adult echinoderms are radially symmetrical while their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. Annelids, arthropods and molluscs stay bilateral.

nuggets.title: Germ layers and the coelom
lines: Diploblastic animals have two germ layers, outer ectoderm and inner endoderm, with an undifferentiated mesoglea between them, e.g. coelenterates.
Triploblastic animals have a third germ layer, mesoderm, between ectoderm and endoderm (Platyhelminthes to Chordates).
A body cavity lined by mesoderm is the coelom; such animals are coelomates, e.g. annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates.
In pseudocoelomates the cavity is not lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm, e.g. Aschelminthes.
Animals with no body cavity are acoelomates, e.g. Platyhelminthes.
nuggets.tip: Mesoglea is not a germ layer. Diploblasts lack mesoderm.

questions.why: Mesoderm is absent in diploblastic embryos; they have only ectoderm and endoderm with undifferentiated mesoglea in between.
Mesoderm on both sides: a true coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm, unlike a pseudocoelom where mesoderm is only scattered pouches.
A-R, B-P, C-Q: coelom is lined by mesoderm; pseudocoelom has mesoderm as scattered pouches; acoelomates have no body cavity.
A-P, B-R, C-Q: echinoderms are coelomates, Aschelminthes pseudocoelomates and Platyhelminthes acoelomates.
I only: annelids are true coelomates. Sponges have no coelom, Aschelminthes are pseudocoelomates and Platyhelminthes are acoelomates.

nuggets.title: Segmentation and notochord
lines: In some animals the body is externally and internally divided into segments with serial repetition of at least some organs: metameric segmentation (metamerism).
Earthworm (Annelida) shows metameric segmentation.
The notochord is a mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development in some animals.
Animals with a notochord are chordates; those without it (Porifera to Echinodermata) are non-chordates.

questions.why: Both correct: serial repetition of segments with some organs is metameric segmentation, and the earthworm shows it.
Annelida are triploblastic and metamerically segmented (Latin annulus: little ring). Molluscs, echinoderms and aschelminths are unsegmented.
Dorsal: NCERT describes the notochord as a rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development.
Mesoderm: the notochord is a mesodermally derived rod-like structure. Mesoglea is not a germ layer.

nuggets.title: Phylum Porifera (sponges)
lines: Porifera (pore bearers) are generally marine and mostly asymmetrical, with a cellular level of organisation.
A water canal system: water enters through minute pores ostia into the central spongocoel and leaves through the osculum; it helps in food gathering, respiratory exchange and removal of waste.
Choanocytes (collar cells) line the spongocoel and canals; digestion is intracellular.
The body is supported by a skeleton of spicules or spongin fibres.
Sexes are not separate (hermaphrodite); asexual reproduction by fragmentation, sexual by gametes; fertilisation is internal and development indirect (larval stage).
Examples: Sycon (Scypha), Spongilla (freshwater sponge) and Euspongia (bath sponge).
nuggets.tip: Water route: ostia → spongocoel → osculum. Fertilisation in sponges is internal, not external.

questions.why: Ostia → spongocoel → osculum → outside: water enters through ostia, collects in the spongocoel and exits via the osculum.
Choanocytes (collar cells) line the spongocoel and the canals of sponges.
Both correct: digestion in sponges is intracellular, and the body is supported by spicules or spongin fibres.
Internal, indirect: sponges are hermaphrodite, fertilisation is internal and development is indirect with a larval stage distinct from the adult.
A-Q, B-R, C-P: Sycon is also called Scypha, Spongilla is the freshwater sponge and Euspongia the bath sponge.

nuggets.title: Phylum Coelenterata (Cnidaria)
lines: Cnidarians are aquatic, mostly marine, sessile or free-swimming, radially symmetrical, diploblastic animals with a tissue level of organisation.
Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) with stinging capsules (nematocysts) on tentacles and body are used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey.
A central gastro-vascular cavity with a single opening, the mouth on the hypostome; digestion is extracellular and intracellular.
Corals have a skeleton of calcium carbonate; the two body forms are polyp (sessile, cylindrical, e.g. Hydra, Adamsia) and medusa (umbrella-shaped, free-swimming, e.g. Aurelia).
In metagenesis (e.g. Obelia) polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually.
Examples: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (sea anemone), Pennatula (sea-pen), Gorgonia (sea-fan), Meandrina (brain coral).
nuggets.tip: Metagenesis: polyp → medusa asexually; medusa → polyp sexually. Not the other way round.

questions.why: Hypostome: the gastro-vascular cavity of cnidarians has a single opening, the mouth, located on the hypostome.
Calcium carbonate: NCERT states some cnidarians, e.g. corals, have a skeleton composed of calcium carbonate. Spicules and spongin belong to sponges.
I and II: polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually. Polyps are sessile and cylindrical, medusae umbrella-shaped and free-swimming, so III and IV are wrong.
Alternation of generation between asexual and sexual phases: in Obelia polyps (asexual) and medusae (sexual) alternate. Drastic change in form after embryonic development is metamorphosis.
A-Q, B-P, C-R, D-S: Gorgonia sea-fan, Meandrina brain coral, Pennatula sea-pen, Adamsia sea anemone.

nuggets.title: Phylum Ctenophora (comb jellies)
lines: Ctenophores, commonly called sea walnuts or comb jellies, are exclusively marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic, with tissue level organisation.
The body bears eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, which help in locomotion.
Digestion is both extracellular and intracellular.
Bioluminescence (the property of a living organism to emit light) is well marked in ctenophores.
Sexes are not separate; reproduction only by sexual means; fertilisation is external with indirect development.
Examples: Pleurobrachia and Ctenoplana.
nuggets.tip: Ctenophores have no cnidoblasts and no asexual reproduction; comb plates are for locomotion, not digestion.

questions.why: Ctenophora: exclusively marine, radial, diploblastic animals with eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, both kinds of digestion and only sexual reproduction.
Ctenoplana and Beroe are ctenophores, which lack cnidoblasts (NCERT calls them radially symmetrical). Hydra, Aurelia and sea anemone are cnidarians; starfish is an echinoderm.
Ctenophores: NCERT notes bioluminescence (emission of light by a living organism) is well marked in ctenophores.
External, indirect: ctenophores reproduce only sexually, with external fertilisation and indirect development.
Both: ctenophores are commonly known as sea walnuts or comb jellies. Adamsia is a sea anemone (cnidarian).

nuggets.title: Phylum Platyhelminthes (flatworms)
lines: Flatworms have a dorso-ventrally flattened body; they are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and acoelomate with organ level of organisation.
They are mostly endoparasites of animals including humans; parasitic forms have hooks and suckers and absorb nutrients directly through the body surface.
Specialised cells called flame cells help in osmoregulation and excretion.
Sexes are not separate; fertilisation is internal and development passes through many larval stages.
Some members like Planaria possess high regeneration capacity.
Examples: Taenia (tapeworm), Fasciola (liver fluke).
nuggets.tip: Flame cells do both excretion and osmoregulation. Wuchereria is NOT a flatworm (it's an aschelminth).

questions.why: A and R true, R explains A: they are called flatworms because their body is dorso-ventrally flattened.
Platyhelminthes are triploblastic, acoelomate and bilaterally symmetrical. Annelids are coelomate; ctenophores and cnidarians are diploblastic and radial.
Both: flame cells in flatworms help in both osmoregulation and excretion.
Planaria possesses high regeneration capacity. Fasciola and Taenia are parasitic flatworms; hookworm is an aschelminth.
A-R, B-Q, C-S, D-P: Taenia flame cells, Paramoecium contractile vacuole, Periplaneta urecose glands, Pheretima nephridia.

nuggets.title: Phylum Aschelminthes (roundworms)
lines: Aschelminths are circular in cross-section (roundworms); they may be free-living, aquatic, terrestrial or parasitic in plants and animals.
They are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and pseudocoelomate, with organ-system level of body organisation.
The alimentary canal is complete with a well-developed muscular pharynx; an excretory tube removes body wastes from the body cavity through the excretory pore.
Sexes are separate (dioecious); often females are longer than males; fertilisation is internal and development may be direct or indirect.
Examples: Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filaria worm), Ancylostoma (hookworm).
nuggets.tip: Aschelminthes: no true coelom and no metamerism. Females longer than males.

questions.why: Neither true coelom nor metamerism: Ascaris is a pseudocoelomate and unsegmented roundworm.
Excretory tube and excretory pore: in aschelminths an excretory tube removes body wastes from the body cavity through the excretory pore. Nephridia are annelid organs.
Complete alimentary canal with muscular pharynx is NCERT's line for Ascaris. Females (not males) are longer, there is no true coelom, and nephridia are annelid organs.
A-R, B-P, C-Q: roundworm is Ascaris, Ancylostoma is hookworm and Wuchereria is filaria worm.
Fertilisation is external is the incorrect statement: aschelminths are dioecious with internal fertilisation, and females are often longer than males.

nuggets.title: Phylum Annelida
lines: Annelids may be aquatic (marine and freshwater) or terrestrial, free-living or sometimes parasitic; they show organ-system level organisation and bilateral symmetry.
They are triploblastic, metamerically segmented and coelomate; the name comes from Latin annulus (little ring) because the body is marked into segments (metameres).
Longitudinal and circular muscles help in locomotion; aquatic annelids like Nereis have lateral appendages, parapodia, which help in swimming.
A closed circulatory system is present; nephridia help in osmoregulation and excretion.
The neural system has paired ganglia connected by lateral nerves to a double ventral nerve cord.
Nereis is dioecious; earthworms (Pheretima) and leeches (Hirudinaria) are monoecious; reproduction is sexual.
nuggets.tip: Annelids: closed circulation and ventral nerve cord. Parapodia only in Nereis, not in earthworm or leech.

questions.why: Pseudocoelom is not an annelid feature; annelids are true coelomates with segmentation, a ventral nerve cord and a closed circulatory system.
Metamerism: the body is distinctly marked into segments (metameres), hence Annelida (Latin annulus, little ring).
Paired ganglia connected by lateral nerves to a double ventral nerve cord is the annelid neural system. The nerve cord is ventral, not dorsal.
A-Q, B-R, C-P: Nereis is dioecious, Pheretima is the earthworm and Hirudinaria is the blood-sucking leech.
Nereis is dioecious; the other two are monoecious: NCERT says earthworms and leeches are monoecious. Hirudinaria is also aquatic, so option 1 is wrong.

nuggets.title: Phylum Arthropoda
lines: Arthropoda is the largest phylum of Animalia, including insects; over two-thirds of all named species are arthropods.
They have organ-system level organisation, bilateral symmetry, are triploblastic, segmented and coelomate, with a chitinous exoskeleton.
The body has head, thorax and abdomen; they have jointed appendages (arthros: joint, poda: appendages).
Respiratory organs are gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheal system; circulatory system is open; excretion takes place through Malpighian tubules.
Sensory organs: antennae, eyes (compound and simple) and statocysts or balance organs; they are mostly dioecious, fertilisation usually internal, mostly oviparous.
Examples: economically important Apis (honey bee), Bombyx (silkworm), Laccifer (lac insect); vectors Anopheles, Culex, Aedes; gregarious pest Locusta; living fossil Limulus (king crab).
nuggets.tip: Parapodia are annelid (Nereis) structures, not arthropod. Silverfish is an insect, not a fish.
