questions.why: Parapodia are lateral appendages of the annelid Nereis. Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton, segmentation and jointed appendages.
Silver fish is an insect (arthropod). Puffer and flying fish are bony fishes; cuttlefish (Sepia) is a mollusc.
i, ii, iii, iv: arthropod respiratory organs are gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheal system. Coxal glands are not respiratory.
Statocyst: NCERT lists statocysts or balance organs among arthropod sensory organs. Radula is a molluscan feeding organ.
A-Q, B-P, C-R, D-S: Limulus living fossil, Locusta gregarious pest, Bombyx silkworm, Apis honey bee.

nuggets.title: Phylum Mollusca
lines: Mollusca is the second largest animal phylum; molluscs are terrestrial or aquatic, with organ-system level, bilateral symmetry, triploblastic and coelomate body.
The body is covered by a calcareous shell and is unsegmented, with a distinct head, muscular foot and visceral hump.
A soft and spongy layer of skin forms a mantle over the visceral hump; the space between hump and mantle is the mantle cavity, with feather-like gills having respiratory and excretory functions.
The anterior head has sensory tentacles; the mouth contains a file-like rasping organ for feeding, the radula.
Usually dioecious and oviparous with indirect development.
Examples: Pila (apple snail), Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia (cuttlefish), Loligo (squid), Octopus (devil fish), Aplysia (seahare), Dentalium (tusk shell), Chaetopleura (chiton).
nuggets.tip: Mantle is soft and spongy (not tough). Molluscan gills do respiration AND excretion.

questions.why: Head, muscular foot and visceral hump are the three molluscan body regions. Head, thorax and abdomen is the arthropod plan.
Radula: the file-like rasping organ for feeding in the molluscan mouth. The mantle covers the visceral hump.
Only I: feather-like gills lie in the mantle cavity between hump and mantle. Statement II is wrong because NCERT calls the mantle a soft and spongy layer of skin, not tough.
i, ii and iii: molluscan gills are feather-like, have respiratory and excretory functions and lie in the mantle cavity. They are not covered by a shell.
A-R, B-P, C-Q, D-S: Chaetopleura chiton, Dentalium tusk shell, Aplysia seahare, devil fish Octopus.

nuggets.title: Phylum Echinodermata
lines: Echinoderms have an endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles, hence the name (spiny bodied); all are marine with organ-system level.
Adults are radially symmetrical but larvae are bilaterally symmetrical; they are triploblastic and coelomate.
The digestive system is complete, with the mouth on the lower (ventral) side and anus on the upper (dorsal) side.
The most distinctive feature is the water vascular system, which helps in locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration.
An excretory system is absent; sexes are separate, reproduction is sexual, fertilisation usually external and development indirect with a free-swimming larva.
Examples: Asterias (star fish), Echinus (sea urchin), Antedon (sea lily), Cucumaria (sea cucumber), Ophiura (brittle star).
nuggets.tip: Echinoderms: endoskeleton (not exoskeleton) of ossicles, no excretory system, sexes separate.

questions.why: A and C: the water vascular system helps in locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration. Echinoderms have no excretory system.
Endoskeleton: echinoderms have an endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles, which gives them the spiny-bodied name.
Echinodermata: no excretory system, dioecious with external fertilisation and indirect development, water vascular system, ventral mouth and dorsal anus.
A-Q, B-R, C-P, D-T, E-S: Asterias star fish, Echinus sea urchin, Antedon sea lily, Cucumaria sea cucumber, Ophiura brittle star.
I and III: echinoderms are all marine with organ-system level and external fertilisation. Adults are radial, they are coelomate, and fertilisation is not internal.

nuggets.title: Phylum Hemichordata
lines: Hemichordata was earlier a sub-phylum of Chordata but is now placed as a separate phylum under non-chordata.
It is a small group of worm-like marine animals with organ-system level, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate.
The cylindrical body has an anterior proboscis, a collar and a long trunk; a rudimentary structure in the collar called stomochord is similar to the notochord.
The circulatory system is of open type; respiration takes place through gills; the excretory organ is the proboscis gland.
Sexes are separate; fertilisation is external and development indirect. Examples: Balanoglossus and Saccoglossus.
nuggets.tip: Hemichordates have a stomochord, not a true notochord, so they are non-chordates.

questions.why: Balanoglossus: a worm-like marine hemichordate whose cylindrical body has proboscis, collar and trunk. Ophiura is an echinoderm; the others are fishes.
Proboscis gland is the excretory organ of Balanoglossus; gills are its respiratory organs.
iii and iv: hemichordates have an open circulatory system and a body of proboscis, collar and trunk. They are bilateral and have no chitin.
Both correct: hemichordates are dioecious with external fertilisation and indirect development, and their circulation is of open type.
Pharynx with gill slits: hemichordates respire through gills (pharyngeal gill slits), a feature shared with chordates. They lack a true notochord and a dorsal hollow nerve cord.

nuggets.title: Phylum Chordata: hallmarks and protochordates
lines: Three fundamental chordate features: a notochord, a dorsal, hollow, single nerve cord and paired pharyngeal gill slits.
Chordates are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, coelomate with organ-system level, have a post-anal tail and a closed circulatory system with a ventral heart.
Phylum Chordata has three subphyla: Urochordata (Tunicata), Cephalochordata and Vertebrata; the first two are called protochordates and are exclusively marine.
In Urochordata the notochord is present only in the larval tail, e.g. Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum.
In Cephalochordata the notochord extends from head to tail and persists throughout life, e.g. Branchiostoma (Amphioxus or Lancelet).
nuggets.tip: Non-chordates: solid, double, ventral nerve cord and dorsal heart. Chordates: hollow, single, dorsal nerve cord and ventral heart.

questions.why: A dorsal solid nerve cord is not a chordate feature; chordates have a dorsal, hollow, single nerve cord. Notochord, gill slits and a ventral heart are chordate traits.
ii and v: a solid, double, ventral nerve cord and a dorsal heart belong to non-chordates. Notochord, gill slits and post-anal tail are chordate features.
Urochordata, Cephalochordata and Vertebrata are the three subphyla of Chordata. Protochordata is a collective name for the first two, not a subphylum.
Salpa, Ascidia and Doliolum are urochordates. Lancelet and Amphioxus are names of Branchiostoma, a cephalochordate.
A and R true, R explains A: Branchiostoma is a cephalochordate because its notochord runs from head to tail and persists throughout life.

nuggets.title: Vertebrata and class Cyclostomata
lines: Vertebrates have a notochord during the embryonic period, replaced by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column in the adult; thus all vertebrates are chordates but all chordates are not vertebrates.
Vertebrates have a ventral muscular heart with two, three or four chambers, kidneys for excretion and osmoregulation, and paired appendages (fins or limbs).
Vertebrata is divided into Agnatha (lacks jaw) and Gnathostomata (bears jaw); Agnatha has class Cyclostomata.
All living cyclostomes are ectoparasites on some fishes; they have a sucking and circular mouth without jaws, 6–15 pairs of gill slits, and a body devoid of scales and paired fins.

Cranium and vertebral column are cartilaginous; circulation is closed; they are marine but migrate to fresh water for spawning, die within a few days, and larvae return to the ocean after metamorphosis.
Examples: Petromyzon (lamprey) and Myxine (hagfish).
nuggets.tip: Cyclostomes lack PAIRED fins and scales, and are ectoparasites (not endoparasites).

questions.why: Both correct: all vertebrates are chordates but not all chordates are vertebrates, and in vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column in the adult.
Agnatha and Gnathostomata: subphylum Vertebrata is divided by the absence or presence of jaws.
Ectoparasite: all living members of Cyclostomata are ectoparasites on some fishes.
All: cyclostomes are ectoparasites on fishes, have cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column, and lack paired fins.
'Devoid of scales and unpaired fins' is incorrect: NCERT says the body is devoid of scales and paired fins. Circulation is closed and the mouth is circular, sucking and jawless.

nuggets.title: Class Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes)
lines: Marine animals with a streamlined body and a cartilaginous endoskeleton; the mouth is located ventrally; the notochord is persistent throughout life.
Gill slits are separate and without operculum; the tough skin has minute placoid scales; teeth are modified placoid scales that are backwardly directed.
Jaws are very powerful; they are predaceous; due to the absence of air bladder they have to swim constantly to avoid sinking.
The heart is two-chambered (one auricle, one ventricle); some have electric organs (e.g. Torpedo) and some have a poison sting (e.g. Trygon); they are cold-blooded (poikilothermous).
Sexes are separate; in males pelvic fins bear claspers; fertilisation is internal and many are viviparous.
Examples: Scoliodon (dog fish), Pristis (saw fish), Carcharodon (great white shark), Trygon (sting ray).
nuggets.tip: Torpedo = electric organ; Trygon = poison sting. Don't swap them.

questions.why: Torpedo (electric ray) has electric organs. Trygon has a poison sting; Pristis is saw fish and Scoliodon dog fish.
Placoid scale with cartilaginous endoskeleton: Chondrichthyes have minute placoid scales (teeth are modified placoid scales) and a cartilaginous skeleton.
They have to swim constantly to avoid sinking, because cartilaginous fishes lack an air bladder.
Pelvic fins of male: in male cartilaginous fishes the pelvic fins bear claspers.
Internal, viviparous: Chondrichthyes have internal fertilisation and many of them are viviparous.

nuggets.title: Class Osteichthyes (bony fishes)
lines: Includes both marine and freshwater fishes with a bony endoskeleton; the streamlined body has a terminal mouth.
They have four pairs of gills covered by an operculum on each side; the skin has cycloid/ctenoid scales.
An air bladder is present, which regulates buoyancy; the heart is two-chambered; they are cold-blooded.
Sexes are separate; fertilisation is usually external; they are mostly oviparous and development is direct.
Marine examples: Exocoetus (flying fish), Hippocampus (sea horse); freshwater: Labeo (rohu), Catla (katla), Clarias (magur); aquarium: Betta (fighting fish), Pterophyllum (angel fish).
nuggets.tip: Operculum and air bladder = bony fish. Placoid scales and claspers = cartilaginous fish.

questions.why: A-R, B-P, C-Q, D-S: Pterophyllum angel fish, Myxine hagfish, Pristis saw fish, Exocoetus flying fish.
Exocoetus (flying fish) is a bony fish with an air bladder. Torpedo, Scoliodon and Trygon are cartilaginous fishes with no air bladder.
iii and iv: bony fishes have four pairs of gills covered by an operculum and cycloid/ctenoid scales. Placoid scales and claspers are cartilaginous-fish features.
Betta and Pterophyllum are bony aquarium fishes. Trygon and Torpedo are cartilaginous fishes.
A incorrect, B correct: bony fishes have cycloid/ctenoid scales (placoid scales are cartilaginous-fish features), a terminal mouth and gills covered by an operculum.

nuggets.title: Class Amphibia
lines: Amphibians can live in aquatic as well as terrestrial habitats; most have two pairs of limbs; the body is divisible into head and trunk; a tail may be present in some.
The amphibian skin is moist (without scales); the eyes have eyelids; a tympanum represents the ear.
Alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a common chamber called cloaca, which opens to the exterior.
Respiration is by gills, lungs and through skin; the heart is three-chambered (two auricles and one ventricle); they are cold-blooded.
Sexes are separate; fertilisation is external; they are oviparous and development is direct or indirect.
Examples: Bufo (toad), Rana (frog), Hyla (tree frog), Salamandra (salamander), Ichthyophis (limbless amphibia).
nuggets.tip: Frog body: head + trunk only (no neck, no tail in adults). Ichthyophis is the limbless amphibian.

questions.why: Eyes have no eyelids is wrong: NCERT says amphibian eyes have eyelids. Moist skin, two pairs of limbs and a cloaca are all amphibian features.
Three-chambered with two auricles and one ventricle is the amphibian heart; fishes have two chambers and crocodiles, birds and mammals four.
External and oviparous: amphibians have separate sexes, external fertilisation and lay eggs.
Ichthyophis is the limbless amphibian. Cucumaria is a sea cucumber and Pristis a saw fish.
Head, trunk and tail is wrong for Rana: the frog body has only head and trunk. A tympanum, moist scaleless skin and cloaca are correct features.

nuggets.title: Class Reptilia
lines: The class name refers to their creeping or crawling mode of locomotion (Latin repere or reptum: to creep or crawl); they are mostly terrestrial.
The body is covered by dry and cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes; they have no external ear openings, and a tympanum represents the ear.
Limbs, when present, are two pairs; snakes and lizards shed their scales as skin cast.
The heart is usually three-chambered, but four-chambered in crocodiles; reptiles are poikilotherms.
Sexes are separate; fertilisation is internal; they are oviparous and development is direct.

Examples: Chelone (turtle), Testudo (tortoise), Chameleon (tree lizard), Calotes (garden lizard), Crocodilus (crocodile), Hemidactylus (wall lizard); poisonous snakes Naja (cobra), Bangarus (krait), Vipera (viper).
nuggets.tip: Chelone = turtle, Testudo = tortoise. Reptile development is direct, unlike frogs.

questions.why: Creeping or crawling mode of locomotion gives the class its name Reptilia (Latin repere or reptum, to creep or crawl).
Both correct: snakes and lizards shed their scales as skin cast, and reptiles do not have external ear openings.
Only I: reptiles have internal fertilisation; they are oviparous but development is direct, so statement II is wrong.
A-Q, B-T, C-P, D-R, E-S: Chelone turtle, Testudo tortoise, Chameleon tree lizard, Calotes garden lizard, Hemidactylus wall lizard.
One: only II is incorrect, because the reptile heart is usually three-chambered (four-chambered only in crocodiles). Crawling locomotion, skin casting and internal fertilisation are correct.

nuggets.title: Class Aves (birds)
lines: Birds are characterised by feathers and most can fly (except flightless birds like ostrich); they possess a beak.
Forelimbs are modified into wings; hind limbs generally have scales and are modified for walking, swimming or clasping tree branches.
Skin is dry without glands except the oil gland at the base of the tail; the endoskeleton is fully ossified, and long bones are hollow with air cavities (pneumatic).
The digestive tract has additional chambers, the crop and gizzard; the heart is completely four-chambered; they are warm-blooded (homoiothermous).
Respiration is by lungs, with air sacs connected to the lungs to supplement respiration; sexes are separate, fertilisation internal, oviparous and development direct.
Examples: Corvus (crow), Columba (pigeon), Psittacula (parrot), Struthio (ostrich), Pavo (peacock), Aptenodytes (penguin), Neophron (vulture).
nuggets.tip: Crop and gizzard = Aves. Struthio (ostrich) and Aptenodytes (penguin) are flightless.

questions.why: All are correct: birds have forelimbs modified into wings, a completely four-chambered heart, are homoiotherms and are oviparous with direct development.
Neophron (vulture) is a bird with hollow, pneumatic long bones. Hemidactylus is a lizard; Macropus and Ornithorhynchus are mammals.
Aves: NCERT states the bird digestive tract has additional chambers, the crop and gizzard.
Both correct: the bird endoskeleton is fully ossified with hollow, pneumatic long bones, and the digestive tract has crop and gizzard.
A-Q, B-R, C-P, D-T, E-S: Columba pigeon, Psittacula parrot, Struthio ostrich, Aptenodytes penguin, Neophron vulture.

nuggets.title: Class Mammalia
lines: Mammals are found in a variety of habitats: polar ice caps, deserts, mountains, forests, grasslands and dark caves; some can fly or live in water.
The most unique feature is the presence of milk-producing mammary glands; they also have hair on the skin and external ears or pinnae.
They have two pairs of limbs adapted for walking, running, climbing, burrowing, swimming or flying; different types of teeth are present in the jaw.
Heart is four-chambered; they are homoiothermous; respiration is by lungs; sexes are separate, fertilisation internal, and they are viviparous with few exceptions; development is direct.

Oviparous mammal: Ornithorhynchus (platypus). Viviparous: Macropus (kangaroo), Pteropus (flying fox), Rattus, Canis, Felis, Elephas, Delphinus (common dolphin), Balaenoptera (blue whale), Panthera tigris, Panthera leo.
nuggets.tip: Viviparity is NOT shared by birds and mammals; warm-bloodedness is. Platypus lays eggs.

questions.why: Hairs, pinna and mammary glands are unique mammalian features. A tympanic membrane occurs in other vertebrates too, and mammals have direct development.
Whales, dolphins, seals are aquatic mammals. Trygon (sting ray) and sharks are cartilaginous fishes.
Viviparity is not shared: birds are oviparous, while mammals are mostly viviparous. Both breathe by lungs, are warm-blooded and have an ossified endoskeleton.
Ornithorhynchus (platypus) is the oviparous mammal in NCERT. Delphinus, Macropus and Elephas are viviparous.
Mammals: different types of teeth, homoiothermy, mammary glands (their most unique feature), separate sexes with internal fertilisation and mostly viviparous.

nuggets.title: Root systems: tap, fibrous and adventitious
lines: In most dicots, direct elongation of the radicle forms the primary root, which bears lateral roots of several orders: the tap root system, as in mustard.
In monocots the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by many roots arising from the base of the stem: the fibrous root system, as in wheat.
Adventitious roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle, as in grass, Monstera and the banyan tree.
Root functions: absorption of water and minerals, anchorage, storage of reserve food and synthesis of plant growth regulators.
nuggets.tip: Adventitious = from any part except the radicle; fibrous = many roots from the stem base in monocots.

questions.why: Mustard (a dicot) has a tap root system formed by elongation of the radicle. Wheat and grass have fibrous roots; Monstera has adventitious roots.
Adventitious roots arise from any part other than the radicle (e.g., grass, Monstera, banyan). They are not restricted to monocots or dicots.
Fibrous root – wheat; tap root – turnip (a swollen tap root); adventitious root – Monstera. So A-Q, B-P, C-R.
A matches NCERT: the monocot primary root is short-lived and replaced by many roots. B is wrong: roots from the stem base form a fibrous, not tap, root system.
A is wrong: adventitious roots arise from parts other than the radicle. B is correct: NCERT lists synthesis of plant growth regulators as a root function.

nuggets.title: Regions of the root tip
lines: The root apex is covered by a thimble-like root cap that protects the tender apex as it makes its way through the soil.
A few millimetres above the root cap is the region of meristematic activity: very small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide repeatedly.
Cells proximal to it undergo rapid elongation and enlargement (region of elongation) and are responsible for growth of the root in length.
Cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature; the region proximal to it is the region of maturation.
From the region of maturation, some epidermal cells form very fine, delicate, thread-like root hairs that absorb water and minerals.
nuggets.tip: Root hairs: epidermal cells of the region of maturation (not endodermis, not elongation zone).

questions.why: Region of elongation: its cells undergo rapid elongation and enlargement, increasing root length. Meristematic cells divide; maturation-zone cells differentiate.
Root hairs develop from epidermal cells of the region of maturation, which lies proximal to the region of elongation (NEET 2017).
Meristematic cells are very small, thin-walled, with dense protoplasm and divide repeatedly. Large or thick-walled cells are not meristematic.
A is wrong: meristematic cells are thin-walled. B is NCERT: cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature.
A is correct: maturation lies proximal to elongation. B is wrong: root hairs arise from epidermal cells, not endodermal cells.

nuggets.title: Modifications of root
lines: Tap roots of carrot and turnip, and adventitious roots of sweet potato, get swollen and store food.
Prop roots: the hanging roots of the banyan tree that grow down and provide support.
Stilt roots: supporting roots coming out of the lower nodes of the stem in maize and sugarcane.
In Rhizophora growing in swampy areas, many roots come out of the ground and grow vertically upwards (pneumatophores) to get oxygen for respiration.
nuggets.tip: Banyan = prop roots; maize and sugarcane = stilt roots (lower nodes); sweet potato = adventitious, not tap.

questions.why: Sweet potato is a swollen adventitious root that stores food. Carrot and turnip are modified tap roots; potato (not sweet potato) is a stem.
Carrot and turnip: swollen tap roots; sweet potato: swollen adventitious roots. Rhizophora grows in swampy areas and forms upward-growing roots.
The hanging supporting roots of the banyan tree are prop roots. Maize has stilt roots; carrot and sweet potato have storage roots.
II and III are correct. I is wrong: root hairs arise from the region of maturation. IV is wrong: maize and sugarcane have stilt roots; prop roots belong to banyan.
Pneumatophores occur in mangroves like Rhizophora that grow in saline swampy areas, i.e., halophytes. They help get oxygen for respiration.

nuggets.title: Stem: features and underground storage stems
lines: The stem is the ascending part of the axis bearing branches, leaves, flowers and fruits; it develops from the plumule of the embryo of a germinating seed.
The stem bears nodes (where leaves are borne) and internodes, and bears buds, which may be terminal or axillary.
Stems spread branches bearing leaves, flowers and fruits and conduct water, minerals and photosynthates; some store food, support, protect and aid vegetative propagation.
Underground stems of potato, ginger, turmeric, zaminkand and Colocasia store food and act as organs of perennation to tide over conditions unfavourable for growth.
nuggets.tip: Potato is a stem because its 'eyes' are axillary buds.

questions.why: (c) and (d) are correct: stems bear nodes and internodes and develop from the plumule. Absorbing from soil is a root function, and stems bear axillary buds too.
The 'eyes' of a potato tuber are axillary buds at nodes, which is why potato is a modified stem, not a root (NEET 2011).
A is wrong: ginger, turmeric, zaminkand and Colocasia are underground stems, not roots. B is wrong: they help tide over unfavourable conditions.
Underground stems act as organs of perennation, helping the plant survive conditions unfavourable for growth.
Potato, ginger, turmeric and zaminkand are underground stems modified to store food; they are not aerial, mechanical or photosynthetic modifications.

nuggets.title: Stem tendrils, thorns and stems of arid plants
lines: Stem tendrils develop from axillary buds; they are slender, spirally coiled and help plants climb, as in gourds (cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon) and grapevine.
Axillary buds may also become woody, straight and pointed thorns, as in Citrus and Bougainvillea; thorns protect plants from browsing animals.
Some plants of arid regions modify their stems into flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia) structures.
These modified stems contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
nuggets.tip: Pea has leaf tendrils; cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon and grapevine have stem tendrils.

questions.why: Stem tendrils occur in watermelon, cucumber, grapevine and pumpkin (4). Pea has leaf tendrils; Pistia, Eichhornia and Chrysanthemum have no tendrils.
Both correct. NCERT: stem tendrils develop from axillary buds, and axillary buds may also be modified into woody, straight, pointed thorns.
Thorns of Bougainvillea (and Citrus) are modified axillary buds, i.e., stem modifications, not leaves or stipules (NEET 2017).
Underground stem – potato; stem tendril – cucumber; stem thorn – Citrus; flattened stem – Opuntia; fleshy cylindrical stem – Euphorbia.
A is correct. B swaps the examples: Opuntia has a flattened stem and Euphorbia a fleshy cylindrical one.

nuggets.title: Stem modifications for vegetative propagation
lines: In grass and strawberry, subaerially growing stems spread to new niches; when older parts die, new plants are formed.
In mint and jasmine, a slender lateral branch arises from the base of the main axis, grows aerially for some time, then arches downward to touch the ground.
In aquatic plants like Pistia and Eichhornia, a lateral branch with short internodes bears at each node a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots.
In banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum, lateral branches arise from the basal, underground part of the main stem, grow horizontally beneath the soil and come out obliquely upward as leafy shoots.

questions.why: (b), (c), (d), (e) are correct (NEET 2022). (a) is wrong: thorns of Citrus and Bougainvillea are modified axillary buds, not leaflets.
In banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum, lateral branches arise from the basal, underground part of the main stem and emerge obliquely upward as leafy shoots (suckers).
In mint and jasmine the slender lateral branch arises from the base of the main axis, grows aerially and then arches down to touch the ground.
The lateral branch of Pistia and Eichhornia has short internodes, each node bearing a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots.
C is incorrect: grass and strawberry have subaerial (not underground) stems, and new plants form when older parts die. A, B and D match NCERT.

nuggets.title: Leaf: origin and parts
lines: The leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem; it develops at the node, bears a bud in its axil and is the most important organ for photosynthesis.
Leaves originate from shoot apical meristems and are arranged in an acropetal order.
A typical leaf has three parts: leaf base, petiole and lamina; the leaf base may bear two lateral small leaf-like structures called stipules.
In monocots the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem; in some leguminous plants the leaf base becomes swollen, called the pulvinus.
The petiole holds the blade to light; long thin flexible petioles let blades flutter in wind, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface.
The lamina (leaf blade) is the green expanded part with veins and veinlets around a prominent midrib; veins give rigidity and transport water, minerals and food.
nuggets.tip: Pulvinus: some leguminous plants. Sheathing leaf base: monocots.

questions.why: I and II are correct. III is wrong: leaves arise from shoot apical meristems. IV is wrong: leaves are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.
Stipules – lateral leaf-like structures; pulvinus – swollen leaf base; lamina – has veins and veinlets; petiole – holds blade to light; veins – give rigidity to the blade.
Both wrong. The leaf base may (not always) bear stipules, and the swollen leaf base (pulvinus) occurs in some leguminous plants, not monocots.
Both wrong. The sheathing leaf base is seen in monocots, and it is the petiole (not the peduncle) that holds the leaf blade to light.
A is wrong: it is long thin flexible petioles that let blades flutter in wind. B is correct: the leaf blade is the green expanded part with veins and veinlets.

nuggets.title: Venation and simple vs compound leaves
lines: Venation is the arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina: reticulate when veinlets form a network, parallel when veins run parallel within the lamina.
Dicot leaves generally possess reticulate venation, while parallel venation is characteristic of most monocots.
A leaf is simple when its lamina is entire or, if incised, the incisions do not touch the midrib; when incisions reach the midrib, breaking it into leaflets, it is compound.
A bud is present in the axil of the petiole of both simple and compound leaves, but not in the axil of leaflets of a compound leaf.
Pinnately compound: leaflets on a common axis, the rachis (the midrib), as in neem. Palmately compound: leaflets attached at the tip of the petiole, as in silk cotton.
nuggets.tip: Bud in the axil of the petiole = leaf; no bud in the axil of a leaflet.

questions.why: Dicot leaves generally show reticulate venation, while parallel venation characterises most (not all) monocots.
Both wrong. Parallel venation is typical of most, not all, monocots; and in a simple leaf the incisions do not touch the midrib.
Both wrong. Buds are absent in the axil of leaflets of a compound leaf; and the rachis belongs to pinnately, not palmately, compound leaves.
A is correct: the rachis represents the midrib. B is wrong: palmate leaflets attach at the tip of the petiole, not the lamina.
Pinnately compound – neem; simple – mango; palmately compound – silk cotton; leaf base sheathing the stem – monocots.

nuggets.title: Phyllotaxy
lines: Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch; it is usually of three types: alternate, opposite and whorled.
Alternate: a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner, as in china rose, mustard and sunflower.
Opposite: a pair of leaves arises at each node and lies opposite each other, as in Calotropis and guava.
Whorled: more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, as in Alstonia.
nuggets.tip: Calotropis and guava = opposite; Alstonia = whorled.

questions.why: Alternate – china rose, mustard, sunflower; opposite – guava, Calotropis; whorled – Alstonia.
A is wrong: in opposite phyllotaxy the pair of leaves arises at each node, not internode. B is correct for Alstonia.
Both wrong. Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on a stem, not leaflets on a rachis; and alternate phyllotaxy has a single leaf per node.
Mustard – alternate; Alstonia – whorled; Calotropis – opposite.
II and IV are correct: pulvinus occurs in some legumes and guava has opposite leaves. I is wrong (no bud in leaflet axils); III is wrong (it is Australian Acacia).

nuggets.title: Modifications of leaves
lines: Leaves are often modified for functions other than photosynthesis: into tendrils for climbing (as in peas) or into spines for defence (as in cacti).
The fleshy leaves of onion and garlic store food.
In some plants such as Australian Acacia, the leaves are small and short-lived; the petioles expand, become green and synthesise food.
Leaves of certain insectivorous plants such as pitcher plant and venus-fly trap are also modified leaves.

questions.why: Leaf tendrils – pea; leaf spines – cacti; expanded green petiole – Australian Acacia.
A is wrong: in onion and garlic the fleshy leaves store food. B is correct: petioles of Australian Acacia expand, turn green and synthesise food.
Spines of cacti such as Opuntia are modified leaves (NEET 2015). Pea has leaf tendrils, onion fleshy storage leaves, silk cotton palmately compound leaves.
A is correct (Alstonia is whorled). B is wrong: the traps of pitcher plant and venus-fly trap are modified leaves, not spines.
The trap of the venus-fly trap is a modified leaf, as is the pitcher of the pitcher plant.

nuggets.title: Inflorescence: racemose vs cymose
lines: A flower is a modified shoot in which the shoot apical meristem changes to a floral meristem; the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is the inflorescence.
Inflorescences are of two major types, depending on whether the apex develops into a flower or continues to grow.
Racemose: the main axis continues to grow and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession.
Cymose: the main axis terminates in a flower and is limited in growth; flowers are borne in basipetal order.
nuggets.tip: Racemose = acropetal (youngest at the top); cymose = basipetal (oldest at the top).

questions.why: The inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.
Continuous growth (racemose) gives lateral flowers in acropetal succession; limited growth (cymose) gives flowers in basipetal order.
Racemose: main axis continues to grow (R) and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal order (S). Limited growth and basipetal order describe cymose.
Both wrong. Racemose flowers are borne in acropetal order; cymose flowers are borne in basipetal order.
Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong for cymose: flowers are in basipetal order and the main axis does terminate in a flower.

nuggets.title: The flower: whorls, calyx, corolla and perianth
lines: A typical flower has four whorls on the swollen end of the pedicel, the thalamus (receptacle): calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx and corolla are accessory organs; androecium and gynoecium are reproductive organs.
In some flowers like lily, calyx and corolla are not distinct and are together termed the perianth.
A flower with both androecium and gynoecium is bisexual; one with either only stamens or only carpels is unisexual.
Sepals are generally green, leaf-like and protect the flower in bud; the calyx may be gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (sepals free).
Petals are usually brightly coloured to attract insects; corolla shape and colour vary greatly: tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped or wheel-shaped.

questions.why: A is wrong: a typical flower has four whorls; perianth is not a fifth whorl. B is correct: calyx, corolla (or perianth) are accessory; androecium and gynoecium reproductive.
A is wrong: 'perianth' is used when calyx and corolla are not distinct, as in lily. B is correct: a flower with only stamens or only carpels is unisexual.
A is correct. B mislabels the parts: gamosepalous means sepals united and polysepalous means sepals free, not petals.
A is wrong: corolla shape and colour vary greatly, not slightly. B is correct: corolla may be tubular, bell-, funnel- or wheel-shaped.
A flower having both stamens and carpels is bisexual; with only one of them it is unisexual (NEET 2024).

nuggets.title: Floral symmetry, merosity and bracts
lines: Actinomorphic (radial symmetry): divisible into two equal radial halves in any radial plane through the centre, e.g., mustard, Datura, chilli.
Zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry): divisible into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane, e.g., pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia.
Asymmetric (irregular): cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane through the centre, as in Canna.
A flower is trimerous, tetramerous or pentamerous when its floral appendages are in multiples of 3, 4 or 5, respectively.
Flowers with bracts (reduced leaves at the base of the pedicel) are bracteate; those without bracts are ebracteate.
nuggets.tip: Legumes (pea, bean, gulmohur, Cassia) = zygomorphic; Canna = asymmetric.

questions.why: Gulmohar and Cassia are zygomorphic (NEET 2022). Mustard, Datura and chilli are actinomorphic.
Brassica (mustard) flowers are actinomorphic (NEET 2016). Trifolium, Pisum and Cassia are legumes with zygomorphic flowers.
A is wrong: muliathi, a legume, is zygomorphic, not actinomorphic. B is correct: pea, gulmohur, bean and Cassia are zygomorphic.
Both wrong. Bracts are reduced leaves, not petals; and the asymmetric example is Canna, while Cassia is zygomorphic.
I, III and IV are correct. II is wrong: flowers with reduced leaves (bracts) at the base of the pedicel are bracteate, not ebracteate.

nuggets.title: Position of ovary: hypogyny, perigyny, epigyny
lines: Based on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium relative to the ovary on the thalamus, flowers are hypogynous, perigynous or epigynous.
Hypogynous: gynoecium occupies the highest position with other parts below it; ovary superior, e.g., mustard, china rose, brinjal.
Perigynous: gynoecium in the centre, other parts on the rim of the thalamus at almost the same level; ovary half-inferior, e.g., plum, rose, peach.
Epigynous: thalamus margin grows upward, enclosing and fusing with the ovary completely, other parts arising above it; ovary inferior, e.g., guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower.
nuggets.tip: Plum, rose, peach = perigynous (half-inferior). Guava, cucumber = epigynous.

questions.why: Peach is perigynous, so its ovary is half-inferior (NEET 2011). Cucumber and guava are epigynous (inferior ovary); cotton is hypogynous.
Rose is perigynous (NEET 2015). Cucumber and guava are epigynous; china rose is hypogynous.
In an epigynous flower the ovary is inferior (fused with the thalamus) and the other floral parts arise above it (NEET 2021).
Mustard – hypogynous; peach – perigynous; cucumber – epigynous.
A is correct (perigynous). B is wrong: in epigynous flowers the thalamus encloses the ovary completely, not partially.

nuggets.title: Aestivation
lines: Aestivation is the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl.
Valvate: sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin, without overlapping, as in Calotropis.
Twisted: one margin of each appendage overlaps that of the next one, as in china rose, lady's finger and cotton.
Imbricate: margins overlap one another but not in any particular direction, as in Cassia and gulmohur.
Vexillary (papilionaceous), in pea and bean: the largest standard overlaps two lateral wings, which overlap the two smallest anterior petals, the keel.
nuggets.tip: Calotropis = valvate; china rose/cotton = twisted; Cassia/gulmohur = imbricate; pea/bean = vexillary.

questions.why: Valvate – Calotropis; twisted – cotton; imbricate – gulmohar; vexillary – Trifolium (a legume); united sepals – gamosepalous.
A is wrong: in valvate aestivation sepals/petals touch without overlapping. B is correct: china rose, lady's finger and cotton are twisted.
Both wrong. Imbricate margins overlap not in any particular direction; in pea the largest petal is the standard, while the lateral ones are wings.
The large posterior standard petal of a papilionaceous corolla is also called the vexillum (NEET 2016); the keel is called carina.
Overlap in no particular direction is imbricate, seen in Cassia and gulmohar. China rose is twisted and Calotropis valvate.

nuggets.title: Androecium
lines: The androecium is made of stamens; each stamen has a filament and an anther, usually bilobed with two pollen sacs per lobe; a sterile stamen is a staminode.
Stamens attached to petals are epipetalous (brinjal); those attached to the perianth are epiphyllous (lily).
Stamens may be free (polyandrous) or united: one bundle is monoadelphous (china rose), two diadelphous (pea), more than two polyadelphous (Citrus).
There may be variation in the length of filaments within a flower, as in Salvia and mustard.
nuggets.tip: Mono-china rose, Di-pea, Poly-Citrus.

questions.why: Monoadelphous – china rose; diadelphous – pea; polyadelphous – Citrus; epiphyllous – lily (NEET 2024).
Pea has diadelphous stamens, in two bundles (NEET 2021). China rose is monoadelphous and Citrus polyadelphous.
A is wrong: stamens attached to petals are epipetalous, as in brinjal. B is correct: stamens attached to the perianth are epiphyllous, as in lily.
A is correct. B is wrong: china rose stamens are monoadelphous; polyadelphous stamens occur in Citrus.
NCERT gives Salvia and mustard as examples of variation in filament length within a flower.

nuggets.title: Gynoecium and placentation
lines: The gynoecium is made of carpels, each with stigma, style and ovary; the style connects ovary to stigma, and ovules attach to a flattened cushion-like placenta.
Carpels may be free (apocarpous, as in lotus and rose) or fused (syncarpous, as in mustard and tomato).

Marginal: the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and ovules form two rows, as in pea. Axile: ovules on a central axis of a multilocular ovary, as in china rose, tomato, lemon.
Parietal: ovules on the inner wall; the one-chambered ovary becomes two-chambered by a false septum, as in mustard and Argemone.
Free central: ovules on a central axis with no septa, as in Dianthus and Primrose.
Basal: the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and bears a single ovule, as in sunflower and marigold.
nuggets.tip: False septum = parietal (mustard, Argemone). No septa + central axis = free central (Dianthus, Primrose).

questions.why: Both correct. Free carpels (lotus, rose) are apocarpous; fused carpels (mustard, tomato) are syncarpous.
China rose, Petunia and lemon have multilocular ovaries with axile placentation (NEET 2023). Primrose and Dianthus are free central; pea and beans marginal.
Dianthus shows free central placentation (NEET 2016). Argemone and Brassica are parietal; Citrus is axile.
A is correct. B is wrong: the ovary is one-chambered and becomes two-chambered due to the false septum in mustard and Argemone.
A is wrong: ovules on a central axis without septa is free central, not axile. B is correct: basal placentation, single ovule, sunflower and marigold.

nuggets.title: The fruit
lines: The fruit is a mature or ripened ovary developed after fertilisation; a fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary is parthenocarpic.
A fruit consists of a wall or pericarp and seeds; the pericarp may be dry or fleshy.
A thick, fleshy pericarp is differentiated into the outer epicarp, middle mesocarp and inner endocarp.
In mango and coconut the fruit is a drupe: it develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and is one-seeded.
Mango has a thin epicarp, fleshy edible mesocarp and hard stony endocarp; in coconut the mesocarp is fibrous.
nuggets.tip: Parthenocarpic (fruit), not 'parthenogenic'. Mango and coconut: both drupes, both stony endocarp.

questions.why: A is correct. B is wrong: a fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic, not 'parthenogenic'.
Both wrong. The fruit wall is the pericarp (not epicarp), and a fleshy pericarp is divided into epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp.
A is correct: coconut is a drupe with a fibrous mesocarp. B is wrong: the coconut endocarp is hard and stony; its edible part is the endosperm.
Fleshy fruits with a hard stony endocarp are drupes, e.g., mango and coconut (NEET 2009).
ii and iii are common: both drupes have a hard stony endocarp and develop from a monocarpellary superior ovary. Only coconut has a fibrous mesocarp; mango's edible part is mesocarp.

nuggets.title: Structure of a dicotyledonous seed
lines: After fertilisation the ovules develop into seeds; a seed is made of a seed coat and an embryo.
The seed coat has two layers: the outer testa and the inner tegmen.
The hilum is a scar on the seed coat through which the developing seed was attached to the fruit; above it is a small pore, the micropyle.
The embryo has an embryonal axis with radicle and plumule at its two ends, and two cotyledons that are often fleshy and full of reserve food.
In some seeds like castor the endosperm, formed by double fertilisation, is a food-storing tissue; in bean, gram and pea it is absent in mature seeds (non-endospermous).
nuggets.tip: Testa outside, tegmen inside. Castor = endospermous; bean, gram, pea = non-endospermous.

questions.why: A is wrong: testa is the outer layer and tegmen the inner. B is correct: the hilum is the scar where the seed was attached to the fruit.
A is wrong: the micropyle is the small pore above the hilum, not the reverse. B is correct: cotyledons are often fleshy and full of reserve food.
A is correct: castor is endospermous. B is wrong: mature seeds of bean, gram and pea have no endosperm; food is stored in the cotyledons.
Pea seeds are non-albuminous (non-endospermous): food is in the cotyledons (NEET 2014). Maize, wheat and castor have endosperm.
Hilum – scar on the seed coat; micropyle – small pore; proteinous layer – aleurone layer.

nuggets.title: Structure of a monocotyledonous seed
lines: Monocot seeds are generally endospermic, but some, as in orchids, are non-endospermic.
In cereal seeds such as maize, the seed coat is membranous and generally fused with the fruit wall; the endosperm is bulky and stores food.
The outer covering of the endosperm separates it from the embryo by a proteinous layer called the aleurone layer.
The embryo is small and lies in a groove at one end of the endosperm; it has one large, shield-shaped cotyledon, the scutellum, and a short axis with plumule and radicle.
The plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths called the coleoptile and coleorhiza, respectively.
nuggets.tip: Coleoptile covers the plumule; coleorhiza covers the radicle.

questions.why: Both correct per NCERT: in maize the seed coat is membranous and fused with the fruit wall, and a proteinous aleurone layer separates endosperm from embryo.
A is wrong: the plumule is sheathed by the coleoptile and the radicle by the coleorhiza. B is correct: the embryo has a scutellum and a short axis.
The plumule is enclosed in the coleoptile, and the radicle in the coleorhiza.
The scutellum of wheat or maize is the single, shield-shaped cotyledon of the monocot embryo (NEET 2010).
All four statements match NCERT, including that orchid seeds are non-endospermic, so the answer is 'None of these'.

nuggets.title: Semi-technical description and floral formula
lines: A flowering plant is described in a set sequence: habit, vegetative characters (roots, stem, leaves), then floral characters (inflorescence and flower parts).
In a floral formula: Br = bracteate, K = calyx, C = corolla, P = perianth, A = androecium, G = gynoecium; ⊕ = actinomorphic, % = zygomorphic, ⚥ = bisexual.
G with a line below it denotes a superior ovary; G with a line above it denotes an inferior ovary.
Fusion is indicated by enclosing the figure within brackets; adhesion by a line drawn above the symbols of the floral parts.
In a floral diagram the mother axis is a dot on the top; calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium are drawn in successive whorls, calyx outermost and gynoecium in the centre.
nuggets.tip: Brackets = fusion (cohesion); line above symbols = adhesion. Line under G = superior ovary.

questions.why: A is wrong: ⊕ means actinomorphic and G with a line below means a superior ovary. B states both correctly (NEET 2025).
Both wrong. G with a line below denotes a superior ovary; brackets show fusion, while adhesion is shown by a line drawn above the symbols.
Only III and IV are right. K is calyx and C is corolla, and brackets denote fusion, not adhesion.
A is correct. B is wrong: in a floral formula K stands for calyx and C for corolla.
Both wrong. The mother axis is a dot on the top of the floral diagram, and the calyx, not corolla, is the outermost whorl.

nuggets.title: Family Solanaceae (potato family)
lines: Solanaceae, the 'potato family', is widely distributed in the tropics, subtropics and even temperate zones.
Plants are mostly herbs or shrubs, rarely small trees; stem herbaceous, rarely woody, aerial, erect, cylindrical, hairy or glabrous, underground in potato (Solanum tuberosum).
Leaves alternate, simple, rarely pinnately compound, exstipulate, with reticulate venation; inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose as in Solanum.
Flower bisexual, actinomorphic; calyx five, united, persistent, valvate; corolla five, united, valvate; stamens five, epipetalous.
Gynoecium bicarpellary, syncarpous, ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules (axile); fruit a berry or capsule; seeds many, endospermous.
Uses: food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco) and ornamentals (Petunia).
nuggets.tip: Solanaceae: K(5) C(5) A5 epipetalous, G(2) superior; berry or capsule.

questions.why: All five are correct: K(5) (united sepals), epipetalous stamens, bicarpellary gynoecium, valvate petals, and solitary/axillary/cymose inflorescence as in Solanum.
A, C and D are correct: leaves have reticulate venation, are rarely pinnately compound and alternate. They are exstipulate (B wrong) and not opposite (E wrong).
A is correct. B is wrong: Solanaceae leaves are simple and only rarely pinnately compound, not 'mostly'.
Both correct: the gynoecium is bicarpellary and syncarpous, and the fruit is a berry or capsule.
Tobacco is the fumigatory member of Solanaceae. Ashwagandha is medicinal and Petunia ornamental; colchicine is not from this family.

nuggets.title: Meristematic tissues
lines: Growth in plants is largely restricted to specialised regions of active cell division called meristems.
Apical meristems occur at the tips of roots and shoots and produce primary tissues; the shoot apical meristem occupies the distant-most region of the stem axis.
Some cells 'left behind' from the shoot apical meristem during leaf formation and stem elongation constitute the axillary bud, capable of forming a branch or a flower.
The intercalary meristem occurs between mature tissues; it is present in grasses and regenerates parts removed by grazing herbivores.
Apical and intercalary meristems are primary meristems: they appear early in the life of a plant and contribute to the primary plant body.
The secondary or lateral meristem is cylindrical and appears later in mature regions of plants producing a woody axis, e.g., fascicular and interfascicular cambium and cork-cambium.
nuggets.tip: Primary = apical + intercalary. Lateral meristems are cylindrical, not conical.

questions.why: During leaf formation and stem elongation, some cells left behind from the shoot apical meristem form the axillary bud.
A is wrong: the shoot apical meristem lies at the tip of the stem axis, not the root. B is correct: axillary buds can form a branch or a flower.
Both true and R explains A: apical and intercalary meristems appear early and build the primary plant body, hence 'primary meristems'.
A is correct. B is wrong: lateral (secondary) meristems are cylindrical, not conical.
The intercalary meristem occurs between mature tissues, as in grasses, where it regenerates parts removed by grazing herbivores.

nuggets.title: Permanent tissues: parenchyma and collenchyma
lines: Cells formed by meristems become structurally and functionally specialised and lose the ability to divide; they form permanent tissues.
Permanent tissues with all cells similar in structure and function are simple tissues; those with many different cell types are complex tissues.
Parenchyma forms the major component within organs; its cells are generally isodiametric, thin-walled (cellulose), and do photosynthesis, storage and secretion.
Collenchyma occurs in layers below the epidermis in dicots, either as a homogeneous layer or in patches.
Collenchyma cells are thickened at the corners by cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin, often contain chloroplasts, and give mechanical support to growing parts like young stems and petioles.
nuggets.tip: Collenchyma = living, corners thickened with pectin; sclerenchyma = dead, lignified.

questions.why: Actively dividing – meristematic tissue; similar cells – simple tissue; different cell types – vascular (complex) tissue; dead, thick-walled, narrow lumen – sclereids (NEET 2021).
A is wrong: parenchyma forms the major component within organs. B is correct: parenchyma cells are generally isodiametric.
A is wrong: photosynthesis, storage and secretion are functions of parenchyma. B is correct: collenchyma lies in layers below the epidermis in dicots.
Collenchyma corners are thickened by deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin, all three.
Parenchyma – photosynthesis, storage, secretion; collenchyma – cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin; meristem – actively dividing cells; sclerenchyma – thick lignified walls.

nuggets.title: Sclerenchyma: fibres and sclereids
lines: Sclerenchyma consists of long, narrow cells with thick, lignified walls having a few or numerous pits; the cells are usually dead and without protoplasts.
On the basis of form, structure, origin and development, sclerenchyma is either fibres or sclereids.
Fibres are thick-walled, elongated and pointed cells, generally occurring in groups in various parts of the plant.
Sclereids are spherical, oval or cylindrical, highly thickened dead cells with a very narrow lumen.
Sclereids occur in fruit walls of nuts, the pulp of guava, pear and sapota, seed coats of legumes and leaves of tea; sclerenchyma provides mechanical support.

questions.why: Both correct: sclerenchyma cells are usually dead without protoplasts, and fibres are thick-walled, elongated, pointed cells occurring in groups.
Sclereids occur in fruit walls of nuts, seed coats of legumes and leaves of tea, so all of these.
NCERT lists the pulp of guava, pear and sapota as sites of sclereids.
Sclereids are dead cells, so 'living tissue' is the wrong feature. Their shapes, lignified walls, narrow lumen and locations match NCERT.
Sclereids – narrow lumen; parenchyma – isodiametric cells; collenchyma – thickened corners.

nuggets.title: Xylem and its elements
lines: Xylem conducts water and minerals from roots to the stem and leaves, and also provides mechanical strength.
Xylem has four kinds of elements: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma.
Tracheids are elongated, tube-like dead cells with thick lignified walls and tapering ends; thickenings of their inner wall layers vary in form.
A vessel is a long tube of many dead vessel members with lignified walls and a large central cavity, interconnected through perforations in their common walls.
Tracheids and vessels are the main water-transporting elements of flowering plants; vessels characterise angiosperms, and gymnosperms lack vessels.
Xylem fibres have highly thickened walls and obliterated lumens; xylem parenchyma is living, thin-walled (cellulose), stores food and helps radial conduction of water.
nuggets.tip: Only living xylem element: xylem parenchyma. Gymnosperms: no vessels.

questions.why: A is correct. B is wrong: the four xylem elements are tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma; sclereids are not one of them.
Both wrong. Tracheid walls are thick and lignified (not chitinised), and the thickenings of their inner wall layers vary in form.
Gymnosperms lack vessels, so tracheids are their chief water-conducting elements (NEET 2010).
A is false: both parenchyma and collenchyma are living. B is true: gymnosperms lack vessels, which characterise angiosperms (NEET 2024).
Xylem parenchyma – stores food; tracheids and vessels – main water-transporting elements; xylem fibres – obliterated lumen.

nuggets.title: Protoxylem, metaxylem: endarch vs exarch
lines: The first formed primary xylem is protoxylem; the later formed primary xylem is metaxylem.
In stems, protoxylem lies towards the centre (pith) and metaxylem towards the periphery: this is endarch.
In roots, protoxylem lies towards the periphery and metaxylem towards the centre: this is exarch.
Endarch and exarch describe the arrangement of primary xylem.
nuggets.tip: Stem = endarch (protoxylem inside); root = exarch (protoxylem outside).

questions.why: Both wrong (swapped). In roots protoxylem lies towards the periphery (exarch); in stems it lies towards the centre (endarch).
A is false: endarch and exarch describe primary xylem, not secondary. B is true: exarch xylem is the rule in roots (NEET 2023).
Stems have endarch primary xylem; roots have exarch primary xylem.
Both true and R explains A: in the Zea mays root, protoxylem is peripheral and metaxylem central, which is exactly what exarch means.

nuggets.title: Phloem: sieve tubes and companion cells
lines: Phloem transports food materials, usually from leaves to other parts; in angiosperms it has sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
Gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells; they lack sieve tubes and companion cells.
Sieve tube elements are long, tube-like cells arranged longitudinally; their end walls are perforated in a sieve-like manner to form sieve plates.
A mature sieve element has peripheral cytoplasm and a large vacuole but lacks a nucleus; its functions are controlled by the nucleus of companion cells.
Companion cells are specialised parenchyma connected to sieve tube elements by pit fields in their common longitudinal walls; they help maintain the pressure gradient in sieve tubes.
nuggets.tip: Gymnosperms: sieve cells + albuminous cells instead of sieve tubes + companion cells.

questions.why: Both wrong. Sieve tube elements are arranged longitudinally, and a mature sieve element lacks a nucleus.
Both correct: companion cells are specialised parenchyma linked to sieve tube elements by pit fields in their common longitudinal walls.
A is wrong: companion cells maintain the pressure gradient in sieve tubes, not fibres. B is correct: phloem parenchyma is absent in most monocots.
Companion cells are closely associated with sieve tube elements, whose functions their nucleus controls (NEET 2012).
Both correct. Phloem carries food usually from leaves; gymnosperms lack vessels, sieve tubes and companion cells, having sieve cells and albuminous cells instead.

nuggets.title: Phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres, protophloem
lines: Phloem parenchyma has elongated, tapering cylindrical cells with dense cytoplasm and nucleus; it stores food and substances like resins, latex and mucilage.
Phloem parenchyma is absent in most monocots.
Phloem fibres (bast fibres) are sclerenchymatous, much elongated, unbranched, with pointed needle-like apices and thick walls; at maturity they lose protoplasm and die.
Phloem fibres are generally absent in primary phloem but present in secondary phloem; fibres of jute, flax and hemp are used commercially.
The first formed primary phloem, with narrow sieve tubes, is protophloem; the later formed phloem, with bigger sieve tubes, is metaphloem.
nuggets.tip: Phloem fibre is the only dead element of phloem.

questions.why: Phloem (bast) fibres of jute, flax and hemp are used commercially.
Phloem fibres are generally absent in primary phloem and are found in secondary phloem.
First-formed primary phloem has narrow sieve tubes and is called protophloem; later-formed phloem with bigger sieve tubes is metaphloem.
Sclerenchymatous, elongated, unbranched, needle-like, thick-walled dead cells found in secondary phloem are phloem (bast) fibres.
Companion cells – maintain pressure gradient; bast fibres – sclerenchyma; sieve tube cells – lack nucleus; phloem parenchyma – absent in most monocots.

nuggets.title: Tissue systems and the epidermis
lines: On the basis of structure and location there are three tissue systems: epidermal, ground (fundamental) and vascular (conducting).
The epidermal tissue system forms the outermost covering of the whole plant body and comprises epidermal cells, stomata and epidermal appendages (trichomes and hairs).
The epidermis is usually single-layered, of elongated, compactly arranged parenchymatous cells with a little cytoplasm lining the wall and a large vacuole.
The outside of the epidermis is often covered by a waxy thick cuticle that prevents water loss; the cuticle is absent in roots.
nuggets.tip: Three tissue systems, not two. No cuticle on roots.

questions.why: A is wrong: there are three tissue systems (epidermal, ground, vascular). B is correct: the epidermis is the outermost layer of the primary plant body.
A is correct: roots lack a cuticle. B is wrong: stomata are in the epidermis of leaves, not the endodermis.
I, III and V are correct. II is wrong (there are three tissue systems) and IV is wrong (epidermal cells have a large vacuole).
The epidermis is usually single-layered parenchyma with a large vacuole that forms the protective outer covering, so all are correct.
The cuticle is absent in roots, so root epidermis does not bear one; stem and leaf epidermis are covered by a cuticle.

nuggets.title: Stomata and epidermal appendages
lines: Stomata in the leaf epidermis regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange; each is enclosed by two bean-shaped guard cells.
In grasses guard cells are dumb-bell shaped; their outer walls (away from the pore) are thin and inner walls (towards the pore) highly thickened.
Guard cells possess chloroplasts and regulate opening and closing of stomata; specialised epidermal cells near them are subsidiary cells.
The stomatal aperture, guard cells and surrounding subsidiary cells together form the stomatal apparatus.
Root hairs are unicellular elongations of epidermal cells that absorb water and minerals; shoot hairs, trichomes, are usually multicellular, may be secretory and help prevent water loss.
nuggets.tip: Guard cells: bean-shaped in dicots, dumb-bell in grasses; inner wall thick.

questions.why: Both correct: guard cells are dumb-bell shaped in grasses, and guard cells have chloroplasts and regulate stomatal opening and closing.
Only I and V hold. Guard cells are bean-shaped in dicots and dumb-bell in grasses (II, III swapped), and it is the inner walls, towards the pore, that are thick.
A is wrong: root hairs are unicellular. B is correct: trichomes of the shoot system are usually multicellular.
The stomatal apparatus = stomatal aperture + guard cells + surrounding subsidiary cells.
II, III and V are correct. Stomata are not appendages and do not protect, and it is trichomes, not root hairs, that may be branched or unbranched, soft or stiff.

nuggets.title: Ground tissue and vascular tissue systems
lines: All tissues except the epidermis and vascular bundles form the ground tissue, made of simple tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
In primary stems and roots the ground tissue includes cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays; in leaves it is thin-walled, chloroplast-containing mesophyll.
The vascular system consists of the complex tissues xylem and phloem, which together form vascular bundles.
In dicot stems cambium lies between xylem and phloem, so bundles are open; monocot bundles have no cambium and are closed.
Radial: xylem and phloem on different radii alternately, as in roots. Conjoint: on the same radius, common in stems and leaves, with phloem usually outside the xylem.
nuggets.tip: Radial = roots; conjoint = stems and leaves.

questions.why: Ground tissue includes collenchyma, sclerenchyma and parenchyma; epidermis and vascular bundles are excluded by definition.
Xylem and phloem belong to the vascular tissue system; cortex, endodermis and pericycle are part of the ground tissue.
Radial – xylem and phloem on alternate radii; exarch – metaxylem towards centre; endarch – protoxylem towards centre; conjoint – xylem and phloem on the same radius.
A is correct. B is wrong: in conjoint bundles the phloem is usually on the outer side of the xylem.
Cambium between xylem and phloem makes a bundle open, able to form secondary xylem and phloem; without cambium it is closed (NEET 2023).

nuggets.title: Anatomy of the dicot root
lines: The outermost layer of a dicot root is the epiblema; many of its cells protrude as unicellular root hairs.
The cortex has several layers of thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces; its innermost layer is the endodermis.
Endodermis: one layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces; their tangential and radial walls bear water-impermeable, waxy suberin as casparian strips.
Next to it lies the pericycle, a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma, where lateral roots and the vascular cambium (in secondary growth) are initiated.
Pith is small or inconspicuous; parenchyma between xylem and phloem is conjunctive tissue; there are usually two to four xylem and phloem patches.
All tissues on the inner side of the endodermis (pericycle, vascular bundles and pith) constitute the stele.
nuggets.tip: Lateral roots arise from the pericycle (endogenous), not the endodermis or pith.

questions.why: A is wrong: root endodermal cells have no intercellular spaces. B is correct: their tangential and radial walls carry suberin as casparian strips.
A is wrong: the stele includes tissues on the inner side of the endodermis. B is correct: monocot root anatomy resembles the dicot root in many respects.
Casparian strips are suberin deposits on the tangential and radial walls of the root endodermis (NEET 2018).
Lateral roots and the vascular cambium (during secondary growth) are initiated in the pericycle.
II to VI are correct. I is wrong: lateral roots and vascular cambium are initiated in the pericycle, not the pith.

nuggets.title: Anatomy of the monocot root
lines: The monocot root is similar to the dicot root in many respects: it has epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, vascular bundles and pith.
Monocot roots usually have more than six xylem bundles (polyarch), whereas dicot roots have two to four.
Pith is large and well developed in monocot roots.
Monocot roots do not undergo any secondary growth.
nuggets.tip: Monocot root: polyarch, large pith, no secondary growth.

questions.why: Both wrong. Monocot roots are polyarch (more than six xylem bundles), and the large, well-developed pith is a monocot root feature.
Monocot roots are polyarch. Their pith is large and well developed, and there is no cambium or secondary growth.
Dicot root – 2 to 4 xylem bundles, small pith, secondary growth; monocot root – large pith, more than six xylem bundles.
Both roots have epidermis, root hairs and casparian strips; only the absence of secondary growth sets the monocot root apart.
The maize root (monocot) has polyarch (more than six) and exarch xylem bundles; stems are endarch.

nuggets.title: Anatomy of the dicot stem
lines: The dicot stem epidermis is covered by a thin cuticle and may bear trichomes and a few stomata.
Cortex: outer hypodermis of a few layers of collenchyma, middle layers of rounded thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces, and inner endodermis.
Endodermal cells of the stem are rich in starch grains, so the layer is called the starch sheath.
The pericycle lies inside the endodermis, above the phloem, as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma; radially placed parenchyma between bundles forms medullary rays.
Vascular bundles are arranged in a ring (characteristic of dicot stem); each is conjoint, open, with endarch protoxylem; a large parenchymatous pith fills the centre.
nuggets.tip: Dicot stem: collenchymatous hypodermis, starch sheath, ring of open bundles.

questions.why: A is wrong: the cortical parenchyma has conspicuous intercellular spaces. B is correct: the innermost cortical layer is the endodermis.
III, IV and V hold for the dicot stem. Its hypodermis is collenchyma and its pericycle forms semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma, so I and II are wrong.
A is correct for the dicot stem pericycle. B is wrong: a ring of vascular bundles is characteristic of the dicot stem; monocot bundles are scattered.
Medullary rays are a few layers of radially placed parenchyma cells lying between the vascular bundles.
Both true and R explains A: endodermal cells of the dicot stem are rich in starch grains, hence the name starch sheath.

nuggets.title: Anatomy of the monocot stem
lines: The monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and a large number of scattered vascular bundles in parenchymatous ground tissue.
Each vascular bundle is surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath.
Vascular bundles are conjoint and closed; peripheral bundles are generally smaller than the centrally located ones.
Phloem parenchyma is absent, and water-containing cavities are present within the vascular bundles.
nuggets.tip: Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered closed bundles, water cavities.

questions.why: A is correct. B is wrong: monocot stem bundles are conjoint and closed, lacking cambium.
Water-containing cavities within vascular bundles are a monocot stem feature, e.g., maize (NEET 2012).
Barley is a monocot, so its stem bundles are closed and scattered (NEET 2009).
Monocot stem bundles are closed and surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath.
Both wrong: monocot stem bundles are conjoint and closed, and smaller peripheral bundles are a monocot, not dicot, stem feature.

nuggets.title: Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf
lines: A vertical section of a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf through the lamina shows three parts: epidermis, mesophyll and vascular system.
Epidermis covers the upper (adaxial) and lower (abaxial) surfaces; the abaxial epidermis generally bears more stomata, which may even be absent on the adaxial side.
Mesophyll has adaxial palisade parenchyma of elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel, and abaxial spongy parenchyma of oval or round, loosely arranged cells.
Spongy parenchyma has numerous large spaces and air cavities between its cells.
Bundle size depends on vein size; veins vary in thickness in reticulate venation, and bundles are surrounded by thick-walled bundle sheath cells.
nuggets.tip: Palisade = adaxial (upper); spongy = abaxial (lower).

questions.why: Both wrong. Palisade cells are arranged vertically and parallel, and in reticulate venation the veins vary in thickness.
I, II, III and V are correct. IV is wrong: spongy parenchyma cells are loosely arranged, with large spaces and air cavities.
In a dorsiventral leaf, spongy parenchyma is towards the abaxial (lower) side and palisade towards the adaxial (upper) side.
II to VI are correct. Statement I (smaller peripheral bundles) describes the monocot stem, not the dicot leaf.
In dicot leaves the vascular bundles are surrounded by a layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells.

nuggets.title: Isobilateral (monocot) leaf and bulliform cells
lines: In an isobilateral (monocot) leaf, stomata are present on both surfaces of the epidermis.
The mesophyll of an isobilateral leaf is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma.
In grasses, certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins become large, empty, colourless bulliform cells.
Turgid bulliform cells keep the leaf surface exposed; when flaccid under water stress they make the leaves curl inwards to minimise water loss.
The parallel venation of monocot leaves is reflected in the near-similar sizes of vascular bundles, except in the main veins.
nuggets.tip: Bulliform cells: grasses, adaxial, flaccid = leaf curls in.

questions.why: In very dry weather bulliform cells become flaccid, so grass leaves curl inwards to minimise water loss (NEET 2019).
Bulliform cells cause inward curling of monocot leaves under water stress (NEET 2024); they are empty, colourless cells, not photosynthetic or storage cells.
A is wrong: bulliform cells occur in grasses, not pulses. B is correct: when flaccid they curl leaves inwards to reduce water loss.
Both correct: dicot leaf bundles have thick-walled bundle sheath cells, and isobilateral mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy.
Sorghum is a grass with an isobilateral leaf whose mesophyll lacks palisade (NEET 2009). Mustard, soybean and gram are dicots with palisade.

nuggets.title: Tissues and the epithelium
lines: A tissue is a group of similar cells along with intercellular substances that performs a specific function; cell structure varies with function.
Animal tissues are of four basic types: epithelial, connective, muscular and neural.
Epithelium has a free surface facing a body fluid or the outside environment and provides a covering or lining for some part of the body.
Epithelial cells are compactly packed with little intercellular matrix.
Epithelium is of two types: simple (single layer) and compound (two or more layers).
nuggets.tip: Epithelium is avascular; protection, secretion, absorption and diffusion are its jobs, not excitation.

questions.why: A tissue = group of similar cells plus intercellular substances performing a specific function. A single cell is not a tissue.
Epithelial tissue has a free surface facing either a body fluid or the outside environment, so it lines or covers body parts.
Epithelial cells are compactly packed with little intercellular matrix; large matrix is a feature of connective tissue.
Epithelium is not vascularised; it is compactly packed, lines surfaces and helps in protection, secretion and absorption.
Protection, secretion and absorption are epithelial functions; excitation belongs to neural tissue.

nuggets.title: Simple squamous epithelium
lines: Simple epithelium is a single layer of cells that functions as a lining for body cavities, ducts and tubes.
Squamous epithelium is a single thin layer of flattened cells with irregular boundaries.
Squamous epithelium is found in the walls of blood vessels and air sacs of lungs.
It is involved in functions like forming a diffusion boundary.
nuggets.tip: Squamous = flat + diffusion (blood vessels, alveoli); not secretion/absorption.

questions.why: Squamous epithelium is a single thin layer of flattened cells with irregular boundaries; cuboidal cells are cube-like, columnar are tall.
Arteries and veins are lined by flat squamous epithelium, which forms a diffusion boundary.
The cells lining blood vessels are squamous epithelium; smooth muscle lies deeper in the wall, not as the lining.
Absorption and secretion are functions of cuboidal/columnar epithelium; squamous mainly forms a diffusion boundary.
All are true: squamous epithelium is flat with irregular boundaries, lines blood vessels and lung air sacs, and forms a diffusion boundary.

nuggets.title: Cuboidal and columnar epithelium
lines: Cuboidal epithelium is a single layer of cube-like cells, found in ducts of glands and tubular parts of nephrons in kidneys.
Cuboidal epithelium mainly functions in secretion and absorption.
Epithelium of the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of nephron has microvilli.
Columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall, slender cells with nuclei at the base; the free surface may have microvilli.
Columnar epithelium lines the stomach and intestine and helps in secretion and absorption.
nuggets.tip: Brush border = microvilli: PCT (cuboidal) and intestine (columnar).

questions.why: Single layer of cube-like cells = cuboidal epithelium, found in tubular parts of nephrons. Blood vessels and air sacs have squamous.
Cuboidal epithelium with a brush border of microvilli lines the PCT of nephron; salivary ducts have cuboidal epithelium without microvilli.
PCT is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, whose main functions are secretion and absorption.
False: iii (columnar cells of stomach and intestine help in secretion and absorption, not protection) and v (nuclei are basal, not apical).
A is true (tall, slender cells). B is false: lung alveoli are lined by squamous, not columnar, epithelium.

nuggets.title: Ciliated and glandular epithelium
lines: Columnar or cuboidal cells bearing cilia on the free surface form ciliated epithelium, which moves particles or mucus in a specific direction.
Ciliated epithelium lines hollow organs like bronchioles and fallopian tubes.
Some columnar or cuboidal cells become specialised for secretion: glandular epithelium.
Glands are unicellular (isolated glandular cells, e.g. goblet cells of the alimentary canal) or multicellular (clusters, e.g. salivary gland).
nuggets.tip: Goblet cell = unicellular exocrine gland secreting mucus.

questions.why: Hollow tubes like bronchioles and fallopian tubes are lined by ciliated epithelium that moves particles/mucus in one direction.
Bronchioles have ciliated epithelium; kidney tubules have cuboidal, intestine columnar and blood vessels squamous.
Ciliated columnar epithelium occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube); stomach and oesophagus lack it.
Some columnar or cuboidal cells get specialised for secretion and form glandular epithelium.
A goblet cell is a unicellular glandular (secretory) cell of the alimentary canal that secretes mucus.

nuggets.title: Exocrine and endocrine glands
lines: On the basis of mode of pouring secretions, glands are exocrine and endocrine.
Exocrine glands secrete mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, digestive enzymes and other cell products through ducts.
Endocrine glands do not have ducts; their products, called hormones, are secreted directly into the fluid bathing the gland.
Salivary glands are an example of multicellular glands; goblet cells are unicellular.

questions.why: Thyroid is an endocrine (ductless) gland; salivary, mammary and intestinal glands are exocrine with ducts.
Mammary glands are made of clusters of cells and pour milk through ducts: multicellular exocrine.
False: endocrine glands secrete hormones, not enzymes only. Exocrine glands release enzymes, mucus, milk, oil through ducts.
Endocrine glands are ductless; their hormones pass directly into the fluid bathing the gland.
Goblet cell = unicellular gland; salivary gland = multicellular exocrine; thymus = endocrine. So A-Q, B-R, C-P.

nuggets.title: Compound epithelium
lines: Compound epithelium is made of more than one layer (multi-layered) of cells.
It has a limited role in secretion and absorption.
Its main function is to provide protection against chemical and mechanical stresses.
It covers the dry surface of the skin, the moist surface of buccal cavity, pharynx, and inner lining of ducts of salivary glands and pancreatic ducts.
nuggets.tip: Multi-layered = protection; one layer = diffusion, secretion, absorption.

questions.why: Both true: compound epithelium is multi-layered and has only a limited role in secretion and absorption.
Compound epithelium covers the dry skin, moist buccal cavity, pharynx and lines ducts of salivary glands and pancreatic ducts: all of them.
The dry surface of the skin is covered by multi-layered (stratified) squamous compound epithelium for protection.
False: I (it is truly multi-layered, not pseudostratified) and IV (its role in secretion and absorption is limited).
Incorrect: compound epithelium's main function is protection; it has only a limited role in secretion and absorption.

nuggets.title: Cell junctions
lines: All cells in epithelium are held together with little intercellular material; in nearly all animal tissues specialised junctions give structural and functional links.
Tight junctions help to stop substances from leaking across a tissue.
Adhering junctions perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together.
Gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells for rapid transfer of ions, small molecules and sometimes big molecules.
nuggets.tip: Tight = seal, Adhering = glue, Gap = talk.

questions.why: Tight junctions stop substances from leaking across a tissue; gap junctions allow passage between cells.
Adhering junctions perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together.
Gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells for rapid transfer of ions, small and sometimes big molecules.
Assertion true: junctions occur in epithelium and other tissues. Reason false: stopping leakage is the job of tight, not adhering, junctions.
All four are correct per NCERT: tight (stop leakage), adhering (cementing), little intercellular material, and gap (cytoplasmic channels).

nuggets.title: Connective tissue and loose connective tissue
lines: Connective tissues are the most abundant and widely distributed tissues; they link and support other tissues and organs.
