Connective tissue includes cartilage, bone, adipose and blood; in all except blood, cells secrete fibres of collagen or elastin.
Connective tissues are classified into loose, dense and specialised connective tissue.
Areolar tissue (beneath skin) has fibroblasts (fibre-producing cells), macrophages and mast cells; it supports epithelium.
Adipose tissue, a loose connective tissue beneath the skin, stores fats; excess nutrients are converted into fats and stored here.
nuggets.tip: Adipose is LOOSE connective tissue, not specialised.

questions.why: Connective tissue is the most abundant and widely distributed tissue in the animal body.
Areolar tissue contains fibroblasts, macrophages and mast cells; chondroblasts belong to cartilage.
Fibroblasts produce and secrete fibres in connective tissue; macrophages are phagocytic, mast cells secretory.
Areolar tissue is a loose connective tissue; tendon is dense regular, adipose is loose, cartilage is specialised.
Adipose tissue is a type of loose connective tissue located beneath the skin, specialised to store fat.

nuggets.title: Dense connective tissue: tendons, ligaments, skin
lines: In dense connective tissue, fibres and fibroblasts are compactly packed; fibre orientation decides regular or irregular.
In dense regular tissue, collagen fibres lie in rows between many parallel bundles of fibres.
Tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones; ligaments attach one bone to another: both are dense regular tissue.
Dense irregular tissue has fibroblasts and many fibres (mostly collagen) oriented differently; it is present in the skin.
nuggets.tip: Tendon: Muscle to bone (T-M-B). Ligament: bone to bone.

questions.why: Tendons are dense regular tissue, chiefly collagen fibres running in parallel rows (one direction).
Ligaments attach one bone to another; tendons attach muscle to bone.
Both wrong: tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones, and ligaments attach one bone to another.
Dense irregular tissue has many fibres, mostly collagen, oriented differently; parallel fibres mean dense regular.
Both false: ligaments are dense regular tissue, and cartilage is a specialised connective tissue.

nuggets.title: Specialised connective tissue: cartilage, bone, blood
lines: Cartilage, bone and blood are specialised connective tissues.
Cartilage has a solid, pliable intercellular material that resists compression; its cells (chondrocytes) lie in small cavities in the matrix.
Most cartilage of vertebrate embryos is replaced by bone in adults; it persists in the tip of nose, outer ear joints, between adjacent bones of vertebral column, limbs and hands.
Bone has a hard, non-pliable ground substance rich in calcium salts and collagen fibres; bone cells (osteocytes) lie in lacunae.
Bones support and protect soft organs, interact with skeletal muscles for movement, and bone marrow of some bones produces blood cells.
Blood is a fluid connective tissue with plasma, RBCs, WBCs and platelets.
nuggets.tip: Cartilage = pliable; bone = non-pliable. Both have cells in lacunae.

questions.why: Cartilage matrix is solid, pliable and resists compression; bone matrix is non-pliable.
The supporting skeleton of the external ear and nose tip is cartilage, which persists there in adults.
Only ii, iii, iv are right. i is wrong (bone ground substance is non-pliable), v is wrong (bones interact with skeletal, not smooth, muscles).
Both cartilage (chondrocytes) and bone (osteocytes) have cells enclosed in lacunae; only bone matrix is non-pliable.
Mast cells: areolar tissue; bronchiole: ciliated epithelium; blood: specialised CT; nephron tubules: cuboidal. So A-Q, B-P, C-S, D-R.

nuggets.title: Muscle tissue: skeletal, smooth, cardiac
lines: Each muscle is made of long cylindrical fibres containing many fine myofibrils; muscle fibres contract (shorten) and relax in a coordinated way.
Skeletal (striated) muscle is closely attached to skeletal bones; e.g. biceps are striated and voluntary, with fibres bundled in parallel.
Smooth muscle fibres taper at both ends (fusiform), lack striations, are held by cell junctions and are involuntary.
Smooth muscle is found in the walls of internal organs such as blood vessels, stomach and intestine.
Cardiac muscle is contractile tissue found only in the heart; cell junctions fuse adjacent membranes.
Communication junctions (intercalated discs) at some fusion points allow cardiac cells to contract as a unit.
nuggets.tip: Intercalated discs are only in cardiac muscle; smooth muscle has none.

questions.why: Skeletal muscle fibres are cylindrical, striated and multinucleate; spindle-shaped unstriated fibres are smooth muscle.
Smooth muscle fibres are spindle-shaped (fusiform), unbranched, unstriated, uninucleate and involuntary.
Thigh muscles are skeletal: striated and voluntary. Intestine muscle is smooth; heart muscle is striated (cardiac).
Intercalated discs are a feature of cardiac muscle, not smooth muscle; smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary.
Intercalated discs at fusion points let cardiac cells contract as a unit. Cardiac muscle is involuntary and striated.

nuggets.title: Neural tissue
lines: Neural tissue exerts the greatest control over the body's responsiveness to changing conditions.
Neurons, the unit of neural system, are excitable cells.
Neuroglial cells, which make up the rest of the neural system, protect and support neurons.
Neuroglia make up more than one-half the volume of neural tissue in our body.
When a neuron is suitably stimulated, an electrical disturbance travels along its plasma membrane and, at neuron endings, stimulates or inhibits adjacent cells.
nuggets.tip: Neurons excitable; neuroglia support and are more than half the volume.

questions.why: Per NCERT, neural tissue exerts the greatest control over the body's responsiveness to changing conditions.
Neuroglia make up more than one-half the volume of neural tissue in our body.
Both false: neuroglia protect and support neurons (not the reverse), and they form more than half the volume, not a stated 90%.
Wrong: neurons, not nephrons, are the excitable units of the neural system. Nephrons are kidney units.
All four statements match NCERT, so none is false.

nuggets.title: Frog: habitat, habits and body
lines: Frogs live in fresh water and on land; the most common species in India is Rana tigrina.
Frogs are cold-blooded (poikilotherms): body temperature varies with the environment.
In summer and winter they shelter in deep burrows: aestivation (summer sleep) and hibernation (winter sleep).
They can change colour to hide from enemies (camouflage); this protective coloration is called mimicry.
The frog never drinks water but absorbs it through the skin; skin is smooth and slippery due to mucus.
Body is divisible into head and trunk; a neck and tail are absent.

questions.why: The most common Indian frog species is Rana tigrina.
Hibernation is winter sleep; aestivation is summer sleep. Frogs do both in deep burrows.
Frogs are poikilotherms precisely because their body temperature is not constant but varies with the environment.
Only i: the body is divisible into head and trunk; a neck and tail are always absent, not 'sometimes'.
All four are true per NCERT (absorbs water via skin, tympanum beside eyes, limbs for swimming/walking/leaping/burrowing, webbed hindlimb digits).

nuggets.title: Frog: eyes, limbs and sexual dimorphism
lines: Above the mouth are a pair of nostrils; eyes are bulged and covered by a nictitating membrane that protects them in water.
On either side of the eyes a membranous tympanum (ear) receives sound signals.
Hindlimbs end in five digits and are larger and more muscular; forelimbs end in four digits; feet have webbed digits for swimming.
Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimbs, which are absent in females.
nuggets.tip: Hind = 5 digits, fore = 4 digits.

questions.why: The bulged eyes are covered by a transparent nictitating membrane that protects them while in water.
Hindlimbs end in five digits and forelimbs in four digits.
Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimb; the pad is not on the hindlimb.
Only I is wrong: hindlimbs end in five digits and forelimbs in four, not the reverse.

nuggets.title: Frog: digestive system
lines: Frogs are carnivores, so the alimentary canal is short and the intestine is reduced.
Mouth opens into buccal cavity, then pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, intestine, rectum and finally the cloaca.
Food is captured by the bilobed tongue; in the stomach it is digested by HCl and gastric juices.
Liver secretes bile stored in the gall bladder; the duodenum receives bile and pancreatic juice through a common bile duct.
Digested food is absorbed by finger-like folds of the intestine wall called villi and microvilli.

questions.why: Frogs are carnivores, hence their alimentary canal is short and intestine reduced: Reason explains Assertion.
Frogs capture food with their bilobed tongue.
In the frog's stomach, food is digested by HCl and gastric juices secreted from the stomach wall.
The duodenum receives bile from gall bladder and pancreatic juice from pancreas through a common bile duct.
Digested food is absorbed by villi and microvilli of the inner intestine wall, not the stomach or rectum.

nuggets.title: Frog: respiration
lines: Frogs respire on land and in water by two different methods.
In water, the skin acts as the aquatic respiratory organ (cutaneous respiration); dissolved oxygen is exchanged through skin by diffusion.
On land, the buccal cavity, skin and lungs act as respiratory organs; respiration by lungs is pulmonary respiration.
The lungs are a pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper part of the trunk (thorax).
Air enters through nostrils into the buccal cavity and then to lungs; during aestivation and hibernation gas exchange occurs through skin.
nuggets.tip: Skin exchange is by diffusion, not active transport.

questions.why: In water, skin alone acts as the aquatic respiratory organ (cutaneous respiration).
During aestivation and hibernation, gaseous exchange takes place through the skin.
Only I is incorrect: dissolved O2 is exchanged through skin by diffusion, not active transport.
All four are correct: cutaneous + pulmonary respiration, pink lungs in thorax, nostril-buccal cavity-lungs path, skin during aestivation/hibernation.
Frog lungs are a pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper trunk (thorax); on land, skin and buccal cavity also respire.

nuggets.title: Frog: circulatory system
lines: Frogs have a well-developed closed vascular system and a lymphatic system (lymph, lymph channels, lymph nodes).
The heart is a muscular structure with three chambers (two atria, one ventricle), covered by pericardium.
A triangular sinus venosus joins the right atrium and receives blood through the vena cava; the ventricle opens into conus arteriosus on the ventral side.
Special venous connections: hepatic portal system (liver-intestine) and renal portal system (kidney-lower body).
RBCs are nucleated and contain haemoglobin; lymph differs from blood as it lacks a few proteins and RBCs.
nuggets.tip: Frog RBCs are nucleated, unlike human RBCs.

questions.why: The triangular sinus venosus joins the right atrium and receives blood from the vena cava.
The frog's ventricle opens into a sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side of the heart.
Hepatic portal links liver and intestine; renal portal links kidney and lower body, in that order.
Frog RBCs are nucleated, while human RBCs lack a nucleus; both have hepatic portal system, paired cerebral hemispheres, thyroid and parathyroid.
Incorrect: frogs do have a lymphatic system of lymph, lymph channels and lymph nodes.

nuggets.title: Frog: excretory system
lines: Frog excretory system has a pair of kidneys, ureters, cloaca and urinary bladder; kidneys are compact, dark red, bean-like.
Each kidney is made of many structural and functional units called nephrons (uriniferous tubules).
In males, the ureters arise from the kidneys and act as urinogenital ducts; in females ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca.
The thin-walled urinary bladder lies ventral to the rectum, which also opens into the cloaca.
The frog excretes urea, so it is ureotelic.
nuggets.tip: Male frog ureter = urinogenital duct; female = ureter only.

questions.why: Both adult frogs and humans are ureotelic. Frogs have 3-chambered hearts, external fertilisation and nucleated RBCs.
Frog excretory system: pair of kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and cloaca.
Ureters act as urinogenital ducts only in male frogs; in females ureters and oviducts open separately into cloaca.
Male frog cloaca receives the urinogenital duct, urinary bladder and rectum.
The thin-walled urinary bladder lies ventral to the rectum, which also opens into the cloaca.

nuggets.title: Frog: nervous and endocrine control
lines: Control and coordination is highly evolved in frog, with a neural system and endocrine glands.
Endocrine glands include pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads.
Neural system has CNS (brain, spinal cord), PNS (cranial and spinal nerves) and autonomic system; there are ten pairs of cranial nerves.
Forebrain: olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon; midbrain: a pair of optic lobes; hindbrain: cerebellum and medulla oblongata.
Medulla oblongata passes out through the foramen magnum and continues into the spinal cord in the vertebral column.
nuggets.tip: Frog: 10 pairs of cranial nerves (humans 12).

questions.why: Frogs have a highly evolved neural system and endocrine glands for control and coordination.
Only i: parathyroid and pineal body are present, but frogs have ten, not twelve, pairs of cranial nerves.
The frog midbrain has a pair of optic lobes; olfactory lobes are part of the forebrain.
Frog hindbrain consists of cerebellum and medulla oblongata; cerebrum is forebrain.
Touch: sensory papillae; smell: nasal epithelium; cranial nerves: PNS; medulla: exits via foramen magnum. So A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2.

nuggets.title: Frog: sense organs
lines: Sense organs include organs of touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes) and hearing (tympanum with internal ears).
Eyes and internal ears are well-organised structures; the rest are cellular aggregations around nerve endings.
Eyes are a pair of spherical structures in the orbit of the skull; they are simple eyes (one unit).
External ear is absent; only the tympanum is seen externally. The ear is an organ of hearing and balancing (equilibrium).

questions.why: All pairs are correct per NCERT: touch-sensory papillae, smell-nasal epithelium, taste-taste buds, hearing-tympanum with internal ears.
Sensory papillae, taste buds and nasal epithelium are cellular aggregations around nerve endings; eyes and ears are well-organised.
The well-organised sense organs of frog are the eyes and internal ears.
Only II: external ear is absent and the tympanum is seen externally, not internally; the ear serves hearing and balance.
The frog ear is an organ of hearing as well as balancing. Frog eyes are simple, not mosaic; urea is made in liver, not kidney.

nuggets.title: Frog: reproductive system and development
lines: Male: a pair of yellowish ovoid testes attached to the upper part of kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum, the mesorchium.
Vasa efferentia, 10-12 in number, enter the kidneys and open into Bidder's canal, which communicates with the urinogenital duct to the cloaca.
Female: ovaries lie near kidneys with no functional connection to them; a pair of oviducts opens separately into the cloaca.
A mature female lays 2500-3000 ova at a time; fertilisation is external (in water).
Development involves a larval stage, the tadpole, which undergoes metamorphosis to form the adult.
nuggets.tip: Frog: external fertilisation, 2500-3000 eggs, tadpole larva.

questions.why: Vasa efferentia arising from frog testes are 10-12 in number.
Sperm path: testis - vasa efferentia - Bidder's canal (in kidney) - urinogenital duct - cloaca.
False: i and ii. Ovaries lie near (not in) the kidneys and have no functional connection with them.
Both false: a female lays 2500-3000 ova at a time, and fertilisation is external.
Both true: development has a tadpole larval stage, which undergoes metamorphosis into the adult.

nuggets.title: What is a cell: discovery and cell theory
lines: Unicellular organisms are capable of independent existence; anything less than a complete cell does not ensure independent living, so the cell is the fundamental unit of life.
Anton Von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell; Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus.
In 1838 Matthias Schleiden, a German botanist, observed that all plants are composed of different kinds of cells forming tissues.
In 1839 Theodore Schwann, a British zoologist, reported the thin outer layer of animal cells (plasma membrane) and that the cell wall is unique to plant cells.
Schleiden and Schwann together formulated the cell theory, but it did not explain how new cells are formed.
Rudolf Virchow (1855) explained that cells divide and new cells form from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula), giving cell theory its final shape.
nuggets.tip: Schleiden 1838 botanist; Schwann 1839 zoologist; Virchow 1855.

questions.why: A true: Leeuwenhoek first saw a live cell. B false: Robert Brown discovered the nucleus, not the nucleolus.
Schleiden, a German botanist, reported in 1838 that all plants are made of different kinds of cells.
Schwann (1839) reported that animal cells have a thin outer layer, today called the plasma membrane.
Rudolf Virchow (1855) proposed Omnis cellula-e cellula: new cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Schleiden and Schwann's theory could not explain how new cells are formed; Virchow added this later.

nuggets.title: An overview of the cell
lines: Plant cells have a distinct cell wall outside the cell membrane; in animal cells the cell membrane is the outermost structure.
Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus; prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
In both, the semi-fluid cytoplasm is the main arena of cellular activities.
Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, mitochondria, microbodies, vacuoles); prokaryotes lack them.
Plant cells have cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole, absent in animal cells; animal cells have centrioles, absent in almost all plant cells.

questions.why: In prokaryotes there are no membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus, animal cells lack cell walls, and cells never arise de novo.
The cytoplasm is the main arena of cellular activities in both plant and animal cells.
Both wrong: eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles, and prokaryotic cells lack them.
Both wrong: plastids and a large central vacuole are in plant cells; centrioles are in animal cells, absent in almost all plant cells.
Plant cells differ from animal cells in having a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole.

nuggets.title: Cell size and shape
lines: Mycoplasmas, the smallest cells, are only 0.3 µm in length; bacteria are 3 to 5 µm.
The largest isolated single cell is the egg of an ostrich.
Among multicellular organisms, human red blood cells are about 7.0 µm in diameter; nerve cells are some of the longest cells.
Cells may be disc-like, polygonal, columnar, cuboid, thread-like or irregular; shape varies with function.
nuggets.tip: Ascending: Mycoplasma 0.3 µm < bacteria 3-5 µm < RBC 7 µm < ostrich egg.

questions.why: Mycoplasma 0.3 µm, bacteria 3-5 µm, nerve cell among the longest, human RBC 7.0 µm: A-P, B-Q, C-S, D-R.
Incorrect: Mycoplasma is the smallest cell, not the largest; the largest isolated single cell is the ostrich egg.
Ascending order: Mycoplasma (0.3 µm) < bacteria (3-5 µm) < human RBC (7 µm) < ostrich egg.
Round and biconcave describes RBCs, not WBCs (WBCs are amoeboid).
Both true: human RBCs are about 7.0 µm in diameter, and cell shape varies with the function performed.

nuggets.title: Prokaryotic cells
lines: Prokaryotic cells are represented by bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms).
They are generally smaller and multiply more rapidly than eukaryotic cells, and vary greatly in shape and size.
The four basic bacterial shapes are bacillus (rod), coccus (spherical), vibrio (comma) and spirillum (spiral).
Genetic material is basically naked, not enveloped by a nuclear membrane; genomic DNA is a single circular chromosome.
Many bacteria have small circular DNA outside genomic DNA, the plasmids, which confer unique traits such as antibiotic resistance.
Except ribosomes, no organelles like those in eukaryotes are found; a specialised membranous structure, the mesosome, is characteristic.
nuggets.tip: Plasmids are extra; normal metabolism does not depend on them.

questions.why: Prokaryotes: blue-green algae, mycoplasma, PPLO, bacteria, cyanobacteria. Euglenoids and algae are eukaryotes.
Bacillus rod-like, coccus spherical, vibrio comma-shaped, spirillum spiral.
A false: prokaryotic (not eukaryotic) cells are smaller and multiply faster. B true: prokaryotic organisation is fundamentally similar.
A false: prokaryotic DNA is naked, not enclosed by a nuclear membrane. B true: plasmids are small circular DNA outside genomic DNA.
Plasmids give unique phenotypes like antibiotic resistance and are used in genetic engineering, but are not needed for normal metabolism.

nuggets.title: Bacterial cell envelope
lines: Most prokaryotic cells, particularly bacteria, have a chemically complex cell envelope: a tightly bound three-layered structure.
The layers are outermost glycocalyx, then cell wall, then plasma membrane; together they act as a single protective unit.
Bacteria are classified as Gram positive (take up the Gram stain) or Gram negative (do not) based on differences in cell envelope.
Glycocalyx differs among bacteria: a loose sheath is the slime layer, a thick and tough layer is the capsule.
The cell wall determines cell shape and provides strong support to prevent the bacterium from bursting or collapsing.
nuggets.tip: Slime layer = loose; capsule = thick and tough.

questions.why: Bacterial envelope from outside in: glycocalyx, cell wall, plasma membrane.
A true: bacteria have a chemically complex envelope. B false: it is a tightly bound three-layered, not four-layered, structure.
Bacteria that take up the Gram stain are Gram positive; those that do not are Gram negative.
A true: glycocalyx varies among bacteria. B false: a loose sheath is the slime layer; the capsule is thick and tough.
The cell wall gives shape and strong structural support, preventing the bacterium from bursting or collapsing.

nuggets.title: Mesosomes, chromatophores and bacterial appendages
lines: Mesosomes are extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell as vesicles, tubules and lamellae.
Mesosomes help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion, and increase surface area and enzymatic content.
In some prokaryotes like cyanobacteria, membranous extensions into the cytoplasm called chromatophores contain pigments.
Motile bacteria have flagella, made of three parts: filament (longest), hook and basal body.
Pili are elongated tubular structures of a special protein; fimbriae are small bristle-like fibres that help attach bacteria to rocks or host tissues; neither plays a role in motility.
nuggets.tip: Pigment-containing extensions = chromatophores, not mesosomes.

questions.why: A false: pigment-containing extensions in cyanobacteria are chromatophores. B true: mesosomes aid wall formation and DNA replication/distribution.
Chromatophores contain pigments and take part in photosynthesis in cyanobacteria.
Incorrect: the bacterial flagellum has three parts: filament, hook and basal body.
Both wrong (swapped): pili are elongated tubular protein structures; fimbriae are small bristle-like fibres.
Fimbriae help some bacteria attach to rocks in streams and to host tissues.

nuggets.title: Ribosomes and inclusion bodies in prokaryotes
lines: In prokaryotes, ribosomes are associated with the plasma membrane; they are about 15-20 nm and made of two subunits, 50S and 30S, forming 70S.
Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.
Several ribosomes may attach to a single mRNA forming a polysome, which translates the mRNA into proteins.
Reserve material is stored in the cytoplasm as inclusion bodies, not bound by any membrane, e.g. phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules.
Gas vacuoles are found in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.

questions.why: Prokaryotic 70S ribosomes are made of 50S and 30S subunits.
A true: ribosomes are attached to the plasma membrane. B false: several ribosomes attach to a single mRNA, not several mRNAs to one ribosome.
Many ribosomes on one mRNA, making multiple copies of a polypeptide at once, form a polysome (polyribosome).
Both true: reserve material is stored as inclusion bodies, which are not membrane-bound and lie free in the cytoplasm.
Gas vacuoles occur in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.

nuggets.title: Cell membrane: composition
lines: Studies on human RBCs showed the membrane is mainly lipids and proteins; the major lipids are phospholipids arranged in a bilayer.
Lipids are arranged with polar heads towards the outer sides and hydrophobic tails towards the inner part, protecting nonpolar saturated hydrocarbon tails from water.
The membrane also contains cholesterol; biochemical studies showed cell membranes also possess protein and carbohydrate.
Ratio of protein and lipid varies by cell type; human erythrocyte membrane has about 52% protein and 40% lipids.
Based on ease of extraction, membrane proteins are integral (partially or totally buried) or peripheral (on the surface).
nuggets.tip: RBC membrane: proteins 52% > lipids 40%.

questions.why: Human RBC membrane: about 52% proteins and 40% lipids; don't reverse them.
Phospholipids have polar heads facing outward and hydrophobic tails facing inward in the bilayer.
A true: membranes are mainly lipids and proteins. B false: phospholipids form a bilayer, not a monolayer.
A true: proteins are classified by ease of extraction. B false: integral proteins are buried; peripheral ones lie on the surface.
Besides lipids, biochemical investigation revealed cell membranes possess protein and carbohydrate.

nuggets.title: Fluid mosaic model and transport
lines: The widely accepted fluid mosaic model was proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972).
The quasi-fluid nature of lipid enables lateral movement of proteins within the bilayer, measured as its fluidity.
Fluidity is important for cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.
The membrane is selectively permeable; movement without energy is passive transport, and water moves by diffusion called osmosis.
Polar molecules cannot pass through the lipid bilayer and need carrier proteins; transport against the concentration gradient uses energy (active transport, e.g. Na+/K+ pump).
nuggets.tip: Singer and Nicolson, 1972 (not 1927).

questions.why: The quasi-fluid lipid allows lateral movement of proteins within the bilayer.
A false: Singer and Nicolson proposed it in 1972, not 1927. B true: quasi-fluid lipid allows lateral protein movement.
Polar molecules cannot pass through the lipid bilayer and need carrier proteins to cross.
Movement of ions or molecules against the concentration gradient uses ATP: active transport.
Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model. Na+/K+ movement is active; lipids have polar heads outward.

nuggets.title: Cell wall
lines: The cell wall is a non-living rigid structure covering the plasma membrane of fungi and plants; it gives shape and protects from mechanical damage and infection.
Algal cell wall is made of cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals like calcium carbonate; other plants have cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins.
The wall of a young plant cell, the primary wall, can grow; it diminishes as the cell matures and the secondary wall forms on the inner (membrane) side.
The middle lamella, mainly calcium pectate, holds or glues neighbouring cells together.
Cell wall and middle lamellae may be traversed by plasmodesmata, connecting the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.
nuggets.tip: Calcium pectate = middle lamella.

questions.why: Cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals like CaCO3 form the cell wall of algae.
Both wrong: animals have no cell wall (fungi and plants do), and the growing wall of a young cell is the primary wall.
Both true: the middle lamella is mainly calcium pectate, and plasmodesmata traverse wall and middle lamella.
The secondary wall is laid on the inner side (towards the membrane) as the cell matures.
Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic connections between adjacent plant cells through the wall.

nuggets.title: Endomembrane system
lines: Membranous organelles are distinct in structure and function, but ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles form the endomembrane system because their functions are coordinated.
Mitochondria, chloroplast and peroxisomes are not part of the endomembrane system, as their functions are not coordinated with these.
Ribosomes are non-membranous and are not part of the endomembrane system.
Membrane-bound organelles give eukaryotic cells an extensive compartmentalisation of cytoplasm, which prokaryotes lack.

questions.why: The endomembrane system includes ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles; mitochondria and ribosomes are excluded.
Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not part of the endomembrane system.
ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles are grouped as one system because their functions are coordinated: Reason explains Assertion.
A false: the fourth member is vacuoles, not ribosomes. B true: mitochondria, chloroplast, peroxisomes are excluded.
Peroxisomes are not part of the endomembrane system; Golgi, vacuoles and lysosomes are.

nuggets.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
lines: Electron microscopy shows the ER as a network of tiny tubular structures scattered in the cytoplasm.
ER divides the intracellular space into two compartments: luminal (inside ER) and extra-luminal (cytoplasm).
ER with ribosomes on its outer surface is rough ER (RER); it is frequent in cells active in protein synthesis and secretion and is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane.
ER without ribosomes is smooth ER (SER), the major site of lipid synthesis; in animal cells lipid-like steroidal hormones are made in SER.
nuggets.tip: RER = proteins; SER = lipids and steroids.

questions.why: The ER divides the intracellular space into two compartments: luminal and extra-luminal.
Luminal = inside the ER; extra-luminal = cytoplasm.
Cells active in protein synthesis and secretion have extensive RER, so more RER than SER.
Both wrong: ER with ribosomes is RER, and RER (not SER) is the site of protein synthesis and secretion.
SER is the major site for synthesis of lipids; RER makes proteins.

nuggets.title: Golgi apparatus
lines: Camillo Golgi (1898) first observed densely stained reticular structures near the nucleus, later named Golgi bodies.
They consist of flat, disc-shaped sacs or cisternae of 0.5-1.0 µm diameter, stacked parallel and concentrically arranged near the nucleus.
The cis (forming) face is convex and the trans (maturing) face is concave; the two faces are different but interconnected.
Golgi mainly performs packaging; vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face and move to the trans face, for intracellular targets or secretion.
Golgi apparatus is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids.
nuggets.tip: Cis = convex = forming; trans = concave = maturing.

questions.why: Golgi bodies were first observed by Camillo Golgi in 1898.
Golgi cisternae are flat, disc-shaped sacs stacked parallel to each other.
Cis face is convex (forming); trans face is concave (maturing).
Vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face of the Golgi; materials leave from the trans face.
Golgi is the site of formation of glycoproteins (and glycolipids); RER makes proteins, not glycoproteins.

nuggets.title: Lysosomes, vacuoles and microbodies
lines: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles formed by packaging in the Golgi apparatus, rich in hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases).
Lysosomal enzymes are optimally active at acidic pH and can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
The vacuole is a membrane-bound space bounded by a single membrane, the tonoplast; it contains water, sap, excretory product and materials not useful to the cell.
In plant cells vacuoles can occupy up to 90% of cell volume; the tonoplast transports ions against concentration gradient into the vacuole.
In Amoeba, the contractile vacuole is important for osmoregulation and excretion; in protists, food vacuoles form by engulfing food.
Microbodies are many membrane-bound minute vesicles containing various enzymes, present in both plant and animal cells.
nuggets.tip: Lysosomes come from Golgi, not ER.

questions.why: Incorrect: lysosomes are formed by packaging in the Golgi apparatus, not the ER. They are membrane-bound with acid-active hydrolases.
A true: lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes. B false: these enzymes are active at acidic pH.
The tonoplast moves ions against the concentration gradient, so their concentration is higher in the vacuole than in cytoplasm.
In Amoeba the contractile vacuole performs excretion and osmoregulation.
A false: plant vacuoles can occupy up to 90% of the cell volume. B true: contractile vacuole does osmoregulation and excretion.

nuggets.title: Mitochondria
lines: Mitochondria are not easily visible unless specifically stained; their number per cell varies with physiological activity.
Each is sausage-shaped or cylindrical, 0.2-1.0 µm (average 0.5 µm) in diameter and 1.0-4.1 µm long.
It is double membrane-bound; the inner membrane forms infoldings called cristae towards the matrix, increasing surface area; the two membranes have their own specific enzymes.
Mitochondria are sites of aerobic respiration and produce ATP, hence called power houses of the cell.
The matrix has a single circular DNA, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes and components for protein synthesis; mitochondria divide by fission.
nuggets.tip: Cristae = infoldings of inner membrane; matrix = inner compartment.

questions.why: Mitochondrion: diameter 0.2-1.0 µm, length 1.0-4.1 µm.
Incorrect: electron transport enzymes are in the inner membrane (cristae), not the outer one.
A true: number depends on physiological activity. B false: the inner compartment is the matrix; cristae are infoldings.
The matrix contains a single circular DNA, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes and protein-synthesis components.
Mitochondria divide by fission.

nuggets.title: Plastids
lines: Plastids are found in all plant cells and in euglenoids; they bear specific pigments and are classified by pigment type into chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments that trap light energy for photosynthesis.
Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments like carotene and xanthophylls, giving yellow, orange or red colour.
Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids: amyloplasts store starch, elaioplasts oils and fats, aleuroplasts proteins.
Chlamydomonas has a single chloroplast per cell, while a mesophyll cell has 20-40 chloroplasts.
nuggets.tip: Amylo = starch, Elaio = oil, Aleuro = protein.

questions.why: Aleuroplasts store proteins, not carotene; carotenoids are in chromoplasts and chloroplasts.
Amyloplast: carbohydrate (starch); elaioplast: oils/fats; aleuroplast: proteins; thylakoids: flattened sacs. A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q.
Carotenoid pigments of chromoplasts are fat soluble.
Both true: Chlamydomonas has a single chloroplast; a mesophyll cell has 20-40.
A false: plastids are in all plant cells and euglenoids, not animals. B true: chloroplasts have chlorophyll and carotenoids.

nuggets.title: Chloroplast structure
lines: Chloroplasts are mainly in mesophyll cells of leaves; they are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, 5-10 µm long and 2-4 µm wide.
They are double membrane-bound; the inner membrane is relatively less permeable.
The space inside the inner membrane is the stroma, containing flattened sacs called thylakoids; thylakoids stack like piles of coins to form grana.
Flat membranous tubules called stroma lamellae connect thylakoids of different grana; the thylakoid membrane encloses a space called the lumen.
Stroma has enzymes for synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins, small double-stranded circular DNA and 70S ribosomes; chlorophyll is in the thylakoids.
nuggets.tip: Chloroplast ribosomes (70S) are smaller than cytoplasmic (80S).

questions.why: Both true: thylakoids stack like piles of coins to form grana, and the thylakoid membrane encloses the lumen.
Of the two chloroplast membranes, the inner one is relatively less permeable.
Chloroplasts are 5-10 µm long and 2-4 µm wide.
The stroma contains enzymes for the synthesis of both carbohydrates and proteins.
Chloroplast DNA is small, double-stranded and circular, like bacterial DNA.

nuggets.title: Ribosomes
lines: Ribosomes are granular structures first observed under the electron microscope by George Palade (1953).
They are composed of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and proteins and are not surrounded by any membrane.
Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S subunits); prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S).
'S' (Svedberg unit) is the sedimentation coefficient, an indirect measure of density and size.
nuggets.tip: 80S = 60S + 40S; 70S = 50S + 30S (S values are not additive).

questions.why: Ribosomes were first observed by George Palade in 1953.
Ribosomes are made of RNA and proteins; they have no DNA or membrane.
60S + 40S subunits form the eukaryotic 80S ribosome.
Eukaryotic ribosomes 80S, cytoskeleton = filamentous proteins, prokaryotic ribosomes 70S, sedimentation coefficient = Svedberg unit.
Ribosomes are made of RNA and proteins; prokaryotic ones are 70S and they occur in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

nuggets.title: Cytoskeleton, cilia and flagella
lines: The cytoskeleton is an elaborate network of filamentous proteinaceous structures (microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments) in the cytoplasm.
Cytoskeleton functions in mechanical support, motility and maintenance of cell shape.
Cilia are small structures that work like oars, moving the cell or the surrounding fluid; flagella are comparatively longer and responsible for cell movement.
Cilia and flagella are covered with plasma membrane; their core, the axoneme, has nine pairs of peripheral doublets and a pair of central microtubules: the 9+2 array.
Both emerge from centriole-like basal bodies; prokaryotic flagella are structurally different from eukaryotic ones.
nuggets.tip: Cilia short (oars); flagella long (cell movement).

questions.why: The network of filamentous proteins maintaining cell shape is the cytoskeleton.
The cytoskeleton is involved in motility, mechanical support and maintenance of cell shape.
The axoneme has nine peripheral doublets and two central microtubules, which is exactly the 9+2 array: Reason explains Assertion.
Cilia and flagella are covered with plasma membrane; their core is the axoneme.
Both wrong (swapped): cilia are small and work like oars; flagella are longer and move the cell.

nuggets.title: Centrosome and centrioles
lines: Centrosome usually contains two cylindrical centrioles, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar materials.
The two centrioles lie perpendicular to each other, each organised like a cartwheel.
Each centriole has nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin; each fibril is a triplet and adjacent triplets are linked.
The central proteinaceous part of the proximal region is the hub, connected to peripheral triplets by radial spokes.
Centrioles form the basal body of cilia or flagella and the spindle fibres of the spindle apparatus in animal cells.
nuggets.tip: Centriole = 9 triplets (9+0); axoneme = 9 doublets + 2 (9+2).

questions.why: Both true: each peripheral fibril of a centriole is a triplet, and adjacent triplets are linked.
The two centrioles lie perpendicular to each other, each with a cartwheel organisation.
The central part of the proximal region of the centriole is the hub.
The centrosome is surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar materials.
False: the hub is proteinaceous, not nucleic acid. Centrioles lie perpendicular, cartwheel-like, two per centrosome.

nuggets.title: Nucleus
lines: Nucleus was first described by Robert Brown (1831); the material stained by basic dyes was named chromatin by Flemming.
The interphase nucleus has chromatin, nuclear matrix and one or more nucleoli.
The nuclear envelope has two parallel membranes with a perinuclear space of 10-50 nm; the outer membrane is continuous with ER and bears ribosomes.
At places the two membranes fuse to form nuclear pores, through which RNA and protein molecules move in both directions.
Normally there is one nucleus per cell; mature RBCs of many mammals and sieve tube cells of vascular plants lack a nucleus.

questions.why: Both true: Flemming named chromatin (stained by basic dyes), and Robert Brown described the nucleus in 1831.
Both true: a non-dividing nucleus is the interphase nucleus, and the perinuclear space is 10-50 nm.
Nuclear pores allow movement of RNA and protein molecules in both directions between nucleus and cytoplasm.
The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes.
Nucleus is absent in RBCs of many mammals, sieve tube cells of vascular plants and prokaryotic cells: all of these.

nuggets.title: Nucleolus, chromatin and chromosomes
lines: The nucleolus is a spherical structure in the nucleoplasm, not membrane-bound; it is the site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis, larger in cells active in protein synthesis.
Chromatin contains DNA and basic proteins called histones, some non-histone proteins and RNA; a single human cell has about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes.
Every chromosome has a primary constriction, the centromere, bearing disc-shaped kinetochores on its sides.
Based on centromere position: metacentric (middle, equal arms), submetacentric (slightly away), acrocentric (close to end, one very short arm), telocentric (terminal).
Some chromosomes have non-staining secondary constrictions at a constant location, giving a small fragment called the satellite.
nuggets.tip: Kinetochore = disc on centromere; satellite = beyond secondary constriction.

questions.why: The nucleolus is a site of active rRNA synthesis; it is not membrane-bound and is unrelated to spindle formation.
A single human cell has about 2 metres of DNA distributed among its 46 chromosomes.
Acrocentric: one very short, one very long arm; metacentric: equal arms; telocentric: terminal; submetacentric: unequal. A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q.
Disc-shaped structures on the sides of the centromere are kinetochores.
A non-staining secondary constriction gives a small fragment called the satellite.

nuggets.title: Chemical analysis and elemental composition
lines: Living tissue is ground in trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH) and filtered to get an acid-soluble filtrate and an acid-insoluble retentate.
All carbon compounds obtained from living tissues are called biomolecules.
When tissue is fully burnt, carbon compounds are oxidised to gaseous CO2 and water vapour; the remaining ash contains inorganic elements (Ca, Mg, etc.).
All elements of the earth's crust are present in living tissue, but per unit mass living organisms have far more carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
In the human body, oxygen is 65%, carbon 18.5%, hydrogen 9.5% and nitrogen 3.3%; in the earth's crust carbon is only 0.03% and hydrogen 0.14%.
nuggets.tip: Oxygen tops both earth's crust (46.6%) and human body (65%).

questions.why: Tissue is ground in trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH) to separate acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions.
Ash is the material left after burning tissue; it contains inorganic elements, while carbon compounds escape as CO2 and water vapour.
Earth's crust: hydrogen 0.14%, carbon 0.03%, oxygen 46.6%, nitrogen very little. So A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q.
Oxygen has the highest weight percentage in both earth's crust (46.6%) and human body (65%).
Human body by weight: O (65%) > C (18.5%) > H (9.5%) > N (3.3%).

nuggets.title: Amino acids
lines: Amino acids are organic compounds with an amino group and an acidic group on the same carbon, the α-carbon; hence called α-amino acids.
They are substituted methanes: the four valencies are occupied by hydrogen, carboxyl group, amino group and a variable R group.
Based on R group there are many amino acids, but only twenty types occur in proteins: R is hydrogen in glycine, methyl in alanine, hydroxy methyl in serine.
By number of amino and carboxyl groups they are acidic (glutamic acid), basic (lysine) and neutral (valine); aromatic ones are tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan.
Due to ionisable -NH2 and -COOH groups, amino acid structure changes with pH; the form with both charges is the zwitterionic form.
nuggets.tip: Substituted METHANES, not ethanes.

questions.why: Amino acids are substituted methanes with H, -COOH, -NH2 and an R group on the four valencies.
R group is hydrogen in glycine and methyl in alanine; hydroxy methyl gives serine.
Glutamic acid acidic, lysine basic, valine neutral, tryptophan aromatic: A-Q, B-P, C-S, D-R.
Aromatic amino acids per NCERT: tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan.
A form carrying both positive and negative charges at the same time is the zwitterionic form.

nuggets.title: Lipids and fatty acids
lines: Lipids are generally water insoluble; they may be simple fatty acids, with a carboxyl group attached to an R group (methyl, ethyl or higher -CH2 groups).
Palmitic acid has 16 carbons and arachidonic acid 20 carbons, each including the carboxyl carbon.
Saturated fatty acids lack double bonds; unsaturated ones have one or more C=C double bonds.
Glycerol is trihydroxy propane; fatty acids esterified with glycerol form mono-, di- and triglycerides, i.e. fats and oils.
Oils have a lower melting point (e.g. gingelly oil) and stay liquid in winters.
Lipids with phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound are phospholipids, e.g. lecithin in cell membranes; neural tissues have lipids with more complex structures.
nuggets.tip: Count INCLUDES carboxyl carbon: palmitic 16, arachidonic 20.

questions.why: Both false: arachidonic acid has 20 carbons including the carboxyl carbon, and it is unsaturated.
Lipids: water insoluble; arachidonic: unsaturated; saturated: no double bond; palmitic: saturated. A-Q, B-P, C-S, D-R.
Oils have a lower melting point, so they remain liquid in winters.
Lecithin is a phospholipid found in the cell membrane.
Correct: b (lecithin is a phospholipid) and c (glycerol is trihydroxy propane). Single bonds = saturated; palmitic has 16 C, arachidonic 20 C.

nuggets.title: Nitrogen bases, nucleosides and nucleotides
lines: Living organisms have heterocyclic compounds as nitrogen bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil and thymine.
Adenine and guanine are substituted purines; cytosine, uracil and thymine are substituted pyrimidines; thymine is also called 5-methyl uracil.
A nitrogen base attached to a sugar is a nucleoside (adenosine, guanosine, thymidine, uridine, cytidine).
If a phosphate is also esterified to the sugar, it is a nucleotide (adenylic acid, thymidylic acid, guanylic acid, uridylic acid, cytidylic acid).
Nucleic acids like DNA and RNA consist of nucleotides only; they function as genetic material.
nuggets.tip: -osine/-idine = nucleoside; -ylic acid = nucleotide.

questions.why: Adenine, guanine: nitrogen bases; uridine, cytidine: nucleosides; guanylic, uridylic acid: nucleotides; DNA, RNA: nucleic acids.
Adenylic, uridylic and cytidylic acids are nucleotides; uridine is a nucleoside.
A true: base + sugar = nucleoside. B false: adenylic acid is a nucleotide (it has phosphate).
Thymine, the base found only in DNA, is also called 5-methyl uracil.
A true: polynucleotide sugar is ribose or deoxyribose. B false (swapped): deoxyribose is in DNA, ribose in RNA.

nuggets.title: Primary and secondary metabolites
lines: In animal tissues, compounds like amino acids, sugars and fats are primary metabolites, with identifiable functions in normal physiology.
Plant, fungal and microbial cells also make secondary metabolites: alkaloids, flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics, pigments, scents, gums and spices.
Examples: pigments (carotenoids, anthocyanins), alkaloids (morphine, codeine), terpenoids (monoterpenes, diterpenes), essential oils (lemon grass oil).
Toxins (abrin, ricin), lectins (concanavalin A), drugs (vinblastin, curcumin), polymeric substances (rubber, gums, cellulose).
Many secondary metabolites are useful to humans, though their roles in the host are not all known.
nuggets.tip: Abrin and ricin = toxins; concanavalin A = lectin.

questions.why: Pigment: anthocyanins; alkaloid: codeine; terpenoid: diterpenes; essential oil: lemon grass oil. A-R, B-S, C-Q, D-P.
Toxin: ricin; drug: curcumin; polymeric substance: rubber; lectin: concanavalin A. A-P, B-R, C-S, D-Q.
Ricin is a toxin, not a drug; drugs are vinblastin and curcumin.
Abrin and ricin are toxins; the lectin example is concanavalin A.
Amino acids and glucose are primary metabolites; morphine, vinblastin, curcumin, rubber and gums are secondary.

nuggets.title: Acid-soluble pool and biomacromolecules
lines: The acid-soluble pool has compounds of molecular weight 18 to around 800 daltons, and roughly represents the cytoplasmic composition.
The acid-insoluble fraction has four types of organic compounds: proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids.
Except lipids, these have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above; these are biomacromolecules, while those below one thousand daltons are micromolecules.
Lipids (molecular weight not above 800 Da) appear in the acid-insoluble fraction because broken membranes form vesicles that are not water soluble; lipids are not strictly macromolecules.
Macromolecules from cytoplasm and organelles form the acid-insoluble fraction; together both fractions represent the cellular pool.
nuggets.tip: Lipids: small molecules, yet in the acid-insoluble fraction.

questions.why: Both false: lipids go to the acid-insoluble fraction, and their molecular weight does not exceed 800 Da.
Membranes break into pieces forming vesicles that are not water soluble, so lipids land in the acid-insoluble fraction.
Cytoplasmic composition: acid-soluble pool; macromolecules and organelles: acid-insoluble; lipids: not strictly macromolecules.
Acid-insoluble compounds (except lipids) have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above.
Both true: the acid-soluble pool roughly represents cytoplasmic composition; macromolecules form the acid-insoluble fraction.

nuggets.title: Average composition of cells
lines: Water is the most abundant chemical in living organisms (70-90% of total cellular mass).
Proteins form 10-15%, nucleic acids 5-7%, carbohydrates 3%, lipids 2% and ions 1% of cellular mass.
Biomacromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides) are polymers; proteins are heteropolymers of amino acids.
Lipids are not strictly macromolecules (molecular weight does not exceed 800 Da) but appear in the acid-insoluble fraction because they form membranes and vesicles.

questions.why: Nucleic acids 5-7%, carbohydrates 3%, proteins 10-15%, lipids 2%: A-Q, B-R, C-S, D-P.
Order: water (70-90) > proteins (10-15) > nucleic acids (5-7) > carbohydrates (3) > lipids (2).
Only correct match: nucleic acids 5-7%. Water is 70-90%, proteins 10-15%, carbohydrates 3%.
Proteins are macromolecules (heteropolymers of amino acids) found in the acid-insoluble pool, not micromolecules.
Both true: below 1000 Da are micromolecules; acid-insoluble ones are biomacromolecules.

nuggets.title: Proteins and their functions
lines: Proteins are polypeptides: linear chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; each protein is a heteropolymer.
Essential amino acids must be supplied through diet (dietary proteins); non-essential ones our body can make.
Proteins transport nutrients across membranes, fight infections, act as hormones and enzymes.
Collagen: intercellular ground substance; trypsin: enzyme; insulin: hormone; antibody: fights infectious agents; GLUT-4: glucose transport into cells.
Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.
nuggets.tip: RuBisCO = biosphere; collagen = animal world.

questions.why: Collagen: intercellular ground substance; trypsin: enzyme; insulin: hormone; antibody: fights infectious agents.
GLUT-4 enables glucose transport into cells; insulin hormone; trypsin enzyme; collagen ground substance.
RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere; collagen in the animal world.
A true. B false: essential amino acids cannot be made by our body and must come from diet.
A true: a protein is a polymer of amino acids. B false: it is a heteropolymer (about 20 kinds of amino acids).

nuggets.title: Polysaccharides
lines: Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose; inulin is a polymer of fructose.
In a polysaccharide chain like glycogen, the right end is the reducing end and the left end the non-reducing end; glycogen is stored in animals.
Starch forms helical secondary structures that hold I2, giving a blue colour.
Cellulose lacks complex helices, cannot hold I2, and gives no colour; plant cell walls and cotton fibre are cellulose.
Complex polysaccharides have amino-sugars and modified sugars (glucosamine, N-acetyl galactosamine) as building blocks; arthropod exoskeleton has chitin.
nuggets.tip: Starch + iodine = blue; cellulose + iodine = no colour.

questions.why: A false: cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose. B true: inulin is a polymer of fructose.
A true: starch holds I2 in its helical portion. B false: the starch-I2 complex is blue, not red.
Cellulose lacks complex helices, so it cannot hold iodine and gives no blue colour.
Glycogen is the storage form of glucose in animals; plants store starch.
Arthropod exoskeleton is chitin, a complex polysaccharide polymer of the amino-sugar N-acetyl glucosamine.

nuggets.title: Structure of proteins
lines: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids (positional information); the left end is the first, N-terminal, amino acid and the right end the last, C-terminal.
A protein thread is not an extended rigid rod; only some portions form a helix (secondary structure), and in proteins only right-handed helices are seen.
The long chain also folds upon itself like a hollow woollen ball: the tertiary structure, absolutely necessary for many biological activities of proteins.
Some proteins are assemblies of more than one polypeptide: quaternary structure; adult human haemoglobin has 4 subunits (two α and two β).
nuggets.tip: Left = N-terminal (first); right = C-terminal (last).

questions.why: A false: the left end is the first amino acid (N-terminal) and the right end the last (C-terminal). B true: Hb has 2α + 2β.
Only right-handed helices are observed in proteins. The first amino acid is N-terminal, and quaternary structures need not be two subunits.
Only B: a protein thread does not exist throughout as a rigid rod; only some portions are helical.
Folding like a hollow woollen ball gives the tertiary structure.
A true: an assembly of polypeptides is quaternary structure. B false: adult Hb has 4 subunits, not 6.

nuggets.title: Enzymes: nature and active site
lines: Almost all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids behave like enzymes and are called ribozymes.
An enzyme, like any protein, has primary to tertiary structure; in the tertiary structure the backbone folds to form crevices or pockets called the active site.
Inorganic catalysts work efficiently at high temperatures and pressures, while enzymes get damaged at high temperatures (above 40°C).
Enzymes from organisms living in hot vents and sulphur springs are stable and retain catalytic power up to 80°-90°C; thermal stability is valued in such thermophiles.

questions.why: The crevice or pocket (active site) is formed in the tertiary structure of the enzyme protein.
A true. B false (swapped): inorganic catalysts work at high temperature and pressure; enzymes are damaged above 40°C.
Enzymes from thermophiles in hot vents and sulphur springs stay active at 80°-90°C.
A true: nucleic acids acting like enzymes are ribozymes. B false: ribozymes are RNA, not DNA.
Ribozyme is a non-proteinaceous (RNA) enzyme; ligase, DNase and lysozyme are proteins.

nuggets.title: Chemical reactions and their rates
lines: A physical change is a change in shape (or state) without breaking bonds, e.g. ice melting; a chemical reaction breaks bonds and forms new ones, e.g. hydrolysis of starch into glucose.
Rate of a physical or chemical process is the amount of product formed per unit time.
Rate doubles or decreases by half for every 10°C change in either direction.
Without enzyme, about 200 molecules of H2CO3 form per hour; with carbonic anhydrase in the cytoplasm, about 600,000 molecules every second.
Glucose to pyruvic acid needs ten enzyme-catalysed reactions; under anaerobic conditions pyruvate forms lactic acid in skeletal muscle and ethanol in yeast.
nuggets.tip: Carbonic anhydrase: ~10 million-fold faster.

questions.why: Both true: change in shape without breaking bonds is physical; breaking and forming bonds is a chemical reaction.
Both false (swapped): ice melting is a physical change; hydrolysis of starch into glucose is a chemical reaction.
Rate of reaction doubles or halves for every 10°C change.
With carbonic anhydrase, about 600,000 H2CO3 molecules form every second.
Anaerobically, skeletal muscle forms lactic acid; yeast fermentation forms ethanol.

nuggets.title: How enzymes speed up reactions
lines: The substrate binds the enzyme's active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex (ES); this complex is short-lived.
While bound, a new structure of the substrate called the transition state forms; many altered unstable states exist between substrate and product.
The difference in average energy of substrate and transition state is the activation energy; enzymes bring this energy barrier down.
If product P is at a lower energy level than substrate S, the reaction is exothermic and needs no external energy to form product.

questions.why: The transition state formed during enzyme action is transient and unstable.
The new substrate structure while bound is the transition state, formed for a transient period.
Activation energy = energy of transition state minus energy of substrate.
When P lies lower than S, energy is released: an exothermic reaction.
Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy barrier.

nuggets.title: Nature of enzyme action: the catalytic cycle
lines: Substrate S must diffuse towards the active site; formation of the ES complex is obligatory.
Step 1: the substrate binds to the active site, fitting into it.
Step 2: binding induces the enzyme to alter its shape, fitting more tightly around the substrate.
Step 3: the active site breaks the chemical bonds of the substrate, forming the enzyme-product complex.
Step 4: the enzyme releases products and the free enzyme is ready for another substrate: E + S → ES → EP → E + P.
nuggets.tip: The enzyme comes out unchanged.

questions.why: Order: substrate binds active site (4) → enzyme changes shape (1) → substrate bonds broken (2) → products released (3).
Sequence: substrate binding (V) → ES complex (I) → substrate bonds broken (IV) → products released (III) → free enzyme (II).
The substrate diffuses towards the active site, and ES complex formation is obligatory.
Correct: a and c. The active site breaks bonds of the substrate, not of the product.

nuggets.title: Factors affecting enzyme activity
lines: Enzyme activity is affected by conditions that alter the protein's tertiary structure: temperature, pH, substrate concentration and specific chemicals.
Each enzyme shows highest activity at an optimum temperature and optimum pH; activity declines above and below the optimum.
Low temperature keeps the enzyme temporarily inactive, while high temperature destroys activity because proteins are denatured by heat.
Velocity rises with substrate concentration and reaches a maximum, Vmax, beyond which it does not rise further, as all enzyme molecules are saturated.

questions.why: Both false: activity is highest (not lowest) at the optimum temperature, and it declines above and below it.
Low temperature preserves the enzyme in a temporarily inactive state; high temperature denatures it.
Both true: low temperature inactivates temporarily, heat denatures; a substrate-like inhibitor is a competitive inhibitor.
Velocity rises with substrate concentration until Vmax, then does not increase further.
Both true: conditions altering the tertiary structure (temperature, pH, substrate, specific chemicals) affect enzyme activity.

nuggets.title: Enzyme inhibition
lines: When binding of a chemical shuts off enzyme activity, the process is inhibition and the chemical an inhibitor.
An inhibitor closely resembling the substrate in molecular structure is a competitive inhibitor; it competes with the substrate for the active site.
Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it closely resembles the substrate succinate.
Competitive inhibitors are often used in the control of bacterial pathogens.
nuggets.tip: Malonate mimics succinate.

questions.why: Malonate resembles succinate and competitively inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.
A true. B false: an inhibitor resembling the substrate is a competitive, not non-competitive, inhibitor.
A false: malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase competitively. B true: competitive inhibitors help control bacterial pathogens.
Competitive inhibitors are often used in the control of bacterial pathogens.
Not correct: adding plenty of substrate (succinate) can reverse competitive inhibition by malonate, since both compete for the active site.

nuggets.title: Classification and nomenclature of enzymes
lines: Enzymes are divided into 6 classes, each with 4-13 subclasses, and named by a four-digit number.
Oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases catalyse oxidoreduction between two substrates; transferases transfer a group (other than hydrogen) between substrates.
Hydrolases hydrolyse ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C-C, C-halide or P-N bonds.
Lyases remove groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.
Isomerases inter-convert optical, geometric or positional isomers; ligases link two compounds, e.g. joining C-O, C-S, C-N, P-O bonds.
nuggets.tip: Ligase links; lyase removes (non-hydrolytically).

questions.why: A true: 6 classes, each with 4-13 subclasses. B false: each enzyme is named by a four-digit number.
Oxidoreductases: oxidoreduction; transferases: group transfer; hydrolases: hydrolysis; isomerases: isomer interconversion; ligases: linking.
Glucose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate is an inter-conversion of isomers: an isomerase.
Removal of groups by non-hydrolytic means, leaving double bonds, is done by lyases.
A true: oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases. B false: enzymes linking two compounds are ligases, not lyases.

nuggets.title: Co-factors
lines: Many enzymes have non-protein constituents, co-factors, bound to them; the protein portion is the apoenzyme.
Three kinds of co-factors: prosthetic groups, co-enzymes and metal ions.
Prosthetic groups are organic compounds tightly bound to the apoenzyme, e.g. haem in peroxidase and catalase, part of the active site.
Co-enzymes are organic compounds with only transient association; many contain vitamins, e.g. NAD and NADP contain niacin.
Metal ions form coordination bonds with the active site and substrate, e.g. zinc for carboxypeptidase; removing the co-factor makes the enzyme lose catalytic activity.
nuggets.tip: Haem: peroxidase and catalase; Zn: carboxypeptidase; niacin: NAD/NADP.

questions.why: Statement 1 true (tightly bound = prosthetic group). Statement 2 false: the complete active enzyme is the holoenzyme, not apoenzyme.
Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + co-enzyme (or other co-factor).
Haem is the prosthetic group of peroxidase and catalase and forms part of the active site.
Co-enzymes NAD and NADP contain the vitamin niacin.
Zinc is the metal-ion co-factor of the proteolytic enzyme carboxypeptidase.

nuggets.title: Cell cycle: definition and duration
lines: The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two daughter cells.
Cell growth (increase in cytoplasm) is a continuous process, but DNA synthesis occurs only during one specific stage of the cycle.
A typical human cell in culture divides about once every 24 hours, whereas yeast completes its cell cycle in only about 90 minutes.
The cell cycle has two basic phases: interphase (between two successive M phases) and the M phase (mitosis phase, when actual division occurs).
Of the 24-hour human cell cycle, M phase lasts only about an hour; interphase occupies more than 95% of the duration.
M phase begins with nuclear division, karyokinesis, and usually ends with division of cytoplasm, cytokinesis.
nuggets.tip: Numbers to lock in: human cell 24 h, yeast 90 min, interphase >95%, M phase about 1 h.

questions.why: 24 hrs, 90 min. NCERT: a typical human cell in culture divides roughly every 24 hours, while yeast completes the cycle in about 90 minutes. The reversed option is the trap.
95%. Interphase lasts more than 95% of the human cell cycle; M phase (actual division) lasts only about an hour of the 24 hours.
I and II. M phase is actual division and interphase lies between two M phases; M phase lasts only about an hour. III is wrong: it is interphase, not M phase, that takes over 95%.
A-S, B-Q, C-P, D-R: eukaryotic (human) cycle 24 h, yeast 90 min, M phase is actual cell division, interphase is the phase between two successive M phases.
E-C-A-D-B: G1 → S → G2 (interphase), then M phase, which starts with karyokinesis and usually ends with cytokinesis.

nuggets.title: Interphase: G1, S and G2
lines: Interphase, though called the resting phase, is the time when the cell prepares for division by both cell growth and DNA replication.
G1 phase is the interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication; the cell is metabolically active and grows but does not replicate DNA.
In S phase DNA replicates and its amount per cell doubles (2C → 4C), but the chromosome number does not increase (2n stays 2n).
In animal cells, DNA replication begins in the nucleus during S phase, while the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.
During G2 phase, proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis while cell growth continues.
nuggets.tip: S phase doubles DNA, not chromosome number: a 2n = 8 cell still has 8 chromosomes after S.

questions.why: 8. In S phase DNA content doubles (2C → 4C) but the number of chromosomes stays the same; each chromosome now has two chromatids. 16 is the trap.
S phase. NCERT: in animal cells, during S phase DNA replication begins in the nucleus and the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.
Statement A is wrong: DNA replication begins in the nucleus, not the nucleolus. Statement B is correct: the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm during S phase.
All except iv are correct. S phase lies between G1 and G2, DNA doubles 2C → 4C and centrioles replicate, but the chromosome number does not double.
A-S, B-P, C-Q, D-R: S = DNA replication; G2 = proteins synthesised for mitosis; quiescent stage (G0) = inactive; G1 = interval between mitosis and start of DNA replication.

nuggets.title: G0 phase and which cells divide by mitosis
lines: Some cells in adult animals do not appear to divide (e.g. heart cells), and many others divide only occasionally to replace lost or dead cells.
Cells that do not divide further exit G1 and enter an inactive stage called the quiescent stage (G0) of the cell cycle.
Cells in G0 remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called on to do so depending on the requirement of the organism.
In animals, mitotic division is seen only in diploid somatic cells; in plants, mitosis can occur in both haploid and diploid cells.
Mitosis is usually restricted to diploid cells, but in some lower plants and some social insects haploid cells also divide by mitosis.
nuggets.tip: G0 is called an 'inactive' stage, yet its cells are metabolically ACTIVE: they just do not proliferate.

questions.why: Remain metabolically active. G0 (quiescent) cells stay metabolically active but do not proliferate unless the organism needs them to; they do not become cancerous.
Statement A is wrong: G0 cells are metabolically active. Statement B is right: the centriole/centrosome duplicates during S phase of interphase.
Statement A is wrong because NCERT calls G0 an inactive stage (no proliferation). Statement B is correct: G0 cells remain metabolically active and divide only when called on.
Both correct. In animals mitosis is seen only in diploid somatic cells, while in plants mitotic divisions occur in both haploid and diploid cells.
Statement A is correct: mitosis is usually restricted to diploid cells. Statement B is wrong: NCERT says some lower plants and some social insects, not higher plants or all social insects.

nuggets.title: M phase and prophase
lines: M phase is the most dramatic period of the cell cycle; as parent and progeny cells have the same chromosome number, mitosis is called equational division.
Karyokinesis has four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase; prophase follows the S and G2 phases of interphase.
In prophase, chromosomal material condenses into compact mitotic chromosomes, each made of two chromatids attached at the centromere.
The centrosome, duplicated during interphase, moves towards opposite poles; its radiating microtubules (asters) and spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus.
Cells at the end of prophase do not show Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus or the nuclear envelope.
nuggets.tip: Prophase follows S AND G2, not S immediately.

questions.why: Both correct. M phase involves major reorganisation of virtually all cell components, and since parent and progeny have the same chromosome number it is called equational division.
Option 3 is incorrect: prophase follows the S and G2 phases, not S immediately. Chromatin condensation and initiation of spindle assembly are true prophase events.
All of them. NCERT: cells at the end of prophase, viewed under the microscope, do not show Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope.
A-Q, B-R, C-P, D-S: prophase begins with condensation, centrosome/centriole duplicates in S phase, nucleolus and envelope vanish by end of prophase, morphology is best studied at metaphase.
During prophase the chromosomal material becomes untangled as chromatin condenses. Centrioles duplicate earlier in S phase, and chromatids are joined at the centromere, not centrosome.

nuggets.title: Metaphase
lines: The complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope marks the start of metaphase, the second phase of mitosis.
Condensation of chromosomes is completed at metaphase, so their morphology is most easily studied at this stage.
A metaphase chromosome consists of two sister chromatids held together by the centromere.
Small disc-shaped structures on the surface of centromeres, the kinetochores, are the sites of attachment of spindle fibres.
Chromosomes align at the cell's equator; this plane is called the metaphase plate, with one chromatid of each chromosome connected to fibres from each pole.
nuggets.tip: Spindle fibres attach to kinetochores (on the centromere), not to the centromere directly or to centrosomes.

questions.why: Kinetochores: small disc-shaped structures on the surface of the centromere that serve as attachment sites for spindle fibres at metaphase.
Metaphase. Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores of chromosomes and the chromosomes are brought to the metaphase plate.
A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q: metaphase chromosome = two sister chromatids; metaphase plate = plane of alignment; anaphase = splitting of chromosome; kinetochores = discs on centromeres.
Complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope marks the start of metaphase. DNA and chromosome duplication happen in S phase; spindle formation starts in prophase.
Statement A is false: morphology is best studied at metaphase, not prophase. Statement B is true: chromosome condensation is completed at metaphase.

nuggets.title: Anaphase
lines: At the onset of anaphase, each chromosome at the metaphase plate splits simultaneously as the centromeres split.
The separated chromatids, now called daughter chromosomes, begin migrating towards the two opposite poles.
As each chromosome moves away from the equatorial plate, the centromere is towards the pole (leading edge) and the arms trail behind.
Thus the key anaphase events are splitting of centromeres, separation of chromatids and their movement to opposite poles.
nuggets.tip: Chromosomes move TO the equator in metaphase and AWAY from it in anaphase.

questions.why: In anaphase centromeres split, so the sister chromatids become two daughter chromosomes. Centrosomes are a different structure (spindle poles).
Option 1 is not true: chromosomes move to the equator in metaphase. In anaphase centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles.
A-Q, B-R, C-S, D-P: spindle assembly starts in prophase; protein synthesis for mitosis in interphase (G2); kinetochore attachment in metaphase; chromatids move to poles in anaphase.
Chromosomes will not segregate. APC triggers anaphase, when centromeres split and chromatids separate; without it sister chromatids stay joined and cannot move to opposite poles.
A-R, B-Q, C-P, D-S: kinetochore attachment = metaphase; nucleolus, Golgi, ER reform = telophase; centromeres split = anaphase; centrosomes move to poles = prophase.

nuggets.title: Telophase
lines: In telophase, chromosomes that reach their poles decondense and lose their individuality.
The chromosomes cluster at opposite spindle poles and their identity as discrete elements is lost.
A nuclear envelope develops around each chromosome cluster at each pole, forming two daughter nuclei.
The nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform in telophase (they had disappeared by the end of prophase).
nuggets.tip: Disappear in prophase, reappear in telophase: nucleolus, Golgi, ER, nuclear envelope.

questions.why: Statement A is wrong: in telophase the nuclear envelope re-forms around chromosome clusters (it disintegrates earlier). Statement B is correct: nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform.
All of the above. In telophase chromosomes cluster at the poles and lose identity, a nuclear envelope forms around each cluster, and nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform.
Telophase and prophase. Golgi body and ER disappear by the end of prophase and reform during telophase.
At telophase chromosomes reach their respective poles, decondense and lose their individuality. Condensation happens in prophase, and the equator is the metaphase position.

II and IV only. Centromeres split in anaphase and nucleolus/Golgi/ER reform in telophase. Tetrads appear in pachytene (not leptotene), terminalisation is in diakinesis, crossing over is between non-sister chromatids.

nuggets.title: Cytokinesis and syncytium
lines: In an animal cell, cytokinesis is achieved by a furrow in the plasma membrane that deepens and joins in the centre, dividing the cytoplasm into two.
Plant cells are enclosed by a relatively inextensible cell wall, so they divide by a different mechanism.
In plant cells, wall formation starts in the centre of the cell and grows outward to meet the existing lateral walls.
The new wall begins as a simple precursor, the cell plate, which represents the middle lamella between the walls of two adjacent cells.
Organelles like mitochondria and plastids are distributed between the two daughter cells during cytokinesis.
When karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, a multinucleate condition called syncytium forms, e.g. the liquid endosperm in coconut.
nuggets.tip: Cell plate grows centre → outwards (centrifugal), and becomes the middle lamella.

questions.why: Both statements are swapped. The furrow forms in animal cells; the cell plate forms in plant cells.
Statement A is reversed: syncytium forms when karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis. Statement B is correct: liquid endosperm of coconut is a syncytium.
A-R, B-P, C-Q: animal cytokinesis by a furrow in the plasma membrane, multinucleate condition = syncytium, plant cytokinesis by cell plate.
Option 3 is incorrect: a furrow in the plasma membrane is how animal cells divide. Plant cells form a cell plate in the centre that grows outward and becomes the middle lamella.
Polyploidy. No cell plate means no cytokinesis; the duplicated chromosome sets stay in one cell, multiplying whole chromosome sets.

nuggets.title: Significance of mitosis
lines: Mitosis usually produces diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement.
The growth of multicellular organisms is due to mitosis.
Cell growth disturbs the ratio between nucleus and cytoplasm, so the cell divides to restore the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.
A very significant contribution of mitosis is cell repair: cells of the upper epidermis, the gut lining and blood cells are constantly replaced.
Mitotic divisions in meristematic tissues (apical and lateral cambium) result in continuous growth of plants throughout their life.

questions.why: Both correct. Cell growth disturbs the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, so the cell must divide to restore the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.
Statement A is wrong: epidermal, gut-lining and blood cells are constantly replaced. Statement B is correct: apical and lateral meristems give plants continuous growth.

A-Q, B-S, C-P, D-R: haploid cells of some lower plants/social insects divide by mitosis; mitosis aids cell repair; division restores nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio; upper epidermis cells are constantly dividing.
Statement A is correct (growth and cell repair). Statement B is wrong: mitosis gives diploid daughter cells with an identical genetic complement.
Mitosis produces daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell, as chromosomes are equally distributed.

nuggets.title: Meiosis: overview
lines: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number by half and produces haploid daughter cells; it ensures the haploid phase in the life cycle of sexually reproducing organisms.
Meiosis involves two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division, meiosis I and meiosis II, but only a single cycle of DNA replication.
Meiosis I is initiated after the parental chromosomes have replicated to produce identical sister chromatids at the S phase.
Meiosis involves pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
Four haploid cells are formed at the end of meiosis II.
nuggets.tip: Two divisions, ONE DNA replication (before meiosis I), four haploid cells.

questions.why: Option 1 is incorrect: there is no S phase before meiosis II. DNA replicates only once, at the S phase before meiosis I. The other statements are NCERT facts.
Both incorrect. Meiosis has two divisions but only one DNA replication, and the sister chromatids are produced at the S phase, not G2.
Option 1 does not hold: meiosis gives four haploid cells, not diploid. Pairing/recombination and two divisions with a single DNA replication are correct.
