Two nuclear divisions and one DNA replication: meiosis I and II follow a single round of DNA replication.
Both incorrect. Recombination is between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, and meiosis II ends with four haploid cells, not eight.

nuggets.title: Prophase I: leptotene and zygotene
lines: Prophase of the first meiotic division is typically longer and more complex than mitotic prophase and has five sub-stages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis.
During leptotene, chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope, and their compaction continues throughout this stage.
In zygotene, chromosomes start pairing together; this association is called synapsis and the paired chromosomes are homologous chromosomes.
Electron micrographs show that synapsis is accompanied by formation of a complex structure, the synaptonemal complex.
The complex formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is called a bivalent or a tetrad; zygotene is short compared to pachytene.
nuggets.tip: Zygotene = pairing (synapsis) + synaptonemal complex. Not 'kinetochore complex'.

questions.why: Zygotene. Homologous chromosomes start pairing (synapsis) in zygotene; leptotene only shows gradual condensation.
Statement A is correct: in leptotene chromosomes gradually become visible under the light microscope. Statement B is wrong: pairing (synapsis) begins in zygotene, not diakinesis.
Only i is correct: chromosome compaction continues through leptotene. Statement ii is wrong because chromosomes become visible under the light microscope, not electron microscope.
Both incorrect: synapsis is accompanied by the synaptonemal complex, not a kinetochore complex; a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is called a bivalent or tetrad.
Electron microscope. NCERT notes that electron micrographs of zygotene show synapsis is accompanied by formation of the synaptonemal complex.

nuggets.title: Prophase I: pachytene and crossing over
lines: In pachytene, the four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct and clearly appear as tetrads.
Pachytene is marked by recombination nodules, the sites where crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between two homologous chromosomes and leads to recombination of genetic material.
Crossing over is an enzyme-mediated process; the enzyme involved is recombinase.
By the end of pachytene, crossing over is complete, leaving the homologous chromosomes linked at the sites of crossing over.
nuggets.tip: Recombinase, recombination nodules, crossing over: all pachytene.

questions.why: Pachytene. Crossing over between non-sister chromatids happens in pachytene and is mediated by the enzyme recombinase.
Pachytene. It is characterised by recombination nodules, the sites at which crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
Statement A is wrong: tetrads become distinct in pachytene, not zygotene. Statement B is correct: recombination nodules mark crossing over sites in pachytene.
Recombinase brings about crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. The synaptonemal complex forms earlier in zygotene.
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. Exchange between sister chromatids gives no new combination; between non-homologous chromosomes is not crossing over.

nuggets.title: Prophase I: diplotene
lines: The beginning of diplotene is recognised by the dissolution of the synaptonemal complex.
The recombined homologous chromosomes of the bivalents then separate from each other except at the sites of crossovers.
These X-shaped structures where homologues remain attached are called chiasmata.
In oocytes of some vertebrates, diplotene can last for months or years.
nuggets.tip: Chiasmata become visible in diplotene; terminalisation happens later in diakinesis.

questions.why: Statement A is correct: diplotene begins with dissolution of the synaptonemal complex. Statement B is wrong: the prolonged diplotene is in oocytes of some, not all, vertebrates.
A - Diplotene, B - Pachytene. Diplotene may last months or years in oocytes of some vertebrates; tetrads become clearly visible in pachytene.
Diplotene starts with dissolution of the synaptonemal complex. Synapsis is zygotene; recombination nodules and crossing over are pachytene.
Both true. Chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope in leptotene, and diplotene begins with dissolution of the synaptonemal complex.
Chiasmata: X-shaped points where homologous chromosomes stay attached at crossover sites after separating in diplotene.

nuggets.title: Prophase I: diakinesis and recap
lines: The final stage of meiotic prophase I, diakinesis, is marked by terminalisation of chiasmata.
During diakinesis, chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle is assembled to prepare homologous chromosomes for separation.
By the end of diakinesis, the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down; diakinesis is the transition to metaphase I.
Sequence of prophase I: leptotene → zygotene (synapsis) → pachytene (crossing over) → diplotene (chiasmata) → diakinesis (terminalisation).
nuggets.tip: Mnemonic: Lazy Zebras Pick Daisies Daily (L-Z-P-D-D).

questions.why: Diakinesis. Terminalisation of chiasmata is the distinctive feature of diakinesis, the last sub-stage of prophase I.
All of the above. Diakinesis shows terminalisation of chiasmata, and by its end the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1: crossing over in pachytene, alignment at equatorial plate in metaphase I, terminalisation in diakinesis, pairing in zygotene.
A-Q, B-S, C-P, D-R: diakinesis = terminalisation of chiasmata, pachytene = recombination nodules, zygotene = synaptonemal complex, leptotene = thin thread-like chromosomes.
II, I, III, IV: synapsis (zygotene) → crossing over (pachytene) → terminalisation of chiasmata (diakinesis) → nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear at end of diakinesis.

nuggets.title: Metaphase I to interkinesis
lines: In metaphase I, bivalent chromosomes align on the equatorial plate and microtubules from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of homologous chromosomes.
In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes separate, while sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres.
In telophase I, the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear and cytokinesis follows, forming a dyad of cells.
The stage between the two meiotic divisions is interkinesis; it is generally short lived and has no DNA replication.
Interkinesis is followed by prophase II, a much simpler prophase than prophase I.
nuggets.tip: Anaphase I separates homologues; anaphase II separates sister chromatids.

questions.why: Statement A is correct: bivalents align on the equatorial plate in metaphase I. Statement B describes metaphase I, not anaphase I, so it is incorrect.
Statement A is wrong: in anaphase I only homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids stay joined at centromeres. Statement B is correct for telophase I.
Statement A is wrong: interkinesis is generally short lived. Statement B is correct: there is no DNA replication during interkinesis.
Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I, while sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres until anaphase II.
A-R, B-P, C-Q, D-S: terminalisation in diakinesis, bivalents align in metaphase I, homologues separate in anaphase I, nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear in telophase I.

nuggets.title: Meiosis II
lines: Meiosis II starts immediately after cytokinesis, usually before chromosomes have fully elongated, and resembles a normal mitosis.
In prophase II, the nuclear membrane disappears by the end of the stage and chromosomes again become compact.
In metaphase II, chromosomes align at the equator and microtubules from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of sister chromatids.
Anaphase II begins with simultaneous splitting of the centromere of each chromosome, letting sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
In telophase II, nuclear envelopes enclose the chromosome groups and cytokinesis follows, forming a tetrad of cells (four haploid daughter cells).
nuggets.tip: Chromosome number halves in meiosis I; meiosis II keeps it the same, like mitosis.

questions.why: Anaphase II. The centromere of each chromosome splits only in anaphase II; in anaphase I sister chromatids stay joined at the centromere.
A-R, B-S, C-Q, D-P: nuclear membrane disappears by end of prophase II, alignment at equator in metaphase II, meiosis ends with telophase II, centromeres split in anaphase II.
1 and 2. In telophase II nuclear envelope and nucleolus reappear around the chromosome groups, and cytokinesis follows to form a tetrad of cells.
Mitosis. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids without changing chromosome number, so it resembles a normal mitosis.
48. The chromosome number is halved in meiosis I; meiosis II only separates sister chromatids, so cells keep 48 chromosomes.

nuggets.title: Significance of meiosis
lines: Meiosis is the mechanism by which the specific chromosome number of each species is conserved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms.
Paradoxically, this conservation is achieved through a process that reduces the chromosome number by half.
Meiosis produces the haploid phase (gametes), and fertilisation restores the diploid phase in the life cycle.
Meiosis increases genetic variability in the population from one generation to the next.
These variations are very important for the process of evolution.

questions.why: Both correct. Meiosis conserves the species-specific chromosome number across generations and increases genetic variability from one generation to the next.
Both correct. Meiosis gives the haploid phase in sexually reproducing organisms, and fertilisation restores the diploid phase.
All of these. Meiosis maintains chromosome number across generations and increases genetic variability, which is important for evolution.
All of the above. In diploid organisms meiosis halves the chromosome number to form gametes and introduces variation through crossing over.
Both incorrect: the names are swapped. Mitosis keeps the chromosome number (diploid daughter cells); meiosis halves it (haploid daughter cells).

nuggets.title: What we know: leaf experiments
lines: Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process by which green plants use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds; it is the basis of life on earth.
Testing a variegated leaf, or a leaf partly covered with black paper, for starch shows photosynthesis occurs only in green parts and only in the presence of light.
In the half-leaf experiment, part of a leaf is enclosed in a test tube with KOH-soaked cotton (which absorbs CO2), while the other half is exposed to air.
The exposed half tests positive for starch and the enclosed half tests negative, proving that CO2 is required for photosynthesis.
nuggets.tip: KOH absorbs CO2: no CO2 in the tube, so no starch in that half.

questions.why: Green, presence. Starch appears only in green regions of a variegated leaf and only in the uncovered (lit) part, so photosynthesis needs chlorophyll and light.
Both correct. KOH in the tube absorbs CO<sub>2</sub>, so the enclosed half cannot make starch while the half exposed to air tests starch-positive.
KOH soaked in cotton absorbs CO2 from the air inside the test tube in the half-leaf experiment.
Carbon dioxide. The only difference between the two halves is CO2 availability (removed by KOH), so the experiment shows CO2 is required.

nuggets.title: Early experiments: Priestley, Ingenhousz, Sachs
lines: Joseph Priestley (1733–1804) showed in 1770 that a candle in a closed bell jar goes out and a mouse suffocates, but a mint plant restores the air.
Priestley hypothesised that plants restore to the air whatever breathing animals and burning candles remove; he discovered oxygen in 1774.
Jan Ingenhousz (1730–1799) showed that sunlight is essential for the plant process that purifies air fouled by candles or animals.
Using an aquatic plant, Ingenhousz saw small bubbles around green parts in bright sunlight but not in the dark, and identified them as oxygen.
Julius von Sachs (1854) showed that glucose is made when plants grow, is usually stored as starch, and that chlorophyll lies in chloroplasts.
nuggets.tip: Priestley = air and mint in a bell jar; Ingenhousz = light and green parts; Sachs = glucose stored as starch.

questions.why: Statement A is wrong: Priestley's experiments revealed the essential role of air, not water, in plant growth. Statement B is his hypothesis, so it is correct.
Both correct. Ingenhousz showed sunlight is essential for purifying the air, and that an aquatic plant gives bubbles around green parts only in bright light.
Statement A is wrong: Sachs showed glucose (not sucrose) is produced. Statement B is correct: glucose is usually stored as starch.
Both incorrect. Priestley discovered oxygen (not hydrogen) in 1774, and Ingenhousz showed green parts release oxygen, not CO2.
A-R, B-S, C-P, D-Q: Ingenhousz = sunlight essential; Priestley = plants restore the air; Engelmann = first action spectrum; Sachs = glucose made in green parts.

nuggets.title: Engelmann and the action spectrum
lines: T.W. Engelmann (1843–1909) split light into its spectral components with a prism and illuminated the green alga Cladophora.
The alga was placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria, which were used to detect the sites of O2 evolution.
The bacteria accumulated mainly in the region of blue and red light of the split spectrum.
This gave the first action spectrum of photosynthesis, which roughly resembles the absorption spectra of chlorophyll a and b.
nuggets.tip: Engelmann used Cladophora (a green alga), not Chlamydomonas or a blue-green alga.

questions.why: Both incorrect. Engelmann used Cladophora (not Chlamydomonas), and the aerobic bacteria detected sites of O2 evolution, not CO2.
Option 1 is incorrect: Cladophora is a green alga, not a blue-green alga. A prism, aerobic bacteria and clustering in blue and red light are all correct.
Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: bacteria gathered mainly in blue and red light, not violet and red.
Chlorophyll a and b. Engelmann's action spectrum roughly matches the absorption spectra of chlorophyll a and b, which peak in blue and red light.
Chlorophyll a absorbs most strongly in the red and blue regions, and most photosynthesis also occurs in blue and red light, so the two spectra match closely.

nuggets.title: Van Niel: O2 comes from water
lines: Cornelius van Niel (1897–1985), a microbiologist, worked on purple and green bacteria.
He showed photosynthesis is essentially a light-dependent reaction in which hydrogen from a suitable oxidisable compound reduces CO2 to carbohydrates.
In green plants H2O is the hydrogen donor and is oxidised to O2; in purple and green sulphur bacteria H2S is the donor, oxidised to sulphur or sulphate, not O2.
He inferred that the O2 evolved by green plants comes from H2O, not CO2; this was later proved by radioisotopic techniques.
Correct overall equation: 6CO2 + 12H2O → C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2.
nuggets.tip: Write 12 H2O on the left: all 6 O2 come from water.

questions.why: Both correct. Water is the H donor in green plants (oxidised to O<sub>2</sub>); in purple and green sulphur bacteria H<sub>2</sub>S is the donor and gives sulphur or sulphate.
Statement A is wrong: van Niel showed photosynthesis is essentially light-dependent. Statement B is correct: hydrogen from an oxidisable compound reduces CO2.
Anoxygenic photosynthesis. These bacteria use H2S, not water, as the hydrogen donor, so no O2 is released.
Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: radioisotope techniques proved the O2 released comes from water, not CO2.
O2. Oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from splitting of water, so labelled water oxygen appears in the evolved O2.

nuggets.title: Where photosynthesis takes place
lines: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in green leaves, but also in other green parts; the mesophyll cells of leaves have a large number of chloroplasts.
Chloroplasts align along the walls of mesophyll cells so that they receive the optimum quantity of incident light.
Within the chloroplast is a membranous system of grana and stroma lamellae, set in a fluid matrix called the stroma.
The membrane system traps light energy and synthesises ATP and NADPH (light reactions); enzymatic reactions in the stroma fix CO2 into sugar, which forms starch.
Light reactions are directly light driven; the carbon reactions are called dark reactions, but this does not mean they occur in darkness or are light-independent.
nuggets.tip: Grana/thylakoid membranes = light reactions; stroma = sugar synthesis (Calvin cycle).

questions.why: Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: the membranous system is grana and stroma lamellae, while the stroma is the fluid matrix, not a membrane.
Statement A is wrong: photosynthesis occurs mainly in leaves, not the stem. Statement B is correct: mesophyll cells have many chloroplasts that fix CO2.
Both correct. Thylakoid membranes trap light and make ATP and NADPH, while stromal enzymes incorporate CO<sub>2</sub> into sugar, which forms starch.
A-R, B-P, C-Q, D-S: grana = light reactions, stroma = sugar synthesis, photosynthesis = physico-chemical process, chloroplasts = abundant in mesophyll cells.
The grana membranes both capture light and form ATP and NADPH; CO2 fixation happens in the stroma.

nuggets.title: Pigments and their colours
lines: Leaf pigments of any green plant can be separated by paper chromatography, showing that leaf colour is due to four pigments, not one.
Chlorophyll a appears bright or blue-green and chlorophyll b appears yellow-green in the chromatogram.
Xanthophylls appear yellow and carotenoids appear yellow to yellow-orange.
Pigments are substances that can absorb light at specific wavelengths.
Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment associated with photosynthesis.
nuggets.tip: Xanthophyll = yellow; carotenoid = yellow to yellow-orange. Students often swap them.

questions.why: A-T, B-P, C-S, D-R: chlorophyll b yellow-green, carotenoids yellow-orange, chlorophyll a blue-green, xanthophylls yellow.
Statement A is correct. Statement B swaps the colours: xanthophylls are yellow and carotenoids are yellow to yellow-orange.
Both correct. Chlorophyll a is the major light-trapping pigment; chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory pigments.
Both incorrect. NCERT uses paper chromatography, and it shows leaf colour is due to four pigments, not a single one.
Option 2 is incorrect: chlorophyll a, not b, is the chief pigment. The other statements about pigments, chromatography and photo-oxidation are correct.

nuggets.title: Chlorophyll a and accessory pigments
lines: The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a shows maximum absorption in the blue and red regions.
The action spectrum shows that most photosynthesis takes place in the blue and red regions; some also occurs at other wavelengths.
Chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory pigments: they absorb light and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a.
Accessory pigments allow a wider range of wavelengths of incoming light to be used for photosynthesis.
They also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
nuggets.tip: Accessory pigments protect from photo-OXIDATION (not photo-reduction).

questions.why: Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: accessory pigments protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation, not photoreduction.
2 and 3. Accessory pigments pass absorbed energy to chlorophyll a and widen the usable range of wavelengths. Chlorophyll a itself is not an accessory pigment.
Photo-oxidation. Accessory pigments such as xanthophylls and carotenoids protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
Chlorophyll a. Accessory pigments absorb light and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a, the chief pigment of the reaction centre.
Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment of photosynthesis; chlorophyll b, carotenes and xanthophylls are accessory pigments.

nuggets.title: Light reaction and photosystems
lines: The light reactions (photochemical phase) include light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release and formation of ATP and NADPH.
Pigments are organised into two discrete light harvesting complexes (LHC) within Photosystem I and Photosystem II.
PS I and PS II are named in the sequence of their discovery, not the sequence in which they function.
Each LHC has hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins; all pigments except one molecule of chlorophyll a form the antennae.
A single chlorophyll a molecule forms the reaction centre: in PS I its absorption peak is at 700 nm (P700), in PS II at 680 nm (P680).
nuggets.tip: PS I = P700, PS II = P680. Naming follows discovery, not the order of working.

questions.why: Both correct. Light reactions cover light absorption, water splitting, O<sub>2</sub> release and ATP and NADPH formation, and are also called the photochemical phase.
Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: PS I and PS II are named in the sequence of their discovery; PS II actually works first.
Statement A is wrong: LHC pigments are bound to proteins, not lipids. Statement B is correct: all pigments except one chlorophyll a molecule form the antenna.
Statement A is correct: one chlorophyll a molecule is the reaction centre. Statement B is reversed: PS I peaks at 700 nm, PS II at 680 nm.
680 nm. The reaction centre chlorophyll a of PS II is P680; that of PS I is P700.

nuggets.title: Electron transport: the Z scheme
lines: In PS II, the reaction centre absorbs 680 nm red light; its electrons are excited and passed to an electron acceptor.
From the acceptor, electrons move downhill through an electron transport system of cytochromes to the pigments of PS I.
PS I electrons, excited by 700 nm light, go to another acceptor and then downhill to reduce NADP+ to NADPH + H+.
This path forms a characteristic shape when all carriers are placed in sequence on a redox potential scale, so it is called the Z scheme.
The electrons lost by PS II are replaced by electrons from water, so electron flow is H2O → PS II → PS I → NADP+.
nuggets.tip: Non-cyclic order: water → PS II → ETS → PS I → NADP+.

questions.why: Statement A is wrong: in non-cyclic photophosphorylation PS II works first, then PS I. Statement B is correct: they are linked by an electron transport chain.
H2O → PS II → PS I. Water replaces electrons lost from PS II; they then flow via the ETS to PS I and on to NADP+.
The Z shape appears when all the carriers are placed in sequence on a redox potential scale.
The electrons ultimately come from PS II, which is linked to water splitting. Water replaces PS II electrons, which pass via PS I to NADP+.
PS I, NADP+. Electrons from the acceptor of PS I, plus protons, are needed to reduce NADP+ to NADPH + H+.

nuggets.title: Splitting of water
lines: PS II continuously supplies electrons, which are replaced by electrons from the splitting of water.
The water-splitting complex is associated with PS II, which is located on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane.
Water splits as 2H2O → 4H+ + O2 + 4e−.
The protons and O2 formed are released into the lumen of the thylakoid; O2 is one of the net products of photosynthesis.
nuggets.tip: Each water molecule gives 2 H+; 6 H2O gives 12 H+.

questions.why: Statement A is wrong: the water-splitting complex is associated with PS II, not PS I. Statement B is correct: water gives H+, oxygen and electrons.
Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: the protons (not electrons) accumulate in the lumen; the electrons go to PS II.
Inner side of the thylakoid membrane, facing the lumen, which is why protons and O2 from water are released into the lumen.
Photolysis of water. P680 is the reaction centre of PS II, the photosystem associated with the water-splitting complex.
12. 2H2O → 4H+ + O2 + 4e−, so each water gives 2 H+ and 6 water molecules give 12 H+.

nuggets.title: Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation
lines: Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light.
When PS II and PS I work in series, non-cyclic photophosphorylation occurs, producing both ATP and NADPH + H+.
In cyclic photophosphorylation only PS I works; the excited electron returns to PS I via the ETS instead of reducing NADP+.
Cyclic flow probably occurs in the stroma lamellae, whose membranes lack PS II and NADP reductase; grana lamellae have both PS I and PS II.
Cyclic photophosphorylation forms only ATP, and also occurs when only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available.
nuggets.tip: Cyclic: PS I only, ATP only, no NADPH, no O2.

questions.why: ATP. In cyclic flow the electron returns to PS I and NADP+ is not reduced, so only ATP forms (no NADPH, no O2).
Cyclic flow makes only ATP, not NADPH. The Calvin cycle needs both (3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2), so photosynthesis cannot continue.
ii and iv. Only PS I works in cyclic flow, and stroma lamellae lack PS II and NADP reductase. The Z scheme needs both photosystems, and cyclic flow gives no NADPH.
Statement A is wrong: cyclic flow forms only ATP, not NADPH. Statement B is correct: it also occurs when only light beyond 680 nm is available.
All of them. Cyclic photophosphorylation occurs in stroma lamellae, operates with light beyond 680 nm, and forms ATP without NADPH.

nuggets.title: Chemiosmotic hypothesis
lines: ATP synthesis is linked to development of a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane (chemiosmotic hypothesis).
In photosynthesis, protons accumulate inside the membrane, in the lumen; in respiration, they accumulate in the intermembrane space of mitochondria.
The primary electron acceptor, on the outer side of the membrane, passes electrons to an H carrier, which moves a proton from the stroma into the lumen.
NADP reductase lies on the stroma side, and the protons it uses to reduce NADP+ are removed from the stroma.
Chemiosmosis requires a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase.
nuggets.tip: Highest H+ concentration (lowest pH) in the chloroplast is in the thylakoid lumen.

questions.why: Protons accumulate within the lumen of the thylakoids. Accumulation in the intermembrane space happens in mitochondria during respiration.
Lumen of thylakoids. Water splitting and the H carrier both add protons to the lumen, while NADP reduction removes them from the stroma.
Membrane, proton pump, proton gradient and ATP synthase. A proton gradient (not an electron gradient) drives ATP synthase.
Statement A is wrong: CF0 forms a channel for facilitated diffusion of protons, not simple diffusion. Statement B is correct: CF1 faces the stroma.
Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: the primary electron acceptor is on the outer (stroma) side of the membrane, not the inner side.

nuggets.title: ATP synthase and use of the gradient
lines: Protons decrease in the stroma and accumulate in the lumen, creating a gradient and a measurable decrease in pH in the lumen.
The gradient breaks down as protons move back across the membrane to the stroma through the CF0 channel of ATP synthase.
CF0 is embedded in the thylakoid membrane and forms a transmembrane channel for facilitated diffusion of protons.
CF1 protrudes on the outer surface facing the stroma; energy from the gradient changes its conformation so it synthesises ATP.
ATP and NADPH formed on the stroma side are used immediately in the stroma to fix CO2 and synthesise sugars.
nuggets.tip: CF0 = channel in membrane; CF1 = stroma-facing part that makes ATP.

questions.why: Both correct. Protons fall in the stroma and build up in the lumen, creating a proton gradient and a measurable drop in lumen pH.
CF1 particle. Breakdown of the gradient causes a conformational change in CF1, which synthesises ATP; CF0 is only the proton channel.
Splitting of water releases H+ into the lumen. The H carrier moves protons from stroma to lumen, and NADP reductase removes them from the stroma, so options 2 and 3 are wrong.
Synthesis of ATP. Puncturing the membrane destroys the proton gradient between lumen and stroma, so ATP synthase cannot make ATP.
ATP and NADPH are made on the stromal side because the Calvin cycle in the stroma needs them immediately.

nuggets.title: Biosynthetic phase: C3 and C4 discovery
lines: The biosynthetic phase is not directly light-dependent but depends on light-reaction products ATP and NADPH, plus CO2 and H2O.
Melvin Calvin used radioactive 14C in algal photosynthesis studies and found the first CO2 fixation product is a 3-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA).
Plants whose first product is the C3 acid PGA follow the C3 pathway; those whose first product is the C4 acid oxaloacetic acid (OAA) follow the C4 pathway.
As the first product was a C3 acid, scientists first guessed the acceptor was a 2-carbon molecule; it proved to be the 5-carbon ketose sugar RuBP.
nuggets.tip: The Calvin cycle does not run at night because it needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.

questions.why: Statement A is wrong: the biosynthetic phase is not directly light-dependent, but it depends on light-reaction products. Statement B is correct: Calvin found a 3-carbon acid.
Alga. Calvin's 14C studies on algal photosynthesis showed the first CO2 fixation product is 3-PGA.
Both incorrect. Statement A swaps the acids: the C3 product is PGA and the C4 product is OAA. The Calvin pathway occurs in all photosynthetic plants.
C2 compound. Since the first product had 3 carbons, scientists expected a 2-carbon acceptor; it turned out to be the 5-carbon RuBP.
The Calvin cycle is not directly light-dependent, but it uses ATP and NADPH from the light reaction; without light those run out.

nuggets.title: Calvin cycle: three stages
lines: The Calvin cycle occurs in all photosynthetic plants, whether they have C3 or C4 pathways, and has three stages: carboxylation, reduction, regeneration.
Carboxylation: CO2 is fixed with RuBP by RuBP carboxylase, giving two molecules of 3-PGA; this is the most crucial step.
RuBisCO (RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase) is the most abundant enzyme in the world and can show both carboxylation and oxygenation activity.
Reduction: 2 ATP for phosphorylation and 2 NADPH for reduction are used per CO2 fixed, forming glucose.
Regeneration of the CO2 acceptor RuBP needs one ATP for phosphorylation, so the cycle can continue.
nuggets.tip: Order: Carboxylation → Reduction → Regeneration.

questions.why: Carboxylation, reduction, regeneration: CO2 fixed onto RuBP, PGA reduced using ATP and NADPH, then RuBP regenerated.
2 molecules of 3-PGA. RuBisCO adds CO2 to the 5-carbon RuBP, and the 6-carbon product splits into two 3-PGA.
Six. Regenerating each RuBP needs one ATP for phosphorylation, so 6 RuBP need 6 ATP.
A-T, B-S, C-R, D-Q: PEP is 3-carbon, RuBP 5-carbon, OAA 4-carbon, acetyl CoA 2-carbon.
It is called the C3 cycle because its first stable product, 3-PGA, is a 3-carbon compound. The acceptor RuBP is a 5-carbon sugar.

nuggets.title: Calvin cycle: ATP and NADPH count
lines: For every CO2 entering the Calvin cycle, 3 ATP and 2 NADPH are required.
To make one molecule of glucose, 6 turns of the cycle are needed.
So one glucose needs 6 CO2, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
Out: one glucose, with 18 ADP and 12 NADP returned for the light reactions.
The light reactions provide ATP and NADPH to the Calvin cycle, which is why the two phases are tightly linked.
nuggets.tip: Per CO2: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH. Per glucose: multiply by 6 = 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.

questions.why: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. Each CO2 needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, and one glucose needs 6 CO2 (6 turns).
3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2: 2 ATP + 2 NADPH in reduction and 1 ATP in regeneration of RuBP.
Both correct. Each CO<sub>2</sub> needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, and 6 turns of the cycle are needed to make one glucose.
One glucose, 18 ADP, 12 NADP. Inputs are 6 CO2, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH; the outputs are glucose plus ADP and NADP sent back to the light reactions.
6 : 18 : 12. Six turns fix 6 CO2, using 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per turn, giving 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

nuggets.title: C4 plants: Kranz anatomy
lines: C4 plants are adapted to dry tropical regions; their first CO2 fixation product is a C4 acid, yet the Calvin cycle is their main biosynthetic pathway.
C4 leaves have Kranz anatomy: large bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles; Kranz means 'wreath', reflecting the arrangement of cells.
Bundle sheath cells may form several layers around the vascular bundles.
They have a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and no intercellular spaces.
Examples of C4 plants include maize and sorghum.
nuggets.tip: Bundle sheath: many chloroplasts, thick walls, no intercellular spaces.

questions.why: Thick walls, no intercellular spaces and a large number of chloroplasts: NCERT's three hallmarks of bundle sheath cells in Kranz anatomy.
Statement A is correct. Statement B is wrong: the large cells around vascular bundles in C4 plants are bundle sheath cells, not mesophyll.
Wreath, reflection. Kranz means wreath, a reflection of how bundle sheath cells are arranged around the vascular bundle.
'Single layer' is incorrect: bundle sheath cells may form several layers. No intercellular spaces, many chloroplasts and thick walls are correct.
Sugarcane, a C4 grass like maize and sorghum, has Kranz anatomy. Wheat, mustard and potato are C3 plants.

nuggets.title: C4 (Hatch and Slack) pathway
lines: In the Hatch and Slack pathway, the primary CO2 acceptor is the 3-carbon phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), present in the mesophyll cells.
The enzyme for this fixation is PEP carboxylase (PEPcase); mesophyll cells of C4 plants lack RuBisCO.
The C4 acid OAA formed in mesophyll becomes malic acid or aspartic acid, which is transported to the bundle sheath cells.
In bundle sheath cells, the C4 acid is broken down to release CO2 and a 3-carbon molecule.
The 3-carbon molecule returns to the mesophyll, where it is converted to PEP again, completing the cycle.
nuggets.tip: PEP (3C) + CO2 → OAA (4C), in mesophyll, by PEPcase.

questions.why: Both correct. PEP is the primary CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor in mesophyll cells, and C<sub>4</sub> mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO.
PEP carboxylase. In C4 plants, PEPcase fixes CO2 onto PEP in mesophyll cells; RuBisCO acts later in the bundle sheath.
Oxaloacetic acid. Sorghum is a C4 plant; its first stable product is the 4-carbon OAA, not 3-PGA.
Mesophyll. OAA formed by PEPcase in mesophyll cells is converted there to malic acid (or aspartic acid) before moving to the bundle sheath.
CO2 and a 3C molecule. Decarboxylation of the C4 acid in the bundle sheath releases CO2, and the 3-carbon remainder returns to mesophyll.

nuggets.title: C4 plants: division of labour
lines: The CO2 released in bundle sheath cells enters the C3 (Calvin) pathway.
Bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase; mesophyll cells have PEPcase but lack RuBisCO.
The Calvin pathway occurs in all mesophyll cells of C3 plants, but in C4 plants it runs only in the bundle sheath cells.
Thus the basic pathway that makes sugars, the Calvin pathway, is common to both C<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>4</sub> plants.
nuggets.tip: Mesophyll: PEPcase, no RuBisCO. Bundle sheath: RuBisCO, no PEPcase.

questions.why: Statement A is reversed: bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO and lack PEPcase. Statement B is correct: in C4 plants the Calvin cycle runs in bundle sheath cells.
Both incorrect. PEPcase is in the mesophyll cells (not bundle sheath), so mesophyll cells do have PEPcase; they lack RuBisCO instead.
RuBisCO, PEPcase. Bundle sheath cells of C4 plants are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase.
Mesophyll cells. The 3-carbon molecule from decarboxylation in the bundle sheath goes back to mesophyll to regenerate PEP.
Both. OAA is converted in mesophyll to malic acid or aspartic acid, either of which is carried to bundle sheath cells.

nuggets.title: Photorespiration
lines: RuBisCO's active site can bind both CO2 and O2; it has a much greater affinity for CO2, and their relative concentration decides which binds.
In C3 plants some O2 binds RuBisCO, so instead of two PGA, RuBP forms one phosphoglycerate and one phosphoglycolate; this is photorespiration.
Photorespiration makes neither sugar nor ATP or NADPH; it releases CO2 while using ATP, so it is wasteful. Its biological function is not yet known.
Photorespiration does not occur in C4 plants: their mechanism raises CO2 at the enzyme site, so RuBisCO acts as a carboxylase.
As a result, C4 plants have better productivity and yields and tolerate higher temperatures.
nuggets.tip: RuBisCO prefers CO2 over O2; photorespiration happens only because O2 is abundant around C3 RuBisCO.

questions.why: Statement A is wrong: RuBisCO has a much greater affinity for CO2 than O2. Statement B is correct: O2 binding gives one phosphoglycerate and one phosphoglycolate.
Photorespiration occurs in C3 plants but is absent in C4 plants, whose CO2-concentrating mechanism keeps RuBisCO working as a carboxylase.
Statement A is true: O2 binding to RuBisCO lowers CO2 fixation in C3 plants. Statement B is false: C4 plants lack photorespiration.
3 (b, d, e). Photorespiration makes no sugar, ATP or NADPH, and its function is unknown. (a) is wrong because fixation decreases; (c) is wrong because CO2 (not O2) is released.
In C4 plants, decarboxylation of the C4 acid raises CO2 concentration in bundle sheath cells, so RuBisCO works as a carboxylase and photorespiration is avoided.

nuggets.title: Factors: Blackman's law and light
lines: Photosynthesis is affected by internal (plant) factors, such as leaf number, size, age and orientation and chlorophyll amount, and external factors: sunlight, temperature, CO2, water.
Blackman's (1905) law of limiting factors: if a process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is set by the factor nearest its minimal value.
At low light intensities there is a linear relationship between incident light and CO2 fixation; at higher intensities other factors become limiting.
Light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight, so light is rarely limiting except for plants in shade or dense forests.
Increasing incident light beyond a point causes breakdown of chlorophyll and a decrease in photosynthesis.
nuggets.tip: Light saturation is at 10% of full sunlight, not 1%.

questions.why: Minimal. Blackman's law says the rate is set by the factor nearest its minimal value; that factor directly changes the rate when its quantity changes.
Statement A is correct: CO2 fixation rises linearly with light at low intensities. Statement B is wrong: light saturation occurs at 10% of full sunlight, not 1%.
10 per cent. Light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight, so light is rarely a limiting factor in nature.
Plants in shade or dense forests. Because saturation needs only about 10% of full sunlight, light limits photosynthesis mainly for shaded plants.
Very high light intensity causes breakdown of chlorophyll (photo-oxidative damage), lowering the photosynthetic rate.

nuggets.title: Factors: CO2, temperature and water
lines: CO2 is the major limiting factor for photosynthesis; its atmospheric concentration is very low, between 0.03 and 0.04%.
C4 plants show CO2 saturation at about 360 µL L−1; C3 plants respond to higher CO2 and saturate only beyond 450 µL L−1.
Higher productivity of C3 plants with more CO2 is used for greenhouse crops like tomatoes and bell pepper, grown in CO2-enriched air.
Dark reactions are enzymatic and temperature-controlled; C4 plants and tropical plants have a higher temperature optimum than C3 and temperate plants.
Water stress closes stomata, reducing CO2 availability, and makes leaves wilt, reducing their surface area and metabolic activity.
nuggets.tip: CO2 saturation: C4 at 360, C3 beyond 450 µL/L. Current CO2 levels limit C3 plants.

questions.why: Statement A is correct: CO2 is the major limiting factor. Statement B swaps the values: C4 saturates at 360 and C3 beyond 450 µL L−1.
Statement A is correct: C3 greenhouse crops such as tomatoes and bell pepper give higher yields with extra CO2. Statement B is wrong: C3 and C4 plants respond differently.
Statement A is reversed: C4 plants have the higher temperature optimum. Statement B is correct: tropical plants have higher optima than temperate plants.
360 µL L−1. C4 plants saturate at about 360 µL L−1, while C3 plants keep responding until beyond 450 µL L−1.
Both true, and the reason explains it: water stress closes stomata, cutting CO2 supply and lowering photosynthesis.

nuggets.title: Respiration: breaking C–C bonds for ATP
lines: All energy for life processes comes from oxidation of macromolecules (food); green plants and cyanobacteria make their own food by photosynthesis.
Cellular respiration is the breakdown of food within cells by breaking C–C bonds through oxidation to release energy for ATP synthesis.
Compounds oxidised during respiration are respiratory substrates; usually carbohydrates, but proteins, fats and even organic acids can be used.
Energy is not released in one step but in a series of slow step-wise reactions controlled by enzymes, and is trapped as chemical energy in ATP.
ATP acts as the energy currency of the cell; its energy is used for energy-requiring processes of the organism.
The carbon skeleton produced during respiration is used as precursors for biosynthesis of other molecules in the cell.

questions.why: Respiration: oxidation of C–C bonds of organic molecules to release energy for cell use. Photorespiration and photosynthesis are different processes in the chloroplast.
Both correct. Energy of substrates is not released in a single step; it is released stepwise under enzyme control and trapped as chemical energy of ATP.
A incorrect, B correct. NCERT calls ATP the energy currency of the cell, and its trapped energy is used in various energy-requiring processes.
Both incorrect. The cell catabolises (not anabolises) glucose, and oxidises it in several small steps (not large ones) so that each step can be coupled to ATP synthesis.
Respiration = breaking C–C bonds (R); substrates = compounds oxidised (P); ATP = energy currency (S); carbon skeletons = precursors for biosynthesis (Q).

nuggets.title: Do plants breathe?
lines: Plants, unlike animals, have no specialised organs for gaseous exchange; they use stomata and lenticels, and gases move by diffusion.
Each plant part takes care of its own gas-exchange needs; there is very little transport of gases from one plant part to another.
Plants do not present great demands for gas exchange: roots, stems and leaves respire at much lower rates than animals.
Distance gases must diffuse is small because most living cells lie close to the surface and loosely packed parenchyma has interconnected air spaces.
During photosynthesis large volumes of gases are exchanged, and O<sub>2</sub> released within leaves is available to their cells.
In respiration O2 is used and CO2, water and energy are released; combustion of glucose also needs O2.
nuggets.tip: Gas exchange in plants is by diffusion, not osmosis.

questions.why: All are correct. NCERT gives exactly these reasons: low demand for gas exchange, each part meets its own needs, and short diffusion distances even in bulky plants.
Both true and linked: plants need no special respiratory organs because each part handles its own gas exchange and there is very little transport of gases between parts.
A correct, B incorrect. Plants lack special breathing systems, but stomata and lenticels allow gas exchange by diffusion, not osmosis.
A incorrect, B correct. Plants need O2 (not CO2) for respiration and give out CO2; they do have systems that ensure O2 availability.
A correct, B incorrect. Respiration uses O2 and releases CO2, water and energy; combustion also requires O2.

nuggets.title: Glycolysis: the EMP pathway
lines: Glycolysis (Greek glycos = sugar, lysis = splitting) was worked out by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas, hence the EMP pathway.
In anaerobic organisms glycolysis is the only process in respiration; it occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and is present in all living organisms.
Glucose undergoes partial oxidation to form two molecules of pyruvic acid through a chain of ten enzyme-controlled reactions.
In plants glucose comes from sucrose, the end product of photosynthesis, or from storage carbohydrates.
Sucrose is converted into glucose and fructose by the enzyme invertase; both readily enter the glycolytic pathway.
nuggets.tip: EMP = Embden, Meyerhof, Parnas.

questions.why: Glycolysis was given by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas, so it is called the EMP pathway. Other options jumble their first names.
Invertase converts sucrose into glucose and fructose, which both enter glycolysis. Maltase acts on maltose; hexokinase phosphorylates glucose.
Glycolysis is partial oxidation of one glucose into two molecules of pyruvic acid; complete oxidation needs the Krebs cycle and ETS.
A true, R false. Glycolysis is the EMP pathway, but it is the only respiratory process in anaerobic organisms, not aerobic ones.
Both correct. Glycolysis is a chain of ten enzyme-controlled reactions converting glucose to pyruvate, and pyruvic acid is its key product.

nuggets.title: Glycolysis: the key steps
lines: Glucose and fructose are phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase; this is isomerised to fructose-6-phosphate.
ATP is utilised at two steps: glucose → glucose-6-phosphate, and fructose-6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is split into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).
When PGAL is oxidised to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA), two hydrogen atoms are removed and NAD+ → NADH + H+.
BPGA → 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA) is energy yielding and the energy is trapped as ATP.
Another ATP is formed when PEP is converted to pyruvic acid.
nuggets.tip: ATP used: glucose & F-6-P steps. ATP made: BPGA → PGA and PEP → pyruvate.

questions.why: Both true and R explains A: ATP is spent converting glucose → glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, using one ATP. Invertase splits sucrose; phosphatases remove phosphate.
NADH + H+ forms when PGAL is oxidised to BPGA, the only oxidation step of glycolysis, where two H atoms go to NAD+.
Both correct. BPGA → PGA is energy yielding and forms ATP; a second ATP forms when PEP is converted to pyruvic acid.
Correct order: F-1,6-bisP splits into DHAP + PGAL (iii) → PGAL to BPGA (iv) → BPGA to 3-PGA (i) → 3-PGA to 2-phosphoglycerate (ii).

nuggets.title: Glycolysis: ATP balance and fates of pyruvate
lines: Per glucose, glycolysis uses 2 ATP and directly forms 4 ATP by substrate-level steps, giving a net gain of 2 ATP.
Glycolysis also yields 2 NADH + H+ per glucose, and needs no oxygen at any step.
Pyruvic acid is the key product of glycolysis; its metabolic fate depends on the cellular need.
There are three major fates of pyruvate: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration.
Under aerobic conditions pyruvate enters mitochondria for complete oxidation to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O; under anaerobic conditions it is fermented.

questions.why: 2 ATP are used in glycolysis: at glucose → glucose-6-phosphate and at fructose-6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. 4 is the number of ATP formed.
Glucose → 2 pyruvate forms 4 ATP but spends 2 ATP, so the net gain is 2 ATP (plus 2 NADH).
ATP is synthesised at BPGA → 3-PGA and PEP → pyruvic acid. Fructose-6-P → fructose-1,6-bisP uses ATP.
Pyruvic acid has three major fates: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration, so all of these.
Zero: glycolysis needs no O2; that is why it is common to aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

nuggets.title: Fermentation: alcohol and lactic acid
lines: In fermentation, glucose is incompletely oxidised under anaerobic conditions by a set of reactions that convert pyruvic acid to CO2 and ethanol (yeast) or lactic acid.
In yeast, enzymes pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase convert pyruvic acid to CO2 and ethanol.
Some bacteria produce lactic acid from pyruvic acid; in animal muscle cells during exercise, low O2 leads pyruvate to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase.
In both fermentations, the reducing agent NADH + H+ is reoxidised to NAD+.
CO2 is released only in alcoholic fermentation; lactic acid fermentation neither uses O2 nor releases CO2.
nuggets.tip: Yeast: decarboxylase + alcohol dehydrogenase. Muscle: lactate dehydrogenase.

questions.why: Yeast uses pyruvic acid decarboxylase (removes CO2) and then alcohol dehydrogenase to give ethanol. Lactate dehydrogenase makes lactic acid instead.
In muscle cells under low O2, pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase, using NADH + H+.
Lactate fermentation releases no CO2: pyruvate is reduced directly to lactic acid. Alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration both release CO2.
In lactic acid fermentation neither O2 is used nor CO2 liberated; pyruvate (3C) becomes lactate (3C) without decarboxylation.
A true, R false. Fermentation is incomplete oxidation of glucose to lactic acid/ethanol, but it occurs in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes, not prokaryotes only.

nuggets.title: Fermentation: why it is inefficient
lines: In lactic acid and alcohol fermentation, less than 7% of the energy in glucose is released, and not all of it is trapped as ATP.
The processes are hazardous: either acid or alcohol is produced.
Yeasts poison themselves to death when the concentration of alcohol reaches about 13%.
Fermentation gives a net gain of only 2 ATP per glucose and is only a partial breakdown of glucose.
Fermentation takes place in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes; organisms needing more energy use aerobic respiration.
nuggets.tip: Fermentation numbers: <7% energy, 13% alcohol, net 2 ATP.

questions.why: Fermentation releases less than 7% of the energy of glucose, and not all of it is trapped as ATP.
A incorrect, B correct. Less than 7% energy is released but not all of it is trapped as ATP; yeast dies at about 13% alcohol.
Yeasts poison themselves to death when alcohol concentration reaches about 13%.
A correct, B incorrect. Net gain is only 2 ATP per glucose, and fermentation is a partial, not complete, breakdown of glucose.
A correct, B incorrect. Fermentation occurs in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes, not multicellular eukaryotes.

nuggets.title: Aerobic respiration: the overview
lines: Aerobic respiration leads to complete oxidation of organic substances in the presence of O2, releasing CO2, water and a large amount of energy.
This type of respiration is most common in higher organisms and takes place within the mitochondria.
Pyruvate formed by glycolysis in the cytoplasm is transported from the cytoplasm into the mitochondria.
Event 1, in the matrix: complete oxidation of pyruvate by stepwise removal of all H atoms, leaving three molecules of CO2.
Event 2, on the inner mitochondrial membrane: electrons removed with the H atoms pass to O2 with simultaneous synthesis of ATP.
nuggets.tip: One pyruvate → 3 CO<sub>2</sub> (1 in link reaction + 2 in Krebs cycle).

questions.why: Both incorrect. Complete oxidation of pyruvate leaves three CO2, not two; and electron passage to O2 is coupled to synthesis of ATP, not ADP.
A correct, B incorrect. Aerobic respiration is complete oxidation in the presence of O2, but it is most common in higher organisms.
Aerobic respiration is complete oxidation of organic substances in the presence of O2; incomplete oxidation without O2 is fermentation.
Both the TCA cycle (matrix) and ETS (inner membrane) take place in mitochondria; glycolysis is the step in the cytoplasm.

nuggets.title: Link reaction: pyruvate to acetyl CoA
lines: In the mitochondrial matrix pyruvate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation catalysed by pyruvic dehydrogenase.
Pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH + H+, in the presence of Mg2+.
The pyruvic dehydrogenase reactions need several coenzymes, including NAD+ and coenzyme A.
Two molecules of NADH are produced from the two pyruvic acids formed from one glucose.
Acetyl CoA then enters the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle in the mitochondrial matrix.
nuggets.tip: Pyruvate loses CO<sub>2</sub> (not O<sub>2</sub>) in the link reaction.

questions.why: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA in the presence of Mg2+, as NCERT's equation shows.
Both correct. Pyruvate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase, which needs several coenzymes including NAD+ and CoA.
A incorrect, B correct. Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA releases CO2, not O2; acetyl CoA then enters the Krebs cycle in the matrix.
The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex works in the mitochondrial matrix, after pyruvate moves in from the cytoplasm.
Pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH + H+; no O2 or water is formed.

nuggets.title: TCA cycle: start and decarboxylations
lines: The TCA cycle was first elucidated by Hans Krebs and is also called the citric acid cycle.
It starts with condensation of the acetyl group with oxaloacetic acid (OAA) and water to give citric acid, catalysed by citrate synthase; CoA is released.
Citrate is then isomerised to isocitrate.
Two successive decarboxylations follow, forming α-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl-CoA.
Carbon counts: OAA and succinic acid are 4C, α-ketoglutaric acid is 5C, citric and isocitric acid are 6C.
nuggets.tip: Acetyl CoA condenses with OAA, not with pyruvic acid.

questions.why: The first TCA reaction, acetyl CoA + OAA + water → citric acid, is catalysed by citrate synthase. Pyruvate dehydrogenase works before the cycle.
Citric acid undergoes isomerisation to form isocitrate, then two successive decarboxylations follow.
Both false. Acetyl CoA (not pyruvate) condenses with OAA and water, and the enzyme is citrate synthase, not pyruvate synthase.
Oxidative decarboxylation occurs when acetyl CoA forms from pyruvate and when succinyl CoA forms from α-ketoglutarate.
Succinic acid is 4C, α-ketoglutaric acid 5C and citric acid 6C. Oxaloacetic acid is 4C and pyruvic acid 3C, so the other options fail.

nuggets.title: TCA cycle: products and regeneration
lines: During conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinic acid a molecule of GTP is synthesised (substrate-level phosphorylation).
In a coupled reaction GTP is converted to GDP with simultaneous synthesis of ATP from ADP.
Succinyl-CoA is further oxidised to OAA, so OAA is regenerated and the cycle continues.
There are three points where NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+ and one point where FAD+ is reduced to FADH2.
Continued oxidation of acetyl CoA needs continued replenishment of OAA and regeneration of NAD+ and FAD+ from NADH and FADH2.
Per pyruvate: Pyruvic acid + 4NAD+ + FAD+ + 2H2O + ADP + Pi → 3CO2 + 4NADH + 4H+ + FADH2 + ATP.
nuggets.tip: Krebs per turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>, 1 GTP.

questions.why: Wrong statement: the cycle starts by condensing acetyl CoA with oxaloacetic acid, not pyruvic acid. The other three statements match NCERT.
A correct, B incorrect. GTP forms at succinyl-CoA → succinic acid, but NAD+ is reduced at three points and FAD+ at one, not the reverse.
Both incorrect. The cycle needs replenishment of OAA (not citric acid), and regeneration of NAD+ and FAD+ from NADH and FADH2.
Succinyl-CoA → succinic acid involves no oxidation; it is the substrate-level step forming GTP. The other steps are dehydrogenations or decarboxylations.
GTP is synthesised during conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinic acid; GTP then gives ATP in a coupled reaction.

nuggets.title: Electron transport system: the complexes
lines: The electron transport system (ETS), the pathway through which electrons pass from one carrier to another, is present in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Electrons from NADH are oxidised by NADH dehydrogenase (complex I) and transferred to ubiquinone, located within the inner membrane.
Ubiquinone also receives electrons from FADH2 via complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), which is generated in the citric acid cycle.
Reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) is oxidised by cytochrome bc1 complex (complex III), which passes electrons to cytochrome c.
Cytochrome c is a small protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane and is a mobile carrier between complexes III and IV.
Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase, containing cytochromes a and a3 and two copper centres.
nuggets.tip: Mobile carriers: ubiquinone and cytochrome c.

questions.why: Both false. Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase and complex III is cytochrome bc1; cytochrome c shuttles electrons between complexes III and IV.
A correct, B incorrect. Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase with cytochromes a, a3 and two (not three) copper centres.
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) has cytochromes a and a3 and two copper centres.
Complex I = NADH dehydrogenase, II = succinate dehydrogenase, III = cytochrome bc<sub>1</sub> complex, IV = cytochrome c oxidase.
A incorrect, B correct. ETS passes electrons (not protons) from one carrier to another, and it lies in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

nuggets.title: Oxidative phosphorylation
lines: When electrons pass from complex I to IV, they are coupled to ATP synthase (complex V) for production of ATP from ADP and Pi.
The number of ATP made depends on the nature of the electron donor: one NADH gives 3 ATP, one FADH2 gives 2 ATP.
Role of O2 is limited to the terminal stage, but it is vital: it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen as the final hydrogen acceptor.
Unlike photophosphorylation, where light makes the proton gradient, here the energy of oxidation-reduction is used, so it is called oxidative phosphorylation.
nuggets.tip: NADH → 3 ATP, FADH<sub>2</sub> → 2 ATP. Never the reverse.

questions.why: Incorrect statement: one NADH + H+ gives 3 ATP and one FADH2 gives 2, not the reverse. The other three statements are NCERT facts.
Both true and R explains A: ATP yield depends on the nature of the electron donor, so NADH gives 3 ATP and FADH2 gives 2.
Both correct. O2 is vital because it drives the process by removing hydrogen, acting as the final hydrogen acceptor.
O2 is the final hydrogen acceptor. ETS is in the inner membrane (not matrix), NADH gives 3 ATP, and redox energy, not light, makes the gradient.
Oxidative phosphorylation is ATP formation using energy of electrons removed during substrate oxidation. Direct phosphate transfer from a substrate is substrate-level phosphorylation.

nuggets.title: ATP synthase and the proton gradient
lines: Energy released by the electron transport chain is used to make ATP with the help of ATP synthase (complex V).
Complex V has two major components, F1 and F0.
The F1 headpiece is a peripheral membrane protein complex and contains the site for synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
F0 is an integral membrane protein complex that forms the channel through which protons cross the inner membrane.
Protons pumped into the intermembrane space flow back to the matrix through F0, down the proton gradient, driving ATP synthesis at F1.
nuggets.tip: F<sub>1</sub> = peripheral head (makes ATP); F<sub>0</sub> = integral channel (passes H<sup>+</sup>).

questions.why: Both incorrect. F1 is a peripheral (not central) protein complex, and F0 is an integral (not peripheral) complex forming the proton channel.
A correct, B incorrect. Energy of ETS is used by ATP synthase, but complex V is made of F1 and F0, not F1 and F2.
F0 is an integral membrane protein complex that forms the channel for protons across the inner membrane.
Protons are pumped into and accumulate in the intermembrane space; their return to the matrix through F0 drives ATP synthesis.
Chemiosmosis: ATP forms because a proton gradient builds across the inner membrane and protons flow back through ATP synthase.

nuggets.title: Respiratory balance sheet
lines: Net ATP per glucose can be calculated only on assumptions: a sequential, orderly pathway (glycolysis → TCA cycle → ETS) functions.
Assumption: NADH made in glycolysis is transferred into the mitochondria and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation.
Assumption: no intermediate is used to make other compounds, and only glucose is respired, with no alternative substrates entering.
On these assumptions there is a net gain of 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration; in living systems all pathways work simultaneously, so it is theoretical.
Fermentation is partial breakdown with net 2 ATP and slow NADH → NAD<sup>+</sup>; aerobic respiration is complete breakdown with vigorous NADH reoxidation.
nuggets.tip: 38 ATP is a theoretical figure valid only under the balance-sheet assumptions.

questions.why: All three are NCERT's assumptions: a sequential pathway, glycolytic NADH entering mitochondria, and no intermediates diverted or other substrates added.
Both correct. Under the balance-sheet assumptions, with glucose as the substrate, aerobic respiration gives a net gain of 38 ATP.
Fermentation does partially break down glucose, but it occurs in the cytoplasm (not mitochondria) and its NADH → NAD<sup>+</sup> is slow, not vigorous.
All are incorrect for anaerobic respiration: it occurs in the cytoplasm, breaks glucose down only partially, and nets 2 ATP, not 38.
The NADH made in glycolysis is transferred into mitochondria and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation, an assumption of the balance sheet.

nuggets.title: Respiration as an amphibolic pathway
lines: Glucose is the favoured substrate; other carbohydrates are converted into glucose before use.
Fats are broken into glycerol and fatty acids; fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA, and glycerol enters after conversion to PGAL.
Proteins are degraded by proteases, and the resulting amino acids enter the pathway at some stage within the Krebs cycle or even as pyruvate or acetyl CoA.
When fatty acids are synthesised, acetyl CoA is withdrawn from the pathway, so respiratory intermediates are also used in synthesis.
Because it involves both catabolism and anabolism, the respiratory pathway is better called an amphibolic pathway rather than a catabolic one.
nuggets.tip: Acetyl CoA is the common entry point for fats, carbohydrates and proteins.

questions.why: The respiratory pathway is amphibolic: it breaks down substrates (catabolism) and supplies intermediates such as acetyl CoA for synthesis (anabolism).
Both true and R explains A: the pathway is amphibolic because its intermediates are used in both breakdown and synthesis.
Both correct. Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA before entering, and glycerol enters after conversion to PGAL.
Acetyl CoA is common to the respiratory breakdown of fats (via fatty acids), carbohydrates (via pyruvate) and proteins (some amino acids).
Both correct. Fatty acids are broken to acetyl CoA for respiration, and acetyl CoA is withdrawn from the pathway when fatty acids must be synthesised.

nuggets.title: Respiratory quotient (RQ)
lines: Respiratory quotient (RQ) = volume of CO2 evolved / volume of O2 consumed; it depends on the type of respiratory substrate.
When carbohydrates are completely oxidised, equal amounts of CO2 and O2 are evolved and consumed, so RQ is 1.
When fats are used, RQ is less than 1; for tripalmitin, 2(C51H98O6) + 145O2 → 102CO2 + 98H2O, giving RQ 0.7.
When proteins are respiratory substrates, the ratio is about 0.9.
In living organisms respiratory substrates are often more than one; pure proteins or fats are never used as respiratory substrates.
nuggets.tip: RQ: carbohydrate 1, protein 0.9, fat (tripalmitin) 0.7.

questions.why: RQ of tripalmitin = 102 CO2 / 145 O2 = 0.7. 0.9 is the RQ of proteins.
RQ = CO2 evolved / O2 consumed = 102/145 ≈ 0.7, the RQ of the fat tripalmitin.
Both correct. RQ is CO2 evolved / O2 consumed, and its value depends on the type of respiratory substrate.
A incorrect, B correct. Fats give RQ less than 1 (tripalmitin 0.7); proteins give about 0.9.
A correct, B incorrect. Pure proteins or fats are never used as substrates; tripalmitin's RQ is 0.7, not 0.6.

nuggets.title: Growth: definition and the open form of growth
lines: Growth is one of the most fundamental and conspicuous characteristics of a living being.
Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts or even of an individual cell.
Growth is accompanied by metabolic processes (both anabolic and catabolic) that occur at the expense of energy.
Plant growth is unique: plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout life because of meristems at certain locations.
Meristem cells can divide and self-perpetuate; their products lose the capacity to divide and make up the plant body.
New cells are always being added to the plant body by meristem activity: this is the open form of growth.
nuggets.tip: Swelling of wood in water is reversible, so it is NOT growth; expansion of a leaf is growth.

questions.why: Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size. A temporary or reversible change (e.g. turgor swelling) is not growth, and growth never means a decrease.
NCERT: growth is accompanied by metabolic processes, both anabolic and catabolic, that occur at the expense of energy. Hence 'Both 1 and 2'.
Expansion of a leaf is an irreversible increase in size, so it is growth. Swelling of wood in water is reversible physical imbibition, not growth.
Continuous addition of new cells by meristem activity is the open form of growth, the reason plant growth is generally indeterminate.
Both true and linked: plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout life (due to meristems), which is why plant growth is indeterminate (open).

nuggets.title: Primary and secondary growth
lines: Root apical meristem and shoot apical meristem are responsible for the primary growth of plants.
Primary growth principally contributes to the elongation of the plant along its axis.
In dicotyledonous plants and gymnosperms, the lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork-cambium) appear later in life.
Lateral meristems increase the girth of the organs in which they are active; this is secondary growth.
nuggets.tip: Apical = length (primary); lateral (vascular + cork cambium) = girth (secondary).

questions.why: Root and shoot apical meristems cause primary growth, i.e. elongation along the axis. Increase along the radius/girth is due to lateral meristems.
In dicots and gymnosperms the lateral meristems, vascular cambium and cork-cambium, appear later in life and bring about secondary growth.
I, III and IV are correct. II is wrong: girth increases due to lateral meristems (vascular and cork cambium), not apical meristems.
Only the lateral meristems increase girth. Shoot and root apical meristems cause elongation along the axis (primary growth).
Meristem cells divide and self-perpetuate (A–S); constant addition of cells = open growth (B–R); apical meristem = primary growth (C–P); vascular and cork cambium = secondary growth (D–Q).

nuggets.title: Growth is measurable
lines: At the cellular level, growth is principally a consequence of increase in the amount of protoplasm.
Since protoplasm is hard to measure directly, we measure a quantity more or less proportional to it.
Growth parameters: increase in fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number.
One single maize root apical meristem can give rise to more than 17,500 new cells per hour.
Cells in a watermelon may increase in size by up to 3,50,000 times.
Growth of a pollen tube is measured as its length; growth of a dorsiventral leaf as increase in surface area.
nuggets.tip: Maize root = cell NUMBER (17,500/hour); watermelon = cell SIZE (3,50,000 times).

questions.why: Growth at the cellular level is principally a consequence of increase in the amount of protoplasm, not of any single organelle.
All six (fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number) are listed by NCERT as growth parameters, so the answer is 6.
A single maize root apical meristem gives rise to more than 17,500 new cells per hour. 3,50,000 is the watermelon cell-size figure.
Pollen tube growth is measured as length; a dorsiventral leaf's growth as increase in surface area.
I, II and IV are NCERT facts. III is wrong: a dorsiventral leaf's growth is measured as increase in surface area, not volume.

nuggets.title: Phases of growth: meristematic, elongation, maturation
lines: The period of growth has three phases: meristematic, elongation and maturation.
Meristematic cells at root and shoot apex divide constantly; they are rich in protoplasm with large conspicuous nuclei.
Meristematic cell walls are primary, thin and cellulosic, with abundant plasmodesmatal connections.
Cells just next to the meristematic zone, away from the tip (proximal), are in elongation: increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, new wall deposition.
Further from the apex lies the maturation zone, where cells attain maximal size in wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications.
Most tissues and cell types studied in plant anatomy represent the maturation phase.
nuggets.tip: Meristematic = large nuclei, thin walls; elongation = vacuolation; maturation = wall thickening.

questions.why: Meristematic cells are rich in protoplasm and possess large conspicuous nuclei; 'inconspicuous nuclei' is the trap.
Meristematic cell walls are primary in nature, thin and cellulosic, with abundant plasmodesmatal connections, so all of the above.
Elongation-phase cells lie proximal to the meristematic zone, i.e. just next to it and away from the tip.
Increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new cell wall deposition characterise the elongation phase, not the dividing meristematic phase.
Meristematic = constantly dividing cells (A–Q); elongation = increased vacuolation (B–P); maturation = maximal size in wall thickening (C–R).

nuggets.title: Growth rate and arithmetic growth
lines: The increased growth per unit time is termed the growth rate; it may be arithmetic or geometrical.
In arithmetic growth, after mitosis only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates and matures.
The simplest example of arithmetic growth is a root elongating at a constant rate.
Plotting length against time in arithmetic growth gives a linear curve.
Arithmetic growth is expressed as Lt = L0 + rt, where r is the growth rate (elongation per unit time).

questions.why: In arithmetic growth one daughter cell keeps dividing while the other differentiates and matures. In geometric growth both keep dividing.
A root elongating at a constant rate is the simplest expression of arithmetic growth, giving a straight line against time.
Arithmetic growth: Lt = L0 + rt. W1 = W0ert is the exponential (geometric) equation.
A root elongating at a constant rate shows arithmetic growth, which is why its length–time plot is linear; Reason explains Assertion.
Arithmetic growth: one daughter cell continues to divide while the other matures; exemplified by a root elongating at a constant rate.

nuggets.title: Geometric growth and the sigmoid curve
lines: In geometric growth, both progeny cells after mitosis retain the ability to divide and continue to do so.
Initial growth is slow (lag phase), then increases rapidly at an exponential rate (log or exponential phase).
With limited nutrient supply, growth slows down, leading to a stationary phase.
Growth plotted against time gives a typical sigmoid or S-curve, characteristic of organisms growing in a natural environment.
Exponential growth: W1 = W0ert; W0 initial size, W1 final size, t time, e base of natural logarithms.
r is the relative growth rate, a measure of the ability to produce new plant material, called the efficiency index.
nuggets.tip: Sigmoid order: lag → log (exponential) → stationary.

questions.why: When both progeny cells retain the ability to divide and continue dividing, growth is geometric. In arithmetic growth only one keeps dividing.
With limited nutrient supply growth slows down, leading to the stationary phase of the sigmoid curve.
Sigmoid growth runs lag → log (exponential) → stationary, i.e. C, A, B.
Exponential (geometric) growth is W1 = W0ert. Lt = L0 + rt is arithmetic growth.
In W1 = W0ert, r is the relative growth rate, also the measure of the ability to produce new plant material, called the efficiency index. So all apply.

nuggets.title: Absolute vs relative growth rate
lines: Quantitative comparisons of growth of living systems can be made in two ways: absolute and relative growth rate.
Absolute growth rate: measurement and comparison of total growth per unit time.
Relative growth rate: growth per unit time expressed on a common basis, e.g. per unit initial parameter.
Two leaves of different sizes can show the same absolute increase in area, yet the smaller leaf has the higher relative growth rate.
nuggets.tip: Absolute = total gain per time; relative = gain divided by initial size.

questions.why: Total growth per unit time is the absolute growth rate. Dividing it by the initial size gives the relative growth rate.
Growth per unit time expressed per unit initial parameter is the relative growth rate.
Relative rate = gain/initial size: A = 7/7 = 100%, B = 10/20 = 50%. So A has the higher relative growth rate.
Absolute rate is total gain per time: A gained 7 cm2, B gained 10 cm2 in 3 days, so B has the higher absolute growth rate.
Statement A is wrong: comparisons are made in two ways (absolute and relative), not five. Statement B is NCERT's definition of absolute growth rate.

nuggets.title: Conditions for growth
lines: Plant cells grow by cell enlargement, which requires water; growth is intimately linked to the plant's water status.
Turgidity of cells helps in extension growth; water also provides the medium for enzymatic activities.
Oxygen helps in releasing metabolic energy essential for growth activities.
Nutrients (macro and micro essential elements) are needed to synthesise protoplasm and act as a source of energy.
Every plant has an optimum temperature range for growth; any deviation could be detrimental to its survival.
Environmental signals such as light and gravity also affect certain phases/stages of growth.

questions.why: NCERT: turgidity of cells helps in extension growth. Plasticity and elasticity are not the terms used.
Water provides the medium for the enzymatic activities needed for growth.
Oxygen helps in releasing metabolic energy (through respiration) essential for growth activities.
Every plant has an optimum temperature range; any deviation from it could be detrimental to its survival.
A is wrong: turgidity helps extension growth, it does not inhibit it. B is correct: oxygen helps release metabolic energy.

nuggets.title: Differentiation: structure matches function
lines: Cells derived from root and shoot apical meristems and cambium differentiate and mature to perform specific functions.
During differentiation cells undergo few to major structural changes in both their cell walls and protoplasm.
To form a tracheary element, cells lose their protoplasm and develop strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary walls.
Such walls let tracheary elements carry water to long distances even under extreme tension.
Differentiation in plants is open: cells/tissues arising from the same meristem have different structures at maturity.
Final structure depends on location: cells away from the root apical meristem become root-cap cells; those pushed to the periphery become epidermis.
nuggets.tip: Open differentiation: same meristem, different mature structures, decided by position.

questions.why: Maturation of meristem-derived cells into cells performing specific functions is differentiation; de- and redifferentiation come later.
During differentiation cells change in both cell walls and protoplasm, e.g. tracheary elements lose protoplasm and gain lignified walls.
Tracheary elements lose protoplasm and develop strong lignocellulosic secondary walls to carry water to long distances even under extreme tension.
Differentiation is open because cells/tissues arising from the same meristem have different structures at maturity.
Incorrect statement: cells pushed to the periphery from the root apical meristem mature as epidermis, not pith.

nuggets.title: Dedifferentiation and redifferentiation
lines: Living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide can regain it under certain conditions: dedifferentiation.
Formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from fully differentiated parenchyma cells is dedifferentiation.
Dedifferentiated cells divide and produce cells that again lose the capacity to divide and mature: redifferentiation.
Secondary xylem, secondary phloem and cork of a woody dicot are products of redifferentiation.
Parenchyma cells made to divide in plant tissue culture to form a callus are undergoing dedifferentiation.
nuggets.tip: Meristem → differentiation → dedifferentiation → redifferentiation.

questions.why: Sequence: divisions in primary meristem → differentiation → dedifferentiation (e.g. cork cambium forms) → redifferentiation (cork, secondary tissues).
Dedifferentiated tissues produce cells that again lose the ability to divide and mature for specific functions: redifferentiation.
Secondary xylem, secondary phloem and cork are produced by dedifferentiated cambia and mature again, so all are products of redifferentiation.
Mature mesophyll cells regaining the ability to divide to form callus is dedifferentiation.
Fully differentiated parenchyma regaining division to form interfascicular cambium is dedifferentiation, not redifferentiation.

nuggets.title: Development and plasticity
lines: Development includes all changes an organism goes through in its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence.
A cell's development: meristematic cell → cell division → plasmatic growth → differentiation → maturation → mature cell.
Plasticity: plants follow different pathways in response to environment or phases of life to form different kinds of structures.
Heterophylly in cotton, coriander and larkspur: juvenile leaves differ in shape from mature leaves (phase of life).
In buttercup, leaves produced in air differ from those produced in water (environment).
Development = growth + differentiation; it is controlled by intrinsic (genetic, PGRs) and extrinsic (light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition) factors.
nuggets.tip: Cotton/coriander/larkspur = phase of life; buttercup = environment (air vs water).

questions.why: All changes from seed germination to senescence make up development.
Correct sequence: meristematic cell → plasmatic growth → differentiation → mature cell.
Plasticity (heterophylly) is shown by coriander, buttercup and cotton (also larkspur). Maize is not an NCERT example.
Cotton heterophylly is due to phase of life (A–R), buttercup's due to environment (B–P), and development = growth + differentiation (C–Q).
Assertion is NCERT. Reason is wrong: development is controlled by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors, not extrinsic only.

nuggets.title: Plant growth regulators: nature and groups
lines: PGRs are small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition, also called plant growth substances or phytohormones.
Chemical classes: indole compounds (IAA), adenine derivatives (N6-furfurylamino purine, kinetin), carotenoid derivatives (ABA).
Gibberellic acid (GA3) is a terpene; ethylene (C2H4) is a gas.
Growth promoters (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins) aid cell division, enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting and seed formation.
Growth inhibitors act in dormancy, abscission and responses to wounds and stresses; ABA is the main inhibitor.
