Ethylene could fit either group but is largely an inhibitor of growth activities.
nuggets.tip: IAA = indole, kinetin = adenine, ABA = carotenoid, GA = terpene, ethylene = gas.

questions.why: Indole compounds = IAA (A–P), adenine derivatives = kinetin (B–R), carotenoid derivatives = ABA (C–Q), terpenes = GA<sub>3</sub> (D–S).
Promoters drive cell division, enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting and seed formation (1, 2, 3, 5, 6). Dormancy and abscission are inhibitor roles.
Abscisic acid is a growth inhibitor. Auxins and gibberellins are promoters; ethylene can fit either group.
Ethylene is the gaseous PGR, and it is also the one that could fit either group but is largely an inhibitor.
ABA is a derivative of carotenoids. IAA and NAA are auxins; GA is a terpene.

nuggets.title: Discovery of plant growth regulators
lines: Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin saw coleoptiles of canary grass bend towards unilateral light (phototropism); this led to auxin.
F.W. Went isolated auxin from the tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings.
Bakanae (foolish seedling) disease of rice is caused by the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi; E. Kurosawa reproduced it with sterile fungal filtrate, giving gibberellic acid.
F. Skoog found tobacco internode callus proliferated only if auxin was supplemented with vascular extract, yeast extract, coconut milk or DNA; Skoog and Miller crystallised kinetin.
In the mid-1960s, inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin were purified and later proved chemically identical: abscisic acid.
Cousins confirmed a volatile substance from ripened oranges hastened ripening of stored unripened bananas: ethylene.
nuggets.tip: Canary grass = Darwin; oat = Went; rice = Kurosawa; tobacco = Skoog; oranges/bananas = Cousins.

questions.why: Charles and Francis Darwin observed phototropic bending of coleoptiles of canary grass.
F.W. Went isolated auxin from tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings, not canary grass (Darwin) or rice.
E. Kurosawa showed that sterile filtrate of Gibberella fujikuroi reproduced bakanae symptoms in uninfected rice seedlings.
Darwins: canary grass phototropism (A–S); Went: auxin from oat (B–R); Kurosawa: rice (C–P); Skoog: tobacco internodes (D–T); Cousins: oranges (E–Q).
Inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin proved chemically identical and were named abscisic acid.

nuggets.title: Auxins: nature and effects on rooting, flowering and abscission
lines: Auxin (Greek auxein: to grow) was first isolated from human urine; the term is applied to IAA and other natural and synthetic compounds.
IAA and IBA are natural auxins isolated from plants; NAA and 2,4-D are synthetic auxins.
Auxins help to initiate rooting in stem cuttings, an application widely used for plant propagation.
Auxins promote flowering, e.g. in pineapples.
Auxins prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages but promote abscission of older mature leaves and fruits.
Auxins induce parthenocarpy, e.g. in tomatoes.

questions.why: Auxin was first isolated from human urine; Went later isolated it from oat coleoptile tips.
All correct: auxein = to grow, first isolated from human urine; IAA and IBA are natural; NAA and 2,4-D are synthetic auxins.
Auxin's ability to initiate rooting in stem cuttings is applied widely for plant propagation.
Early fruit and leaf drop is prevented by auxins; ethylene does the opposite by promoting abscission.
Both are true NCERT lines, but promoting abscission of older leaves does not explain preventing early drop, so Reason is not the explanation.

nuggets.title: Auxins: apical dominance, herbicides, xylem
lines: In higher plants the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of lateral (axillary) buds: apical dominance.
Removal of shoot tips (decapitation) usually makes lateral buds grow; it is widely used in tea plantations and hedge-making.
Auxins are widely used as herbicides; 2,4-D kills dicotyledonous weeds.
2,4-D does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants, so gardeners use it to prepare weed-free lawns.
Auxin also controls xylem differentiation and helps in cell division.
nuggets.tip: Decapitation removes apical dominance, making tea bushes and hedges dense.

questions.why: Pruning removes the auxin-producing apex, freeing axillary buds from apical dominance, so lateral branches grow and the hedge becomes dense.
Decapitation (removing shoot tips) is widely used in tea plantations and hedge-making; parthenocarpy is a separate auxin effect.
2,4-D, a synthetic auxin, is widely used to kill dicotyledonous weeds.
2,4-D kills dicot weeds but does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants such as grasses, hence weed-free lawns.
Auxin controls xylem differentiation and helps in cell division; phloem differentiation is not the NCERT line.

nuggets.title: Gibberellins: nature, fruits and malting
lines: There are more than 100 gibberellins (GA1, GA2, GA3…) from fungi and higher plants; GA3 was the first discovered and most studied.
All GAs are acidic.
GAs increase the length of axis, used to increase the length of grape stalks.
GAs make apples elongate and improve their shape.
GAs delay senescence, so fruits can be left on the tree longer to extend the market period.
GA3 is used to speed up the malting process in the brewing industry.

questions.why: NCERT reports more than 100 gibberellins from widely different organisms such as fungi and higher plants.
All gibberellins are acidic in nature (gibberellic acids).
GAs cause apples to elongate and improve their shape; sweetness is not an NCERT effect.
GAs delay senescence, so fruits stay on the tree longer and the market period is extended.
A is wrong: gibberellins delay senescence. B is correct: GA3 speeds up malting in brewing.

nuggets.title: Gibberellins: sugarcane, conifers and bolting
lines: Sugarcane stores carbohydrate as sugar in its stem; spraying it with gibberellins increases stem length.
This raises sugarcane yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.
Spraying juvenile conifers with GAs hastens the maturity period, leading to early seed production.
Gibberellins promote bolting (internode elongation just prior to flowering) in beet, cabbages and many plants with rosette habit.
nuggets.tip: Bolting = internode elongation just before flowering in rosette plants, caused by GA.

questions.why: Gibberellin spray on sugarcane increases stem length and yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.
Gibberellins increase sugarcane stem length and hence yield. Auxin, cytokinin and ABA do not have this NCERT use.
Gibberellic acid sprayed on juvenile conifers hastens maturity and leads to early seed production.
Auxin is linked to apical dominance as gibberellin is linked to bolting, internode elongation before flowering in rosette plants.
Incorrect statement: GAs on conifers cause early (not late) seed production. The other statements are true.

nuggets.title: Cytokinins
lines: Cytokinins have specific effects on cytokinesis; they were discovered as kinetin, a modified adenine (a purine), from autoclaved herring sperm DNA.
Kinetin does not occur naturally in plants; the natural cytokinin zeatin was isolated from corn kernels and coconut milk.
Natural cytokinins are synthesised where rapid cell division occurs: root apices, developing shoot buds and young fruits.
Cytokinins help produce new leaves, chloroplasts in leaves, lateral shoot growth and adventitious shoot formation.
Cytokinins help overcome apical dominance.
They promote nutrient mobilisation, which helps delay leaf senescence.
nuggets.tip: Kinetin is synthetic (herring sperm DNA); zeatin is natural (corn, coconut milk).

questions.why: Both correct: kinetin (modified adenine, a purine) came from autoclaved herring sperm DNA, and kinetin does not occur naturally in plants.
Zeatin was isolated from both corn kernels and coconut milk.
I is wrong: adenine is a purine, not a pyrimidine. V is wrong: ABA is a growth inhibitor. II, III and IV are true.
Natural cytokinins are made where rapid cell division occurs: root apices, developing shoot buds and young fruits, so all of them.
Cytokinins delay leaf senescence by promoting nutrient mobilisation.

nuggets.title: Ethylene: physiological effects
lines: Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR, synthesised in large amounts by tissues undergoing senescence and by ripening fruits.
It causes horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings.
Ethylene promotes senescence and abscission and enhances respiration during fruit ripening: the respiratory climactic.
It breaks seed and bud dormancy, initiates germination in peanut seeds and sprouting of potato tubers.
It promotes rapid internode/petiole elongation in deep water rice, keeping upper shoot parts above water.
It promotes root growth and root hair formation, increasing the absorption surface.
nuggets.tip: Peanut SEEDS germinate, potato TUBERS sprout: a common swap trap.

questions.why: Ethylene causes apical hook formation in dicot seedlings, swelling of the axis and horizontal growth of seedlings, so all of them.
The rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening, enhanced by ethylene, is the respiratory climactic.
A is wrong: respiratory climactic is a rise, not a decrease, in respiration. B is correct: peanut seed germination and potato tuber sprouting.
Ethylene promotes rapid internode/petiole elongation in deep water rice so leaves stay above water.
The gaseous PGR ethylene promotes root growth and root hair formation. Overcoming apical dominance is cytokinin; weed-killing is auxin; malting is GA.

nuggets.title: Ethylene in agriculture and ethephon
lines: Ethylene is used to initiate flowering and to synchronise fruit-set in pineapples; it also induces flowering in mango.
Ethylene is the most widely used PGR in agriculture, as it regulates so many physiological processes.
Ethephon, the most widely used source of ethylene, is absorbed readily in aqueous solution, transported and releases ethylene slowly.
Ethephon hastens fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples and accelerates abscission in flowers and fruits (thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut).
Ethephon promotes female flowers in cucumbers, thereby increasing the yield.
nuggets.tip: Cucumber + ethylene = more female flowers = more yield.

questions.why: Ethylene initiates flowering and synchronises fruit-set in pineapples.
Ethylene regulates so many processes that it is the most widely used PGR in agriculture.
Ethephon is the most widely used compound as a source of ethylene.
Ethephon accelerates abscission in flowers and fruits, used for thinning of cotton, cherry and walnut, so all of them.
Ethylene (via ethephon) promotes female flowers in cucumbers, raising yield.

nuggets.title: Abscisic acid: the stress hormone
lines: ABA was discovered for its role in regulating abscission and dormancy.
ABA acts as a general plant growth inhibitor and an inhibitor of plant metabolism; it inhibits seed germination.
ABA stimulates the closure of stomata in the epidermis.
ABA increases the tolerance of plants to various kinds of stresses, so it is called the stress hormone.
ABA plays a role in seed development, maturation and dormancy, helping seeds withstand desiccation.
In most situations ABA acts as an antagonist to GAs.
nuggets.tip: ABA vs GA: ABA induces dormancy; GA breaks it.

questions.why: ABA is a general growth inhibitor, an inhibitor of plant metabolism and stimulates stomatal closure, so all of them.
ABA is the stress hormone because it increases the tolerance of plants to various stresses; it does not remove the stress.
ABA is called the stress hormone. Ethylene, GA3 and IAA are not.
In most situations ABA acts as an antagonist to gibberellins.
A is correct (stomatal closure, stress tolerance). B is wrong: ABA is an antagonist, not a protagonist, to GAs.

nuggets.title: PGRs act together
lines: PGRs play individualistic or synergistic roles, which may be complementary or antagonistic.
One PGR has diverse effects, and diverse PGRs can manifest similar effects.
Dormancy, abscission, senescence and apical dominance are each influenced by more than one PGR.
Extrinsic factors such as temperature and light control plant growth and development, including flowering, via PGRs.
Example of antagonism: auxin causes apical dominance while cytokinins help overcome it; ABA likewise antagonises GAs.

questions.why: PGRs can act individualistically or synergistically, and their roles may be complementary or antagonistic, so both.
Both are NCERT points: one PGR has diverse effects and diverse PGRs can produce similar effects.
Temperature and light act through PGRs to control flowering (and other developmental events).
Gibberellin hastens maturity of juvenile conifers, auxin controls xylem differentiation and ABA increases stress tolerance.
IAA: weed-free lawns (A–S); ABA: stomatal closure (B–R); ethylene: fruit ripening (C–T); GA: bolting (D–Q); cytokinin: herring sperm DNA (E–P).

nuggets.title: Respiratory organs across animals
lines: Lower invertebrates like sponges, coelenterates and flatworms exchange O2 and CO2 by simple diffusion over their entire body surface.
Earthworms use their moist cuticle; insects have a network of tracheal tubes to transport atmospheric air within the body.
Special vascularised structures called gills are used by most aquatic arthropods and molluscs (branchial respiration).
Vascularised bags called lungs are used by terrestrial forms (pulmonary respiration).
Among vertebrates, fishes use gills; reptiles, birds and mammals respire through lungs.
Amphibians like frogs respire through lungs and also through their moist skin (cutaneous respiration).
nuggets.tip: Earthworm = moist cuticle; insect = trachea; prawn = gills; frog = lungs + skin.

questions.why: NCERT: lower invertebrates like sponges, coelenterates and flatworms exchange gases by simple diffusion over the entire body surface.
Prawn is an aquatic arthropod, so it uses gills; cockroach is an insect, so it uses tracheal tubes.
Earthworm: moist skin/cuticle (A–P); terrestrial arthropods: trachea (B–S); fishes: gills (C–Q); birds and reptiles: lungs (D–R).
Amphibians such as frogs also respire through moist skin: cutaneous respiration. Earthworms lack trachea, and fishes use gills, not lungs.
A is NCERT. B is wrong: fishes are vertebrates, and amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals respire mainly through lungs, not skin.

nuggets.title: Nose to larynx: the upper passage
lines: A pair of external nostrils leads through the nasal passage into the nasal chamber, which opens into the nasopharynx, part of the pharynx.
The pharynx is the common passage for food and air.
Nasopharynx opens through the glottis of the larynx into the trachea.
Larynx is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production, hence called the sound box.
During swallowing, the glottis is covered by the epiglottis, a thin elastic cartilaginous flap, preventing entry of food into the larynx.
nuggets.tip: Epiglottis = thin ELASTIC cartilage, not bone; it guards the glottis.

questions.why: The nasopharynx opens through the glottis of the larynx region into the trachea.
The epiglottis is a thin elastic cartilaginous flap that covers the glottis during swallowing.
Food entering the windpipe triggers coughing; this follows improper closure of the glottis by the epiglottis during swallowing.
Both are true NCERT lines, but the epiglottis covering the glottis does not explain sound production by the larynx, so Reason is not the explanation.
Incorrect statement: the epiglottis is a thin elastic cartilaginous flap, not a bony one. The other statements are NCERT facts.

nuggets.title: Trachea, bronchial tree and alveoli
lines: Trachea is a straight tube extending up to the mid-thoracic cavity; it divides at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi.
Each bronchus divides repeatedly into secondary and tertiary bronchi and bronchioles, ending in very thin terminal bronchioles.
Trachea, primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings.
Each terminal bronchiole gives rise to very thin, irregular-walled and vascularised bag-like structures called alveoli.
The branching network of bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli makes up the lungs.
nuggets.tip: Cartilage rings stop at the initial bronchioles; alveoli have none.

questions.why: Trachea divides at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi.
Air path: trachea → primary → secondary → tertiary bronchi → initial bronchioles → alveoli.
Incomplete cartilaginous rings support the trachea, bronchi and initial bronchioles only, not all bronchioles.
Alveoli are very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures, not thick or non-vascular.
Both wrong: trachea divides at the 5th (not 6th) thoracic vertebra, and the larynx is a cartilaginous (not tendinous) box.

nuggets.title: Lungs, pleura and the two functional parts
lines: The two lungs are covered by a double-layered pleura, with pleural fluid between them that reduces friction on the lung surface.
The outer pleural membrane is in close contact with the thoracic lining; the inner pleural membrane is in contact with the lung surface.
From external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles is the conducting part; alveoli and their ducts form the respiratory or exchange part.
The conducting part transports air to the alveoli, clears it of foreign particles, humidifies it and brings it to body temperature.
The exchange part is the site of actual diffusion of O2 and CO2 between blood and atmospheric air.
nuggets.tip: Conducting part ends at TERMINAL bronchioles; no gas exchange happens there.

questions.why: Pleural fluid lies between the two layers of the double-layered pleura and reduces friction on the lung surface.
The conducting part runs from the external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles; alveoli and their ducts are the exchange part.
Both are NCERT: external nostrils to terminal bronchioles = conducting part; alveoli and their ducts = respiratory/exchange part.
Providing the surface for O2 and CO2 diffusion is the job of the exchange part (alveoli), not the conducting part.
II and III are correct. I is wrong: the conducting part brings air to body temperature; it does not 'cool down' the air.

nuggets.title: Thoracic chamber and the steps of respiration
lines: Lungs lie in the thoracic chamber, which is anatomically an air-tight chamber.
It is formed dorsally by the vertebral column, ventrally by the sternum, laterally by the ribs and below by the dome-shaped diaphragm.
Any change in thoracic cavity volume is reflected in the lung (pulmonary) cavity; we cannot directly alter pulmonary volume.
Respiration steps: (i) breathing or pulmonary ventilation, (ii) diffusion across the alveolar membrane, (iii) transport of gases by blood.
(iv) Diffusion of O2 and CO2 between blood and tissues; (v) utilisation of O2 by cells for catabolic reactions and release of CO2 (cellular respiration).
nuggets.tip: Dorsal = vertebral column, ventral = sternum: a common swap.

questions.why: Thoracic chamber: dorsally vertebral column, ventrally sternum, laterally ribs, lower side diaphragm.
A is NCERT. B swaps the sides: the vertebral column is dorsal and the sternum is ventral.
Both wrong: thoracic volume changes are reflected in the pulmonary (not abdominal) cavity, and we cannot directly alter pulmonary volume.
Order: pulmonary ventilation → diffusion across alveolar membrane → transport by blood → diffusion between blood and tissues → O2 use by cells.
Drawing in atmospheric air and releasing CO2-rich alveolar air is breathing, also called pulmonary ventilation, so both.

nuggets.title: Inspiration: how air is drawn in
lines: Air moves in and out by creating a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere.
Inspiration occurs when the pressure within the lungs (intra-pulmonary pressure) is less than the atmospheric pressure.
Inspiration is initiated by contraction of the diaphragm, increasing thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis.
Contraction of external inter-costal muscles lifts the ribs and sternum, increasing thoracic volume in the dorso-ventral axis.
The rise in thoracic volume increases pulmonary volume, which lowers intra-pulmonary pressure below atmospheric, so air moves into the lungs.
nuggets.tip: Diaphragm = antero-posterior; external intercostals = dorso-ventral.

questions.why: Diaphragm contraction enlarges the thorax antero-posteriorly; external intercostal contraction lifts ribs and sternum, enlarging it dorso-ventrally.
Contraction of the diaphragm increases thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis.
Inspiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure, so air flows down the gradient into the lungs.
Sequence: muscle contraction → thoracic volume rises → lungs expand → pulmonary volume rises → intra-pulmonary pressure falls → air moves in.
Assertion is NCERT. Reason is wrong: inspiration is initiated by contraction (not relaxation) of the diaphragm and external intercostals.

nuggets.title: Expiration, breathing rate and spirometer
lines: Expiration takes place when intra-pulmonary pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure.
Relaxation of the diaphragm and inter-costal muscles returns diaphragm and sternum to normal, reducing thoracic and pulmonary volume.
Additional muscles in the abdomen help increase the strength of inspiration and expiration.
On average, a healthy human breathes 12–16 times per minute.
The volume of air in breathing movements is estimated with a spirometer, which helps in clinical assessment of pulmonary functions.

questions.why: Normal expiration involves relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, not their contraction.
During expiration there is a reduction in both thoracic and pulmonary volume, raising intra-pulmonary pressure.
Additional muscles in the abdomen can increase the strength of inspiration and expiration.
A spirometer estimates the volume of air in breathing and helps clinical assessment of pulmonary functions.
I and II are wrong: a healthy human breathes 12–16 times/min (not 72), and volumes are measured by a spirometer (not barometer).

nuggets.title: Respiratory volumes: TV, IRV, ERV, RV
lines: Tidal volume (TV): air inspired or expired during normal respiration, approx. 500 mL.
A healthy man can thus inspire or expire about 6000 to 8000 mL of air per minute.
Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV): additional air inspired by forcible inspiration, averaging 2500–3000 mL.
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV): additional air expired by forcible expiration, averaging 1000–1100 mL.
Residual volume (RV): air remaining in the lungs even after forcible expiration, averaging 1100–1200 mL.

questions.why: TV ≈ 500 mL × 12–16 breaths per minute ≈ 6000–8000 mL per minute.
IRV, the extra air inspired by forcible inspiration, averages 2500–3000 mL.
ERV, the extra air expired by forcible expiration, averages 1000–1100 mL; 1100–1200 mL is the RV.
Alveoli do not collapse even after forceful expiration because of the residual volume, air that can never be expelled.

nuggets.title: Respiratory capacities: IC, EC, FRC, VC, TLC
lines: Inspiratory capacity (IC) = TV + IRV: total air a person can inspire after a normal expiration.
Expiratory capacity (EC) = TV + ERV: total air a person can expire after a normal inspiration.
Functional residual capacity (FRC) = ERV + RV: air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration.
Vital capacity (VC) = ERV + TV + IRV: maximum air breathed in after forced expiration, or out after forced inspiration.
Total lung capacity (TLC) = RV + ERV + TV + IRV, or VC + RV: air in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration.
nuggets.tip: Only FRC and TLC include RV; VC never does.

questions.why: EC = TV + ERV (A–Q); FRC = ERV + RV (B–S); VC = ERV + TV + IRV (C–P); IC = TV + IRV (D–R).
Vital capacity = IRV + ERV + TV. Adding RV gives total lung capacity instead.
Expiratory capacity = TV + ERV = 500 + 1000 = 1500 mL. Residual volume is not part of EC, so it is a distractor.
VC is the maximum air breathed in after forced expiration or out after forced inspiration, and equals ERV + TV + IRV, so all.

nuggets.title: Exchange of gases: diffusion and its factors
lines: Alveoli are the primary sites of gas exchange; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues.
O2 and CO2 are exchanged by simple diffusion, based on pressure/concentration gradient.
Rate of diffusion depends on pressure gradient, solubility of gases and thickness of the membranes involved.
Solubility of CO2 is 20–25 times higher than O2, so far more CO2 diffuses per unit partial-pressure difference.
The diffusion membrane has three major layers: thin squamous alveolar epithelium, alveolar capillary endothelium and the basement substance between them.
Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre, favouring diffusion.

questions.why: Exchange between alveoli and blood, and blood and tissues, occurs by simple diffusion; no carrier or ATP is used.
NCERT factors: pressure gradient, solubility of gases and membrane thickness (i, iii, v). 'Oxygen gradient' and 'reactivity' are not listed.
CO2 is 20–25 times more soluble than O2.
Both are NCERT: CO<sub>2</sub> is 20–25 times more soluble, and the membrane is alveolar squamous epithelium, capillary endothelium and basement substance.
Because of its higher solubility, CO2 diffusing per unit partial-pressure difference is much higher than O2. Exchange is passive, and the membrane is under 1 mm.

nuggets.title: Partial pressures of O2 and CO2
lines: Atmospheric air: pO2 159 mm Hg, pCO2 0.3 mm Hg.
Alveoli: pO2 104 mm Hg, pCO2 40 mm Hg.
Deoxygenated blood: pO2 40, pCO2 45; oxygenated blood: pO2 95, pCO2 40 (mm Hg).
Tissues: pO2 40, pCO2 45 mm Hg.
The gradient for O<sub>2</sub> runs alveoli → blood → tissues; for CO<sub>2</sub> it runs the opposite way, tissues → blood → alveoli.
nuggets.tip: 159/0.3 air, 104/40 alveoli, 95/40 oxygenated, 40/45 deoxygenated and tissues.

questions.why: Alveolar air has pO2 104 and pCO2 40 mm Hg. 159/0.3 is atmospheric air; 95/40 is oxygenated blood.
pO<sub>2</sub> in mm Hg: atmosphere 159, alveoli 104, deoxygenated blood 40, oxygenated blood 95, tissues 40.
pCO<sub>2</sub> in mm Hg: atmosphere 0.3, alveoli 40, deoxygenated blood 45, oxygenated blood 40, tissues 45.
II–V match the NCERT table. I is wrong: pCO2 of deoxygenated blood is 45 mm Hg; 95 is pO2 of oxygenated blood.
Alveolar pO2 (104) is more than that of blood reaching the lungs (40), so O2 diffuses into blood.

nuggets.title: Transport of oxygen and the dissociation curve
lines: About 97% of O2 is transported by RBCs; the remaining 3% is carried dissolved in plasma.
Haemoglobin, a red iron-containing pigment in RBCs, binds O2 reversibly to form oxyhaemoglobin.
Each haemoglobin molecule can carry a maximum of four molecules of O2.
Binding of O2 with haemoglobin is primarily related to partial pressure of O2; pCO2, H+ concentration and temperature can interfere.
Percentage saturation of Hb with O2 plotted against pO2 gives a sigmoid curve: the oxygen dissociation curve.

questions.why: Both are NCERT: about 97% of O2 is carried by RBCs and the remaining 3% dissolved in plasma.
Each haemoglobin molecule can carry a maximum of four O2 molecules.
Binding of O2 with Hb is primarily related to pO2. pCO2, H+ and temperature only interfere with it.
Plotting % saturation of Hb against pO2 gives a sigmoid curve, the oxygen dissociation curve.
Only D is correct (sigmoid curve). Binding depends primarily on pO<sub>2</sub>; CO<sub>2</sub> diffuses more than O<sub>2</sub>; RBCs carry 97% of O<sub>2</sub>, not 70%.

nuggets.title: Loading in alveoli, unloading in tissues
lines: In the alveoli: high pO2, low pCO2, lesser H+ concentration and lower temperature favour formation of oxyhaemoglobin.
In the tissues: low pO2, high pCO2, high H+ concentration and higher temperature favour dissociation of O2 from oxyhaemoglobin.
So O<sub>2</sub> gets bound to haemoglobin at the lung surface and gets dissociated at the tissues.
Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood can deliver around 5 mL of O2 to the tissues under normal physiological conditions.
nuggets.tip: Lungs: high O2, low CO2, low H+, low temp = loading. Tissues: the reverse = unloading.

questions.why: Oxyhaemoglobin forms in alveoli with high pO2, low pCO2, less H+ and lower temperature.
High pO2 and lesser H+ favour oxyhaemoglobin formation; high pCO2 and high temperature favour dissociation.
Dissociation in tissues is favoured by higher H+, high pCO2 and low pO2 (ii, iii, iv). Lower temperature and high pH favour binding.
Under normal conditions every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of O2 to tissues; 4 mL is the CO2 figure.
A is wrong: oxyhaemoglobin forms at lower temperature in alveoli. B correctly lists the tissue conditions for O2 dissociation.

nuggets.title: Transport of carbon dioxide
lines: About 20–25% of CO2 is carried by haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin; about 70% as bicarbonate; about 7% dissolved in plasma.
CO2 binding to Hb is related to pCO2; pO2 is a major factor affecting this binding.
In tissues (high pCO<sub>2</sub>, low pO<sub>2</sub>) more CO<sub>2</sub> binds; in alveoli (low pCO<sub>2</sub>, high pO<sub>2</sub>) CO<sub>2</sub> dissociates from carbamino-haemoglobin.
RBCs have a very high concentration of carbonic anhydrase; minute quantities are present in plasma too.
CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> ⇌ HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>: bicarbonate forms at tissues and CO<sub>2</sub> is released at alveoli.
Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately 4 mL of CO2 to the alveoli.
nuggets.tip: CO2 split: 70% bicarbonate, 20–25% carbamino-Hb, 7% dissolved.

questions.why: About 70% of CO2 is carried to the lungs as bicarbonate ions, formed with the help of carbonic anhydrase.
Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO2 to the alveoli; 5 mL is the O2 delivered to tissues.
CO2 dissociates from carbamino-haemoglobin in the alveoli, where pO2 is high and pCO2 is low.
Wrong statement: NCERT says pO2 is a major factor affecting CO2 binding to Hb, so binding IS affected by pO2.
Both wrong: carbamino-haemoglobin carries 20–25% of CO2 (not 40–45%), and carbonic anhydrase is also present in minute quantities in plasma.

nuggets.title: Regulation of respiration
lines: Respiratory rhythm is regulated by the neural system; the respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla is primarily responsible.
The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the functions of the respiratory rhythm centre.
Neural signals from the pneumotaxic centre can reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate.
A chemosensitive area adjacent to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to CO2 and H+; their increase activates it to signal the rhythm centre.
Receptors on the aortic arch and carotid artery also recognise changes in CO2 and H+ and signal the rhythm centre.
The role of oxygen in regulating respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.
nuggets.tip: Rhythm centre = medulla; pneumotaxic centre = pons. O2 barely matters; CO2 and H+ do.

questions.why: The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla is primarily responsible; the pneumotaxic centre only moderates it.
The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the function of the respiratory rhythm centre; it does not act on the lungs directly.
Receptors on the aortic arch and carotid artery recognise changes in CO2 and H+ concentration, not O2.
Both wrong: the rhythm centre is in the medulla and the pneumotaxic centre is in the pons. The statements swap them.
I is wrong: pneumotaxic signals reduce the duration of inspiration, not expiration. II is NCERT: O2's role is quite insignificant.

nuggets.title: Disorders of the respiratory system
lines: Asthma is difficulty in breathing causing wheezing, due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles.
Emphysema is a chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged, decreasing the respiratory surface.
Cigarette smoking is one of the major causes of emphysema.
Occupational respiratory disorders arise in industries such as grinding or stone-breaking, where so much dust is produced that the body's defence cannot cope.
Long exposure causes inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissues) and serious lung damage; workers should wear protective masks.
nuggets.tip: Asthma = inflamed bronchi/bronchioles (wheezing); emphysema = damaged alveolar walls.

questions.why: Wheezing in asthma is due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles. Fibrosis with alveolar damage is the distractor from other disorders.
In emphysema, alveolar walls are damaged, so the respiratory surface for gas exchange is drastically reduced.
Asthma = inflammation of bronchioles; emphysema = decreased respiratory surface due to damaged alveolar walls.
Long exposure to industrial dust causes inflammation leading to fibrosis, the proliferation of fibrous tissues.
Asthma = inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles (A–P); emphysema = damaged alveolar walls, reduced surface (B–Q); occupational disorders = fibrosis (C–R).

nuggets.title: Blood and plasma
lines: Blood is a special connective tissue made of a fluid matrix, plasma, and formed elements.
Plasma is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid forming nearly 55% of blood; it is 90–92% water and 6–8% proteins.
Plasma proteins: fibrinogen for coagulation, globulins for defence mechanisms, and albumins for osmotic balance.
Plasma also carries small amounts of minerals (Na<sup>+</sup>, Ca<sup>++</sup>, Mg<sup>++</sup>, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>, Cl<sup>–</sup>), glucose, amino acids and lipids, all in transit.
Factors for blood coagulation are present in plasma in an inactive form; plasma without clotting factors is called serum.
nuggets.tip: Globulins = defence, albumins = osmotic balance, fibrinogen = clotting.

questions.why: Both correct. Blood is a special connective tissue of plasma and formed elements, and plasma is straw-coloured, viscous and about 55% of blood.
Plasma is 90–92% water and 6–8% proteins. 55% is plasma's share of blood, not its water content.
Fibrinogen → blood clotting (Q), globulin → defence mechanism (R), albumin → osmotic balance (P).
Serum is plasma without clotting factors; it still has antibodies, globulins and albumins.
Both 2 and 3 are wrong: plasma carries glucose, amino acids and lipids but not starch, and clotting factors are present in an inactive form.

nuggets.title: Erythrocytes (RBCs)
lines: Erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets are the formed elements, forming nearly 45% of blood.
RBCs are the most abundant cells in blood: about 5–5.5 million mm–3 in a healthy adult man.
In adults RBCs are formed in the red bone marrow; in most mammals they lack a nucleus and are biconcave.
RBCs carry haemoglobin, a red, iron-containing complex protein; a healthy person has 12–16 g of it per 100 mL of blood.
RBCs have an average life span of 120 days, after which they are destroyed in the spleen, the graveyard of RBCs.
nuggets.tip: RBC: 5–5.5 million/mm<sup>3</sup>, Hb 12–16 g/100 mL, life span 120 days.

questions.why: A healthy adult man has 5 to 5.5 million RBCs per mm3 of blood.
A healthy individual has 12–16 g of haemoglobin in every 100 mL of blood.
Both correct. RBCs lack a nucleus in most mammals and are biconcave; their iron-containing haemoglobin transports respiratory gases.
In adults erythrocytes are formed in the red bone marrow. The spleen destroys old RBCs; it does not make them in adults.
Both incorrect. Haemoglobin is 12–16 g (not 20–30 g) per 100 mL, and it is RBCs, not WBCs, that live 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen.

nuggets.title: Leucocytes: count and types
lines: Leucocytes are colourless due to the lack of haemoglobin; they are nucleated and number 6000–8000 mm–3.
Leucocytes are generally short lived.
Granulocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils; agranulocytes are lymphocytes and monocytes.
Neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs (60–65%) and basophils the least (0.5–1%).
Other shares: lymphocytes 20–25%, monocytes 6–8%, eosinophils 2–3%.
nuggets.tip: Descending order: Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils.

questions.why: Leucocytes are white because they lack haemoglobin; they do have a nucleus, but that is not what makes them colourless.
WBCs average 6000–8000 per mm3 of blood, far fewer than RBCs.
A correct, B incorrect. Neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs (60–65%) and basophils the least (0.5–1%), not the reverse.
Neutrophils 60–65% (Q), basophils 0.5–1% (P), monocytes 6–8% (S), eosinophils 2–3% (R).
Neutrophils (60–65%) > lymphocytes (20–25%) > monocytes (6–8%) > eosinophils (2–3%) > basophils (0.5–1%).

nuggets.title: Leucocytes: functions
lines: Neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic cells that destroy foreign organisms entering the body.
Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin, and are involved in inflammatory reactions.
Eosinophils resist infections and are also associated with allergic reactions.
Lymphocytes are of two major types, B and T, and both are responsible for immune responses of the body.
nuggets.tip: Basophils: histamine, serotonin, heparin.

questions.why: II and III are correct: basophils secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin and are involved in inflammation. They are the least abundant and are granulocytes.
Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin. Neutrophils are phagocytes; T-lymphocytes give immune responses.
Both correct. Neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic; basophils secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin and take part in inflammation.
A correct, B incorrect. Eosinophils resist infection and are linked to allergy, but B- and T-lymphocytes are responsible for immune responses.
Neutrophils – phagocytic (R); basophils – inflammatory reactions (P); eosinophils – allergic reactions (S); lymphocytes – immune responses (Q).

nuggets.title: Platelets (thrombocytes)
lines: Platelets, also called thrombocytes, are cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes, special cells in the bone marrow.
Blood normally contains 1,50,000–3,50,000 platelets mm–3.
Platelets release a variety of factors that are involved in coagulation of blood.
A reduction in platelet number can lead to clotting disorders, causing excessive loss of blood from the body.

questions.why: Platelets are cell fragments of megakaryocytes, special cells in the bone marrow; they are not whole cells.
Platelet count is 1.5–3.5 lakh per mm3 (1,50,000–3,50,000). 6000–8000 is the WBC count.
Both correct. Thrombocytes are fragments of bone-marrow megakaryocytes, and they release factors involved in coagulation.
A fall in thrombocytes (platelets) causes clotting disorders and excessive blood loss, because platelets release clotting factors.
RBC 5–5.5 million (Q), WBC 6000–8000 (P), platelets 1.5–3.5 lakh (S), haemoglobin 12–16 g/100 mL (R), all per the NCERT values.

nuggets.title: ABO blood groups
lines: ABO grouping is based on the presence or absence of two surface antigens, A and B, on RBCs.
Plasma of different individuals contains two natural antibodies, anti-A and anti-B (proteins produced in response to antigens).
Group A has antigen A and anti-B; group B has antigen B and anti-A; group AB has both antigens and no antibodies; group O has no antigens but both antibodies.
Group O blood can be donated to persons of any group, so O individuals are called universal donors.
Persons with group AB can accept blood from AB and all other groups, so they are called universal recipients.
nuggets.tip: Blood group is named by the antigen on RBCs, not by the antibody in plasma.

questions.why: Both correct. ABO grouping depends on antigens A and B on RBCs, and plasma carries two natural antibodies, anti-A and anti-B.
Both incorrect. The labels are swapped: group O is the universal donor and group AB is the universal recipient.
AB is the universal recipient because it has both A and B antigens on RBCs but no antibodies in plasma, so donor RBCs are not attacked.
A has anti-B (S), B has anti-A (Q), AB is the universal recipient (R), O is the universal donor (P).
Incorrect: blood groups are named by the antigens on RBCs, not by plasma antibodies. B blood cannot go to A because A plasma has anti-B.

nuggets.title: Rh grouping and erythroblastosis foetalis
lines: An Rh antigen, similar to the one in Rhesus monkeys, is present on the RBCs of nearly 80% of humans (Rh+ve); those without it are Rh–ve.
An Rh–ve person exposed to Rh+ve blood forms specific antibodies against the Rh antigens.
In an Rh–ve mother with an Rh+ve foetus, the placenta keeps the two bloods apart, so the first pregnancy is not affected.
During delivery of the first child the mother may be exposed to small amounts of foetal Rh+ve blood and starts making anti-Rh antibodies.
In later pregnancies these antibodies can leak into foetal blood and destroy foetal RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice: erythroblastosis foetalis.
It can be avoided by giving the mother anti-Rh antibodies immediately after delivery of the first child.
nuggets.tip: Risk: Rh–ve mother + Rh+ve foetus, in the second pregnancy onwards.

questions.why: A correct, B incorrect. About 80% of humans are Rh+ve, but it is an Rh–ve person exposed to Rh+ve blood who forms anti-Rh antibodies.
Both correct. Rh incompatibility can be fatal or cause severe anaemia and jaundice in the baby, and anti-Rh antibodies given to the mother after the first delivery prevent it.
Erythroblastosis foetalis needs an Rh–ve mother carrying an Rh+ve foetus, which happens when the father is Rh+ve.
Anti-Rh antibodies are given after delivery when the mother is Rh–ve and the child Rh+ve, to stop her making antibodies against later Rh+ve foetuses.
Nearly 80% of humans carry the Rh antigen on their RBCs and are Rh+ve.

nuggets.title: Coagulation of blood
lines: At a cut, a dark reddish-brown scum, the clot or coagulum, forms; it is mainly a network of fibrin threads trapping dead and damaged formed elements.
Fibrins form from inactive fibrinogens in plasma by the enzyme thrombin.
Thrombins form from inactive prothrombin in plasma by the enzyme complex thrombokinase.
Thrombokinase forms through a cascade of linked enzymic reactions involving many plasma factors that are present in an inactive state.
Injury stimulates platelets to release factors that start coagulation; factors released by tissues at the injury site can also start it.
Calcium ions play a very important role in clotting.
nuggets.tip: Sequence: thrombokinase → prothrombin to thrombin → fibrinogen to fibrin.

questions.why: Both correct. The clot is a network of fibrin threads trapping dead and damaged formed elements, and Ca2+ is very important in clotting.
Both correct. Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and thrombokinase converts inactive prothrombin to thrombin.
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin. Thrombokinase acts one step earlier, converting prothrombin to thrombin.
I incorrect, II correct. The coagulum is a network of fibrin (not thrombin) threads; the spleen is the graveyard of RBCs.
Both incorrect, sources swapped. Injury makes platelets release clotting factors, and factors from tissues at the injury site can also start clotting.

nuggets.title: Lymph (tissue fluid)
lines: As blood passes through capillaries, some water and small water-soluble substances move out into spaces between cells; this is interstitial or tissue fluid.
Tissue fluid has the same mineral distribution as plasma; exchange of nutrients and gases between blood and cells happens through it.
The lymphatic system, a network of vessels, collects this fluid and drains it back to the major veins; the fluid in it is called lymph.
Lymph is a colourless fluid with specialised lymphocytes responsible for the immune responses of the body.
Lymph also carries nutrients and hormones; fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals of the intestinal villi.
nuggets.tip: Lacteals (in intestinal villi) absorb fat into lymph.

questions.why: Fluid that leaks out of capillaries into spaces between cells is called interstitial fluid or tissue fluid.
Tissue fluid has the same mineral distribution as plasma; it does not carry RBCs.
Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals present in the intestinal villi.
Both correct. Lymph is colourless and carries lymphocytes for immunity, and it also carries nutrients and hormones; fats are absorbed via lacteals.
Lymph carries nutrients and hormones, and the lymphatic system drains tissue fluid back to the major veins, so all are correct.

nuggets.title: Open and closed circulation
lines: Circulatory patterns are of two types: open and closed.
In the open system, found in arthropods and molluscs, blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces or body cavities called sinuses.
In the closed system, found in annelids and chordates, blood is always circulated through a closed network of blood vessels.
The closed pattern is considered more advantageous because the flow of fluid can be more precisely regulated.
All vertebrates have a muscular chambered heart.
nuggets.tip: Earthworm (annelid) is closed; cockroach (arthropod) is open.

questions.why: Open circulation occurs in arthropods and molluscs; annelids and chordates have a closed system.
Both incorrect. The groups are swapped: open circulation is in arthropods and molluscs, closed is in annelids and chordates.
In open circulation blood leaves vessels into open spaces or body cavities called sinuses; neither the heart nor the vessels are open.
Periplaneta (cockroach) is an arthropod, so its circulation is open. Hirudinaria is an annelid, and bats and whales are chordates: all closed.
A correct, B incorrect. Fishes have a 2-chambered heart, but crocodiles have a 4-chambered heart, not 3.

nuggets.title: Vertebrate hearts: single to double circulation
lines: Fishes have a 2-chambered heart (an atrium and a ventricle); amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) have a 3-chambered heart with two atria and one ventricle.
Crocodiles, birds and mammals have a 4-chambered heart with two atria and two ventricles.
In fishes the heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated by the gills and supplied to body parts: single circulation.
In amphibians and reptiles the left atrium receives oxygenated blood and the right atrium deoxygenated blood; they mix in the single ventricle: incomplete double circulation.
In birds and mammals oxygenated and deoxygenated blood pass to ventricles of the same side without mixing: double circulation.
nuggets.tip: Crocodile is the reptile exception with a 4-chambered heart.

questions.why: Single circulation – Pisces (R); incomplete double – Amphibians (Q); double – Aves and Mammalia (P).
A incorrect, B correct. In fishes the heart pumps deoxygenated blood and the gills oxygenate it. In amphibians/reptiles the bloods mix in the single ventricle.
Not true: amphibians and reptiles have incomplete double circulation. The other statements about the human heart are NCERT facts.
A whale is a mammal, so it has double circulation with two separate pathways. Shark has single circulation; frog and lizard mix blood.
Among reptiles, only the crocodile has a 4-chambered heart; turtles and tortoises have 3 chambers.

nuggets.title: Human heart: position and chambers
lines: The heart is a mesodermally derived organ in the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, about the size of a clenched fist.
It is protected by a double-walled membranous bag, the pericardium, which encloses the pericardial fluid.
It has four chambers: two relatively small upper atria and two larger lower ventricles.
A thin muscular inter-atrial septum separates the atria; a thick-walled inter-ventricular septum separates the ventricles.
The atrium and ventricle of the same side are separated by a thick fibrous tissue, the atrio-ventricular septum, which has an opening between them.
nuggets.tip: Inter-atrial septum is thin; inter-ventricular septum is thick.

questions.why: The heart is mesodermal in origin and lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted to the left.
The heart is protected by a double-walled membranous bag, the pericardium, enclosing pericardial fluid.
Both incorrect. The heart is muscular (not bony) and mesodermal (not ectodermal) in origin.
A incorrect, B correct. The heart's protective bag is the pericardium (pleura covers the lungs); the heart has two small atria and two larger ventricles.
Both incorrect. Thickness is reversed: the inter-atrial septum is thin and muscular, while the inter-ventricular septum is thick-walled.

nuggets.title: Heart valves
lines: The opening between the right atrium and right ventricle is guarded by the tricuspid valve, formed of three muscular flaps or cusps.
The opening between the left atrium and left ventricle is guarded by the bicuspid or mitral valve.
Openings of the right and left ventricles into the pulmonary artery and aorta have semilunar valves.
Valves let blood flow only one way, from atria to ventricles and from ventricles to the pulmonary artery or aorta, and prevent backflow.
The entire heart is made of cardiac muscles; the walls of ventricles are much thicker than those of atria.
nuggets.tip: Tricuspid = right side; bicuspid (mitral) = left side.

questions.why: Tricuspid: right atrium–right ventricle (R); bicuspid: left atrium–left ventricle (P); semilunar: right ventricle–pulmonary artery (Q).
Both correct. A thick fibrous atrio-ventricular septum separates atrium and ventricle, and the right AV opening has the 3-flapped tricuspid valve.
Both correct. The mitral valve guards the left AV opening, and semilunar valves guard the openings of the ventricles into the pulmonary artery and aorta.
Bicuspid – left atrium to left ventricle (R); tricuspid – right atrium to right ventricle (Q); semilunar – ventricles into pulmonary artery and aorta (P).
Semilunar valves sit at the openings of the ventricles into the aorta and the pulmonary artery, not in veins.

nuggets.title: Nodal tissue and the pacemaker
lines: Nodal tissue is specialised cardiac musculature; the SAN lies in the right upper corner of the right atrium, and the AVN in the lower left corner of the right atrium near the AV septum.
The AV bundle runs from the AVN through the AV septa to the top of the interventricular septum and divides into right and left bundle branches.
These branches give minute fibres throughout the ventricular musculature, the Purkinje fibres; together with the bundle branches they form the bundle of His.
Nodal musculature can generate action potentials without any external stimulus, so it is autoexcitable.
The SAN generates the maximum number of action potentials, 70–75 min–1, initiating and maintaining rhythm, so it is the pacemaker.
Our heart normally beats about 72 times per minute.
nuggets.tip: Conduction: SAN → AVN → AV bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.

questions.why: SAN – right upper corner of right atrium (R); AVN – lower left corner of right atrium (Q); bundle of His – fibres with bundle branches (S); Purkinje fibres – throughout ventricles (P).
Impulse path: SA node → AV node → AV bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres (E-C-A-D-B).
A correct, B incorrect. The SAN lies in the right upper corner of the right atrium, but it generates 70–75 action potentials per minute, not 40–45.
The SAN can generate the maximum number of action potentials, 70–75 per minute, which sets the heart rate.
The SA node fires the most action potentials, so it sets and maintains the rhythm as the pacemaker. The AVN only relays the impulse.

nuggets.title: Cardiac cycle: the sequence of events
lines: In joint diastole all four chambers are relaxed; tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open and semilunar valves closed.
During joint diastole, blood from pulmonary veins and vena cava flows through the atria into the left and right ventricles.
The SAN then generates an action potential, and both atria contract together (atrial systole), raising blood flow into the ventricles by about 30%.
The impulse passes via the AVN and AV bundle to the ventricles (ventricular systole); rising pressure closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves, and further rise opens the semilunar valves.
When ventricles relax, falling pressure closes the semilunar valves; when it falls below atrial pressure, the AV valves open again.
nuggets.tip: Order: joint diastole → atrial systole → ventricular systole → ventricular diastole.

questions.why: In joint diastole all chambers are relaxed and AV valves are open, so blood moves freely from atria to ventricles. Rising ventricular pressure closes AV valves, not semilunar ones.
Atrial systole increases blood flow into the ventricles by only about 30%; most filling happens during joint diastole.
In joint diastole all chambers relax, AV valves are open, blood flows into ventricles and semilunar valves are shut. Impulse conduction from SAN begins the next atrial systole.
A correct, B incorrect. Ventricular systole increases ventricular pressure, which closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves.
A cardiac cycle runs atrial systole → ventricular systole → joint diastole, then repeats.

nuggets.title: Cardiac output and heart sounds
lines: A cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in one heartbeat; at 72 beats per minute each cycle lasts about 0.8 s.
In each cycle each ventricle pumps out about 70 mL of blood: the stroke volume.
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, about 5000 mL (5 L) per minute per ventricle; the body can change both values.
The first heart sound, lub, comes from closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves.
The second heart sound, dub, comes from closure of the semilunar valves; both sounds have clinical diagnostic significance.
nuggets.tip: Lub = AV valves close; dub = semilunar valves close.

questions.why: Both correct. Stroke volume is blood pumped by each ventricle per cycle (about 70 mL); cardiac output is blood pumped by each ventricle per minute.
Cardiac output = 70 mL × 72 beats/min = 5040 mL/min; × 60 min = 302,400 mL = 302.4 L per hour.
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 55 mL × 70 = 3850 mL per minute.
Lub is from closure of the bicuspid and tricuspid valves, followed by dub from closure of the semilunar valves. Valve opening makes no sound.
A correct, B incorrect. Lub and dub are right, but the ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, not the lungs.

nuggets.title: ECG: the waves
lines: An ECG is a graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle, recorded by an electrocardiograph.
The P-wave represents electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to contraction of both atria.
The QRS complex represents depolarisation of the ventricles, which starts ventricular contraction.
Contraction starts shortly after Q, which marks the beginning of systole.
The T-wave represents return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state (repolarisation); the end of the T-wave marks the end of systole.
nuggets.tip: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation.

questions.why: The QRS complex represents depolarisation of the ventricles, which starts ventricular contraction. Ventricular repolarisation is the T-wave.
P – atrial depolarisation (R); Q – beginning of systole (P); QRS – ventricular depolarisation (S); T – ventricular repolarisation (Q).
Both correct. P-wave is atrial depolarisation leading to atrial contraction; QRS is ventricular depolarisation starting ventricular contraction.
Wrong interpretation: the P-wave is depolarisation of both atria, not only the left one. The other three options are correct.
ECG – electrical activity of heart (Q); P – atrial depolarisation (S); QRS – ventricular depolarisation (P); T – ventricular repolarisation (R).

nuggets.title: ECG: recording and reading
lines: For a standard ECG the patient is connected to the machine with three electrical leads: one to each wrist and one to the left ankle.
For a detailed evaluation of heart function, multiple leads are attached to the chest region.
Each peak in the ECG is named by a letter from P to T, and each corresponds to a specific electrical activity of the heart.
Counting the QRS complexes in a given time gives the heartbeat rate of the individual.
ECGs from different individuals have roughly the same shape; any deviation indicates a possible abnormality or disease, so it has great clinical significance.
nuggets.tip: Standard ECG leads: both wrists + left ankle (no right ankle).

questions.why: Standard ECG leads go to each wrist and the left ankle, so the right ankle is the exception.
Incorrect: the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, which starts ventricular, not atrial, contraction.
Only II is correct. Ventricular contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole; it is the QRS complex, not an "RST complex", that starts it.
P = depolarisation of atria is correct. Systole starts shortly after Q, T is ventricular repolarisation (its end marks the end of systole), and R is part of ventricular depolarisation.
Incorrect: the end of the T-wave, not its start, marks the end of systole. The other statements are NCERT facts.

nuggets.title: Double circulation and portal systems
lines: Pulmonary circulation: deoxygenated blood pumped into the pulmonary artery goes to the lungs, and oxygenated blood returns by pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
Systemic circulation: oxygenated blood from the aorta reaches tissues through arteries, arterioles and capillaries; deoxygenated blood returns through veins and vena cava to the right atrium.
Systemic circulation supplies nutrients, O<sub>2</sub> and other essential substances to tissues and takes CO<sub>2</sub> and other harmful substances away.
The hepatic portal system is a unique vascular connection between the digestive tract and liver; the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before systemic circulation.
A special coronary system of blood vessels serves only to circulate blood to and from the cardiac musculature.
nuggets.tip: Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

questions.why: Both correct. These are exactly NCERT's definitions of pulmonary circulation (right ventricle → lungs → left atrium) and systemic circulation (aorta → tissues → vena cava → right atrium).
Only II is correct. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood; the hepatic portal vein carries blood from intestine to liver before systemic circulation.
The hepatic portal system is the unique vascular link between the digestive tract and the liver.
The coronary circulation serves only the cardiac musculature; systemic circulation supplies the whole body.
Pulmonary circulation runs right side (deoxygenated) → lungs (oxygenated) → left atrium, through the pulmonary artery and pulmonary veins.

nuggets.title: Regulation of cardiac activity
lines: Normal heart activity is regulated intrinsically, i.e. auto-regulated by specialised muscles (nodal tissue), so the heart is called myogenic.
A special neural centre in the medulla oblongata can moderate cardiac function through the autonomic nervous system (ANS).
Sympathetic neural signals increase the rate of heartbeat and the strength of ventricular contraction, and so the cardiac output.
Parasympathetic neural signals decrease the rate of heartbeat and the speed of conduction of action potential, and so the cardiac output.
Adrenal medullary hormones can also increase the cardiac output.
nuggets.tip: Sympathetic speeds the heart up; parasympathetic slows it down.

questions.why: Both correct. The heart is myogenic (auto-regulated by nodal tissue), and the medulla oblongata centre moderates it through the ANS.
Both incorrect. The effects are swapped: sympathetic signals increase rate and strength, and parasympathetic signals decrease rate and conduction speed.
Parasympathetic signals reduce both heart rate and cardiac output, by slowing the heartbeat and impulse conduction.
Only IV is correct: adrenal medullary hormones raise cardiac output. The heart is myogenic (not neurogenic), the medulla acts via the ANS, and parasympathetic signals slow the heart.
A neural centre in the medulla oblongata moderates cardiac function through the ANS (both sympathetic and parasympathetic parts).

nuggets.title: Hypertension and coronary artery disease
lines: Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg: 120 is the systolic (pumping) pressure and 80 the diastolic (resting) pressure.
If repeated checks show BP of 140/90 mm Hg or higher, the person has hypertension.
High blood pressure leads to heart diseases and also affects vital organs like the brain and kidney.
Coronary artery disease (CAD), often called atherosclerosis, affects the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle.
CAD is caused by deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue, which make the lumen of arteries narrower.
nuggets.tip: Hypertension needs repeated readings of 140/90 or more, not a single check.

questions.why: Hypertension means repeated BP readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher; 120/80 is normal.
Very high BP such as 190/110 mm Hg can harm vital organs like the brain and kidney. 120/80, not 100/55, is the normal value.
In a BP reading the upper value is the systolic (pumping) pressure and the lower value is the diastolic (resting) pressure.
Coronary artery disease is often referred to as atherosclerosis.
All are correct: atherosclerosis (CAD) affects the vessels supplying heart muscle and is caused by calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous deposits narrowing the lumen.

nuggets.title: Angina, heart failure and heart attack
lines: Angina pectoris is acute chest pain that appears when not enough O2 reaches the heart muscle.
Angina can occur in men and women of any age but is more common among the middle-aged and elderly; it results from conditions that affect blood flow.
Heart failure is when the heart is not pumping blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs; it is called congestive heart failure because congestion of the lungs is a main symptom.
Cardiac arrest is when the heart stops beating.
Heart attack is when the heart muscle is suddenly damaged by an inadequate blood supply.
nuggets.tip: Heart failure is not the same as cardiac arrest or heart attack.

questions.why: A incorrect, B correct. Sudden damage to heart muscle from inadequate blood supply is a heart attack; cardiac arrest means the heart stops beating.
Heart failure: heart is not pumping blood effectively. Heart attack: heart muscle suddenly damaged by inadequate blood supply.
Heart failure – ineffective pumping (Q); cardiac arrest – heart stops beating (P); heart attack – sudden muscle damage from poor blood supply (R).
Angina pectoris is acute chest pain due to too little blood (O2) reaching heart muscle. The other three pairs mix up the definitions.
A correct, B incorrect. CAD narrows arteries with calcium, fat and cholesterol deposits; angina occurs when not enough O2 reaches the heart muscle.

nuggets.title: Nitrogenous wastes: ammonia, urea, uric acid
lines: Animals accumulate ammonia, urea, uric acid, CO2, water and ions like Na+, K+, Cl−, phosphate, sulphate by metabolic activities or excess ingestion.
These substances have to be removed from the body totally or partially.
Ammonia, urea and uric acid are the major forms of nitrogenous wastes excreted by animals.
Ammonia is the most toxic form and requires a large amount of water for its elimination.
Uric acid, being the least toxic, can be removed with a minimum loss of water.
nuggets.tip: Toxicity and water need run together: ammonia > urea > uric acid.

questions.why: Both correct. Wastes accumulate by metabolism or excess ingestion, and ammonia, urea and uric acid are the major nitrogenous wastes, exactly as NCERT states.
Uric acid < urea < ammonia. Ammonia is the most toxic nitrogenous waste and uric acid the least toxic.
Both incorrect. The statements are reversed: ammonia is the most toxic and uric acid the least toxic, removable with minimum water loss.
Uric acid. Being least toxic, it can be removed with a minimum loss of water (as pellet or paste); ammonia needs the most water.
A only. All three are nitrogenous wastes, but they differ in toxicity and water need, and none is made in the kidney (urea is formed in the liver).

nuggets.title: Ammonotelism and the move to land
lines: The process of excreting ammonia is ammonotelism; many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects are ammonotelic.
Ammonia is readily soluble and is generally excreted by diffusion across body surfaces or through gill surfaces (in fish) as ammonium ions.
Kidneys do not play any significant role in the removal of ammonia.
Terrestrial adaptation necessitated the production of less toxic urea and uric acid for conservation of water.
nuggets.tip: Ammonotelic = mostly aquatic (bony fish, aquatic amphibians/insects); marine fishes are ureotelic.

questions.why: A correct, B incorrect. Bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects are ammonotelic, but ammonia is readily soluble, which is why it diffuses out as ammonium ions.
Requires less water is the odd one: ammonia needs a large amount of water, which aquatic animals have. Solubility, toxicity and diffusion all support ammonotelism.
Only I. Ammonia leaves by diffusion across body or gill surfaces as ammonium ions; NCERT says kidneys do not play a significant role in its removal.
Fish kidney removing NH3 is incorrect: ammonia leaves through gills/body surface, not via kidneys. The other statements (uric acid pellets, urea in kidney matrix) are NCERT lines.
Conservation of water. NCERT: terrestrial adaptation necessitated less toxic wastes like urea and uric acid so that water is conserved.

nuggets.title: Ureotelic and uricotelic animals
lines: Mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes mainly excrete urea and are called ureotelic animals.
In ureotelic animals, ammonia from metabolism is converted into urea in the liver, released into blood and filtered and excreted by the kidneys.
Some urea may be retained in the kidney matrix of some ureotelic animals to maintain a desired osmolarity.
Reptiles, birds, land snails and insects excrete uric acid as pellet or paste with minimum water loss and are uricotelic.
nuggets.tip: Frog adult and humans are both ureotelic; tadpole is ammonotelic.

questions.why: Both correct. Land life needed less toxic wastes to save water, and mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes are ureotelic.
Urea, liver, kidney. In mammals ammonia is converted to urea in the liver; blood carries it to the kidneys, which filter and excrete it.
Urea, osmolarity. Some urea may be retained in the kidney matrix of some ureotelic animals to maintain a desired osmolarity.
Birds, reptiles and insects are uricotelic. Mammals are ureotelic, fishes/protozoans mostly ammonotelic, and frogs are ureotelic.
Pavo (peacock), a bird, is uricotelic and passes uric acid as pellet or paste. Salamandra and Ornithorhynchus are ureotelic; Hippocampus (bony fish) is ammonotelic.

nuggets.title: Excretory structures in invertebrates
lines: Most invertebrates have simple tubular excretory structures, whereas vertebrates have complex tubular organs called kidneys.
Protonephridia or flame cells are the excretory structures in Platyhelminthes (e.g., Planaria), rotifers, some annelids and the cephalochordate Amphioxus.
Protonephridia are primarily concerned with ionic and fluid volume regulation, i.e., osmoregulation.
Nephridia of earthworms and other annelids remove nitrogenous wastes and maintain fluid and ionic balance.
Malpighian tubules of most insects including cockroaches, and antennal (green) glands of crustaceans like prawns, remove nitrogenous wastes and aid osmoregulation.
nuggets.tip: Amphioxus is a chordate with flame cells (protonephridia).

questions.why: Both correct. Flame cells occur in flatworms, rotifers, some annelids and Amphioxus, and they are mainly concerned with ionic and fluid volume regulation.
Osmoregulation and excretion. Flame cells (protonephridia) of flatworms are excretory structures primarily concerned with ionic and fluid volume regulation.
A-S, B-P, C-R, D-Q. Protonephridia: flatworms; Malpighian tubules: insects; nephridia: annelids; antennary (green) glands: crustaceans.
A incorrect, B correct. Malpighian tubules are excretory structures of most insects, not annelids (which have nephridia); green glands serve prawns.
Three: Planaria, rotifer and Amphioxus have protonephridia. Prawn has green glands, cockroach Malpighian tubules, fish and frog kidneys; Hydra has none.

nuggets.title: Human excretory system: kidney position and size
lines: The human excretory system has a pair of kidneys, one pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.
Kidneys are reddish brown, bean-shaped, between the levels of last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra, close to the dorsal inner wall of abdominal cavity.
Each adult kidney measures 10–12 cm in length, 5–7 cm in width and 2–3 cm in thickness, weighing on average 120–170 g.
Towards the centre of its inner concave surface is a notch, the hilum, through which ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter.
nuggets.tip: Kidneys lie close to the DORSAL inner wall; length 10–12 cm, width 5–7 cm.

questions.why: Both correct. One pair each of kidneys and ureters, one bladder and one urethra; kidneys lie between last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra near the dorsal wall.
T12–L3. NCERT places the kidneys between the levels of the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra.
Reddish brown, bean-shaped is right. Option 2 is wrong because kidneys lie close to the dorsal (not ventral) inner wall, so '1 and 2' also fails.
Hilum, inner concave surface. The notch through which ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter lies at the centre of the inner concave surface.
Pair of ureters. Humans have paired kidneys, one pair of ureters, but a single urinary bladder and a single urethra.

nuggets.title: Internal structure of the kidney
lines: Inner to the hilum is a broad funnel-shaped space, the renal pelvis, with projections called calyces.
The outer layer of the kidney is a tough capsule; inside are an outer cortex and an inner medulla.
The medulla is divided into a few conical masses called medullary pyramids projecting into the calyces.
The cortex extends in between the medullary pyramids as renal columns called Columns of Bertini.
nuggets.tip: Columns of Bertini are CORTEX dipping into medulla, not medulla into cortex.

questions.why: Renal pelvis, calyces. Inner to the hilum lies the funnel-shaped renal pelvis whose projections are calyces.
Tough capsule, medulla, cortex. The kidney is covered by a tough capsule; inside, the medulla is inner and the cortex is outer.
Both correct. Medullary pyramids project into the calyces, and cortex extends between pyramids as Columns of Bertini.
Cortex into medulla. Columns of Bertini are cortical tissue extending between the medullary pyramids.
Renal pelvis is the wrong term: the cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns (Columns of Bertini). The pelvis is the funnel inside the hilum.

nuggets.title: The nephron: glomerulus and renal tubule
lines: Each kidney has nearly one million complex tubular structures called nephrons, the functional units.
Each nephron has two parts: the glomerulus and the renal tubule.
Glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries formed by the afferent arteriole, a fine branch of renal artery; blood leaves it through the efferent arteriole.
The renal tubule begins with a double-walled cup, Bowman's capsule, enclosing the glomerulus; together they form the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle).
The tubule continues as the highly coiled PCT, the hairpin-shaped Henle's loop (descending and ascending limbs) and the highly coiled DCT.
DCTs of many nephrons open into a straight collecting duct; collecting ducts converge and open into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids in the calyces.
nuggets.tip: Afferent brings blood IN to the glomerulus; efferent takes it away.

questions.why: Both correct. Each kidney has nearly one million nephrons, and each nephron has a glomerulus and a renal tubule.
Glomerulus, afferent, renal artery, efferent. The afferent arteriole (branch of renal artery) forms the glomerulus; the efferent arteriole drains it.
A incorrect, B correct. The glomerulus is formed by the afferent arteriole; the efferent arteriole carries blood away from it.
Both incorrect. The double-walled cup is Bowman's capsule, which encloses the glomerulus; together they form the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle), not the renal tubule.
1 and 3. Glomerulus with Bowman's capsule is called both the renal corpuscle and the Malpighian body; Malpighian tubules are insect excretory organs.

nuggets.title: Cortical vs juxta medullary nephrons; vasa recta
lines: The Malpighian corpuscle, PCT and DCT lie in the cortex, whereas the loop of Henle dips into the medulla.
In the majority of nephrons, the loop of Henle is too short and extends only very little into the medulla: cortical nephrons.
In some nephrons the loop of Henle is very long and runs deep into the medulla: juxta medullary nephrons.
The efferent arteriole forms a fine capillary network around the renal tubule called the peritubular capillaries.
A minute vessel of this network runs parallel to Henle's loop forming the U-shaped vasa recta, absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons.
nuggets.tip: Cortical nephrons: majority, short loop, vasa recta reduced. Juxta medullary: long loop.

questions.why: Loop of Henle runs deep into medulla in juxta medullary nephrons. Their corpuscle is still in the cortex, and cortical nephrons, not these, are the majority.
Assertion true, Reason false. Nephrons are cortical or juxta medullary, but it is the juxta medullary nephrons that have the long loop of Henle.
Efferent arteriole. After leaving the glomerulus, the efferent arteriole forms the peritubular capillary network around the renal tubule.
Cortical nephrons. Vasa recta is absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons, whose short loops barely enter the medulla.
A-Q, B-P, C-S, D-R. Corpuscle, PCT, DCT lie in the cortex; loop of Henle dips into medulla; collecting ducts open into pelvis; vasa recta is U-shaped.

nuggets.title: Glomerular filtration
lines: Urine formation involves three processes: glomerular filtration, reabsorption and tubular secretion.
On average 1100–1200 mL of blood is filtered by the kidneys per minute, roughly 1/5th of the blood pumped out by each ventricle per minute.
Glomerular capillary blood pressure filters blood through 3 layers: glomerular endothelium, Bowman's capsule epithelium and a basement membrane between them.
Epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule, the podocytes, are arranged so as to leave minute spaces called filtration slits or slit pores.
Almost all plasma constituents except proteins pass into Bowman's capsule, so this filtration is called ultrafiltration.
nuggets.tip: Podocytes are epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule, not of the glomerulus.

questions.why: 1100–1200 mL. This is the blood filtered by kidneys per minute; 125 mL/min is the filtrate formed (GFR), a common trap.
Epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule. Podocytes form the inner wall of Bowman's capsule and leave filtration slits between them.
Podocytes create slit pores for filtration. Henle's loop has minimal reabsorption, and the afferent arteriole brings blood to (not away from) the glomerulus.
All plasma constituents except proteins pass into Bowman's capsule. Podocytes belong to Bowman's capsule, and filtration is the first, not last, step.
Glomerulus. Filtration of blood by glomerular capillary blood pressure is the first step of urine formation; PCT, DCT and collecting duct reabsorb and secrete.

nuggets.title: GFR and the juxta glomerular apparatus
lines: The amount of filtrate formed by the kidneys per minute is the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
GFR in a healthy individual is approximately 125 mL/minute, i.e., 180 litres per day.
Kidneys have built-in mechanisms for regulation of GFR; one is carried out by the juxta glomerular apparatus (JGA).
JGA is a special sensitive region formed by cellular modifications in the DCT and the afferent arteriole at their location of contact.
A fall in GFR activates JG cells to release renin, which stimulates glomerular blood flow and brings GFR back to normal.
nuggets.tip: Renin (kidney enzyme) vs rennin (milk-curdling enzyme): watch the spelling.

questions.why: Both correct. GFR is the filtrate formed per minute, about 125 mL/min or 180 L/day in a healthy person.
125 mL/min. GFR in a healthy individual is about 125 mL per minute (180 L/day); 'per second' and other daily figures are distractors.
DCT and afferent arteriole. JGA is formed by cellular modifications where the DCT contacts the afferent arteriole.
A correct, B incorrect. JG cells release renin in response to a fall, not a rise, in GFR (and it is renin, not rennin).
JG cells release renin. A fall in GFR activates JG cells, and renin raises glomerular blood flow and GFR back to normal.

nuggets.title: Tubular reabsorption and secretion
lines: About 180 L of filtrate forms per day but only 1.5 L urine is released, so nearly 99 per cent of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules.
Tubular epithelial cells reabsorb glucose, amino acids, Na+ etc. actively, whereas nitrogenous wastes are absorbed by passive transport.
Reabsorption of water occurs passively in the initial segments of the nephron.
During urine formation, tubular cells secrete H+, K+ and ammonia into the filtrate (tubular secretion).
Tubular secretion is important for maintaining the ionic and acid–base balance of body fluids.

questions.why: 99 %. Of 180 L filtrate per day only about 1.5 L is passed as urine, so nearly 99 per cent is reabsorbed.
Reabsorbed into the blood. The renal tubules return about 99 % of the filtrate to the blood; only ~1 % leaves as urine.
Nearly 99 % of filtrate is reabsorbed. The descending limb is permeable to water, the DCT does reabsorb HCO3−, and the ascending limb transports electrolytes.
Both correct. Glucose, amino acids and Na+ are reabsorbed actively, nitrogenous wastes passively, and water passively in initial segments.
A correct, B incorrect. Tubular cells secrete H+, K+ and ammonia, and this secretion does help maintain ionic and acid–base balance.

nuggets.title: PCT and Henle's loop
lines: The PCT is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium, which increases the surface area for reabsorption.
Nearly all essential nutrients and 70–80 per cent of electrolytes and water are reabsorbed by the PCT.
PCT maintains pH and ionic balance by selective secretion of H+, ammonia and K+ into the filtrate and absorption of HCO3− from it.
In Henle's loop reabsorption is minimum, but it maintains the high osmolarity of medullary interstitial fluid.
The descending limb is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, so filtrate gets concentrated as it moves down.
The ascending limb is impermeable to water but allows transport of electrolytes actively or passively, so filtrate gets diluted as it moves up.
nuggets.tip: Descending limb: water out. Ascending limb: salts out, water stays.

questions.why: Cuboidal epithelium. The PCT is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium that increases the surface area for reabsorption.
PCT. Nearly all essential nutrients and 70–80 % of electrolytes and water are reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
All of the above. PCT secretes H+, ammonia and K+ into the filtrate and absorbs HCO3−, maintaining pH and ionic balance.
