Both false. The descending limb is permeable to water and almost impermeable to electrolytes, and the PCT has cuboidal, not columnar, brush border epithelium.
Ascending limb of Henle's loop. It is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes, which dilutes the filtrate as it rises.

nuggets.title: DCT and collecting duct
lines: Conditional reabsorption of Na+ and water takes place in the DCT.
DCT also reabsorbs HCO3− and selectively secretes H+, K+ and NH3 to maintain pH and sodium–potassium balance in blood.
The collecting duct is a long duct extending from the cortex of the kidney to the inner parts of the medulla.
Large amounts of water can be reabsorbed from the collecting duct to produce concentrated urine.
The collecting duct passes small amounts of urea into the medullary interstitium to keep up osmolarity, and secretes H+ and K+ for pH and ionic balance.
nuggets.tip: Glucose is reabsorbed in PCT, never in DCT: a favourite mismatch.

questions.why: DCT. Conditional reabsorption of Na+ and water occurs in the distal convoluted tubule.
A correct, B incorrect. The DCT is capable of reabsorbing HCO3− and selectively secreting H+, K+ and NH3.
DCT–absorption of glucose is wrong: glucose and other nutrients are reabsorbed in the PCT. The other pairs match NCERT.
A incorrect, B correct. The collecting duct runs from cortex to the inner parts of the medulla (not ureter); it reabsorbs much water to concentrate urine.
Collecting duct. It allows small amounts of urea into the medullary interstitium to keep up its osmolarity.

nuggets.title: Counter current mechanism: concentrating urine
lines: Mammals can produce concentrated urine; Henle's loop and vasa recta play a significant role in this.
Filtrate in the two limbs of Henle's loop, and blood in the two limbs of vasa recta, flow in opposite directions, forming a counter current.
Their proximity and counter current maintain osmolarity rising from 300 mOsmolL−1 in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmolL−1 in the inner medulla.
The gradient is mainly due to NaCl and urea; NaCl from the ascending limb is exchanged with the descending limb of vasa recta and returned by its ascending portion.
Small amounts of urea enter the thin segment of the ascending limb and are transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule.
The gradient helps easy passage of water from the collecting tubule, concentrating urine nearly four times the initial filtrate.
nuggets.tip: Counter current = Henle's loop + vasa recta; gradient solutes = NaCl + urea.

questions.why: 300 and 1200 mOsmolL−1. Interstitial osmolarity rises from about 300 in the cortex to about 1200 in the inner medulla.
NaCl and urea. The medullary gradient is mainly caused by NaCl and urea; glucose and ammonia are not part of it.
Descending limb of vasa recta. NaCl transported out by the ascending limb of Henle's loop is exchanged with the descending limb of vasa recta.
A incorrect, B correct. Only small amounts of urea enter the thin ascending limb; urine can become nearly four times as concentrated as the filtrate.
Water passes from collecting tubule to interstitium, concentrating the urine. The gradient pulls water out of, not into, the tubule.

nuggets.title: Regulation by ADH (vasopressin)
lines: Kidney function is monitored by hormonal feedback involving the hypothalamus, JGA and, to a certain extent, the heart.
Osmoreceptors in the body are activated by changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration.
Excessive loss of fluid stimulates the hypothalamus to release antidiuretic hormone (ADH) or vasopressin from the neurohypophysis.
ADH facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis; a rise in body fluid volume switches off osmoreceptors and suppresses ADH.
ADH also has constrictory effects on blood vessels, raising blood pressure, which increases glomerular blood flow and thereby GFR.
nuggets.tip: Drinking lots of water suppresses ADH; dehydration raises it.

questions.why: Osmoreceptors, loss, hypothalamus. Fluid loss activates osmoreceptors, which make the hypothalamus release ADH from the neurohypophysis.
Both correct. Fluid loss triggers vasopressin release, and ADH increases water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis.
Drinking lots of water suppresses ADH. A rise in body fluid volume switches off osmoreceptors. Water loss in summer increases, not suppresses, ADH.
II, III, IV. ADH prevents diuresis, ANF causes vasodilation, and ADH raises BP. Fluid loss activates osmoreceptors, and ADH's BP rise increases GFR.
A correct, B incorrect. ADH constricts vessels and raises BP; a rise in BP increases glomerular blood flow and GFR.

nuggets.title: Renin–angiotensin mechanism and ANF
lines: Renin from JG cells converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I and further to angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II, a powerful vasoconstrictor, increases glomerular blood pressure and thereby GFR.
Angiotensin II activates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which causes reabsorption of Na+ and water from distal parts of the tubule.
This renin–angiotensin mechanism leads to an increase in blood pressure and GFR.
Increased blood flow to the atria makes the heart release Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF), which causes vasodilation and decreases blood pressure.
ANF therefore acts as a check on the renin–angiotensin mechanism.
nuggets.tip: Angiotensin II = vasoconstrictor; ANF = vasodilator.

questions.why: Both incorrect. JG cells release renin on a fall in GFR, and angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor, not a vasodilator.
Both correct. Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which reabsorbs Na+ and water from distal tubule parts.
ANF. ANF is released when blood flow to the atria increases; a fall in BP/volume instead triggers renin, aldosterone and ADH.
Increase in aldosterone. Aldosterone causes reabsorption of Na+ and water from the distal parts of the tubule.
Heart. ANF, released by the atria, causes vasodilation and acts as a check on the renin–angiotensin mechanism.

nuggets.title: Micturition and characteristics of urine
lines: Urine formed by nephrons is stored in the urinary bladder till a voluntary signal is given by the CNS.
The signal is initiated by stretching of the bladder as it fills; stretch receptors on its wall send signals to the CNS.
CNS sends motor messages to contract bladder smooth muscles and simultaneously relax the urethral sphincter, releasing urine; the neural mechanism is the micturition reflex.
An adult excretes on average 1 to 1.5 litres of urine per day; it is light yellow, slightly acidic (pH 6.0) with a characteristic odour.
On average 25–30 g of urea is excreted out per day.
Presence of glucose (glycosuria) and ketone bodies (ketonuria) in urine indicates diabetes mellitus.
nuggets.tip: Sphincter RELAXES during micturition while the bladder contracts.

questions.why: Urinary bladder, CNS. Urine is stored in the bladder until a voluntary signal from the central nervous system initiates its release.
A correct, B incorrect. Bladder stretch starts the signal, but the CNS causes relaxation (not contraction) of the urethral sphincter while the bladder contracts.
A incorrect, B correct. An adult passes 1–1.5 L urine per day, not 2–2.5 L; urine is light yellow, slightly acidic with characteristic odour.
25–30 g. On average 25–30 grams of urea is excreted per day (grams, not mg).
Ketonuria and glycosuria. Glucose and ketone bodies in urine indicate diabetes mellitus; uremia and renal calculi are kidney disorders.

nuggets.title: Role of other organs in excretion
lines: Besides kidneys, lungs, liver and skin also help in the elimination of excretory wastes.
Lungs remove large amounts of CO2 (approximately 200 mL/minute) and significant quantities of water every day.
Liver secretes bile containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs, passed out with digestive wastes.
Sweat is a watery fluid containing NaCl, small amounts of urea, lactic acid, etc.; its primary function is to cool the body surface.
Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through sebum, which gives a protective oily covering to the skin.
Small amounts of nitrogenous wastes can also be eliminated through saliva.
nuggets.tip: Sterols and waxes leave via sebum, not sweat.

questions.why: 200 mL/minute. NCERT: lungs remove large amounts of CO2, approximately 200 mL per minute, plus significant water daily.
A-Q, B-S, C-P, D-R. Lungs remove CO2; liver secretes bilirubin and biliverdin in bile; sweat carries NaCl and urea; sebum carries sterols and waxes.
A incorrect, B correct. Sweat contains NaCl and small amounts of urea and lactic acid (not uric acid); sebaceous glands remove sterols, hydrocarbons, waxes.
Cooling of body surface. Sweat helps remove some wastes, but NCERT says its primary function is to facilitate a cooling effect on the body surface.
Saliva eliminates small amounts of nitrogenous waste. Sterols and waxes leave via sebum (not sweat), and sweat has lactic acid, not pyruvic acid.

nuggets.title: Disorders: uremia, dialysis, transplant, calculi
lines: Malfunctioning kidneys lead to accumulation of urea in blood, a condition called uremia, which is highly harmful and may lead to kidney failure.
In haemodialysis, blood from a convenient artery is pumped into a dialysing unit after adding an anticoagulant like heparin.
The unit has a coiled cellophane tube in dialysing fluid of plasma-like composition minus nitrogenous wastes; cleared blood returns via a vein after adding anti-heparin.
Kidney transplantation is the ultimate method for acute renal failure; a donor, preferably a close relative, minimises rejection by the host's immune system.
Renal calculi are stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts (oxalates, etc.) formed within the kidney; glomerulonephritis is inflammation of glomeruli.
nuggets.tip: Dialysis: blood out via artery, back via vein; heparin before, anti-heparin after.

questions.why: Accumulation of urea in blood. Uremia results from kidney malfunction; glucose in urine is glycosuria.
Assertion correct, Reason incorrect. Blood is drawn from an artery with heparin, but the cleared blood is returned through a vein after adding anti-heparin.
No urea. Dialysing fluid is like plasma except it lacks nitrogenous wastes, so urea diffuses out of the blood along its concentration gradient.
Both correct. The porous cellophane passes molecules by concentration gradient, and kidney transplantation is the ultimate correction for acute renal failure.
A-Q, B-P, C-R. Uremia: urea accumulates in blood; renal calculi: crystallised oxalate salts; glomerulonephritis: inflammation of glomeruli.

nuggets.title: Types of movement and locomotion
lines: Cells of the human body exhibit three main types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary and muscular.
Amoeboid movement is seen in macrophages and leucocytes; pseudopodia form by streaming of protoplasm, involving cytoskeletal elements like microfilaments.
Ciliary movement occurs in internal tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium, e.g., removal of dust from the trachea and passage of ova through the female reproductive tract.
Movement of limbs, jaws and tongue requires muscular movement.
Voluntary movements causing change of place are locomotion; locomotory structures need not be different from those affecting other movements (e.g., cilia of Paramoecium, tentacles of Hydra).
Locomotion requires a perfectly coordinated activity of muscular, skeletal and neural systems.

questions.why: Both correct. Red fibres are rich in myoglobin, and pseudopodial (amoeboid) movement involves cytoskeletal microfilaments.
A correct, B incorrect. Locomotion is a voluntary movement, but dust is removed from the trachea by coordinated beating of cilia, not villi.
Statement 2 is incorrect. NCERT says locomotory structures need not be different from those affecting other movements, e.g., Paramoecium cilia or Hydra tentacles.
Both correct. Ciliary movement occurs in internal tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium, and muscle bundles are held together by the fascia.

nuggets.title: Muscle: origin, properties and types
lines: Muscle is a specialised tissue of mesodermal origin.
About 40–50 per cent of the body weight of a human adult is contributed by muscles.
Muscles have special properties: excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.
Based on location, three types of muscles are identified: skeletal, visceral and cardiac.

questions.why: Mesodermal. Muscle is a specialised tissue of mesodermal origin.
40–50 per cent. Muscles contribute about 40–50 % of the body weight of an adult human.
A correct, B incorrect. Muscles form 40–50 % of body weight, but their properties are excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity, not 'connectivity'.
I, II, III, V. Excitability, contractility, elasticity and extensibility are muscle properties; 'secretability' is not.
Skeletal, visceral and cardiac. NCERT classifies muscles into these three types on the basis of their location.

nuggets.title: Skeletal, visceral and cardiac muscles
lines: Skeletal muscles are closely associated with skeletal components, look striped (striated) and are under voluntary control of the nervous system.
Skeletal muscles are primarily involved in locomotory actions and changes of body posture.
Visceral muscles lie in the inner walls of hollow visceral organs like the alimentary canal and reproductive tract; they are smooth (unstriated) and involuntary.
Visceral muscles assist transport of food through the digestive tract and of gametes through the genital tract.
Cardiac muscles are muscles of the heart; cells assemble in a branching pattern, and they are striated but involuntary.
nuggets.tip: Heart muscle: striated like skeletal, involuntary like smooth.

questions.why: Thigh: striated and voluntary. Thigh muscle is skeletal. Heart muscle is striated (not smooth) and intestinal muscle is smooth (not striated).
Statement 3 is incorrect. Muscles in the inner walls of the alimentary canal are visceral: smooth and involuntary, not striated.
Muscles of the heart. Cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary; alimentary canal muscles are smooth, and locomotory/eyelid muscles are voluntary.
A correct, B incorrect. Smooth muscles are unstriated, but they lie in walls of hollow visceral organs; skeletal muscles are the ones close to bones.
All. Smooth (visceral) muscles move food along the gut (peristalsis), transport gametes through the genital tract and act in the urinary bladder wall.

nuggets.title: Structure of a skeletal muscle fibre
lines: Each skeletal muscle is made of a number of muscle bundles or fascicles held together by a collagenous connective tissue layer called fascia.
Each muscle bundle contains a number of muscle fibres, each lined by the plasma membrane called sarcolemma enclosing the sarcoplasm.
A muscle fibre is a syncytium, as its sarcoplasm contains many nuclei.
The endoplasmic reticulum, i.e., sarcoplasmic reticulum, of muscle fibres is the store house of calcium ions.
The sarcoplasm has many parallel filaments called myofibrils; their striated look is due to the distribution pattern of actin and myosin.
nuggets.tip: Fascicle = bundle; fascia = collagenous layer holding bundles together.

questions.why: Fascia. Muscle bundles (fascicles) are held together by a collagenous connective tissue layer called fascia.
Collagenous connective tissue. NCERT describes the fascia as a collagenous connective tissue layer.
Both correct. A muscle fibre is a multinucleate syncytium, and its sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium ions.
A-Q, B-R, C-P. Sarcolemma is the plasma membrane, sarcoplasmic reticulum stores Ca2+, and myofibrils show alternate dark and light bands.
II and III only. SR stores Ca2+ and striations come from actin–myosin distribution. Bundles are held by fascia (not fascicle), and the sarcomere lies between Z lines.

nuggets.title: Light and dark bands: actin and myosin
lines: Each myofibril has alternate dark and light bands on it.
The light band contains actin and is called the I-band or isotropic band.
The dark band contains myosin and is called the A-band or anisotropic band.
Actin and myosin are rod-like structures arranged parallel to each other and to the longitudinal axis of the myofibrils.
Actin filaments are thinner than myosin filaments, so they are called thin and thick filaments respectively.
nuggets.tip: A-band = Anisotropic = dArk = myosin; I-band = Isotropic = light = actin.

questions.why: I-band and A-band. The light band is the isotropic I-band and the dark band is the anisotropic A-band.
Actin, isotropic band. The light band contains actin and is called the I-band or isotropic band.
Myosin filaments. The dark anisotropic A-band contains myosin (thick filaments).
Thin and thick. Actin filaments are thinner than myosin filaments, hence thin and thick filaments respectively.
Both 1 and 2. Actin and myosin rods lie parallel to each other and parallel to the longitudinal axis of the myofibril.

nuggets.title: Z line, M line, H zone and the sarcomere
lines: In the centre of each I-band is an elastic fibre, the Z line, which bisects it; thin filaments are firmly attached to the Z line.
Thick filaments in the A-band are held together in the middle by a thin fibrous membrane, the M line.
The A and I bands are arranged alternately throughout the length of the myofibrils.
The portion of myofibril between two successive Z lines is the sarcomere, the functional unit of contraction.
At rest, edges of thin filaments partially overlap free ends of thick filaments; the central part of thick filaments not overlapped is the H zone.
nuggets.tip: Z in I-band; M in A-band; H zone is the un-overlapped middle of A-band.

questions.why: Z-line. The elastic fibre bisecting each I-band is the Z line, to which thin filaments are firmly attached.
A band. The M line is a thin fibrous membrane holding the thick filaments together in the middle of the A-band.
Between two successive Z-lines. This portion of the myofibril is the sarcomere, the functional unit of contraction.
I and IV. Z line lies in the centre of the light band, which has only thin filaments. Thin filaments attach to the Z line (not M), and the un-overlapped part is the H zone.
Central gap between actin filaments in the A-band. The H zone is the central part of thick filaments not overlapped by thin filaments.

nuggets.title: Thin filament: actin, tropomyosin, troponin
lines: Each actin (thin) filament is made of two 'F' (filamentous) actins helically wound to each other.
Each F actin is a polymer of monomeric 'G' (globular) actins.
Two filaments of tropomyosin run close to the F actins throughout their length.
A complex protein, troponin, is distributed at regular intervals on the tropomyosin.
In the resting state, a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on the actin filaments.
nuggets.tip: Troponin sits on tropomyosin, not directly at random on actin.

questions.why: Globular actin. Each F (filamentous) actin is a polymer of monomeric G (globular) actins.
Tropomyosin. Troponin, a complex protein, is distributed at regular intervals on the tropomyosin.
Only I. Each thin filament has two F actins wound helically, but two (not one) tropomyosin filaments run close to them.
Subunit of troponin. At rest, a troponin subunit masks the active binding sites for myosin on actin.
Meromyosin. Meromyosins are monomers of the thick (myosin) filament; thin filaments contain F-actin, tropomyosin and troponin.

nuggets.title: Thick filament: myosin and meromyosin
lines: Each myosin (thick) filament is also a polymerised protein, made of many monomeric proteins called meromyosins.
Each meromyosin has a globular head with a short arm and a tail.
The head with short arm is heavy meromyosin (HMM); the tail is light meromyosin (LMM).
HMM projects outwards at regular distance and angle from the surface of the polymerised myosin filament and is known as the cross arm.
The globular head is an active ATPase enzyme with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin.
nuggets.tip: Myosin head has an ATPase plus binding sites for ATP and actin, not Ca<sup>2+</sup>.

questions.why: Meromyosin. Many monomeric meromyosins polymerise to form each myosin (thick) filament.
Globular head with a short arm and a tail. These are the two important parts of each meromyosin.
Cross arm. The HMM (head plus short arm) projects outwards from the myosin filament at regular distance and angle.
ATPase enzyme. The globular head of myosin is an active ATPase with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin.
None correct. Myosin is the thick filament, and its head has active sites for actin, not troponin.

nuggets.title: Initiating contraction: motor unit and NMJ
lines: Muscle contraction is explained by the sliding filament theory: thin filaments slide over thick filaments.
Contraction is initiated by a signal sent by the CNS via a motor neuron.
A motor neuron along with the muscle fibres connected to it constitutes a motor unit.
The junction between a motor neuron and the sarcolemma of the muscle fibre is the neuromuscular junction or motor end plate.
The neural signal releases acetylcholine there, generating an action potential in the sarcolemma that spreads and releases Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm.
nuggets.tip: Signal travels by a MOTOR neuron, not a sensory neuron.

questions.why: Thin filaments over thick filaments. This is the core of the sliding filament theory.
A motor neuron plus the muscle fibres it stimulates. NCERT: a motor neuron with the muscle fibres connected to it forms a motor unit.
Both 2 and 3. The motor neuron–sarcolemma junction is called the neuromuscular junction or motor end plate.
Acetylcholine. Released at the neuromuscular junction, it generates an action potential in the sarcolemma.
A incorrect, B correct. The CNS signal travels via a motor neuron; repeated activation does lead to lactic acid accumulation.

nuggets.title: Cross bridge cycle and relaxation
lines: Increased Ca2+ binds a subunit of troponin on actin, removing the masking of active sites for myosin.
Using energy from ATP hydrolysis, the myosin head binds the exposed active sites on actin to form a cross bridge.
The cross bridge pulls actin towards the centre of the A-band; the Z lines are pulled inwards, shortening the sarcomere.
Myosin releases ADP and Pi and returns to relaxed state; a new ATP binds and the cross bridge is broken.
The cycle repeats until Ca2+ is pumped back to the sarcoplasmic cisternae, masking actin filaments again and causing relaxation.
nuggets.tip: ATP is used twice: hydrolysis energises cross-bridge formation; fresh ATP breaks it.

questions.why: Binds troponin to unmask actin's active sites for myosin. Ca2+ does not act on myosin ATPase directly or detach the myosin head.
Troponin, myosin. Ca2+ binds troponin and exposes the binding sites for myosin on the actin filament.
Cross bridge is broken. After ADP and Pi are released, binding of a new ATP to the myosin head breaks the cross bridge.
Pumping of Ca2+ into sarcoplasmic cisternae. This re-masks actin's active sites, ending cross-bridge cycling and relaxing the fibre.
VII→III→I→IV→VI→II→V. CNS signal, ACh release, sarcolemma action potential, Ca2+ release, unmasking, cross bridge, then actin pulled to the A-band centre.

nuggets.title: Band changes during contraction
lines: During contraction, the I-bands get reduced, whereas the A-bands retain their length.
The Z lines attached to actins are pulled inwards, so the sarcomere shortens.
Actin and myosin filaments themselves do not shorten; they only slide past each other.
As thin filaments slide towards the centre of the A-band, the H zone narrows.
nuggets.tip: A-band constant; I-band and H zone shrink; sarcomere shortens.

questions.why: I bands, A bands. In contraction the I bands get reduced while the A bands retain their length.
(a), (c), (d), (e). H zone narrows/vanishes, I band shortens, myosin hydrolyses ATP and Z lines move in; the A band does not widen.
A band remains same. The sarcomere shortens and I band reduces, but A-band length and filament lengths stay constant.
Neither filament shortens. Actin and myosin slide past each other without changing length.
Size of A-band remains the same. The H zone gets smaller and I-bands decrease; fibre length shortens.

nuggets.title: Fatigue, myoglobin, red and white fibres
lines: Repeated activation of muscles can lead to accumulation of lactic acid due to anaerobic breakdown of glycogen, causing fatigue.
Muscle contains a red coloured oxygen-storing pigment called myoglobin.
Red fibres have high myoglobin and plenty of mitochondria using stored O2 for ATP; they are aerobic muscles.
White fibres have little myoglobin, few mitochondria but a high amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum, and depend on anaerobic processes.
nuggets.tip: Red = aerobic, many mitochondria; white = anaerobic, more SR.

questions.why: Lactic acid from anaerobic respiration. Repeated activation causes anaerobic breakdown of glycogen, and lactic acid accumulation causes fatigue.
Lactic acid. It accumulates in fatigued muscle from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen; pyruvic acid is the trap.
I, II, IV. Red fibres have high myoglobin, plenty of mitochondria and are aerobic; high sarcoplasmic reticulum is a white-fibre feature.
White muscle fibres. They have few mitochondria but a high amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum.
A incorrect, B correct. Red fibres are aerobic; they have many mitochondria and less sarcoplasmic reticulum.

nuggets.title: Coordination and the neural system in animals
lines: Coordination is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another.
The neural system and the endocrine system jointly coordinate and integrate all organ activities so they function in a synchronised fashion.
The neural system gives an organised network of point-to-point connections for quick coordination; the endocrine system gives chemical integration through hormones.
The neural system of all animals is made of highly specialised cells called neurons, which can detect, receive and transmit different kinds of stimuli.
Neural organisation is very simple in lower invertebrates: in Hydra it is a network of neurons.
Insects have a better organised system with a brain plus a number of ganglia and neural tissues; vertebrates have a more developed neural system.
nuggets.tip: Neural = point-to-point and quick; endocrine = chemical (hormones), not enzymes.

questions.why: Coordination is the interaction of two or more organs that complement each other's functions; NCERT defines it at the organ level, not cells or organelles.
Both true: the neural system gives point-to-point connections for quick coordination and the endocrine system gives chemical integration through hormones.
A is false: neural organisation is very simple in lower invertebrates. B is true: insects have a brain with a number of ganglia and neural tissues.
Hydra has the simplest neural organisation, a network of neurons; Pheretima (earthworm) and Salamandra are more organised.
I, III and V are true. II is false: endocrine integration is through hormones, not enzymes. IV is false: lower invertebrates have a very simple organisation.

nuggets.title: Human neural system: CNS, PNS and nerve fibres
lines: The human neural system has two parts: the central neural system (CNS) and the peripheral neural system (PNS).
The CNS includes the brain and spinal cord and is the site of information processing and control.
The PNS comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS (brain and spinal cord).
PNS nerve fibres are of two types: afferent fibres and efferent fibres.
Afferent fibres carry impulses from tissues/organs to the CNS; efferent fibres carry regulatory impulses from the CNS to peripheral tissues/organs.
nuggets.tip: Afferent = Arrives at CNS; Efferent = Exits CNS.

questions.why: The CNS (brain and spinal cord) is the site of information processing and control; the PNS and ANS only carry impulses.
Afferent fibres carry impulses from tissues/organs to the CNS; carrying impulses from the CNS outward is the job of efferent fibres.
Efferent fibres carry regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues/organs.
Both false: the two terms are swapped. Afferent fibres go tissues → CNS and efferent fibres go CNS → peripheral tissues.
A is true. B is false: the PNS comprises all nerves associated with the CNS, not nerves unconnected to it.

nuggets.title: PNS divisions: somatic, autonomic and visceral
lines: The PNS is divided into the somatic neural system and the autonomic neural system.
The somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles.
The autonomic neural system carries impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles of the body.
The autonomic neural system is further classified into the sympathetic and parasympathetic neural systems.
The visceral nervous system is part of the PNS: the whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses carrying impulses between the CNS and the viscera, in both directions.
nuggets.tip: Sympathetic/parasympathetic are divisions of the autonomic system, not of the whole neural system.

questions.why: The somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal (voluntary) muscles; the autonomic system serves smooth muscles.
The autonomic neural system carries impulses from the CNS to involuntary organs and smooth muscles; sympathetic and parasympathetic are its subdivisions.
CNS includes brain and spinal cord (Q); PNS is all nerves associated with the CNS (S); autonomic goes to involuntary organs (R); somatic goes to skeletal muscles (P).
Both true: the visceral nervous system is part of the PNS and is the complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses linking the CNS and the viscera both ways.
False: III (autonomic splits into sympathetic and parasympathetic, not CNS/PNS), IV (afferent is sensory, efferent is motor) and V (the neural system splits into CNS and PNS).

nuggets.title: Structure of a neuron
lines: A neuron is a microscopic structure with three major parts: cell body, dendrites and axon.
The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical cell organelles and granular bodies called Nissl's granules.
Dendrites are short, repeatedly branched fibres projecting from the cell body; they also have Nissl's granules and carry impulses towards the cell body.
The axon is a long fibre with a branched distal end; it carries impulses away from the cell body to a synapse or a neuro-muscular junction.
Each axon branch ends in a bulb-like synaptic knob, which has synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitters.
nuggets.tip: Nissl's granules are in the cell body and dendrites, not in the axon.

questions.why: A neuron is microscopic and has three major parts: cell body, dendrites and axon. Cyton and soma are other names for the cell body, not separate parts.
Incorrect: dendrites are repeatedly branched, not unbranched. They are short, contain Nissl's granules and carry impulses towards the cell body.
Cell body has cytoplasm with organelles (R); dendrites are short, repeatedly branched fibres (S); synaptic knob holds vesicles (Q); axon is long with a branched distal end (P).
Both true: each axon branch ends in a synaptic knob with vesicles of neurotransmitters, and axons carry impulses to a synapse or a neuro-muscular junction.
III–VI are correct. I is wrong: a neuron is microscopic. II is wrong: the third part is the axon, not 'exon'.

nuggets.title: Types of neurons and myelination
lines: By the number of axons and dendrites, neurons are multipolar (one axon, two or more dendrites), bipolar (one axon, one dendrite) or unipolar (cell body with one axon only).
Multipolar neurons occur in the cerebral cortex, bipolar in the retina of the eye, and unipolar usually in the embryonic stage.
Axons are of two types: myelinated and non-myelinated.
Myelinated fibres are enveloped by Schwann cells, which form a myelin sheath around the axon; the gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths are nodes of Ranvier.
Myelinated fibres occur in spinal and cranial nerves.
An unmyelinated fibre is enclosed by a Schwann cell that forms no myelin sheath; such fibres are common in the autonomous and somatic neural systems.
nuggets.tip: Myelinated = spinal and cranial nerves; unmyelinated = autonomous and somatic systems. Easy to swap in exams.

questions.why: All pairs fit NCERT: multipolar = one axon and two or more dendrites, unipolar = cell body with one axon only, bipolar = one axon and one dendrite.
Both false: a multipolar neuron has one axon and two or more dendrites, and bipolar neurons occur in the retina. The cerebral cortex has multipolar neurons.
The gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths are the nodes of Ranvier. A synapse or synaptic gap lies between two neurons, not along one axon.
i, ii and iii match NCERT. iv is wrong: gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths are nodes of Ranvier; a synaptic cleft lies between two neurons.
Both false: the locations are swapped. Myelinated fibres occur in spinal and cranial nerves, and unmyelinated fibres in the autonomous and somatic systems.

nuggets.title: Resting membrane: polarisation and resting potential
lines: Neurons are excitable cells because their membranes are in a polarised state; ion channels on the membrane are selectively permeable to different ions.
At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to K+, nearly impermeable to Na+, and impermeable to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm.
The axoplasm has high K+, negatively charged proteins and low Na+; the fluid outside has low K+ and high Na+, forming a concentration gradient.
The sodium-potassium pump maintains these gradients by active transport, moving 3 Na+ outwards for 2 K+ into the cell.
As a result, the outer surface of the axonal membrane is positive and the inner surface negative, so the membrane is polarised.
The electrical potential difference across the resting plasma membrane is the resting potential.
nuggets.tip: Pump: 3 Na<sup>+</sup> OUT, 2 K<sup>+</sup> IN. Inside = K<sup>+</sup> rich; outside = Na<sup>+</sup> rich.

questions.why: At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+; the reverse order is the tempting trap.
The Na+-K+ pump moves 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in by active transport, which maintains the resting gradients.
All four are true of a polarised membrane: outside positive, inside negative, impermeable to axoplasmic proteins, and more permeable to K<sup>+</sup> than to Na<sup>+</sup>.
A is true. B is false: the pump moves 3 Na+ (not 2) outwards for 2 K+ into the cell.
I, III and IV are correct. II is wrong: the resting axolemma is more permeable to K+. V is wrong: the pump uses active transport.

nuggets.title: Action potential: depolarisation and repolarisation
lines: A stimulus at a site on the polarised membrane makes that site freely permeable to Na+, causing a rapid influx of Na+.
This reverses the polarity: the outer surface becomes negative and the inner surface positive, so the membrane is depolarised.
The potential difference across the membrane at that site is the action potential, which is in fact termed a nerve impulse.
Current flows along the inner surface from the excited site to the next site, so the impulse is conducted along the axon by repeating this sequence.
The stimulus-induced rise in Na+ permeability is extremely short-lived and is quickly followed by a rise in permeability to K+.
Within a fraction of a second, K+ diffuses outside the membrane and restores the resting potential, so the fibre can respond to stimulation again.
nuggets.tip: Na<sup>+</sup> IN → depolarise (inside +); K<sup>+</sup> OUT → repolarise (inside −).

questions.why: A stimulus makes that site freely permeable to Na+, causing a rapid Na+ influx. K+ permeability rises only afterwards.
The action potential comes from a rapid influx of Na+ from ECF into ICF; K+ efflux comes later and restores the resting potential.
Inside the membrane is negative at rest, becomes positive during depolarisation, and returns to negative when K+ efflux restores the resting potential.
Repolarisation follows a rise in K+ permeability, and K+ diffuses outside (efflux). Na+ influx is depolarisation.
II–V are correct. I is wrong: Na+ moving into the cell with the inside turning positive is depolarisation, not polarisation (inside negative).

nuggets.title: Synapse: electrical vs chemical
lines: A nerve impulse passes from one neuron to another through junctions called synapses.
A synapse is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap, the synaptic cleft.
There are two types of synapse: electrical and chemical.
At electrical synapses the two membranes are in very close proximity and current flows directly from one neuron to the other, much like conduction along a single axon.
Transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster than across a chemical synapse; electrical synapses are rare in our system.
nuggets.tip: Electrical = close contact, fast, rare. Chemical = cleft plus neurotransmitter, slower, common.

questions.why: Incorrect: a chemical synapse is slower. Transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster because current flows directly.
Both true: electrical synapses are always faster than chemical ones, and they are rare in our system.
At an electrical synapse current flows directly between closely placed membranes, so transmission is very similar to conduction along a single axon.
I, II, III, V and VI are true. IV is false: electrical synapses need no neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine; current passes directly.
NCERT names two types of synapse: electrical and chemical.

nuggets.title: Chemical synapse and neurotransmitters
lines: At a chemical synapse, a fluid-filled space called the synaptic cleft separates the pre- and post-synaptic membranes.
Neurotransmitters are the chemicals that carry impulses across chemical synapses; axon terminals hold vesicles filled with them.
When an impulse reaches the axon terminal, the synaptic vesicles move to the membrane, fuse with it and release neurotransmitters into the cleft.
Released neurotransmitters bind specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, opening ion channels so that ions enter.
This ion entry generates a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron, which may be excitatory or inhibitory.
nuggets.tip: Receptors sit on the POST-synaptic membrane; vesicles are released from the PRE-synaptic side.

questions.why: Neurotransmitter receptors are on the post-synaptic membrane; the pre-synaptic terminal only releases the transmitter from its vesicles.
The impulse reaches the axon terminal, vesicles release transmitter into the synaptic cleft, it binds the post-synaptic membrane, and the post-synaptic neuron responds.
Sequence: transmitter released into the cleft (C), it binds receptors (A), ion channels open (D), and a new potential is generated (B).
A is true. B is false: neurotransmitters bind receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, not the pre-synaptic one.
The new potential in the post-synaptic neuron may be excitatory or inhibitory, depending on the transmitter and its receptor.

nuggets.title: Brain: functions, meninges and main divisions
lines: The brain is the central information-processing organ and acts as the command and control system of the body.
It controls voluntary movements, balance, vital involuntary organs (lungs, heart, kidneys), thermoregulation, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms, endocrine glands and behaviour.
It is also the site for processing vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts.
The brain is protected by the skull and covered by cranial meninges: outer dura mater, very thin middle arachnoid, and inner pia mater in contact with brain tissue.
The brain has three major parts: forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain; the forebrain consists of the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.
nuggets.tip: Meninges, outer to inner: Dura, Arachnoid, Pia (DAP). Pia touches the brain.

questions.why: NCERT lists all of these as brain functions: voluntary movements, vital involuntary organs, balance, thermoregulation, hunger and thirst.
From inner to outer: pia mater (touches brain), arachnoid (very thin middle layer), dura mater (outer).
Inside the bony skull (cranium), the brain is covered by the cranial meninges; the arachnoid is only one of the three layers.
A is true. B is false: the order is reversed. Dura mater is the outer layer and pia mater the inner layer.
I–III are true. IV–VI are wrong: dura mater is outer, arachnoid is the very thin middle layer, and pia mater is inner.

nuggets.title: Cerebrum: hemispheres, cortex and association areas
lines: The cerebrum forms the major part of the human brain; a deep cleft divides it longitudinally into left and right cerebral hemispheres.
The hemispheres are connected by a tract of nerve fibres called the corpus callosum.
The cerebral cortex is a layer of cells covering the hemispheres and thrown into prominent folds; it is called grey matter because neuron cell bodies concentrated there give it a greyish look.
The cortex has motor areas, sensory areas and large regions that are neither clearly sensory nor motor, called association areas.
Association areas handle complex functions such as intersensory associations, memory and communication.
Myelinated fibres of the tracts form the inner part of the hemispheres and look opaque white, so they are called white matter.
nuggets.tip: Cortex = grey (cell bodies); inner part = white (myelinated tracts).

questions.why: Both true: the hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum, a tract of nerve fibres, and the cerebrum forms the major part of the brain.
The cerebral cortex is grey matter because neuron cell bodies are concentrated there; myelinated axons make up the inner white matter.
Association areas are neither clearly sensory nor motor; they handle intersensory association, memory and communication.
III and IV are false: association areas lie in the cortex (grey matter), not white matter only, and they are not clearly motor. I and II are true.
Cerebrum divides into two hemispheres (Q), joined by the corpus callosum (P); the cortex has motor, sensory and association regions (S); association areas handle memory and communication (R).

nuggets.title: Thalamus, hypothalamus and limbic system
lines: The cerebrum wraps around the thalamus, a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling.
The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus and has centres that control body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking.
The hypothalamus also contains groups of neurosecretory cells that secrete hormones called hypothalamic hormones.
The inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres and deep structures such as the amygdala and hippocampus form the limbic system.
Together with the hypothalamus, the limbic system regulates sexual behaviour, expression of emotions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) and motivation.
nuggets.tip: Temperature, hunger and thirst = hypothalamus (not thalamus). Emotions and sexual behaviour = limbic system plus hypothalamus.

questions.why: The cerebrum wraps around the thalamus, a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling; the hypothalamus lies at its base.
The hypothalamus has the centres for body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking; the thalamus only coordinates sensory and motor signals.
Both true: the hypothalamus has neurosecretory cells that secrete hypothalamic hormones, and the limbic system includes the amygdala and hippocampus.
The limbic system with the hypothalamus regulates sexual behaviour and the expression of excitement, pleasure, rage and fear.
Wrongly paired: fibre tracts that interconnect brain regions describe the pons, not the limbic system, which handles emotions and sexual behaviour.

nuggets.title: Midbrain and brain stem
lines: The midbrain lies between the thalamus/hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain.
A canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain.
The dorsal portion of the midbrain consists mainly of four round swellings (lobes) called corpora quadrigemina.
The midbrain and hindbrain form the brain stem, made of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.
The brain stem forms the connection between the brain and the spinal cord.
nuggets.tip: Corpora quadrigemina are DORSAL in the midbrain; the cerebellum is not part of the brain stem.

questions.why: All true: the midbrain lies between the thalamus/hypothalamus and the pons, the cerebral aqueduct passes through it, and its dorsal part has four lobes.
Corpora quadrigemina, the four round swellings, lie in the dorsal portion of the midbrain.
Both false: the names are swapped. The canal is the cerebral aqueduct, and the four dorsal lobes are the corpora quadrigemina.
I, II, III and V are correct. IV is wrong: corpora quadrigemina are on the dorsal, not ventral, portion of the midbrain.
The brain stem is the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum belongs to the hindbrain but is not part of the brain stem.

nuggets.title: Hindbrain: pons, cerebellum and medulla
lines: The hindbrain comprises the pons, cerebellum and medulla (medulla oblongata).
The pons consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.
The cerebellum has a very convoluted surface to provide additional space for many more neurons.
The medulla of the brain is connected to the spinal cord.
The medulla contains centres that control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.
nuggets.tip: Pons = connecting tracts; cerebellum = convoluted surface for more neurons; medulla = respiration, heart and gastric centres.

questions.why: I, II and IV are correct. III is wrong: the cerebellum has no visual area; visual areas lie in the cerebral cortex.
The pons consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.
The cerebellum has a very convoluted surface to give additional space for many more neurons.
The medulla has centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions, so all options are correct.
The pons connects brain regions (R); the hypothalamus has neurosecretory cells (S); the medulla controls respiration and gastric secretion (Q); the cerebellum gives extra space for neurons (P).

nuggets.title: Endocrine glands and hormones: the basics
lines: Endocrine glands lack ducts and are hence called ductless glands; their secretions are called hormones.
Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts.
Hormones are released into the blood and carried to target organs that may be located distantly.
Invertebrates have very simple endocrine systems with few hormones, whereas vertebrates have a large number of chemicals acting as hormones.
Organised endocrine bodies in humans: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus and gonads (testis and ovary).
The neural and endocrine systems jointly coordinate and regulate the physiological functions of the body.
nuggets.tip: Hormones are NON-nutrient and act as INTERcellular (not intracellular) messengers.

questions.why: Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals produced in trace amounts. They carry signals; they are not nutrients and are never made in bulk.
Hormones travel from the secreting cell to distant target cells, so they are intercellular messengers. Second messengers like cAMP act inside the cell, not hormones.
A is correct: endocrine glands are ductless and their secretions are hormones. B is wrong because hormones are non-nutrient chemicals, not nutrient chemicals.
Parathyroid and adrenal are purely endocrine. Testis and ovary also produce gametes, pancreas has an exocrine part, so other pairs are not 'only endocrine'.
Coordination is two-way: hypothalamic neurons regulate the pituitary, and hormones in turn influence neural activity. The neural and endocrine systems jointly coordinate functions.

nuggets.title: Hypothalamus: releasing and inhibiting hormones
lines: The hypothalamus is the basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain) and regulates a wide spectrum of body functions.
It contains groups of neurosecretory cells called nuclei which produce hormones.
Hypothalamic hormones are of two types: releasing hormones (stimulate pituitary secretion) and inhibiting hormones (inhibit it).
GnRH stimulates pituitary synthesis and release of gonadotrophins; somatostatin inhibits release of growth hormone from the pituitary.
Hormones reach the anterior pituitary through a portal circulatory system; the posterior pituitary is under direct neural regulation via axons.
nuggets.tip: Somatostatin is an INHIBITING hormone: it inhibits GH release.

questions.why: Both correct: the hypothalamus is the basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain) and contains neurosecretory cells called nuclei that make hormones.
The hypothalamus releases releasing hormones (stimulate pituitary) and inhibiting hormones (inhibit pituitary secretion).
Both wrong: GnRH stimulates (not inhibits) gonadotrophin release, and somatostatin inhibits (not stimulates) growth hormone release.
Both correct: hypothalamic hormones pass down axons to nerve endings; those for the anterior pituitary reach it via the portal circulation.
GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH. Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone, so options pairing it are wrong.

nuggets.title: Pituitary gland: location and parts
lines: The pituitary lies in a bony cavity called sella tursica and is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.
It is divided anatomically into an adenohypophysis and a neurohypophysis.
Adenohypophysis has two portions: pars distalis (anterior pituitary) and pars intermedia.
Pars distalis produces GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH; pars intermedia secretes only MSH.
In humans the pars intermedia is almost merged with pars distalis.
Neurohypophysis (pars nervosa) stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, which are synthesised by the hypothalamus.
nuggets.tip: Pars intermedia = only MSH. Pars distalis = 6 hormones (GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH).

questions.why: Both correct: the pituitary sits in the sella tursica, is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk, and has an adenohypophysis and a neurohypophysis.
Pars distalis produces six hormones: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH. MSH comes from pars intermedia; oxytocin and ADH from the neurohypophysis.
A is wrong: pars intermedia secretes only MSH; prolactin comes from pars distalis. B is correct: pars nervosa stores and releases hypothalamic hormones.
MSH is secreted by the pars intermedia, the middle (intermediate) lobe of the pituitary.

nuggets.title: Anterior pituitary hormones and GH disorders
lines: Over-secretion of GH causes abnormal growth called gigantism; low secretion causes stunted growth called pituitary dwarfism.
Excess GH in adults, especially in middle age, causes acromegaly: severe disfigurement, especially of the face.
Prolactin regulates growth of mammary glands and milk formation; TSH stimulates synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones.
ACTH stimulates synthesis and secretion of steroid hormones called glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex.
In males LH stimulates androgen secretion from testis; in females LH induces ovulation and maintains the corpus luteum, while FSH stimulates follicle growth.
MSH acts on melanocytes and regulates pigmentation of the skin.
nuggets.tip: Gigantism = excess GH in children; acromegaly = excess GH in adults.

questions.why: Both are swapped: excess GH causes gigantism, while low GH causes pituitary dwarfism.
After adolescence the bone growth (epiphyseal) plates close, so excess GH in adults cannot increase height; instead it causes acromegaly.
Both correct: prolactin regulates mammary gland growth and milk formation; TSH stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion.
Both correct: ACTH stimulates glucocorticoid secretion from the adrenal cortex, and MSH acts on melanocytes to regulate skin pigmentation.
Both correct: in females LH induces ovulation of mature follicles and maintains the corpus luteum, and FSH stimulates growth of ovarian follicles.

nuggets.title: Posterior pituitary: oxytocin and vasopressin
lines: The neurohypophysis only stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin; both are synthesised by the hypothalamus and carried axonally.
Oxytocin acts on smooth muscles; in females it causes vigorous uterine contraction at child birth and milk ejection from the mammary gland.
Vasopressin acts mainly at the kidney, stimulating resorption of water and electrolytes by the distal tubules, so it is called anti-diuretic hormone (ADH).
Impaired synthesis or release of ADH reduces the kidney's ability to conserve water, causing water loss and dehydration: diabetes insipidus.
nuggets.tip: Posterior pituitary is not a 'true' gland: it stores, it does not synthesise.

questions.why: Both correct: oxytocin causes vigorous uterine contraction at birth and milk ejection; vasopressin acts on distal tubules to reduce water loss, hence ADH.
The neurohypophysis collects and stores vasopressin and oxytocin made by the hypothalamus; it does not secrete (synthesise) them.
ADH is synthesised in the hypothalamus but stored and released by the pituitary. Prolactin, MSH and LH are made in the pituitary itself.
The posterior pituitary only stores and releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons, so it is not a true endocrine gland. It has no duct.
Deficient ADH means less water reabsorption from distal tubules, causing dilute urine and dehydration: diabetes insipidus, not diabetes mellitus.

nuggets.title: Pineal gland: melatonin
lines: The pineal gland is located on the dorsal side of the forebrain.
It secretes melatonin, which regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body.
Melatonin helps maintain the normal rhythm of the sleep-wake cycle and body temperature.
Melatonin also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and our defence capability.
nuggets.tip: Pineal is on the DORSAL forebrain; diurnal rhythm is 24-hour, not 12-hour.

questions.why: A is wrong: the pineal is on the dorsal (not ventral) side of the forebrain. B is correct: melatonin regulates the 24-hour rhythm.
Melatonin from the pineal regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm including the sleep-wake cycle.
Melatonin influences metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle and defence capability. The pineal is in the forebrain (not midbrain) and the rhythm is 24-hour.
Melatonin is secreted by the pineal body (pineal gland) on the dorsal side of the forebrain.
Correct match: melatonin, pineal, sleep-wake cycle. Oxytocin does not grow mammary glands, and ANF comes from the atrial wall and lowers BP.

nuggets.title: Thyroid gland: structure and hormones
lines: The thyroid has two lobes on either side of the trachea, interconnected by a thin flap of connective tissue called the isthmus.
It is composed of follicles and stromal tissues; each follicle has follicular cells enclosing a cavity.
Follicular cells synthesise thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); iodine is essential for their normal synthesis.
Thyroid hormones regulate basal metabolic rate, support RBC formation, control carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism and influence water and electrolyte balance.
The thyroid also secretes a protein hormone, thyrocalcitonin (TCT), which regulates (lowers) blood calcium levels.
nuggets.tip: Isthmus links the two lobes; follicles make T3/T4. TCT lowers blood Ca2+.

questions.why: A is correct: two lobes lie on either side of the trachea. B is wrong: the connecting flap is the isthmus; follicles are the hormone-making units.
TSH comes from the anterior pituitary, not the hypothalamus. The other statements on follicles, T4, T3 and TCT are correct.
Sleep-wake rhythm is controlled by melatonin and immune development by the thymus. Thyroid hormones do control BMR, RBC formation and water-electrolyte balance.
Thyrocalcitonin is made by the thyroid and decreases blood Ca2+. Raising Ca2+ is the job of parathyroid hormone.
Thyroxine regulates BMR, supports erythropoiesis and influences water-electrolyte balance. Blood calcium is regulated by TCT, not thyroxine.

nuggets.title: Thyroid disorders: hypothyroidism, cretinism, Graves'
lines: Iodine deficiency in diet causes hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, commonly called goitre.
Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development of the baby, leading to stunted growth (cretinism), mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism.
In adult women, hypothyroidism may cause the menstrual cycle to become irregular.
Cancer or nodules of the thyroid can raise hormone output: hyperthyroidism, which adversely affects body physiology.
Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism: enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, increased BMR and weight loss.
nuggets.tip: Protruding eyeballs = HYPERthyroidism (Graves'), not deficiency.

questions.why: Iodine is essential for T3/T4 synthesis, so iodine deficiency causes hypothyroidism and goitre (thyroid enlargement).
Maternal hypothyroidism in pregnancy causes defective development of the baby, leading to cretinism (stunted growth, mental retardation).
Hypothyroidism lowers BMR, reduces support for RBC formation and in adult women can make the menstrual cycle irregular: all of them.
Stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ and abnormal skin describe cretinism, caused by maternal hypothyroidism, e.g. iodine deficiency in diet.
Exophthalmos (protruding eyeballs) occurs in Graves' disease, a form of hyperthyroidism. Cretinism and goitre are linked to deficiency.

nuggets.title: Parathyroid gland: PTH and blood calcium
lines: Humans have four parathyroid glands on the back side of the thyroid gland, one pair in each lobe.
They secrete a peptide hormone, parathyroid hormone (PTH); its secretion is regulated by circulating Ca2+ levels.
PTH increases blood Ca2+: it stimulates bone resorption (dissolution/demineralisation), Ca2+ reabsorption by renal tubules and Ca2+ absorption from digested food.
PTH is therefore a hypercalcemic hormone; along with TCT it plays a significant role in calcium balance.
nuggets.tip: PTH raises Ca2+ (hypercalcemic); TCT lowers it.

questions.why: There are four parathyroid glands, located on the back side of the thyroid gland, one pair in each lobe.
Both correct: PTH stimulates bone resorption, Ca2+ reabsorption by renal tubules and Ca2+ absorption from digested food.
PTH is a peptide hormone that raises blood calcium, so it is hypercalcemic. Thyrocalcitonin is the hypocalcemic one.
PTH increases blood Ca2+ and Ca2+ absorption from food, and has no stated role in carbohydrate metabolism, so (b), (d), (e) are not its effects.
Parathormone raises blood Ca2+; its deficiency therefore lowers blood calcium. Calcitonin deficiency would not lower it.

nuggets.title: Thymus: thymosins and immunity
lines: The thymus is a lobular structure between the lungs, behind the sternum, on the ventral side of the aorta.
It secretes peptide hormones called thymosins, which play a major role in differentiation of T-lymphocytes that provide cell-mediated immunity.
Thymosins also promote production of antibodies to provide humoral immunity.
The thymus is degenerated in old individuals, decreasing thymosin production and weakening immune responses of old persons.
nuggets.tip: Thymosins -> T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity), not B-lymphocytes.

questions.why: A is correct: the thymus is lobular and lies ventral to the heart and aorta. B is wrong: thymosins differentiate T-lymphocytes, not B-lymphocytes.
The thymus (via thymosins) drives T-lymphocyte differentiation, so damage to it in a child leads to loss of cell-mediated immunity.
Thymosins play a major role in the differentiation of T-lymphocytes. Raising blood sugar or calcium is done by other hormones.
Parathyroid (PTH) stimulates bone resorption; thymosins also promote antibody production; T-lymphocytes give cell-mediated immunity; thymus degeneration weakens immunity in the old.
Catecholamines are stress (emergency) hormones, MSH regulates pigmentation, thymosins affect immune response and melatonin regulates diurnal rhythm.

nuggets.title: Adrenal medulla: hormones of fight or flight
lines: A pair of adrenal glands lies at the anterior part of each kidney; the central tissue is the adrenal medulla and the outer is the adrenal cortex.
Adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), collectively called catecholamines.
Catecholamines are secreted rapidly during stress or emergency, so they are called emergency hormones or hormones of Fight or Flight.
They increase alertness, pupillary dilation, piloerection, sweating, heart beat, strength of heart contraction and rate of respiration.
They stimulate glycogenolysis (raising blood glucose) and also lipolysis and proteolysis.
nuggets.tip: Catecholamines come from the MEDULLA; corticoids from the cortex.

questions.why: Fight or flight activates the adrenal medulla, which rapidly releases epinephrine and norepinephrine. Other options name wrong glands or effects.
Adrenaline and noradrenaline (catecholamines) are the emergency hormones of fright, fight and flight.
Sudden fear (an earthquake) triggers rapid adrenaline release from the adrenal medulla, raising heart rate, alertness and blood glucose.
Both correct: catecholamines stimulate glycogenolysis (raising blood glucose); glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis.
Adrenaline increases heart beat, strength of heart contraction and rate of respiration: all of them.

nuggets.title: Adrenal cortex: corticoids and Addison's disease
lines: The adrenal cortex has three layers, inner to outer: zona reticularis, zona fasciculata and zona glomerulosa; it secretes hormones called corticoids.
Glucocorticoids (mainly cortisol) stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis and inhibit cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids.
Cortisol maintains the cardiovascular system and kidney functions, produces anti-inflammatory reactions, suppresses the immune response and stimulates RBC production.
Aldosterone (main mineralocorticoid) acts on renal tubules to reabsorb Na+ and water and excrete K+ and phosphate, maintaining electrolytes, fluid volume, osmotic pressure and BP.
Small amounts of androgenic steroids from the cortex help grow axial, pubic and facial hair during puberty.
Underproduction of cortex hormones alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue: Addison's disease.
nuggets.tip: Inner to outer: R-F-G (reticularis, fasciculata, glomerulosa).

questions.why: From inside to outside the cortex layers are zona reticularis, zona fasciculata, zona glomerulosa; the glomerulosa is outermost.
A is correct: medulla is central, cortex is outer. B is wrong: the cortex has three layers, including zona glomerulosa.
A is wrong: cortisol produces anti-inflammatory reactions and suppresses immunity. B is correct about aldosterone's roles.
Adrenaline comes from the adrenal medulla, so cortex injury will not affect it. Aldosterone, cortisol and adrenal androgens are cortical.
Both correct: Graves' disease shows thyroid enlargement, protruding eyes, high BMR, weight loss; low cortex hormones cause Addison's disease.

nuggets.title: Pancreas: insulin, glucagon and diabetes
lines: The pancreas is a composite gland acting as both exocrine and endocrine gland.
Its endocrine part is the Islets of Langerhans: about 1 to 2 million islets, forming 1 to 2 per cent of pancreatic tissue.
α-cells secrete glucagon and β-cells secrete insulin; both are peptide hormones.
Glucagon acts mainly on hepatocytes, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis: it is a hyperglycemic hormone.
Insulin acts on hepatocytes and adipocytes, enhancing cellular glucose uptake and glycogenesis: it is a hypoglycemic hormone.
Prolonged hyperglycemia causes diabetes mellitus, with loss of glucose in urine and formation of harmful ketone bodies; it is treated with insulin therapy.
nuggets.tip: Alpha = glucagon (raises sugar); Beta = insulin (lowers sugar).

questions.why: A normal human pancreas has about 1 to 2 million islets of Langerhans, forming only 1 to 2 per cent of pancreatic tissue.
Both correct: glucagon acts on hepatocytes to stimulate glycogenolysis; insulin acts on hepatocytes and adipocytes to increase glucose uptake and use.
Converting glycogen to glucose (glycogenolysis) is glucagon's action. Insulin increases glucose uptake and oxidation and forms hepatic glycogen.
Mismatched: insulin does not stimulate gluconeogenesis; it lowers blood sugar. Glucagon causes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Both wrong because the names are swapped: hyperglycemia with ketone bodies is diabetes mellitus; ADH impairment causing water loss is diabetes insipidus.

nuggets.title: Testis: androgens
lines: A pair of testes lies in the scrotal sac; the testis is both a primary sex organ and an endocrine gland.
Testis has seminiferous tubules and stromal/interstitial tissue; Leydig (interstitial) cells in the intertubular spaces produce androgens, mainly testosterone.
Androgens regulate development, maturation and functions of male accessory sex organs such as epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate and urethra.
Androgens stimulate muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness and low pitch of voice, and play a major stimulatory role in spermatogenesis.
Androgens act on the CNS to influence male sexual behaviour (libido) and produce anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.
nuggets.tip: Androgens -> LOW pitch of voice; oestrogens -> high pitch.

questions.why: A is correct: the testes lie in the scrotal sac outside the abdomen. B is wrong: Leydig cells produce androgens, not progesterone.
A is wrong: it is androgens, not progesterone, that regulate male accessory sex organs. B is correct: androgens stimulate spermatogenesis and are anabolic.
Androgens cause a low pitch of voice, not a high pitch. The other options (spermatogenesis, libido, anabolic effects) are correct.
Muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness and low pitch of voice are effects of testosterone (androgens) from Leydig cells.
A is correct: LH stimulates androgen secretion from testis. B is wrong: spermatogenesis is regulated by FSH and androgens, not oestrogen.

nuggets.title: Ovary: oestrogen and progesterone
lines: Females have a pair of ovaries in the abdomen; each produces one ovum during each menstrual cycle.
Ovary has ovarian follicles and stromal tissues and produces two groups of steroid hormones: estrogen and progesterone.
Estrogen is made mainly by growing ovarian follicles; after ovulation the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes mainly progesterone.
Estrogens stimulate growth of female accessory sex organs, development of growing follicles, secondary sex characters (e.g. high pitch of voice) and mammary gland development.
Progesterone supports pregnancy and acts on mammary glands to stimulate formation of alveoli and milk secretion.
nuggets.tip: Corpus luteum = mainly progesterone. Milk EJECTION is oxytocin, not progesterone.

questions.why: Both correct: ovaries produce one ovum each cycle, and contain follicles and stroma that make the steroid hormones estrogen and progesterone.
A is correct: growing ovarian follicles make estrogen. B is wrong: the corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone, not androgens.
Assertion is true: the corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone. Reason is false: milk ejection is caused by oxytocin.
Oxytocin: uterine contraction in labour; prolactin: lactation; LH: ovulation; progesterone: implantation and maintenance of pregnancy.
Growth of ovarian follicles, mammary gland development and high pitch of voice are female secondary sex effects of estrogens.

nuggets.title: Hormones of heart and kidney
lines: The atrial wall of the heart secretes a peptide hormone, atrial natriuretic factor (ANF).
ANF is released when blood pressure is increased; it causes dilation of blood vessels and so decreases blood pressure.
ANF therefore acts as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.
Juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce a peptide hormone, erythropoietin, which stimulates erythropoiesis (RBC formation).
nuggets.tip: ANF lowers BP (vasodilation); it is released on HIGH BP, not low.

questions.why: A is wrong: ANF decreases blood pressure. B is correct: juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce erythropoietin, which stimulates RBC formation.
Erythropoietin, which stimulates RBC formation, is produced by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney, not bone marrow or pancreas.
ANF causes vasodilation and lowers BP, opposing the renin-angiotensin system, so it acts as a check on renin-angiotensin.
ANF dilates blood vessels and therefore decreases blood pressure. It does not raise BP or increase water reabsorption.
ANF is released when BP rises, so a fall in BP will not release it. Low BP instead triggers renin, aldosterone and ADH.

nuggets.title: Gastrointestinal hormones and growth factors
lines: Endocrine cells in the gastrointestinal tract secrete four major peptide hormones: gastrin, secretin, CCK and GIP.
Gastrin acts on gastric glands to stimulate secretion of HCl and pepsinogen.
Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas to stimulate secretion of water and bicarbonate ions.
Cholecystokinin (CCK) acts on both pancreas and gall bladder, stimulating pancreatic enzymes and bile juice; GIP inhibits gastric secretion and motility.
Several non-endocrine tissues secrete growth factors, essential for normal growth of tissues and their repair.
nuggets.tip: CCK acts on BOTH pancreas and gall bladder.

questions.why: Both correct: gastrin stimulates HCl and pepsinogen from gastric glands; secretin stimulates water and bicarbonate from exocrine pancreas.
A is wrong: CCK acts on both pancreas and gall bladder, not only on pancreas. B is correct about growth factors.
GIP (gastric inhibitory peptide) inhibits both gastric secretion and motility.
Target sites: CCK on pancreas, GIP on gastric glands, ANF from the heart, ADH acts on the kidney: A-S, B-R, C-Q, D-P.
Secretin is produced in the small intestine and stimulates the exocrine pancreas to release water and bicarbonate.

nuggets.title: Chemical nature of hormones
lines: On chemical nature hormones are of four groups: peptide/polypeptide/protein, steroids, iodothyronines and amino-acid derivatives.
Peptide/protein hormones include insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones.
Steroid hormones include cortisol, testosterone, estradiol and progesterone.
Iodothyronines are the thyroid hormones; epinephrine is an amino-acid derivative.
nuggets.tip: Epinephrine = amino-acid derivative, not steroid or peptide.

questions.why: Protein: insulin and glucagon; steroid: cortisol and estradiol; iodothyronines: thyroid hormones; amino-acid derivatives: epinephrine and norepinephrine.
Glucagon is a peptide hormone. Cortisol, testosterone and progesterone are steroids.
Epinephrine is an amino-acid derived hormone. Estradiol and estriol are steroids.
All 10 are peptide hormones: erythropoietin, thymosin, PTH, ANF, the four GI hormones, insulin and glucagon.
Both correct: thyroid hormones are iodothyronines and epinephrine is an amino-acid derivative; receptors inside the cell (mostly nuclear) are intracellular receptors.

nuggets.title: Mechanism of hormone action
lines: Hormones act by binding to specific proteins called hormone receptors, located in the target tissues only.
Receptors on the cell membrane are membrane-bound receptors; those inside the cell are intracellular receptors, mostly nuclear receptors.
Hormones binding membrane-bound receptors normally do not enter the cell; they generate second messengers such as cyclic AMP, IP3, Ca2+, which regulate metabolism.
Protein hormones such as FSH act via membrane receptors; steroid hormones and iodothyronines act via intracellular receptors.
Hormone-receptor complexes of intracellular receptors interact with the genome to regulate gene expression or chromosome function.
nuggets.tip: Steroids and thyroid hormones: intracellular receptors. Protein hormones: membrane receptors + second messengers.

questions.why: Both correct: membrane-receptor hormones act via second messengers (cAMP, IP3, Ca2+); intracellular receptors regulate gene expression.
Both wrong: hormone receptors are proteins, not lipids, and receptors on the cell membrane are membrane-bound, not nuclear, receptors.
cAMP, cGMP and Ca2+ serve as second messengers; sodium does not.
Lipid-soluble steroids like cortisol and testosterone cross the membrane and bind intracellular (mostly nuclear) receptors. Insulin, glucagon and oxytocin are peptides.
Steroid hormones enter the cell, and the hormone-receptor complex interacts with the genome (DNA) to change gene expression. They do not use cAMP.

nuggets.title: Flower and stamen: the anther
lines: Flowers are the sites of sexual reproduction; the whorl of stamens, the androecium, is the male reproductive organ and the gynoecium is the female one.
A stamen has a long slender stalk, the filament, and a terminal, generally bilobed anther; the filament's proximal end attaches to the thalamus or petal.
A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed, and each lobe has two thecae, so the anther is dithecous; a longitudinal groove separates the thecae.
The anther is a four-sided (tetragonal) structure with four microsporangia at its corners, two in each lobe.
Microsporangia develop further into pollen sacs, which extend along the length of the anther and are packed with pollen grains.
nuggets.tip: Bilobed × 2 thecae = 4 microsporangia per typical anther.

questions.why: The whorl of stamens is the androecium, the male reproductive organ. The corolla and calyx are non-essential whorls; the gynoecium is female.
The filament's proximal end attaches to the thalamus or the petal; the anther is at its distal (terminal) end.
A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed and each lobe has two thecae, so it is dithecous.
A typical bilobed anther has 4 microsporangia, one at each corner, two in each lobe.
The microsporangia develop into pollen sacs, so pollen sac = microsporangium. The embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

nuggets.title: Microsporangium: wall layers and sporogenous tissue
lines: In transverse section a microsporangium is near-circular, surrounded by four wall layers: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum.
The outer three wall layers protect the microsporangium and help in dehiscence of the anther to release pollen.
The innermost layer, the tapetum, nourishes the developing pollen grains.
Tapetal cells have dense cytoplasm and generally more than one nucleus.
In a young anther, compactly arranged homogenous cells called the sporogenous tissue occupy the centre of each microsporangium.
nuggets.tip: Order, outer to inner: Epidermis, Endothecium, Middle layers, Tapetum.

questions.why: The outermost wall layer is the epidermis and the innermost is the tapetum. The endothecium lies just inside the epidermis.
The outer three wall layers (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers) give protection and help in dehiscence; nourishment is the tapetum's job.
Both are true: the tapetum is the innermost layer, its cells have dense cytoplasm and usually more than one nucleus, and it nourishes the developing pollen.
A is true. B is false: the sporogenous tissue is made of compactly arranged homogenous cells and occupies the centre of each microsporangium.
The assertion matches NCERT. The reason is false: the tapetum nourishes the developing pollen grains, not the microspore mother cells.

nuggets.title: Microsporogenesis
lines: As the anther develops, each cell of the sporogenous tissue is a potential pollen mother cell (PMC) or microspore mother cell.
Each PMC undergoes meiosis to form a cluster of four haploid cells, the microspore tetrad.
The formation of microspores from a PMC through meiosis is called microsporogenesis.
As the anther matures and dehydrates, the microspores separate and develop into pollen grains.
Each microsporangium holds several thousand pollen grains, released when the anther dehisces.
nuggets.tip: 1 PMC → 1 meiosis → 4 microspores → 4 pollen grains.

questions.why: Each sporogenous cell is a potential pollen (microspore) mother cell; it becomes microspores only after meiosis.
In microsporogenesis, meiosis occurs in the microspore mother cells (PMCs), giving haploid microspore tetrads.
A diploid microspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form a haploid microspore tetrad, which separates into haploid microspores.
A is false: sporogenous cells undergo meiosis to form microspore tetrads, not mitosis or megaspores. B is true: pollen grains are the male gametophytes.
One PMC gives 4 microspores, i.e. 4 pollen grains, after meiosis, so 100 pollen grains need 100 ÷ 4 = 25 PMCs.

nuggets.title: Pollen grain wall: exine, sporopollenin and germ pores
lines: Pollen grains are generally spherical, about 25–50 µm in diameter, with a two-layered wall.
The hard outer layer, the exine, is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known.
Sporopollenin withstands high temperatures and strong acids and alkali, and no enzyme that degrades it is known; so pollen is well preserved as fossils.
The exine has prominent apertures called germ pores, where sporopollenin is absent.
The inner wall, the intine, is a thin, continuous layer made of cellulose and pectin.
nuggets.tip: Exine = sporopollenin (no germ pores in sporopollenin). Intine = cellulose plus pectin.

questions.why: NCERT gives pollen grains a diameter of about 25–50 micrometres.
Sporopollenin forms the exine of the pollen grain; the intine is cellulose and pectin, and the tapetum and endothecium are anther wall layers.
Germ pores are apertures in the exine where sporopollenin is absent; the regions that resist acids and heat are the sporopollenin parts.
All four describe the exine: it is hard, made of sporopollenin, withstands heat, strong acids and alkali, and no known enzyme degrades it.
Only IV is wrong: the exine's apertures without sporopollenin are germ pores. The micropyle is an opening in the ovule.

nuggets.title: Pollen grain cells and shedding stage
lines: A mature pollen grain contains two cells: the vegetative cell and the generative cell.
The vegetative cell is bigger, has an abundant food reserve and a large, irregularly shaped nucleus.
The generative cell is small, spindle-shaped, with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus, and floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell.
In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at the 2-celled stage.
In the rest, the generative cell divides mitotically into two male gametes before shedding, so pollen is shed at the 3-celled stage.
nuggets.tip: Over 60% of angiosperms shed pollen 2-celled; the rest shed it 3-celled.

questions.why: The vegetative cell is bigger, has abundant food reserve and a large irregularly shaped nucleus; the generative cell is small and spindle-shaped.
I, II and IV describe the generative cell. III is wrong: the abundant food reserve belongs to the vegetative cell.
The microspore divides by mitosis into vegetative and generative cells, and the generative cell divides mitotically to form two male gametes.
A is true: about 40% of angiosperms shed pollen at the 3-celled stage (over 60% at 2-celled). B is false: the intine is a continuous layer.
