A 3-celled pollen grain has 1 vegetative cell and 2 male gametes; the generative cell has already divided into the two gametes.

nuggets.title: Pollen and humans: allergy, nutrition, viability, storage
lines: Pollen of many species causes severe allergies and bronchial afflictions, sometimes leading to chronic respiratory disorders such as asthma and bronchitis.
Parthenium (carrot grass) came into India as a contaminant with imported wheat, has become ubiquitous, and causes pollen allergy.
Pollen is rich in nutrients; pollen tablets and syrups are sold as food supplements and are claimed to boost the performance of athletes and race horses.
Pollen viability varies: rice and wheat pollen lose viability within 30 minutes, while some Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae pollen stay viable for months.
Pollen can be stored for years in liquid nitrogen (−196 °C) in pollen banks for crop breeding programmes.
nuggets.tip: Rice and wheat: 30 minutes. Rosaceae, Leguminosae, Solanaceae: months. Storage at −196 °C.

questions.why: All are true: Parthenium (carrot grass) came with imported wheat, became ubiquitous, and causes pollen allergy.
All are NCERT facts: pollen tablets and syrups are sold as food supplements and are claimed to boost the performance of athletes and race horses.
Pollen of some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae stays viable for months; Poaceae cereals (rice, wheat) lose viability within 30 minutes.
I, III and IV are correct. II is wrong: rice and wheat pollen lose viability within 30 minutes, not 30 seconds.
Pollen is stored for years in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C, in pollen banks.

nuggets.title: Pistil and the ovule (megasporangium)
lines: The gynoecium may be monocarpellary or multicarpellary; multiple pistils may be fused (syncarpous, Papaver) or free (apocarpous, Michelia).
Each pistil has a stigma (landing platform for pollen), a style (elongated slender part) and an ovary (swollen basal part) whose cavity, the locule, holds the placenta.
Ovules (megasporangia) arise from the placenta; an ovary may have one ovule (wheat, paddy, mango) or many (papaya, watermelon, orchids).
The ovule is attached to the placenta by a stalk, the funicle; the body of the ovule fuses with the funicle at the hilum.
One or two integuments encircle the nucellus except at the tip, where a small opening, the micropyle, lies; the opposite basal end is the chalaza.
The nucellus is a mass of cells with abundant reserve food and holds the embryo sac (female gametophyte); an ovule generally has a single embryo sac.
nuggets.tip: Ovule = integumented megasporangium. Single ovule: wheat, paddy, mango; many: papaya, watermelon, orchids.

questions.why: A syncarpous pistil (fused) is seen in Papaver (Q), an apocarpous gynoecium in Michelia (P), and a single pistil is monocarpellary (R).
Only I is correct. II is wrong because orchids have many ovules; III is wrong because wheat has a single ovule.
The ovule is technically the megasporangium (integumented); the carpel is the megasporophyll and the embryo sac develops from the megaspore.
Funicle is the stalk of the ovule (Q), chalaza the basal part (R), micropyle the small opening (P), and integuments the covering (S).
Both false: the micropyle is a small opening, and the basal part opposite the micropyle is the chalaza, not the nucellus.

nuggets.title: Megasporogenesis and embryo sac development
lines: Ovules generally differentiate a single megaspore mother cell (MMC) in the micropylar region of the nucellus.
The MMC undergoes meiosis to produce four megaspores; this is megasporogenesis.
In most flowering plants one megaspore is functional and three degenerate; the functional megaspore develops into the embryo sac, a monosporic development.
The functional megaspore nucleus divides mitotically three times, giving the 2-, 4- and 8-nucleate stages; these divisions are strictly free nuclear.
After the 8-nucleate stage, cell walls are laid down, organising the typical female gametophyte (embryo sac).
nuggets.tip: Mature embryo sac from MMC: 1 meiosis plus 3 mitoses (free nuclear).

questions.why: In most angiosperms reduction division (meiosis) occurs in the MMC. The filiform apparatus is in the synergids, not the egg, and there are only 3 antipodals.
The functional megaspore develops into the embryo sac (female gametophyte); the whole ovule becomes the seed.
Assertion true: the MMC undergoes meiosis to give four megaspores. Reason false: the MMC is diploid, and only the megaspores are haploid.
Three free-nuclear mitotic divisions give 8 nuclei, and cell walls are laid down only after the 8-nucleate stage.
MMC → 4 megaspores needs 1 meiosis; the functional megaspore then undergoes 3 mitotic divisions to reach the 8-nucleate embryo sac.

nuggets.title: Structure of the mature embryo sac
lines: Six of the eight nuclei get cell walls; the remaining two polar nuclei lie below the egg apparatus in the large central cell.
At the micropylar end, three cells form the egg apparatus: two synergids and one egg cell.
Synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip, the filiform apparatus, which guides pollen tubes into the synergid.
Three cells at the chalazal end are the antipodals.
A typical angiosperm embryo sac at maturity is 8-nucleate and 7-celled.
nuggets.tip: Egg apparatus = micropylar; antipodals = chalazal; filiform apparatus = synergids at the micropylar tip.

questions.why: 7 cells (3 antipodals, 2 synergids, 1 egg, 1 central cell) hold 8 nuclei, since the central cell has 2 polar nuclei.
The filiform apparatus of synergids guides the entry of the pollen tube into the synergid.
Only IV is right. The egg apparatus has 2 synergids and one egg, the central cell has two polar nuclei, and the filiform apparatus is at the micropylar tip.
Assertion true: 8-nucleate, 7-celled. Reason false: the 2 polar nuclei are in the central cell; the egg apparatus is 2 synergids plus 1 egg.
The three antipodal cells lie at the chalazal end; the egg apparatus is at the micropylar end.

nuggets.title: Kinds of pollination: autogamy, geitonogamy, xenogamy
lines: Autogamy is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower; in open flowers it needs synchrony in pollen release and stigma receptivity, and anthers close to the stigma.
Chasmogamous flowers have exposed anthers and stigma; cleistogamous flowers do not open at all.
Viola (common pansy), Oxalis and Commelina produce both chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers.
Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous and give assured seed-set even without pollinators.
Geitonogamy is the transfer to another flower of the same plant: functionally cross-pollination using an agent, but genetically similar to autogamy.
Xenogamy is the transfer to the stigma of a different plant; it is the only type that brings genetically different pollen to the stigma.
nuggets.tip: Geitonogamy = functionally cross, genetically self.

questions.why: Autogamy in an open flower needs synchrony of pollen release and stigma receptivity and anthers and stigma lying close together.
Cleistogamous flowers never open, so they are invariably autogamous; chasmogamous flowers can show autogamy, geitonogamy or xenogamy.
Commelina bears cleistogamous flowers, which are autogamous and give assured seed-set without pollinators.
Both true: transfer to a different plant is xenogamy, and geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination but genetically like autogamy.
Only xenogamy (pollen from a different plant) brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma.

nuggets.title: Wind pollination (anemophily)
lines: Plants use two abiotic agents, wind and water, and one biotic agent, animals; most plants use biotic agents, and wind is the more common abiotic agent.
Wind pollination needs light, non-sticky pollen grains produced in large numbers.
Wind-pollinated flowers have well-exposed stamens and a large, often feathery stigma to trap air-borne pollen.
They often have a single ovule in each ovary and numerous flowers packed into an inflorescence, such as the corn cob.
The tassels of the corn cob are the stigma and style, which wave in the wind to trap pollen; wind pollination is common in grasses.
nuggets.tip: Corn tassels = stigma plus style (pollen traps), not anthers.

questions.why: All are wind-pollination features: light, non-sticky pollen, well-exposed stamens and a large, often feathery stigma.
Light, non-sticky pollen in large numbers plus long, feathery stigmas are adaptations for wind pollination.
A single ovule per ovary and flowers packed into an inflorescence are features of wind-pollinated flowers.
Corn tassels are the stigma and style, which wave in the wind to trap pollen grains; they do not disperse pollen.
III–VII fit wind pollination. Large coloured flowers (I) and nectar (II) belong to animal-pollinated flowers.

nuggets.title: Water pollination (hydrophily)
lines: Water pollination is quite rare, limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons.
Examples are Vallisneria and Hydrilla in fresh water and several marine sea-grasses such as Zostera.
Not all aquatic plants use water: in water hyacinth and water lily the flowers rise above the water and are pollinated by insects or wind.
In Vallisneria, the female flower reaches the surface on a long stalk, and male flowers or pollen released onto the surface are carried passively by water currents.
In sea-grasses, female flowers stay submerged; pollen is released into the water, is long and ribbon-like, and is carried passively. Most such pollen has a mucilaginous covering against wetting.
Like wind-pollinated flowers, water-pollinated flowers are not very colourful and do not produce nectar.
nuggets.tip: Water hyacinth and water lily are aquatic but pollinated by insects or wind.

questions.why: In water hyacinth and water lily the flowers emerge above water and are pollinated by insects or wind, not by water.
Water hyacinth does not use water for pollination; Vallisneria, Hydrilla and Zostera do.
II–V are correct. I is wrong: water-pollinated flowers such as Vallisneria are not colourful and produce no nectar.
In many sea-grasses pollen grains are long and ribbon-like and are carried passively inside the water.
Both false, with wind and water swapped: wind is the more common abiotic agent, and water pollination is rare (about 30 genera).

nuggets.title: Insect and animal pollination
lines: Bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds and bats pollinate flowers; among animals, insects, particularly bees, are the dominant pollinators.
Larger animals such as primates (lemurs), arboreal rodents and reptiles (gecko and garden lizards) also act as pollinators in some species.
Insect-pollinated flowers are mostly large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar; flowers pollinated by flies and beetles give off foul odours.
Floral rewards are nectar and pollen; some flowers offer a safe place to lay eggs, e.g. the tallest flower, Amorphophallus (about 6 feet).
A species of moth and the plant Yucca cannot complete their life cycles without each other; the moth lays eggs in the locule of the ovary.
Pollen/nectar robbers take pollen or nectar without bringing about pollination.
nuggets.tip: Amorphophallus is about 6 feet tall (feet, not metres).

questions.why: Incorrect: bees, not moths and butterflies, are the dominant insect pollinators. The other statements match NCERT.
Large, colourful, fragrant, nectar-rich flowers are typical of insect-pollinated plants.
Amorphophallus rewards its pollinators with a safe place to lay eggs; being the tallest flower is not a reward.
The moth species and Yucca cannot complete their life cycles without each other; the moth lays eggs in the ovary's locule.
Only IV is wrong: wind-pollinated flowers have light, non-sticky pollen. Amorphophallus is about 6 feet tall, so I is correct.

nuggets.title: Outbreeding devices
lines: Most flowering plants have hermaphrodite flowers, and continued self-pollination causes inbreeding depression, so plants have evolved devices to prevent it.
In some species pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised: pollen is released before the stigma is receptive, or the reverse.
In others, the anther and stigma are placed at different positions so pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower.
Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that stops self-pollen from fertilising ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.
Unisexual flowers: monoecious castor and maize prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy; dioecious papaya prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
nuggets.tip: Monoecious (castor, maize) = stops autogamy only. Dioecious (papaya) = stops autogamy and geitonogamy.

questions.why: Continued self-pollination results in inbreeding depression, which is why outbreeding devices evolved.
When pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised, self-pollination is prevented and cross-pollination is favoured.
Self-incompatibility is the genetic mechanism that blocks self-pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.
Castor and maize are monoecious: male and female flowers on the same plant prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy.
A dioecious plant bears only male or only female flowers, so both autogamy and geitonogamy are prevented.

nuggets.title: Pollen–pistil interaction
lines: Pollination does not guarantee the right kind of pollen; the pistil recognises pollen as compatible (accepted) or incompatible (rejected).
This recognition comes from a continuous dialogue mediated by chemical components of the pollen interacting with those of the pistil.
After compatible pollination, the pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube through one of the germ pores, which grows through the stigma and style to the ovary.
In plants that shed 2-celled pollen, the generative cell divides into two male gametes during growth of the pollen tube in the stigma.
The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and the embryo sac through one of the synergids, guided by the filiform apparatus.
All events from pollen deposition on the stigma until pollen tubes enter the ovule together form the dynamic process of pollen–pistil interaction.
nuggets.tip: Pollen–pistil interaction ends when the pollen tube enters the ovule, before fertilisation.

questions.why: Order: pollen deposited on stigma, pollen tube develops, tube enters the ovule, then the embryo sac, then male gametes are released.
NCERT defines pollen–pistil interaction as all events from pollen deposition on the stigma until pollen tubes enter the ovule. It can reject pollen too, so option 1 is wrong.
When pollen is shed 2-celled, the generative cell forms two male gametes during growth of the pollen tube in the stigma.
The pollen tube enters the embryo sac through one of the synergids, guided by the filiform apparatus.
The pistil recognises whether pollen is of the right (compatible) or wrong (incompatible) type and accepts or rejects it.

nuggets.title: Artificial hybridisation: emasculation and bagging
lines: In artificial hybridisation, only the desired pollen is used and the stigma is protected from unwanted pollen, through emasculation and bagging.
If the female parent has bisexual flowers, anthers are removed from the bud with forceps before they dehisce; this is emasculation.
Emasculated flowers are covered with a bag, generally of butter paper, to keep unwanted pollen off the stigma (bagging).
When the stigma becomes receptive, pollen from the desired male parent is dusted on it and the flower is rebagged.
If the female parent has unisexual flowers, emasculation is not needed; female buds are simply bagged before the flowers open.
nuggets.tip: Sequence: emasculation → bagging → artificial pollination → rebagging.

questions.why: Order: emasculation, then bagging, then dusting desired pollen when the stigma is receptive (artificial pollination), then rebagging.
Both are NCERT steps: bagging keeps unwanted pollen off the emasculated stigma, and the flower is rebagged after the desired pollen is dusted.
A is incorrect: emasculation must be done before the anther dehisces. B is correct: anthers are removed with forceps.
Emasculation removes anthers from bisexual flowers; unisexual female flowers have no anthers, so it is not needed.
The bag used to cover emasculated flowers is generally made of butter paper.

nuggets.title: Double fertilisation
lines: After entering a synergid, the pollen tube releases the two male gametes into the cytoplasm of the synergid.
One male gamete fuses with the egg nucleus (syngamy), forming the diploid zygote.
The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell, forming the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN); this is triple fusion.
Since two types of fusion, syngamy and triple fusion, occur in one embryo sac, the process is double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.
After triple fusion the central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC) and develops into the endosperm, while the zygote develops into the embryo.
nuggets.tip: Syngamy = 2 nuclei → 2n zygote. Triple fusion = 3 nuclei → 3n PEN.

questions.why: One male gamete fuses with the egg (syngamy) and the other with the polar nuclei of the central cell (triple fusion).
Fusion of a male gamete with the central cell's polar nuclei is triple fusion; syngamy is fusion with the egg.
The PEN forms by fusion of two polar nuclei and one male gamete, three haploid nuclei, so it is triploid.
Synergids are haploid (n), the zygote is diploid (2n) and the PEN is triploid (3n). Antipodals are also haploid.
A is true: double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms. B is false: other plant groups also form embryos.

nuggets.title: Endosperm development
lines: Post-fertilisation events are endosperm and embryo development, maturation of ovules into seeds, and maturation of the ovary into fruit.
Endosperm development precedes embryo development: the PEC divides repeatedly into triploid endosperm tissue full of reserve food for the embryo.
Commonly the PEN undergoes successive nuclear divisions to give free nuclei (free-nuclear endosperm); cell walls form later and the endosperm becomes cellular.
Coconut water from a tender coconut is free-nuclear endosperm, and the surrounding white kernel is cellular endosperm.
Endosperm may be fully consumed by the embryo before seed maturation (pea, groundnut, beans) or persist in the mature seed (castor, coconut).
nuggets.tip: Consumed: pea, groundnut, beans. Persists: castor, coconut.

questions.why: Endosperm development precedes embryo development, so the embryo has assured nutrition.
i is wrong: tender coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm (thousands of nuclei), not cellular. ii is right: the white kernel is cellular endosperm.
Endosperm is fully consumed before seed maturation in pea, groundnut and beans; it persists in castor and coconut.
A is true. B is false: the examples are swapped. Endosperm is consumed in pea, groundnut and beans, and persists in castor and coconut.
Gametogenesis happens before fertilisation; embryogenesis, seed formation and fruit formation are post-fertilisation events.

nuggets.title: Embryo development: dicot and monocot
lines: The embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryo sac, where the zygote lies; most zygotes divide only after some endosperm has formed.
The zygote gives rise to the proembryo and then the globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo; these early stages (embryogeny) are similar in monocots and dicots.
A dicot embryo has an embryonal axis and two cotyledons; above the cotyledons is the epicotyl ending in the plumule (stem tip), and below is the hypocotyl ending in the radicle (root tip).
A monocot embryo has one cotyledon; in the grass family it is the scutellum, placed laterally on the embryonal axis.
In grasses the radicle and root cap are enclosed in the coleorhiza; the epicotyl's shoot apex and leaf primordia are enclosed in a hollow foliar structure, the coleoptile.
nuggets.tip: Coleoptile covers the shoot; coleorhiza covers the root.

questions.why: The zygote lies at the micropylar end of the embryo sac, so the embryo develops there.
ii and iv are true. i is false: pollen release and stigma receptivity are not always synchronised. iii is false: the chalaza is the basal part.
The single, large, shield-shaped cotyledon of the wheat (grass) embryo is the scutellum.
Plumule is the stem tip (R), radicle the root tip (P), hypocotyl lies below the cotyledons (Q), and epicotyl lies above them (S).
Both true: in grasses the cotyledon is the lateral scutellum, and the shoot apex with leaf primordia is enclosed in the coleoptile.

nuggets.title: Seed: structure, types and perisperm
lines: The seed is the final product of sexual reproduction (a fertilised ovule) formed inside the fruit; it has seed coat(s), cotyledon(s) and an embryo axis.
Non-albuminous seeds have no residual endosperm (pea, groundnut); albuminous seeds keep part of it (wheat, maize, barley, castor).
In some seeds, such as black pepper and beet, remnants of the nucellus persist; this residual, persistent nucellus is the perisperm.
The integuments harden into tough protective seed coats; the micropyle remains as a small pore that lets oxygen and water in during germination.
As the seed matures it dries to 10–15 per cent moisture by mass; the embryo's metabolism slows and it may enter dormancy.
nuggets.tip: Perisperm = leftover nucellus (2n); endosperm = 3n.

questions.why: The persistent, residual nucellus in seeds such as black pepper and beet is the perisperm.
Perisperm is leftover nucellus, so it is diploid, whereas the angiosperm endosperm is triploid.
Both true: integuments harden into tough seed coats, and the micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat.
Both true: mature seeds hold only 10–15% moisture by mass, and the ovary develops into the fruit as the ovules mature into seeds.
Albuminous seeds retain endosperm: castor, wheat and maize (3). Gram, bean, pea and groundnut are non-albuminous.

nuggets.title: Fruit formation and significance of seeds
lines: As ovules mature into seeds, the ovary develops into a fruit and the ovary wall becomes the pericarp; fruits may be fleshy (guava, orange, mango) or dry (groundnut, mustard).
In apple, strawberry and cashew the thalamus also forms part of the fruit (false fruits); most fruits develop only from the ovary (true fruits).
Some species, such as banana, form fruits without fertilisation (parthenocarpic fruits, which are seedless); growth hormones can induce parthenocarpy.
Seeds help because pollination and fertilisation do not need water, they aid dispersal, carry food reserves and a protective seed coat, and give new genetic combinations.

A lupine, Lupinus arcticus, from the Arctic Tundra germinated after about 10,000 years of dormancy; a 2000-year-old date palm seed (Phoenix dactylifera) came from King Herod's palace near the Dead Sea.
Orchids and the parasites Orobanche and Striga produce thousands of tiny seeds per fruit.
nuggets.tip: Lupine (Arctic Tundra, 10,000 years) vs date palm (Dead Sea, 2000 years). Easy to swap.

questions.why: Wrong: the outer integument forms the testa, and the inner one forms the tegmen. Ovule → seed, ovary → fruit and ovary wall → pericarp are correct.
Strawberry is a false fruit, because the thalamus contributes to it, like apple and cashew.
A, B and C are NCERT advantages of seeds. D is wrong: seeds are products of sexual reproduction.
Both false: the names are swapped. Lupinus arcticus came from the Arctic Tundra (10,000 years) and Phoenix dactylifera from King Herod's palace (2000 years).
Orchids and the parasites Orobanche and Striga all produce thousands of tiny seeds in each fruit.

nuggets.title: Apomixis and polyembryony
lines: Some species of Asteraceae and grasses produce seeds without fertilisation; this is apomixis, a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.
In some species the diploid egg cell forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation.
In many Citrus and mango varieties, some nucellar cells around the embryo sac divide, protrude into it and develop into embryos.
Such ovules contain many embryos; more than one embryo in a seed is called polyembryony.
Hybrid seeds must be bought every year because characters segregate in their progeny; making hybrids apomictic stops segregation, so farmers can reuse hybrid seed.
nuggets.tip: Apomictic embryos are genetically identical to the parent; there is no meiosis and no fusion.

questions.why: Nucellar polyembryony, with embryos arising from nucellar cells, is reported in Citrus (and mango varieties).
Apomictic hybrid seeds do not segregate characters, so farmers can reuse them instead of buying new hybrid seed every year.
I and II are correct. III is wrong: mango ovules with nucellar embryos have many embryos. IV is wrong: more than one embryo is polyembryony.
Lemon (Citrus) shows polyembryony (R); black pepper has perisperm (P); apple is a false fruit (S); banana is parthenocarpic (Q).
Assertion true: apomixis gives no new variation. Reason false: in apomixis the diploid egg forms without reduction division.

nuggets.title: Reproductive events and the testis
lines: Human reproductive events in order: gametogenesis → insemination → fertilisation → blastocyst formation and implantation → gestation → parturition.
Testes lie outside the abdominal cavity in a pouch, the scrotum, which keeps them 2–2.5 °C below body temperature, as needed for spermatogenesis.
Each testis (about 4–5 cm long, 2–3 cm wide) has about 250 testicular lobules, each with 1–3 highly coiled seminiferous tubules.
Seminiferous tubules are lined by male germ cells (spermatogonia), which form sperms, and Sertoli cells, which nourish the germ cells.
Interstitial spaces outside the tubules contain small blood vessels, immunologically competent cells and Leydig cells, which secrete androgens.
nuggets.tip: Sertoli = nurse cells inside tubules (FSH target); Leydig = androgen makers outside tubules (LH target).

questions.why: Gametogenesis → insemination → fertilisation → implantation → gestation → parturition. Gestation (embryonic development) can only follow implantation, so options placing it earlier are wrong.
NCERT: each testis has about 250 testicular lobules, each holding 1–3 highly coiled seminiferous tubules.
The scrotum keeps testicular temperature 2–2.5 °C lower than internal body temperature, which spermatogenesis needs; it is not about protection or display.
Leydig (interstitial) cells lie outside the seminiferous tubules and synthesise and secrete testicular hormones called androgens.
Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules and provide nutrition to the germ cells; they are not found in the ovary, adrenal or pancreas.

nuggets.title: Male accessory ducts, glands and penis
lines: Male accessory ducts are rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis and vas deferens; tubules open via rete testis into vasa efferentia, which lead to the epididymis.
The epididymis, along the posterior surface of each testis, leads to the vas deferens, which ascends to the abdomen and loops over the urinary bladder.
Vas deferens receives a duct from the seminal vesicle and opens into the urethra as the ejaculatory duct; the urethra opens outside at the urethral meatus.
The penis has special tissue that helps erection; its enlarged tip, the glans penis, is covered by a loose fold of skin called the foreskin.
Male accessory glands: paired seminal vesicles, a prostate and paired bulbourethral glands; their secretions form seminal plasma rich in fructose, calcium and certain enzymes.
Secretions of the bulbourethral glands also help in lubrication of the penis.
nuggets.tip: Sperm route: seminiferous tubules → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.

questions.why: Sperms pass seminiferous tubules → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra → urethral meatus. The inguinal canal is not a sperm duct.
NCERT lists male sex accessory ducts as rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis and vas deferens. The seminal vesicle is an accessory gland, not a duct.
Vasa efferentia carry sperms from the testis (via rete testis) to the epididymis, so blocking them stops transport from testis to epididymis.
Secretions of the male accessory glands (seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands) form seminal plasma, rich in fructose, calcium and certain enzymes.
NCERT: bulbourethral gland secretions help in lubrication of the penis; they do not nourish, activate or speed up sperms.

nuggets.title: Female system: ovary, oviduct and uterus
lines: The female system has a pair of ovaries, accessory ducts (oviducts, uterus, vagina), external genitalia and a pair of mammary glands, mostly in the pelvic region.
Each ovary (2–4 cm long) is covered by thin epithelium enclosing the ovarian stroma, which has a peripheral cortex and an inner medulla.
Each oviduct (10–12 cm) has the funnel-shaped infundibulum whose fimbriae collect the ovum, then the wider ampulla, then the narrow isthmus joining the uterus.
The uterus (womb) is shaped like an inverted pear; it opens into the vagina through the cervix, whose cervical canal forms the birth canal along with the vagina.
Uterine wall: outer thin perimetrium, middle thick smooth-muscle myometrium, and inner glandular endometrium that changes cyclically during the menstrual cycle.
nuggets.tip: Oviduct from ovary side: infundibulum → ampulla → isthmus → uterus. Fertilisation happens in the ampulla.

questions.why: Female accessory ducts are the oviducts, uterus and vagina. Ovaries are primary sex organs, and mammary glands are not ducts.
The oviduct has infundibulum, ampulla and isthmus. The fundus is a part of the uterus, not of the Fallopian tube.
The ampulla lies between the infundibulum and the isthmus, so a block there stops the ovum moving from infundibulum to isthmus.
NCERT: the inner endometrium is a glandular layer; the thick smooth-muscle layer is the myometrium.
Both true: vas deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct to open into the urethra as the ejaculatory duct, and cervical canal plus vagina form the birth canal.

nuggets.title: External genitalia and mammary glands
lines: Female external genitalia: mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen and clitoris.
Mons pubis is a cushion of fatty tissue covered by skin and pubic hair; labia majora are fleshy folds around the vaginal opening, with paired labia minora beneath them.
The clitoris is a tiny finger-like structure at the upper junction of the two labia minora, above the urethral opening.
The hymen partially covers the vaginal opening; it can tear by a sudden fall or jolt, a tampon or sports, so it is not a reliable indicator of virginity.
Each mammary gland has 15–20 mammary lobes with clusters of cells called alveoli, which secrete milk stored in their cavities (lumens).
Milk route: alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct, through which milk is sucked out.

questions.why: The clitoris is the tiny finger-like structure at the upper junction of the two labia minora above the urethral opening; mons pubis is a fatty cushion.
A is true. B is false: the hymen can also tear by a sudden fall or jolt, a vaginal tampon, or sports like horseback riding and cycling, not only at first coitus.
Milk flows alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct, i.e. iv → ii → i → v → iii.
Tubules of each lobe join to form a mammary duct; several mammary ducts join to form a wider mammary ampulla, which connects to the lactiferous duct.
Each mammary lobe contains clusters of cells called alveoli, which secrete milk that is stored in their cavities.

nuggets.title: Spermatogenesis and its hormonal control
lines: Spermatogenesis starts at puberty: spermatogonia (2n = 46) multiply by mitosis, and some become primary spermatocytes.
A primary spermatocyte completes meiosis I to form two equal haploid secondary spermatocytes (23 chromosomes each), which give spermatids after meiosis II.
Spermatids become spermatozoa by spermiogenesis; sperm heads stay embedded in Sertoli cells and are finally released from the tubules by spermiation.
At puberty, increased GnRH from the hypothalamus acts on the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH.
LH acts on Leydig cells to secrete androgens, which stimulate spermatogenesis; FSH acts on Sertoli cells to secrete factors that help spermiogenesis.
nuggets.tip: Spermiogenesis = spermatid → sperm (shape change). Spermiation = release of sperm. Do not swap them.

questions.why: Meiosis I of a primary spermatocyte yields two equal haploid secondary spermatocytes; spermatids appear only after meiosis II.
Spermiogenesis transforms non-motile spermatids into spermatozoa; spermatogenesis is the whole process starting from spermatogonia.
In spermiogenesis spermatozoa are formed from spermatids; in spermiation sperms are released from Sertoli cells into the cavity of the seminiferous tubules.
Spermatogenesis begins at puberty due to a significant increase in GnRH secretion by the hypothalamus, which in turn raises LH and FSH.
FSH acts on Sertoli cells and stimulates secretion of factors that help spermiogenesis; LH acts on Leydig cells to release androgens.

nuggets.title: Sperm structure and semen
lines: A sperm has a head, neck, middle piece and tail, and its whole body is enveloped by a plasma membrane.
The head has an elongated haploid nucleus whose anterior part is covered by a cap-like acrosome filled with enzymes that help fertilisation of the ovum.
The middle piece has numerous mitochondria that produce energy for tail movement, giving the sperm motility essential for fertilisation.
A human male ejaculates about 200–300 million sperms during a coitus.
For normal fertility at least 60% of sperms must have normal shape and size, and at least 40% must show vigorous motility.
Sperms with seminal plasma form semen; the functions of male ducts and glands are maintained by testicular hormones (androgens).
nuggets.tip: 60% normal shape and size, 40% vigorous motility. Examiners love swapping these two numbers.

questions.why: Head holds the haploid nucleus, acrosome is filled with enzymes, middle piece has mitochondria, tail gives motility: A–S, B–P, C–Q, D–R.
The acrosome is filled with enzymes (sperm lysins) that dissolve the egg envelopes and help fertilisation; it is not a sensory or piercing organ.
Assertion is true (200–300 million sperms). Reason swaps the numbers: NCERT needs at least 60% normal shape/size and 40% vigorous motility.
Both false: the acrosome covers the anterior part of the nucleus, and the enzymes are in the acrosome, while the middle piece holds mitochondria.
For normal fertility, at least 40% of ejaculated sperms must show vigorous motility (and at least 60% must have normal shape and size).

nuggets.title: Oogenesis and ovarian follicles
lines: Oogenesis starts during embryonic development, when a couple of million oogonia form in each fetal ovary; no more oogonia are formed after birth.
Oogonia enter prophase I of meiosis and get temporarily arrested as primary oocytes; each, surrounded by granulosa cells, is a primary follicle.
Many follicles degenerate from birth to puberty, so only 60,000–80,000 primary follicles are left in each ovary at puberty.
Primary follicles gain more granulosa layers and a new theca to form secondary follicles, then tertiary follicles with a fluid-filled cavity, the antrum.
In the tertiary follicle the primary oocyte completes unequal meiosis I, forming a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body.
The tertiary follicle matures into the Graafian follicle; the secondary oocyte forms a new membrane, the zona pellucida, and is released at ovulation.
nuggets.tip: One primary spermatocyte → 4 sperms; one primary oocyte → only 1 ovum (the rest are polar bodies).

questions.why: Oogenesis is initiated during embryonic (fetal) development, when oogonia form in the fetal ovary; unlike spermatogenesis, it does not begin at puberty.
Large numbers of follicles degenerate from birth to puberty, leaving only 60,000–80,000 primary follicles in each ovary at puberty.
The tertiary follicle is marked by a fluid-filled cavity called the antrum; primary follicles have none.
One primary spermatocyte forms 4 sperms, but one primary oocyte forms only 1 ovum (the others become polar bodies), so the ratio is 4:1.
The secondary oocyte forms a new membrane, the zona pellucida, around itself.

nuggets.title: Menstrual cycle: the phases
lines: Primate females (monkeys, apes, humans) show the menstrual cycle; the first menstruation, at puberty, is called menarche.
A cycle repeats on average every 28/29 days, and one ovum is released (ovulation) in the middle of each cycle.
Menstrual phase (3–5 days): flow due to breakdown of the endometrial lining and its blood vessels; it occurs only if the released ovum is not fertilised.
Follicular (proliferative) phase: primary follicles grow into a fully mature Graafian follicle while the endometrium regenerates by proliferation.
Luteal (secretory) phase: the remaining parts of the Graafian follicle form the corpus luteum, whose progesterone maintains the endometrium.
Lack of menstruation may indicate pregnancy, but stress or poor health can also cause it; cycles cease around 50 years of age (menopause).
nuggets.tip: Follicular = proliferative; luteal = secretory. Menarche starts the cycles, menopause ends them.

questions.why: The first menstruation, beginning at puberty, is called menarche; menopause is when the cycles stop around 50 years.
I, III and IV are correct. Statement II is wrong: the first menstrual cycle at puberty is menarche, not menopause.
Proliferative = follicular phase, secretory = luteal phase, and menstruation = breakdown of the endometrial lining: A-2, B-3, C-1.
The secretory phase is the luteal phase, running from just after ovulation (about day 15) to day 28, i.e. roughly 13–14 days.
Without fertilisation the corpus luteum degenerates; the fall of progesterone causes breakdown of the endometrium and menstrual flow.

nuggets.title: Hormones, ovulation and corpus luteum
lines: In the follicular phase, pituitary LH and FSH increase gradually, stimulating follicle growth and estrogen secretion by the growing follicles.
LH and FSH peak in the middle of the cycle (about day 14); the rapid rise of LH, the LH surge, ruptures the Graafian follicle and causes ovulation.
After ovulation the remaining Graafian follicle forms the corpus luteum, which secretes large amounts of progesterone to maintain the endometrium.
If fertilisation does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and the endometrium breaks down, starting a new cycle.
If fertilisation and pregnancy occur, the corpus luteum and endometrium are maintained and menstrual cycles stop.

questions.why: Both LH and FSH peak in mid-cycle; the rapid LH surge occurs around the 14th day and induces ovulation.
Wrong statement: during the follicular phase LH and FSH increase gradually, not decrease. The other three statements match NCERT.
The corpus luteum mainly secretes large amounts of progesterone, essential for maintaining the endometrium; hCG comes from the placenta.
The corpus luteum forms after ovulation and degenerates if fertilisation fails, so it is a temporary endocrine gland.
Fertilisation of the ovum is the root cause; maintenance of the corpus luteum, high hormone levels and the endometrium are its consequences.

nuggets.title: Fertilisation and sex determination
lines: Semen is released into the vagina (insemination); sperms swim through the cervix and uterus to the ampullary region of the oviduct, where fertilisation occurs.
Fertilisation happens only if ovum and sperms reach the ampullary region simultaneously, so not every coitus leads to pregnancy.
Contact of a sperm with the zona pellucida induces changes in the membrane that block entry of additional sperms, so only one sperm fertilises an ovum.
Secretions of the acrosome help the sperm enter the ovum cytoplasm through the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane.
Sperm entry makes the secondary oocyte complete meiosis II, forming a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid); fused nuclei form the diploid zygote.
Every ovum carries X while a sperm carries X or Y, so the sex of the baby is decided by the father: XX is female, XY is male.
nuggets.tip: Meiosis II of the oocyte finishes only after sperm entry, not at ovulation.

questions.why: Secretions of the acrosome help one sperm enter the ovum through the zona pellucida; changes in the zona then block other sperms.
The secondary oocyte completes its second meiotic division only after a sperm enters it, giving the second polar body and the haploid ootid.
Sperm entry triggers meiosis II, so the second polar body is extruded after sperm entry but before the sperm and egg nuclei fuse.
Both true: hymen status is not a reliable indicator of virginity, and since only sperms carry X or Y, the father determines the sex of the foetus.
Meiosis II of the secondary oocyte is also unequal, forming a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid).

nuggets.title: Cleavage, blastocyst and implantation
lines: The zygote moves through the isthmus toward the uterus while dividing mitotically (cleavage) into 2, 4, 8, 16 daughter cells called blastomeres.
The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is a morula; it keeps dividing and becomes a blastocyst as it moves further into the uterus.
Blastomeres of the blastocyst form an outer layer, the trophoblast, and an inner group of cells attached to it, the inner cell mass.
The trophoblast layer attaches to the endometrium, while the inner cell mass differentiates as the embryo.
After attachment, uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst, embedding it in the endometrium (implantation); this leads to pregnancy.

questions.why: Cleavage divides the zygote without growth, so a morula has about the same cytoplasm as the zygote but much more DNA (many nuclei).
The blastocyst gets implanted when its trophoblast attaches to the endometrium; the placenta forms only after implantation.
Trophoblast = outer layer attached to endometrium; cleavage = mitotic division of zygote; inner cell mass = future embryo; implantation = embedding: A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1.
Sequence: zygote → cleavage → morula (8–16 cells) → blastocyst → implantation, so the morula lies between zygote and blastocyst.
The trophoblast of the blastocyst attaches to the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus.

nuggets.title: Placenta and pregnancy hormones
lines: After implantation, finger-like chorionic villi appear on the trophoblast and are surrounded by uterine tissue and maternal blood.
Chorionic villi and uterine tissue interdigitate to jointly form the placenta, a structural and functional unit between the embryo and the mother.
The placenta supplies O2 and nutrients to the embryo and removes CO2 and excretory wastes; it joins the embryo through the umbilical cord.
The placenta also acts as an endocrine tissue, producing hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens.
In later pregnancy the ovary secretes relaxin; hCG, hPL and relaxin are produced in women only during pregnancy.
Estrogens, progestogens, cortisol, prolactin and thyroxine also rise in maternal blood, supporting foetal growth and maintenance of pregnancy.
nuggets.tip: Placenta: hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens. Relaxin comes from the ovary; oxytocin from the maternal pituitary.

questions.why: The placenta supplies O2 and nutrients, removes CO2 and wastes and secretes estrogens, but oxytocin comes from the maternal pituitary.
Placental hormones are hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens. Relaxin is ovarian; oxytocin, prolactin and glucocorticoids are not placental.
NCERT: relaxin is secreted by the ovary in the later phase of pregnancy; the corpus luteum is the ovarian structure that produces it.
The placenta produces hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens; LH is secreted by the anterior pituitary, not the placenta.
Chorionic villi and uterine tissue interdigitate and jointly form the placenta, the structural and functional unit between embryo and mother.

nuggets.title: Embryonic development, month by month
lines: Right after implantation the inner cell mass differentiates into outer ectoderm and inner endoderm; mesoderm soon appears between them.
These three germ layers give rise to all adult tissues; the inner cell mass contains stem cells with the potency to give rise to all tissues and organs.
After one month of pregnancy the embryo's heart is formed; the first sign of a growing foetus is the heart sound, heard with a stethoscope.
By the end of the second month limbs and digits develop; by the end of 12 weeks (first trimester) most major organ systems are formed.
First movements of the foetus and appearance of hair on the head are usually seen in the fifth month.
By the end of 24 weeks (second trimester) the body is covered with fine hair, eyelids separate and eyelashes form; by nine months the foetus is fully developed.
nuggets.tip: Heart 1st month, limbs and digits 2nd month, organs by 12 weeks, movements and head hair 5th month, eyelids separate by 24 weeks.

questions.why: Mismatch is b: in the second month limbs and digits develop, while first foetal movements appear in the fifth month. a, c and d match NCERT.
A, C, D and E match NCERT: heart after 1 month, limbs and digits by end of month 2, major organs by 12 weeks (not 8), head hair in month 5.
1st month – heart; 2nd month – limbs and digits; 5th month – hair on head; 6th month (end of 24 weeks) – eyelids separate: A-R, B-S, C-Q, D-P.
The inner cell mass first forms ectoderm and endoderm; the mesoderm soon appears between them, completing the three germ layers.
All four match NCERT: villi appear on the trophoblast after implantation, ICM forms ectoderm and endoderm, implantation leads to pregnancy, and the ICM has stem cells.

nuggets.title: Parturition and lactation
lines: Human pregnancy (gestation) lasts about 9 months; vigorous uterine contractions at its end expel the foetus (parturition).
Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism; signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta cause mild uterine contractions, the foetal ejection reflex.
This reflex triggers release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary, which acts on the uterine muscle to cause stronger contractions.
Stronger contractions stimulate further oxytocin secretion; this continues until the baby is expelled through the birth canal, followed soon by the placenta.
Mammary glands differentiate during pregnancy and produce milk towards its end (lactation); milk of the first few days is colostrum.
Colostrum contains several antibodies absolutely essential to develop resistance in the newborn, so breastfeeding is recommended.
nuggets.tip: The reflex is triggered by the foetus and placenta; oxytocin from the mother's pituitary is the response.

questions.why: The foetal ejection reflex is triggered by signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta; oxytocin release is its consequence.
The foetal ejection reflex triggers release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary, causing strong uterine contractions; the foetal pituitary and relaxin are distractors.
Oxytocin acts on the smooth muscle of the uterus, the myometrium, which shows strong contractions during parturition.
Oxytocin, prostaglandins and a rising estrogen:progesterone ratio help start labour; prolactin drives milk production, not parturition.
Both true, and R explains A: colostrum carries several antibodies essential to develop resistance in the newborn, so early breastfeeding is advised.

nuggets.title: Reproductive health and RCH programmes
lines: According to the WHO, reproductive health means a total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social.
A reproductively healthy society has people with physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects.
India was amongst the first countries to start national-level action plans for reproductive health, called family planning, initiated in 1951.
The improved programmes covering wider reproduction-related areas are popularly named Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes.
Major tasks of RCH: creating awareness about reproduction-related aspects and providing facilities and support for building a reproductively healthy society.
nuggets.tip: WHO's four aspects: physical, emotional, behavioural, social. Not 'mental' or 'sexual habits'.

questions.why: Physical, emotional, behavioural and social: these are the four aspects of total well-being in the WHO definition of reproductive health. 'Mental' or 'development of sex organs' are not the WHO terms.
1951: India initiated national-level 'family planning' programmes in 1951, one of the first countries to do so.
RCH = Reproductive and Child Health Care programmes, the improved family-planning programmes covering wider reproduction-related areas.

A correct, B incorrect: RCH covers wider reproduction-related areas, but its tasks are awareness of reproduction-related aspects and support for a reproductively healthy society, not financial aspects.

nuggets.title: Sex education and medical care for reproductive health
lines: Introduction of sex education in schools gives right information to the young and discourages myths and misconceptions about sex-related aspects.

Proper information about reproductive organs, adolescence and related changes, safe and hygienic sexual practices, STIs and AIDS helps people, especially adolescents, lead a healthy reproductive life.
Fertile couples should be educated on birth control options, care of pregnant mothers, post-natal care, breast feeding and equal opportunities for the male and female child.
Awareness of problems due to uncontrolled population growth and social evils like sex-abuse and sex-related crimes must be created.
Medical assistance and care is needed for pregnancy, delivery, STIs, abortions, contraception, menstrual problems and infertility.

questions.why: Sex education aims to discourage myths and misconceptions about sex-related aspects; it gives right information on safe hygienic practices, STDs and adolescent changes.
i, ii and iii: awareness about organs and adolescence, safe hygienic practices and STD/AIDS awareness are primary steps. MTP is legal in India, so 'ban on MTP' is wrong.
All seven: NCERT lists pregnancy, delivery, STIs, abortions, contraception, menstrual problems and infertility as reproduction-related problems needing medical care.
i to v: sex education, medical assistance, awareness of contraception/STDs, equal opportunity to male and female child and ban on amniocentesis all help. Encouraging myths does the opposite.

nuggets.title: Amniocentesis ban, research and signs of better reproductive health
lines: Amniocentesis is a foetal sex-determination test based on the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid surrounding the developing embryo.
A statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination legally checks the increasing menace of female foeticide.
Research on reproduction-related areas is encouraged: Saheli, a new oral contraceptive for females, was developed at CDRI, Lucknow.
Better awareness, more medically assisted deliveries and better post-natal care have led to decreased maternal and infant mortality rates (MMR, IMR).
Other signs of improved reproductive health: more couples with small families, better detection and cure of STDs and overall increased medical facilities.
nuggets.tip: Amniocentesis itself is not an RCH strategy; the BAN on its misuse for sex determination is.

questions.why: Amniocentesis: a statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination was laid to check the menace of female foeticide.
Amniocentesis determines foetal sex from the chromosomal pattern of cells in the amniotic fluid around the embryo.
Assertion false, Reason true: amniocentesis for sex determination is not an RCH strategy; the statutory ban on it is, as it checks female foeticide.
CDRI, Lucknow (Central Drug Research Institute) developed Saheli, the once-a-week oral contraceptive pill for females.
A, B and C: better detection and cure of disease, better post-natal care and medically assisted deliveries indicate improved reproductive health. MMR decreases, not increases.

nuggets.title: Population explosion and its control
lines: World population of about 2 billion in 1900 rose to about 6 billion by 2000 and 7.2 billion in 2011.
India's population, about 350 million at independence, reached close to 1 billion by 2000 and crossed 1.2 billion in May 2011.
Rapid decline in death rate, MMR and IMR, plus an increase in the number of people in reproductive age, are the probable reasons.
As per the 2011 census, the population growth rate was less than 2 per cent (20/1000/year), a rate at which the population could increase rapidly.
Control measures: motivating smaller families with contraceptives ('Hum Do Hamare Do'), urban couples adopting the 'one child norm' and incentives to small families.
Statutory raising of the marriageable age of females to 18 years and of males to 21 years helps tackle the problem.
nuggets.tip: Population rises when death rate, MMR, IMR fall; number of people in reproductive age rises.

questions.why: A-P, B-R, C-Q: India had about 350 million at independence (1947), reached about a billion by 2000 and crossed 1.2 billion in May 2011.
A fall in death rate, MMR and IMR lets more people survive, causing population explosion. A rise in death rate or MMR would slow growth.
The 2011 census put the growth rate at less than 2 per cent, i.e. under 20/1000/year, still a rate of rapid increase.
Statutory marriageable age is 18 years for females and 21 years for males; the raised age is a population-control measure.
Many young couples in urban working areas have adopted the one child norm, going beyond 'Hum Do Hamare Do'.

nuggets.title: Ideal contraceptive and natural methods
lines: An ideal contraceptive is user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible with no or least side-effects, and does not interfere with sexual drive, desire or the sexual act.
Natural methods work on the principle of avoiding the chances of ovum and sperms meeting.
Periodic abstinence: couples avoid coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation could be expected (fertile period).
Coitus interruptus (withdrawal): the male partner withdraws his penis from the vagina just before ejaculation so as to avoid insemination.
Lactational amenorrhea: ovulation and the cycle do not occur during intense lactation after parturition; effective only up to a maximum of six months.
Natural methods have almost nil side effects, but their chances of failure are also high.
nuggets.tip: Natural methods = periodic abstinence, withdrawal, lactational amenorrhea. No device, no hormone.

questions.why: An ideal contraceptive must be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible with no or least side-effects; each single option lists only part of this.
In periodic abstinence, coitus is avoided from day 10 to 17 of the cycle, the fertile period when ovulation is expected.
A-R, B-P, C-Q: abstinence avoids days 10-17, lactational amenorrhea means no cycle during breast feeding, withdrawal removes the penis before ejaculation.
Lactational amenorrhea is a natural method needing no pills, so 'OCPs have to be used' is untrue. It works up to 6 months with nil side effects but high failure.
Vaults are a barrier method (rubber device covering the cervix). Coitus interruptus, periodic abstinence and lactational amenorrhea are natural methods.

nuggets.title: Barrier methods: condoms, diaphragms, caps, vaults
lines: In barrier methods, ovum and sperms are prevented from physically meeting; barriers are available for both males and females.
Condoms are thin rubber/latex sheaths covering the penis (or vagina and cervix in females) just before coitus, so semen is not released into the female tract.
Nirodh is a popular male condom brand; condoms also protect the user from STIs and AIDS, are disposable and can be self-inserted.
Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are rubber barriers inserted to cover the cervix during coitus; they block sperm entry through the cervix and are reusable.
Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams are usually used along with these barriers to increase their contraceptive efficiency.
nuggets.tip: Condoms are disposable and protect against STIs; diaphragm, cap and vault are reusable and don't.

questions.why: Condoms stop body fluid exchange, so they also protect against STIs and AIDS. Diaphragms and spermicides only reduce conception chances.
Nirodh is the popular brand of condom for males. Mala-D is an oral pill.
Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults cover the cervix and block the entry of sperms through the cervix; they do not affect ovulation or implantation.
A, C and D: cervical caps are reusable barriers preventing sperm-ovum meeting. Only condoms give protection from STDs, so B is wrong.
A is wrong: condoms are made of thin rubber/latex. B is right: diaphragms, caps and vaults block sperm entry through the cervix and are reusable.

nuggets.title: Intra uterine devices (IUDs)
lines: IUDs are inserted by doctors or expert nurses into the uterus through the vagina.
Types: non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and hormone releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20).
IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus; Cu ions released suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms.
Hormone-releasing IUDs also make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to the sperms.
IUDs are ideal for females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children; it is one of the most widely accepted methods of contraception in India.
nuggets.tip: Cu ions: sperm motility. Hormonal IUD: uterus unsuitable + cervix hostile. Lippes loop: no drug.

questions.why: A-R, B-S,P, C-Q,T: Lippes loop is non-medicated; Cu-7 and Multiload 375 release copper; LNG-20 and Progestasert release hormone.
Cu ions from copper IUDs suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity. Making the uterus unsuitable for implantation is the hormonal IUD's action.
Hormone-releasing IUDs such as Progestasert make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms; Cu ions act on sperm motility.
IUDs are one of the most widely accepted contraceptive methods in India, ideal for delaying pregnancy and spacing children.
Lippes loop is a non-medicated IUD; it acts by increasing phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus. CuT/Multiload are copper-releasing.

nuggets.title: Oral pills, injectables, implants and emergency contraception
lines: Oral pills contain small doses of progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations, taken daily for 21 days, starting within the first five days of the cycle.
After a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs) the pills are repeated in the same pattern as long as the female wants contraception.
Pills inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent/retard entry of sperms; they are very effective with lesser side effects.
Saheli, the new oral contraceptive for females, contains a non-steroidal preparation; it is a 'once a week' pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value.
Progestogens alone or with estrogen can be given as injections or implants under the skin; their action is like pills but lasts much longer.
Progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus are effective emergency contraceptives after rape or casual unprotected intercourse.
nuggets.tip: Pills: 21 days on, 7 days off, start within first 5 days. Saheli: once a week, non-steroidal.

questions.why: Pills are taken daily for 21 days, starting within the first 5 days of the cycle, then repeated after a 7-day gap during which menstruation occurs.
All of these: pills inhibit ovulation and implantation and also alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent or retard entry of sperms.
i, iii, v, vi: Saheli was developed at CDRI Lucknow, is once a week, has high contraceptive value and very few side effects. It is non-steroidal, so ii is wrong.
i, ii and iii: progestogens, progestogen-estrogen combinations or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus work as emergency contraceptives. Barriers cannot act after coitus.
Progestogen-estrogen combination within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse is an effective emergency contraceptive. The other hormone pairs are not contraceptives.

nuggets.title: Surgical methods (sterilisation) and side effects
lines: Surgical methods (sterilisation) are advised for the male/female partner as a terminal method to prevent any more pregnancies.
Surgical intervention blocks gamete transport and thereby prevents conception; it does not stop gamete formation.
Vasectomy: a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum.
Tubectomy: a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina.
These techniques are highly effective, but their reversibility is very poor.
Contraceptives are not regular requirements for reproductive health; ill-effects like nausea, abdominal pain, irregular bleeding or even breast cancer should not be ignored.
nuggets.tip: Vasectomy blocks sperm transport; testes still make sperms. Tubectomy does not stop ovulation.

questions.why: In tubectomy, a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied up. Cutting the vas deferens is vasectomy; ovaries and uterus are not removed.
Vasectomy removes or ties up a small part of the vas deferens through a small incision on the scrotum.
Vasectomy blocks sperm transport, not spermatogenesis; the testes keep making sperms. The other pairings are correct.
In vasectomy the incision is made on the scrotum and the vas deferens is cut or tied, so gamete transport is blocked and conception prevented.
Contraceptives are not regular requirements for maintaining reproductive health, so option 1 is incorrect. The other statements match NCERT.

nuggets.title: Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)
lines: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is called MTP or induced abortion.
Nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed in a year all over the world, about 1/5th of all conceived pregnancies.
Government of India legalised MTP in 1971 with strict conditions to avoid its misuse, such as indiscriminate and illegal female foeticide.
MTP (Amendment) Act 2017: up to 12 weeks needs the opinion of one registered medical practitioner; 12 to 24 weeks needs two registered medical practitioners.
MTPs remove unwanted pregnancies after casual intercourse, contraceptive failure or rape, and pregnancies harmful or fatal to the mother or foetus.
MTPs are relatively safe in the first trimester (up to 12 weeks); second-trimester abortions are much more risky.
nuggets.tip: MTP legalised 1971; family planning began 1951. Don't swap them.

questions.why: About 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed every year worldwide, roughly 1/5th of all conceived pregnancies.
India legalised MTP in 1971 with strict conditions to prevent misuse. 1951 is the start of family planning.
At 20 weeks (between 12 and 24 weeks), the 2017 Amendment Act requires the opinion of two registered medical practitioners; one is enough only up to 12 weeks.
MTPs are relatively safe during the first trimester (up to 12 weeks); second-trimester abortions are much riskier.
I and IV: MTPs are advised in the first trimester and need qualified medical personnel. They are not a contraceptive method and are not always surgical.

nuggets.title: Sexually transmitted infections: types and transmission
lines: Infections transmitted through sexual intercourse are called STIs, venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI).
Common STIs: gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV.
Hepatitis-B and HIV also spread by sharing injection needles or surgical instruments, by blood transfusion and from an infected mother to the foetus.
Except hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV, the other STIs are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.
nuggets.tip: Not completely curable: hepatitis-B, genital herpes, HIV. All others are curable if treated early.

questions.why: Gonorrhoea, hepatitis-B and chlamydia are all STIs. Cholera, malaria and haemophilia are not sexually transmitted.
Gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes are all STIs. Malaria, filaria and cancer are not sexually transmitted.
Hepatitis-B and HIV also spread through shared needles, surgical instruments, blood transfusion and from infected mother to foetus.
Genital herpes, with hepatitis-B and HIV, is not completely curable. Gonorrhoea, genital warts and chlamydiasis are curable if treated early.
Gonorrhoea is completely curable if detected early and treated properly. Genital herpes, hepatitis-B and HIV are not.

nuggets.title: STIs: symptoms, complications and prevention
lines: Though all persons are vulnerable, STI incidence is very high in the 15-24 years age group.
Early symptoms are minor: itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swellings in the genital region; infected females may often be asymptomatic.
Late or no treatment leads to pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility or even cancer of the reproductive tract.
Social stigma stops people from going to a qualified doctor, so infections go undetected; they should never go to quacks.
Prevention: avoid sex with unknown or multiple partners, always use condoms during coitus, and consult a qualified doctor early in case of doubt.

questions.why: STI incidence is reported to be very high in the 15-24 years age group.
All of the above: NCERT lists PID, abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility and cancer of the reproductive tract as STI complications.
i, ii, iii, iv: itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swelling are early symptoms. PID is a late complication, not an early symptom.
Patients should go to a qualified doctor, never to quacks. The other statements (15-24 years, asymptomatic females, PID and ectopic pregnancy) are correct.
All of them: avoiding multiple and unknown partners, using condoms and not sharing needles all prevent STIs.

nuggets.title: Infertility and ART: IVF, ZIFT, IUT
lines: Many couples are infertile: unable to produce children in spite of unprotected sexual co-habitation.
Causes may be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological; in India the female is often blamed, but the problem often lies in the male partner.
Infertility clinics help through special techniques called assisted reproductive technologies (ART).
In vitro fertilisation (fertilisation outside the body) followed by embryo transfer (ET) is the 'test tube baby' programme.
Zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres goes into the fallopian tube (ZIFT); embryo with more than 8 blastomeres goes into the uterus (IUT).
Embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation (fusion of gametes within the female) can also be used for such transfer.
nuggets.tip: Up to 8 blastomeres: fallopian tube (ZIFT). More than 8: uterus (IUT).

questions.why: Test tube baby = IVF followed by ET: ova and sperms fuse in the lab and the zygote/embryo is then transferred to the female.
Incorrect: in India the female is often blamed, but the problem more often lies in the male partner. The other three statements are correct.
In ZIFT, the zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube; more than 8 go to the uterus (IUT).
ZIFT and IUT transfer embryos (to fallopian tube and uterus). GIFT transfers an ovum and ICSI injects a sperm into the ovum.
In IVF-based ZIFT, either the zygote or an early embryo up to 8 cells is put into the fallopian tube; larger embryos go to the uterus.

nuggets.title: GIFT, ICSI, artificial insemination and limits of ART
lines: GIFT: an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation.
ICSI (intra cytoplasmic sperm injection) forms an embryo in the laboratory by directly injecting a sperm into the ovum.
Male inability to inseminate or very low sperm count can be corrected by artificial insemination (AI).
In AI, semen from the husband or a healthy donor is artificially introduced into the vagina or into the uterus (IUI, intra-uterine insemination).
ART needs high-precision handling by specialists and costly instruments, so few centres offer it; legal adoption of orphaned children is a good alternative.
nuggets.tip: GIFT transfers a gamete (ovum); ZIFT transfers a zygote. In GIFT fertilisation is in vivo.

questions.why: In GIFT, ova from a donor are transferred into the fallopian tube of the recipient, where fertilisation occurs. Transferring a zygote is ZIFT.
ICSI directly injects a sperm into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory.
NCERT: very low sperm count or inability to inseminate is corrected by artificial insemination, where semen is introduced into vagina or uterus.
IUI (intra-uterine insemination) is the AI technique where semen is artificially introduced into the uterus.
MTP terminates a pregnancy, so it is not an ART. ZIFT, GIFT and ICSI help infertile couples conceive.

nuggets.title: Mendel's hybridisation experiments
lines: Inheritance is the process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny; variation is the degree by which progeny differ from their parents.
Gregor Mendel conducted hybridisation experiments on garden peas for seven years (1856-1863) and proposed the laws of inheritance.
His was the first time statistical analysis and mathematical logic were applied to problems in biology; his large sampling size gave credibility to his data.
Mendel selected 14 true-breeding pea varieties, as pairs similar except for one character with contrasting traits.
A true-breeding line has undergone continuous self-pollination and shows stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations.
nuggets.tip: 14 true-breeding varieties = 7 pairs = 7 characters.

questions.why: Only A is correct: variation is how much progeny differ from parents. B is wrong because NCERT dates this knowledge to 8000-1000 B.C., not A.D.
Mendel's hybridisation experiments on garden pea ran for seven years, 1856-1863.
1 and 3: Mendel first applied statistics to biology and confirmed his inferences over successive generations. His sampling size was large, not small.
Mendel chose 14 true-breeding varieties as 7 pairs, each pair alike except for one character with contrasting traits.
All of them: a true-breeding line comes from continuous self-pollination and shows stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations.

nuggets.title: The seven pea characters Mendel studied
lines: Mendel studied seven characters of garden pea (Pisum sativum), each with two opposing traits.
Characters: stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape and seed colour.
Dominant traits: tall stem, violet flower, axial flower, inflated (full) pod, green pod, round seed, yellow seed.
Recessive traits: dwarf stem, white flower, terminal flower, constricted pod, yellow pod, wrinkled seed, green seed.
nuggets.tip: Pod colour: green dominant. Seed colour: yellow dominant. Don't swap them.

questions.why: Mendel never used trichomes. Seed colour (green/yellow), pod shape (inflated/constricted) and stem height (tall/dwarf) were among his seven characters.
Pod length was not among Mendel's seven characters; seed shape, seed colour and flower position were.
White flower is recessive to violet. Inflated pod, green pod and axial flower are all dominant traits.
Terminal flower position is recessive; axial is dominant. Violet flower, yellow seed and green pod are dominant.
I, II, IV: full pod, yellow seed and green pod are dominant, so they show in both TT-type and Tt-type plants. Dwarf is recessive and needs a homozygous condition.

nuggets.title: Monohybrid cross and key genetic terms
lines: Crossing tall and dwarf pea gave an all-tall F1; selfing F1 gave an F2 with 3/4 tall and 1/4 dwarf plants.
No blending was seen in F<sub>1</sub> or F<sub>2</sub>; the dwarf trait hidden in F<sub>1</sub> reappeared unchanged in F<sub>2</sub>.
Mendel proposed that something is stably passed down, unchanged, through gametes; he called these 'factors', now called genes.
Genes coding for a pair of contrasting traits are alleles, slightly different forms of the same gene.
Genotype is the genetic make-up (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype is the observable trait; TT/tt are homozygous and Tt is heterozygous.
nuggets.tip: F<sub>1</sub> shows only the dominant trait; the recessive one reappears in F<sub>2</sub> at 1/4.

questions.why: In F2 of tall x dwarf, 1/4 of plants were dwarf and 3/4 tall, giving the 3:1 phenotypic ratio.
Dwarf plants reappeared unchanged in F2 after being hidden in F1, showing non-blending of characters.
Mendel called the stably inherited units 'factors'; today they are called genes.
Alleles are different (molecular) forms of a gene coding for a pair of contrasting traits. They are not phenotypes or homozygotes.
Wrong match: genotype is the genetic make-up, not the physical appearance. Physical appearance is the phenotype.

nuggets.title: Punnett square, F2 ratios and test cross
lines: The Punnett square, developed by British geneticist Reginald C. Punnett, shows the probability of all possible genotypes of offspring in a cross.
F1 Tt forms T and t gametes in equal proportion; random fertilisation gives F2 genotypes TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1 and phenotypes tall : dwarf = 3 : 1.
In a test cross, an organism with the dominant phenotype is crossed with the recessive parent to find its genotype.
Test cross of Tt x tt gives tall : dwarf = 1 : 1; if the dominant plant is TT, all progeny are tall.
nuggets.tip: Test cross partner is always the homozygous recessive (tt).

questions.why: Only i is incorrect: the Punnett square was developed by British geneticist Reginald C. Punnett, not Robert. Statement ii correctly defines it.
F2 of a monohybrid cross has genotypes TT : Tt : tt in 1 : 2 : 1; 3 : 1 is the phenotypic ratio.
Crossing a dominant-phenotype organism with the recessive parent to know its genotype is a test cross.
To find whether a black-seeded plant is BB or Bb, cross it with the homozygous recessive bb: all black means BB, 1:1 means Bb.
F1 hybrid (Tt) x recessive parent (tt) gives Tt : tt = 1 : 1.

nuggets.title: Laws of dominance and segregation
lines: Law of Dominance: characters are controlled by discrete units called factors, which occur in pairs.
In a dissimilar pair of factors, one member (dominant) dominates the other (recessive); this explains only one parental trait in F<sub>1</sub> and the 3:1 ratio in F<sub>2</sub>.
Law of Segregation: alleles do not blend, and both characters are recovered as such in F2, though one is absent in F1.
During gamete formation the factors of a pair segregate, so a gamete receives only one of the two factors.
A homozygous parent gives all similar gametes; a heterozygous parent gives two kinds of gametes in equal proportion.
nuggets.tip: Segregation = 'gametes are pure': each gamete gets only one allele of a pair.

questions.why: i and iii: factors are discrete units and in a dissimilar pair one dominates the other. Factors occur in pairs, not triplets.
From monohybrid crosses Mendel proposed the Law of Dominance and the Law of Segregation; independent assortment needed a dihybrid cross.
Law of Segregation: the factors of a pair segregate so each gamete receives only one of the two factors.
By segregation, each germ cell (gamete) receives only one of the paired alleles.
'Gametes are never hybrid' is the Law of Segregation: each gamete carries only one allele of a pair.

nuggets.title: Incomplete dominance and the concept of dominance
lines: In snapdragon (dog flower, Antirrhinum sp.), red (RR) x white (rr) gives an all-pink F1 (Rr): incomplete dominance.
Selfing pink F1 gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white in F2; genotypic and phenotypic ratios are the same, 1 : 2 : 1.
A modified allele may make a normal/less efficient enzyme (phenotype unchanged), or a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme (phenotype changed, recessive).
In pea, BB makes large starch grains and round seeds; bb makes less starch and wrinkled seeds; Bb has round seeds with intermediate-sized grains.
So for seed shape B is dominant, but for starch grain size the alleles show incomplete dominance: dominance depends on the phenotype considered.
nuggets.tip: Incomplete dominance: F<sub>1</sub> is intermediate. Co-dominance: F<sub>1</sub> shows both parents.

questions.why: Incorrect: segregation still applies, since R and r separate and red and white reappear in F2. Only dominance fails, as F1 is pink.
Identical 1 : 2 : 1 genotypic and phenotypic ratios in F2 indicate a monohybrid cross with incomplete dominance.
Pink (Rr) x red (RR) gives RR and Rr in 1 : 1, i.e. red and pink flowers; white (rr) cannot arise.
(a) and (c): phenotype changes only if the modified allele makes no enzyme or a non-functional enzyme. A normal/less efficient enzyme keeps the phenotype.
Seed shape (round vs wrinkled) shows dominant-recessive inheritance, while starch grain size (intermediate in Bb) shows incomplete dominance.

nuggets.title: Co-dominance and multiple alleles: ABO blood groups
lines: In co-dominance, the F1 resembles both parents; ABO blood grouping in humans is a good example.
ABO groups are controlled by gene I; the RBC plasma membrane has sugar polymers whose kind this gene controls.
Gene I has three alleles IA, IB and i; IA and IB make slightly different sugars, while i makes none.
I<sup>A</sup> and I<sup>B</sup> are completely dominant over i, but together both express (co-dominance), giving AB group.
With three alleles there are six genotypes and four phenotypes; more than two alleles at one gene is called multiple alleles, seen only in population studies.
nuggets.tip: A person carries only two of the three ABO alleles.

questions.why: IA and IB each produce a slightly different form of sugar; allele i produces no sugar, so IB and i cannot make identical sugars.
A, B and C: IA/IB are dominant over i, co-dominant with each other, and the I gene has multiple alleles. No incomplete dominance or polygeny.
IAIB x IAi gives IAIA, IAi, IAIB, IBi: 4 genotypes, but only A, AB and B, i.e. 3 phenotypes.
Multiple alleles are alternative forms of one gene, so they lie at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
When the F1 resembles both parents, both alleles express fully: co-dominance. An intermediate F1 would be incomplete dominance.

nuggets.title: Dihybrid cross and independent assortment
lines: Mendel crossed round yellow (RRYY) with wrinkled green (rryy) peas; the F<sub>1</sub> was all round yellow (RrYy).
Selfing F1 gave round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green in 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Each trait pair still segregated 3 : 1 in F2 (yellow : green and round : wrinkled), as in a monohybrid cross.
Law of Independent Assortment: when two pairs of traits combine in a hybrid, segregation of one pair is independent of the other.
RrYy forms four types of gametes, RY, Ry, rY, ry, each with a frequency of 25 per cent.
nuggets.tip: Gamete types = 2<sup>n</sup> (n = heterozygous gene pairs): AaBbCc gives 8.
