questions.why: In a dihybrid cross each pair segregates independently, so round : wrinkled in F2 is 3 : 1 (12 : 4 of 16).
Non-parental types (round green + wrinkled yellow) are 3 + 3 = 6 of 16; 6/16 x 64 = 24.
A 9:3:3:1 ratio shows that the alleles of the two genes are segregating independently (independent assortment).
AaBbCc has three heterozygous pairs that assort independently, giving 23 = 8 types of gametes.
A 1:1:1:1 dihybrid test cross shows the dihybrid made 4 types of gametes in equal numbers; the recessive parent makes only ab.

nuggets.title: Rediscovery of Mendel and the chromosomal theory
lines: Mendel published his work in 1865, but it stayed unrecognised till 1900, partly as his maths-based approach was new and he had no physical proof of factors.
In 1900, de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak independently rediscovered Mendel's results.
By 1902 chromosome movement during meiosis was worked out; Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted chromosome behaviour was parallel to gene behaviour.
Sutton united chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
Thomas Hunt Morgan and colleagues gave its experimental verification, working with the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster.
Drosophila grows on simple synthetic medium, completes its life cycle in about two weeks, gives many progeny per mating and shows clear sexes and many visible variations.
nuggets.tip: Sutton & Boveri proposed the theory; Morgan verified it experimentally.

questions.why: T.H. Morgan, working with Drosophila, verified the chromosomal theory experimentally; Sutton and Boveri only proposed it.
Mendel's work was independently rediscovered in 1900 by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak.
Mendel published his work on inheritance of characters in 1865; the experiments themselves ran 1856-1863.
Sutton united chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles as the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
All four: Drosophila grows on simple synthetic medium, has a ~2-week life cycle, gives many progeny per mating and shows visible sex and genetic variations.

nuggets.title: Linkage, recombination and gene mapping
lines: Morgan made several dihybrid crosses in Drosophila to study sex-linked genes, e.g. yellow-bodied white-eyed females x brown-bodied red-eyed males.
When two genes were on the same chromosome, parental gene combinations were much higher than the non-parental type in the progeny.
Morgan called the physical association of genes linkage and the generation of non-parental gene combinations recombination.
Tightly linked genes show low recombination: white and yellow gave 1.3%, while white and miniature wing gave 37.2% recombination.
Alfred Sturtevant used the recombination frequency between gene pairs on a chromosome as a measure of distance between them and mapped their positions.
Genetic maps are now a starting point for sequencing whole genomes, as in the Human Genome Sequencing Project.
nuggets.tip: Higher recombination = genes farther apart = looser linkage.

questions.why: More parental than recombinant offspring in a dihybrid test cross means the two genes are linked on the same chromosome; unlinked genes give 1:1:1:1.
Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency between gene pairs on one chromosome as a measure of distance to map genes.
Tightly linked genes on the same chromosome show very few recombinations; genes far apart show more.
Morgan found white-yellow tightly linked with 1.3% recombination and white-miniature wing loosely linked with 37.2%.
Distances: a-c 5, c-b 15 (a-b 20), b-d 9 (c-d 24, a-d 29). So the order is a, c, b, d.

nuggets.title: Polygenic inheritance and pleiotropy
lines: Polygenic traits are generally controlled by three or more genes, e.g. human height and human skin colour.
In polygenic inheritance each allele has an additive effect, and the phenotype also reflects the influence of the environment.
For skin colour by genes A, B, C: AABBCC gives the darkest, aabbcc the lightest, and three dominant plus three recessive alleles an intermediate colour.
In pleiotropy, a single gene shows multiple phenotypic expression, usually by affecting metabolic pathways that contribute to different phenotypes.
Example: in phenylketonuria, a mutation in the gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation.
nuggets.tip: Polygeny: many genes, one trait. Pleiotropy: one gene, many traits.

questions.why: Human skin colour is controlled by three or more genes with additive effects: polygenic inheritance.
All dominant alleles (AABBCC) give the darkest skin and all recessive alleles (aabbcc) the lightest, since each allele adds to the effect.
A pleiotropic gene controls multiple traits in an individual, usually by acting on a metabolic pathway.
Phenylketonuria is NCERT's example of pleiotropy: one mutant gene causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation.

nuggets.title: Sex determination: Henking, XO, XY and ZW
lines: Henking (1891) traced a nuclear structure through spermatogenesis in a few insects; only 50% of sperms got it. He named it the X body.
The X body was later named the X-chromosome; chromosomes involved in sex determination are sex chromosomes, and the rest are autosomes.
In grasshopper (XO type), males have only one X chromosome besides autosomes, while females have a pair of X chromosomes.
In XY type (humans, Drosophila), males have X and Y and females XX; both XO and XY are examples of male heterogamety.
In birds, females are heterogametic (ZW) and males homogametic (ZZ), so the egg decides the sex of the chick.
nuggets.tip: Birds: the mother decides sex (ZW female). Humans: the father decides (XY male).

questions.why: Grasshoppers have XO sex determination: males have a single X, females XX. Drosophila and monkeys are XY; birds are ZW.
Incorrect: in fowls (birds) females are ZW, so the egg, not the sperm, decides progeny sex. The other statements are correct.
ZZ - ZW shows female heterogamety: the ZW female makes two kinds of eggs. XX-XO and XX-XY are male heterogamety.
Henking (1891) traced the 'X body' through spermatogenesis in a few insects; this gave the initial clue to the chromosomal basis of sex determination.
Henking (1891) traced this nuclear structure, the 'X body', through spermatogenesis in a few insects.

nuggets.title: Sex determination in humans
lines: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes (same in both sexes) and one pair of sex chromosomes.
Females have a pair of X chromosomes (XX); males have one X and one Y (XY).
Males produce two types of sperm: 50% carry X and 50% carry Y; females produce only one type of ovum, with an X chromosome.
An ovum fertilised by an X-bearing sperm gives a female (XX); one fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm gives a male (XY).
So the genetic make-up of the sperm decides the baby's sex, and each pregnancy has a 50% chance of a male or a female child.
nuggets.tip: Blaming women for daughters is scientifically wrong: the sperm decides sex.

questions.why: The sex of a child is decided by the genetic make-up of the sperm (X or Y) that fertilises the X-bearing egg, not by the woman.
Incorrect: human males produce two types of gametes (X- and Y-bearing sperms) in equal proportion; females produce only one type.
Each fertilisation is independent: X or Y sperm is equally likely, so the chance of a son is always 50%, whatever came before.
Both correct: the male gamete decides the sex, and a Y-bearing sperm fertilising the X egg gives a male (XY).

nuggets.title: Mutation and pedigree analysis
lines: Mutation alters DNA sequences and so changes the genotype and phenotype; besides recombination, it is another cause of variation in DNA.
Loss (deletion) or gain (insertion/duplication) of a DNA segment alters chromosomes; chromosomal aberrations are commonly seen in cancer cells.
A change in a single base pair of DNA is a point mutation, e.g. sickle-cell anaemia; deletions and insertions of base pairs cause frame-shift mutations.
Chemical and physical factors that induce mutations are mutagens; UV radiation can cause mutations in organisms.
Pedigree analysis studies a trait across several generations of a family and is used to trace the inheritance of a trait, abnormality or disease.

questions.why: Mutation alters DNA sequences and so changes both the genotype and the phenotype.
Chromosomal aberrations (deletion, duplication of segments) are commonly observed in cancer cells.
All correct: a single base-pair change gives a point mutation, insertions/deletions cause frame-shifts, and UV is a mutagen.
Genetic variation arises from both mutation and recombination; NCERT names these two as the sources of DNA variation.
Inheritance of a Mendelian disorder in a family is traced by pedigree analysis over several generations.

nuggets.title: Mendelian disorders and haemophilia
lines: Genetic disorders are of two kinds: Mendelian disorders (alteration or mutation in a single gene) and chromosomal disorders.
Common Mendelian disorders: haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia; they may be dominant or recessive.
Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disease: a single protein in the cascade of clotting proteins is affected, so a simple cut keeps bleeding.
A heterozygous carrier female may pass haemophilia to sons; a haemophilic female is extremely rare, needing a carrier mother and a haemophilic father.
The family pedigree of Queen Victoria, a carrier, shows many haemophilic descendants.
nuggets.tip: X-linked recessive: carrier mother to son; a father never passes it to his son.

questions.why: Mendelian disorders are mainly due to alteration or mutation in a single gene; chromosomal disorders involve whole chromosomes.
Haemophilia is a recessive sex-linked disease, so 'dominant' is incorrect. A single clotting-cascade protein is affected.
A carrier female can pass haemophilia to her sons. Aneuploidy is gain/loss of single chromosomes (not whole sets); sickle-cell is qualitative and thalassemia quantitative.
Haemophilia is on the X. A father gives his son a Y, so a haemophilic father cannot pass the gene to his son; he passes it to all daughters.
All true: Queen Victoria's pedigree shows many haemophilics, carrier females pass it to some sons, and haemophilic females are extremely rare.

nuggets.title: Colour blindness
lines: Colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive disorder from a defect in the red or green cone of the eye, causing failure to tell red from green.
The defect is due to mutation in certain genes on the X chromosome.
It occurs in about 8 per cent of males but only about 0.4 per cent of females, since males have only one X.
A daughter is normally not colour blind unless her mother is at least a carrier and her father is colour blind.
A carrier mother is not colour blind herself, as the gene is recessive, but each of her sons has a 50% chance of being colour blind.
nuggets.tip: Males are hemizygous: one recessive X allele is enough to show the trait.

questions.why: Colour blindness affects about 8% of males and only 0.4% of females, because males have one X.
A daughter is colour blind only if she gets the allele from both parents: mother a carrier (or colour blind) and father colour blind.
Colour-blind man x carrier woman: daughters 1/2 colour blind, 1/2 carriers; sons 1/2 colour blind. Overall 50% of progeny are colour blind.
The bride's father was colour blind, so she is a carrier. Carrier x colour-blind man gives half the sons and half the daughters colour blind.
The man's mother was colour blind, so he got her X and is colour blind. Colour-blind woman x colour-blind man: 100% of progeny are colour blind.

nuggets.title: Sickle-cell anaemia
lines: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosome-linked recessive trait, passed from parents to offspring when both partners are carriers.
It is controlled by a single pair of alleles HbA and HbS; only HbSHbS homozygotes show the disease, while heterozygotes are unaffected carriers.
The defect is a substitution of glutamic acid (Glu) by valine (Val) at the sixth position of the beta globin chain of haemoglobin.
It is caused by a single base substitution at the sixth codon of the beta globin gene, from GAG to GUG.
The mutant haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen tension, changing RBCs from biconcave discs to elongated sickle-like cells.
nuggets.tip: Glu (normal) to Val (sickle): GAG to GUG, 6th position, beta chain.

questions.why: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a change in a single base pair of DNA. Valine replaces glutamic acid (not the reverse), RBCs lack nuclei and it is recessive.
Glutamic acid is replaced by valine at the sixth position of the beta globin chain.
In sickle-cell haemoglobin the sixth codon of the mRNA is GUG (valine); the normal codon is GAG (glutamic acid).
Mutant haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen tension, changing RBCs from biconcave discs to sickle shapes.
HbAHbS x HbAHbS gives 1 AA : 2 AS : 1 SS; only HbSHbS is diseased, so 25%.

nuggets.title: Phenylketonuria and thalassemia
lines: Phenylketonuria is an inborn error of metabolism inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
The affected person lacks the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine, so phenylalanine builds up and becomes phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives.
These accumulate in the brain, causing mental retardation, and are also excreted in urine because the kidney absorbs them poorly.
Thalassemia is an autosome-linked recessive blood disease: reduced synthesis of an alpha or beta globin chain forms abnormal haemoglobin and causes anaemia.
Alpha thalassemia: closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16; beta thalassemia: single gene HBB on chromosome 11.
Thalassemia is a quantitative problem (too few globin molecules); sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem (incorrectly functioning globin).
nuggets.tip: Alpha thal: chromosome 16 (2 genes). Beta thal and sickle cell: chromosome 11.

questions.why: False: phenylketonuria is autosomal recessive, not dominant. The other statements (inborn error, lack of phenylalanine-converting enzyme, phenylpyruvic acid) are correct.
In PKU the missing enzyme converts phenylalanine into tyrosine, so phenylalanine accumulates.
Thalassemia is due to less synthesis of globin molecules (quantitative). Sickle-cell anaemia is qualitative: a globin with one wrong amino acid.
Both correct: beta thalassemia is controlled by HBB on chromosome 11, alpha thalassemia by HBA1/HBA2 on chromosome 16 of each parent.
Only b is correct: sickle-cell anaemia is qualitative (faulty globin). Statement a is wrong, as making too few globin molecules is a quantitative problem.

nuggets.title: Chromosomal disorders: aneuploidy, polyploidy and Down's syndrome
lines: Chromosomal disorders are caused by absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes.
Failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division causes gain or loss of a chromosome: aneuploidy.
Failure of cytokinesis after telophase increases a whole set of chromosomes: polyploidy, often seen in plants.
Down's syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21); it was first described by Langdon Down (1866).
Down's individual: short with a small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth and broad palm with a characteristic crease; development is retarded.
nuggets.tip: Down's is an autosomal trisomy; Klinefelter's and Turner's involve sex chromosomes.

questions.why: 2n+1, 2n-1, 2n+2, 2n-2 are gains or losses of single chromosomes: aneuploidy. Polyploidy adds whole sets.
Failure of cytokinesis after telophase adds a whole set of chromosomes: polyploidy.
Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) arises from non-disjunction of an autosome. Klinefelter's and Turner's involve sex chromosomes; sickle-cell is a gene mutation.
A broad palm with a characteristic palm crease is a feature of Down's syndrome, along with furrowed tongue and partly open mouth.
Trisomy of the 21st chromosome is Down's syndrome.

nuggets.title: Klinefelter's and Turner's syndromes
lines: Klinefelter's syndrome is caused by an extra X chromosome, giving the karyotype 47, XXY.
The individual has overall masculine development but also feminine development (gynaecomastia, enlarged breasts), and is sterile.
Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one X chromosome, i.e. 45 with X0.
Turner's females are sterile, as ovaries are rudimentary, and lack other secondary sexual characters.
nuggets.tip: Klinefelter's: 47, XXY male. Turner's: 45, X0 female.

questions.why: Masculine development with gynaecomastia and sterility is Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY).
Sterile female, rudimentary ovaries, no secondary sexual characters and 44 + XO is Turner's syndrome.
Klinefelter's = 44 autosomes + XXY is the right match. Down's is trisomy 21 (not XO), and colour blindness is X-linked (not Y).
Turner's syndrome has 45 chromosomes (44 + X0). Klinefelter's (XXY) and Down's (trisomy 21) have 47.
XY sperm + X egg gives XXY (Klinefelter's); a sperm with no sex chromosome + X egg gives XO (Turner's).

nuggets.title: DNA: nucleotides and the polynucleotide chain
lines: DNA is a long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides; its length is usually defined as the number of nucleotides (or base pairs) in it.
Bacteriophage φ×174 has 5386 nucleotides, bacteriophage lambda 48502 bp, E. coli 4.6 × 106 bp, and haploid human DNA 3.3 × 109 bp.
A nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate; a base joined to the sugar's 1′C by an N-glycosidic linkage forms a nucleoside.
Phosphate linked to the 5′-OH of a nucleoside by a phosphoester linkage makes a nucleotide; two nucleotides join by a 3′→5′ phosphodiester linkage.
Purines: adenine and guanine; pyrimidines: cytosine, uracil and thymine. Thymine (5-methyl uracil) is in DNA; uracil replaces it in RNA.
In RNA every nucleotide has an extra 2′-OH group on ribose; a polynucleotide has a free phosphate at its 5′ end and a free 3′-OH at its 3′ end.
nuggets.tip: Nucleoside = base + sugar. Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate.

questions.why: Two nucleotides are linked by a 3′→5′ phosphodiester linkage; base–sugar is an N-glycosidic bond, and the two strands are held by hydrogen bonds.
A nucleoside is base + pentose sugar; adding a phosphate to its 5′-OH makes a nucleotide.
The nitrogenous base attaches to the 1′ carbon (C1′) of the pentose through an N-glycosidic linkage to form a nucleoside.
φ×174: 5386 nucleotides; lambda: 48502 bp; E. coli: 4.6 × 106 bp; haploid human: 3.3 × 109 bp. So A-P, B-R, C-Q, D-S.
A is wrong: lambda phage has 48502 base pairs, not bases. B is right: haploid human DNA is 3.3 × 109 bp.

nuggets.title: Double helix, Chargaff's rule and central dogma
lines: DNA was first identified as an acidic substance in the nucleus, named 'nuclein', by Friedrich Meischer in 1869.
Watson and Crick (1953) proposed the double helix model using X-ray diffraction data of Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin.
Chargaff's rule: in double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C, so the ratio of purines to pyrimidines is 1.
The two chains have antiparallel polarity; A pairs with T by two H-bonds and G with C by three, so a purine always faces a pyrimidine.
The chains coil in a right-handed fashion; the pitch is 3.4 nm with about 10 bp per turn, so adjacent base pairs are about 0.34 nm apart.
Central dogma (Francis Crick): DNA → mRNA → protein; in some viruses information flows in reverse, RNA → DNA (reverse transcription).
nuggets.tip: One turn = 3.4 nm = 10 bp. Distance between base pairs = 0.34 nm.

questions.why: One turn (pitch) of the B-DNA helix is 3.4 nm and holds about 10 base pairs spaced about 0.34 nm apart.
The two polynucleotide chains run in opposite directions, i.e. they are antiparallel: one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′.
By Chargaff's rule C = G = 17%, so A + T = 66% and A = T = 33% each.
A = T, so T = 30%; the remaining 40% is G + C, giving G = C = 20% each.
RNA → DNA is reverse transcription, DNA → DNA is replication, DNA → mRNA is transcription, and mRNA → polypeptide is translation.

nuggets.title: Packaging of DNA
lines: Human DNA (6.6 × 109 bp × 0.34 nm) would be about 2.2 m long, far more than a typical nucleus (~10–6 m), so it must be packaged.
In prokaryotes like E. coli, negatively charged DNA is held with positively charged proteins in a region called the nucleoid, organised in large loops.
In eukaryotes, positively charged basic proteins called histones are rich in lysine and arginine; eight histone molecules form a histone octamer.
Negatively charged DNA wraps around the positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome, which contains about 200 bp of DNA helix.
Repeating nucleosomes form 'beads-on-string' chromatin; higher-level packaging needs non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins.
Loosely packed, lightly stained, transcriptionally active chromatin is euchromatin; densely packed, dark-staining, inactive chromatin is heterochromatin.

questions.why: Histones are basic proteins rich in lysine and arginine, whose positively charged side chains bind negatively charged DNA.
A typical nucleosome contains about 200 bp of DNA helix wrapped around the histone octamer.
A is wrong: in prokaryotes negatively charged DNA is held by positively charged proteins in the nucleoid. B is correct for nucleosomes.
a, c and d are true. Heterochromatin is transcriptionally inactive (b false), and a nucleosome holds about 200 bp, not 400 (e false).
Histones are basic (positively charged, rich in lysine and arginine), not slightly acidic; eight of them form the histone octamer.

nuggets.title: Griffith and Avery: the transforming principle
lines: In 1928 Frederick Griffith worked with Streptococcus pneumoniae: the S strain (smooth, capsulated, virulent) and the R strain (rough, non-virulent).
Live S killed mice; live R or heat-killed S did not; but heat-killed S plus live R killed mice, and live S bacteria were recovered from them.
Griffith concluded that R bacteria were transformed by a 'transforming principle' from heat-killed S bacteria; its biochemical nature was not defined.
Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty (1933–44) purified DNA, RNA and proteins from heat-killed S cells to identify the transforming substance.
Proteases and RNases did not affect transformation, but DNase inhibited it, so they concluded that DNA is the hereditary material.

questions.why: Only R is correct: the R strain is non-virulent, so mice live. P is wrong (R strain does not kill), and heat-killed S alone does not kill mice (Q wrong).
DNase destroys S-strain DNA, so live R cells are not transformed; transformation is lost only when DNA is digested, proving DNA is the transforming material.
Heat-killed S plus live R bacteria killed the mice, because R cells were transformed into virulent S cells by the transforming principle.
Both true, and R explains A: transformation was blocked only by DNase, not by proteases or RNases, so DNA is the hereditary material.
Griffith used Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), whose S and R strains differ in capsule and virulence.

nuggets.title: Hershey–Chase: the unequivocal proof
lines: The unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material came from Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952), using bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria.
Some phages were grown with radioactive phosphorus (32P) to label DNA, others with radioactive sulfur (35S) to label protein, as DNA lacks S and protein lacks P.
Labelled phages infected E. coli; blending then removed viral coats from the bacteria and centrifugation separated virus particles from bacteria.
Bacteria infected with <sup>32</sup>P phages were radioactive, but those with <sup>35</sup>S phages were not, so only DNA (not protein) enters the bacterium.
nuggets.tip: <sup>32</sup>P = DNA, <sup>35</sup>S = protein. Radioactivity stays with the bacterial pellet only for <sup>32</sup>P.

questions.why: Hershey and Chase (1952) gave the unequivocal proof using bacteriophages; Griffith showed transformation, and Avery et al. did not convince all biologists.
Their proof used bacteriophage, a virus that infects bacteria (a bacterial virus).
35S labelled the protein coat (sulfur is absent in DNA), and 32P labelled DNA (phosphorus is absent in protein).
Steps: infection of E. coli by labelled phages → blending to remove viral coats → centrifugation to separate phages from bacteria.
False statement: 32P (DNA) enters the bacteria, so after centrifugation it is in the bacterial pellet, not the supernatant; 35S coats stay in the supernatant.

nuggets.title: Properties of genetic material and the RNA world
lines: A genetic material must replicate, be chemically and structurally stable, allow slow changes (mutation) for evolution, and express itself as 'Mendelian characters'.
Stability was evident in Griffith's experiment: the heat that killed the bacteria did not destroy the transforming principle.
The 2′-OH group in RNA nucleotides makes RNA reactive and labile; DNA is chemically less reactive and structurally more stable, so it is the predominant genetic material.
Thymine (5-methyl uracil) in place of uracil gives DNA extra stability; RNA viruses, with an unstable genome, mutate and evolve faster.
DNA is preferred for storage of genetic information, while RNA is better for its transmission since it can directly code for proteins.
RNA world: RNA was the first genetic material and also acted as a catalyst; DNA evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable.
nuggets.tip: DNA: storage. RNA: transmission. RNA came first.

questions.why: Genetic material must be stable structurally and chemically; instability is not a required trait, while replication, slow mutation and expression are.
Both match NCERT: RNA was the first genetic material and a catalyst but reactive and unstable; DNA evolved from RNA and its complementary strands resist change.
Both true, and R explains A: DNA is less reactive and more stable than RNA, which makes it the better material for storing genetic information.
Both true: RNA genomes with short life spans mutate and evolve faster, and RNA is better for transmission of information while DNA suits storage.
Thymine (5-methyl uracil) occurs only in DNA; RNA has uracil in its place, while A, G and C occur in both.

nuggets.title: Semiconservative replication: the proof
lines: Watson and Crick proposed semiconservative replication: each parental strand acts as a template, so each daughter DNA has one old and one new strand.
Meselson and Stahl (1958) grew E. coli on 15NH4Cl (15N is a heavy, non-radioactive isotope) for many generations, then shifted it to 14N medium.
DNA was separated by CsCl density gradient centrifugation; E. coli divides about every 20 minutes.
After one generation (20 min) all DNA was hybrid (<sup>15</sup>N/<sup>14</sup>N); after two generations (40 min) hybrid and light DNA were present in equal amounts.
Taylor and colleagues (1958) used radioactive thymidine in Vicia faba (faba beans) to show that DNA in chromosomes also replicates semiconservatively.
nuggets.tip: After n generations only 2 of 2<sup>n</sup> DNA molecules are hybrid; heavy DNA vanishes after generation 1.

questions.why: Meselson and Stahl's first proof of semiconservative replication used the bacterium E. coli.
After 2 generations in 14N, half the DNA is hybrid (15N/14N) and half is light; heavy DNA disappears after the first generation.
After n generations 2 molecules stay hybrid out of 2n; at n = 5 this is 2 hybrid : 30 light = 1 : 15.
60 min = 3 generations, so 10 cells become 80. The 20 original 15N strands sit in 20 hybrid cells, so 60 cells are totally 15N-free.
Griffith – Streptococcus pneumoniae; Hershey–Chase – bacteriophages; Meselson–Stahl – E. coli; Taylor – Vicia faba: A-P, B-R, C-Q, D-S.

nuggets.title: Replication machinery and the fork
lines: Replication is catalysed by DNA-dependent DNA polymerase; E. coli replicates its 4.6 × 106 bp in about 38 minutes (about 2000 bp per second).
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates act both as substrates and as the energy source for polymerisation.
Replication begins at the origin of replication; the long strands cannot be separated fully, so it occurs within a small opening, the replication fork.
DNA polymerase works only in the 5′→3′ direction, so replication is continuous on the 3′→5′ template and discontinuous on the 5′→3′ template.
The discontinuously made fragments (Okazaki fragments) are later joined by DNA ligase; in eukaryotes, replication takes place in the S-phase.

questions.why: Lagging-strand Okazaki fragments are made 5′→3′, i.e. away from the replication fork, and later joined by DNA ligase.
DNA polymerase polymerises only 5′→3′; DNA ligase joins the discontinuously synthesised fragments; replication initiates at the origin of replication: A-Q, B-P, C-R.
DNA polymerase averages about 2000 bp/s; dNTPs serve a dual purpose (substrate + energy); the 3′→5′ template gives continuous and the 5′→3′ template discontinuous replication: A-Q, B-R, C-P, D-S.
Replication starts by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases of the two strands at the origin; the covalent backbone bonds stay intact.
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve a dual purpose: they are the substrates and they also provide energy for polymerisation.

nuggets.title: Transcription unit: template and coding strands
lines: Transcription copies genetic information from one DNA strand into RNA, following complementarity except that uracil pairs with adenine in place of thymine.
A transcription unit has three regions: a promoter, the structural gene, and a terminator.
RNA polymerase also catalyses polymerisation only in the 5′→3′ direction, so the DNA strand with 3′→5′ polarity acts as the template strand.
The other strand (5′→3′) is the coding strand; it is not copied, and its sequence matches the RNA except for thymine in place of uracil.
The promoter lies towards the 5′ end (upstream) of the coding strand, and the terminator towards the 3′ end (downstream).
nuggets.tip: mRNA reads like the coding strand (T → U), not like the template strand.

questions.why: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies the template strand (3′→5′); the coding strand is not copied but matches the RNA sequence.
A transcription unit has a promoter (upstream), the structural gene, and a terminator (downstream); operator and repressor belong to operons.
mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T: AGGTATCGCAT → AGGUAUCGCAU.
RNA polymerase can polymerise only in the 5′→3′ direction, so it must use the template strand with 3′→5′ polarity.
The coding strand is complementary and antiparallel to the template: 3′-ATGC…-5′ pairs with 5′-TACG…-3′.

nuggets.title: Structural genes: cistrons, exons and introns
lines: A cistron is a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide; the structural gene in a transcription unit can be monocistronic or polycistronic.
Structural genes are mostly monocistronic in eukaryotes and polycistronic in bacteria (prokaryotes).
Eukaryotic genes are split genes: coding sequences called exons appear in mature RNA, while intervening sequences called introns do not.
Introns are transcribed but removed before translation, so they are never translated.

questions.why: A cistron is a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide, the equivalent of a structural gene.
Introns are transcribed into hnRNA but spliced out, so they are never translated; exons appear in mature RNA.
A is wrong: a monocistronic mRNA codes for one polypeptide. B is right: the stop (terminator) codon is present on the mRNA.
b, c and e are true for prokaryotes: no introns, coupled transcription–translation, one RNA polymerase. Their genes are polycistronic and need no splicing.
Cistron = DNA segment coding for a polypeptide; monocistronic genes are typical of eukaryotes, polycistronic of bacteria: A-Q, B-P, C-R.

nuggets.title: Transcription in bacteria
lines: Bacteria have a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that transcribes all types of RNA: mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.
RNA polymerase itself only catalyses elongation; it associates transiently with the sigma (σ) factor to initiate and the rho (ρ) factor to terminate transcription.
RNA polymerase binds the promoter, facilitates opening of the helix and elongates; at the terminator, the nascent RNA and the polymerase fall off.
In bacteria mRNA needs no processing and there is no separation of cytosol and nucleus, so translation can begin before transcription is complete.
nuggets.tip: Sigma starts, rho stops.

questions.why: Termination of bacterial transcription is aided by the rho (ρ) factor; the sigma (σ) factor helps initiation.
In prokaryotes one DNA-dependent RNA polymerase carries out initiation (with σ), elongation and termination (with ρ); DNA polymerase replicates DNA.
NCERT: RNA polymerase itself facilitates opening of the helix during transcription and continues elongation; helicase is a replication enzyme.
RNA polymerase associates with the rho factor to terminate bacterial transcription. Capping is at the 5′ end, the template strand is copied, and split genes are eukaryotic.
Bacteria have no separation of cytosol and nucleus, so transcription and translation occur in the same compartment and can be coupled.

nuggets.title: Eukaryotic transcription and RNA processing
lines: Eukaryotes have three RNA polymerases in the nucleus; RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S and 5.8S).
RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of mRNA, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs).
hnRNA undergoes splicing, in which the introns are removed and the exons are joined in a defined order.
hnRNA also undergoes capping (methyl guanosine triphosphate added at the 5′ end) and tailing (200–300 adenylate residues added at the 3′ end).
The fully processed hnRNA, now called mRNA, is transported out of the nucleus for translation.
nuggets.tip: Pol I: big rRNAs. Pol II: hnRNA. Pol III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNA.

questions.why: RNA polymerase II transcribes hnRNA, the mRNA precursor; tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNA come from pol III, and the major rRNAs from pol I.
RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs; 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNAs are made by pol I.
RNA polymerase I makes 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNAs; 5S rRNA is made by RNA polymerase III.
Post-transcriptional events are splicing (B), capping at 5′ (C) and tailing at 3′ (D); hnRNA is processed before it leaves the nucleus, so A is wrong.
Introns are removed during splicing, so the entire gene sequence does not appear in mature RNA; the coding exons are retained.

nuggets.title: The genetic code
lines: Physicist George Gamow argued that 4 bases coding 20 amino acids need a triplet code, giving 43 = 64 codons.
Har Gobind Khorana's chemical synthesis of RNA, Marshall Nirenberg's cell-free protein synthesis and Severo Ochoa's enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase) helped decipher the code.
Of 64 codons, 61 code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) code for none and act as stop codons.
The code is unambiguous and specific (one codon, one amino acid) but degenerate (some amino acids are coded by more than one codon).
Codons are read contiguously without punctuation, and the code is nearly universal: from bacteria to humans, UUU codes for phenylalanine.
AUG has dual functions: it codes for methionine and also acts as the initiator codon.
nuggets.tip: Unambiguous = one codon → one amino acid. Degenerate = one amino acid ← many codons.

questions.why: George Gamow argued that 4 bases must form triplet codons to code 20 amino acids (43 = 64).
The genetic code is unambiguous (each codon specifies one amino acid), so 'ambiguous' is not its feature; specific, degenerate and universal are.
61 codons for 20 amino acids means some amino acids have several codons: this is degeneracy of the code.
Of 64 codons, 3 are stop codons, so 61 codons code for the 20 amino acids.
Because the code is nearly universal, bacteria read the human insulin gene's codons the same way and make the same protein.

nuggets.title: Mutations, reading frame and tRNA
lines: Inserting or deleting one or two bases shifts the reading frame from that point (frameshift); inserting or deleting three bases adds or removes one codon, keeping the frame.
A point mutation, a change of a single base pair (e.g., GAG → GUG in the β-globin gene, Glu → Val), causes sickle-cell anaemia.
tRNA (sRNA) is the adapter molecule: its anticodon loop reads the codon on mRNA, and its amino acid acceptor end carries the amino acid.
tRNA has a clover-leaf secondary structure but is a compact inverted L in 3-D; tRNAs are specific for each amino acid and none exist for stop codons.

questions.why: Deleting base 901 shifts the frame from codon 301 onward, altering codons 301–333, i.e. 33 codons.
Deleting GGU (positions 7–9) removes exactly one codon and keeps the reading frame; single insertions or deletions cause frameshifts.
UAA is a stop codon, so translation stops after the 24th amino acid, giving a polypeptide of 24 amino acids.
The amino acid binds at the amino acid acceptor end, which is the 3′ end of tRNA; the anticodon loop reads mRNA.
tRNA pairs with the mRNA codon through its anticodon loop; the acceptor end carries the amino acid.

nuggets.title: Translation
lines: Translation begins with charging (aminoacylation) of tRNA: amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNAs.
The ribosome, the protein factory, has structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins; when inactive it exists as separate large and small subunits.
Translation begins when the small subunit encounters an mRNA; the large subunit has two sites where adjacent amino acids are bound for peptide bond formation.
In bacteria, 23S rRNA acts as a ribozyme, the catalyst for peptide bond formation.
mRNA has untranslated regions (UTRs) before the start codon (5′ end) and after the stop codon (3′ end), needed for efficient translation.
Initiation is at AUG with the initiator tRNA; at the end, a release factor binds the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the polypeptide.

questions.why: The first phase of translation is aminoacylation (charging) of tRNA, where amino acids are activated by ATP and linked to their tRNAs.
NCERT: translation begins when the small subunit of the ribosome encounters an mRNA.
UTRs lie at both ends: at the 5′ end before AUG and at the 3′ end after the stop codon; they are needed for efficient translation.
The ribosome consists of structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins.
In bacteria, 23S rRNA acts as the ribozyme that catalyses peptide bond formation; it is rRNA, not mRNA or tRNA.

nuggets.title: Gene regulation and lac operon parts
lines: Eukaryotic gene expression can be regulated at transcription, processing (splicing), mRNA transport and translation; in prokaryotes, mainly at transcription initiation.
An operon has a promoter, an operator and structural genes; the lac operon was described by Francois Jacob and Jacques Monod.
The regulatory i gene ('i' for inhibitor) codes for the repressor of the lac operon and is expressed constitutively.
Structural genes: z codes β-galactosidase (lactose → galactose + glucose), y codes permease (lets lactose in), a codes transacetylase.
The three structural genes z, y and a are transcribed together as one polycistronic mRNA.
nuggets.tip: i → repressor, z → β-galactosidase, y → permease, a → transacetylase.

questions.why: a → transacetylase, y → permease, i → repressor, z → β-galactosidase: A-Q, B-R, C-S, D-P.
Permease (y gene product) increases the permeability of the cell to lactose; β-galactosidase hydrolyses it.
An operon consists of a promoter, operator and structural genes; an enhancer is not part of the lac operon.
The i gene is a constitutive regulatory gene, expressed all the time whether or not lactose is present.
Jacob and Monod described the lac operon. Meselson–Stahl used E. coli, Hershey–Chase used phage (not TMV), and Alec Jeffreys developed DNA fingerprinting.

nuggets.title: Lac operon: induction and negative regulation
lines: Without an inducer, the repressor binds the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.
Lactose is the inducer: it (as allolactose in the cell) binds the repressor and inactivates it, so the repressor can no longer bind the operator.
With the operator free, RNA polymerase binds the promoter and transcribes the structural genes, producing the lac enzymes.
A very low level of lac operon expression always occurs, so permease can let some lactose in to act as inducer.
Regulation of the lac operon by the repressor is negative regulation, and the operon is inducible.

questions.why: The i gene's repressor blocks transcription (negative control), and lactose switches the operon on (inducible).
Lactose is the inducer of the lac operon; glucose and galactose are its breakdown products, not inducers.
Allolactose (inducer) binds the repressor protein and inactivates it, so the repressor leaves the operator and transcription proceeds.
With lactose present the inducer binds the repressor, freeing the operator so RNA polymerase can bind the promoter and transcribe z, y and a.
Allolactose acts as the inducer: it inactivates the repressor and switches the operon on.

nuggets.title: Human Genome Project: goals and methods
lines: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was a 13-year project launched in 1990 and completed in 2003.
Goals: identify all ~20,000–25,000 human genes, sequence the 3 billion base pairs, store data in databases, and address ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI).
One approach identified all genes that are expressed as RNA, called Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs).
The other, sequence annotation, blindly sequenced the whole genome (coding and non-coding) and later assigned functions to different regions.
DNA fragments were cloned using vectors such as BAC (bacterial artificial chromosomes) and YAC (yeast artificial chromosomes) and sequenced by automated sequencers.
Model organisms were also sequenced, e.g. bacteria, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans (a free-living non-pathogenic nematode), Drosophila, rice and Arabidopsis.
nuggets.tip: ESTs = genes expressed as RNA. Annotation = sequence everything first, assign function later.

questions.why: The main aim of HGP was to identify and sequence all the genes in human DNA; it did not introduce or remove genes.
HGP was a 13-year project, launched in 1990 and completed in 2003.
ESTs refer to all genes that are expressed as RNA; this was one of the two HGP approaches.
Sequencing the whole genome blindly and then assigning functions to different regions is sequence annotation.
C. elegans – free-living non-pathogenic nematode; Arabidopsis – plant; EST – genes expressed as RNA; annotation – assigning functions: A-R, B-P, C-Q, D-S.

nuggets.title: Salient features of the human genome
lines: The human genome has 3164.7 million bases; the average gene has 3000 bases, and the largest known gene, dystrophin, has 2.4 million bases.
The total number of genes is estimated at about 30,000, and 99.9% of nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all people.
Functions are unknown for over 50% of the discovered genes, and less than 2% of the genome codes for proteins.
Repeated sequences make up a very large portion of the genome; they have no direct coding function but shed light on chromosome structure and evolution.
Chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and chromosome Y the fewest (231).
About 1.4 million locations where single-base DNA differences occur (SNPs) were identified, helping find disease-linked sequences and trace human history.
nuggets.tip: Chromosome 1: most genes (2968). Y: fewest (231). Coding DNA: less than 2%.

questions.why: Chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968), while chromosome Y has the fewest (231).
Not a feature: less than 2% (not 10%) of the genome codes for proteins. About 30,000 genes, over 50% of functions unknown and Y with fewest genes are correct.
Human genome – 3164.7 million bases; average gene – 3000 bases; chromosome 1 – 2968 genes; Y – 231 genes: A-Q, B-P, C-R, D-S.
Dystrophin, the largest known human gene, has 2.4 million bases; the average gene has only 3000.
A single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is a location in the genome where a single DNA base differs between individuals; about 1.4 million were found.

nuggets.title: DNA fingerprinting
lines: As 99.9% of human DNA is identical, DNA fingerprinting compares differences in specific regions of the DNA sequence called repetitive DNA.
In density gradient centrifugation bulk DNA forms a major peak, while repetitive DNA forms small separate peaks, called satellite DNA.
Satellite DNA does not code for proteins but shows a high degree of polymorphism, which is the basis of genetic mapping and DNA fingerprinting.
An inheritable mutation seen in a population at high frequency is a DNA polymorphism; DNA from every tissue of a person shows the same polymorphism.

Steps (Alec Jeffreys, using a VNTR probe): isolate DNA → digest with restriction endonucleases → electrophoresis → blotting onto nitrocellulose or nylon → hybridise with labelled probe → autoradiography.
VNTRs vary in copy number between individuals, ranging from 0.1 to 20 kb; the technique is used in forensic science and in deciding paternity.
nuggets.tip: Mature RBCs have no nucleus, so they are useless for DNA fingerprinting.

questions.why: DNA fingerprinting identifies differences in specific regions of DNA called repetitive DNA, where short sequences are repeated many times.
Its basis is satellite DNA, which is highly repetitive and polymorphic; purine:pyrimidine ratio or DNA amount do not usefully differ between people.
Sequence: digestion by restriction enzymes (C) → electrophoresis (A) → blotting (E) → hybridisation with probe (B) → autoradiography (D).
Labelled VNTR probes are used in the hybridisation step, where they bind complementary DNA fragments on the membrane.
Mature human erythrocytes lack a nucleus, so they carry no nuclear DNA for fingerprinting; skin, semen and hair follicle cells do.

nuggets.title: Origin of universe, earth and early theories of life
lines: The universe is almost 20 billion years old; the Big Bang theory explains its origin as a singular huge explosion unimaginable in physical terms.
The universe expanded, temperature came down, hydrogen and helium formed later, and gases condensed under gravitation to form the galaxies of the present universe.
In the solar system of the Milky Way galaxy, earth was supposedly formed about 4.5 billion years back; life appeared about 500 million years later, i.e., almost 4 billion years back.
Early Greek thinkers believed units of life called spores were transferred to different planets including earth (panspermia), still a favourite idea of some astronomers.
Spontaneous generation held that life came out of decaying and rotting matter like straw and mud.
Louis Pasteur showed life comes only from pre-existing life: in pre-sterilised flasks no life arose from 'killed yeast', while in a flask open to air new organisms arose.
nuggets.tip: Earth: 4.5 billion years old; life appeared ~500 million years later (~4 billion years ago). Universe: ~20 billion years.

questions.why: NCERT describes the Big Bang as a singular huge explosion unimaginable in physical terms. 'Multiple explosions' or 'chemical terms' distort the NCERT line.
Statement A is wrong: earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago (15–20 billion refers to the universe). Statement B is correct: life appeared 500 million years after earth formed.
Spontaneous generation said life arose from decaying and rotting matter like straw and mud. Life from other planets is panspermia; from non-living organic molecules is Oparin–Haldane.
Louis Pasteur, by careful experimentation, showed life comes only from pre-existing life, dismissing spontaneous generation. Oparin–Haldane proposed chemical evolution, not its disproof.
Only A is correct. It was Pasteur (not Darwin) who showed both results: no life from 'killed yeast' in pre-sterilised flasks, but new organisms in the flask open to air.

nuggets.title: Chemical evolution: Oparin–Haldane and Miller
lines: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g., RNA, protein).
Formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution, i.e., formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents.
Conditions on early earth were high temperature, volcanic storms and a reducing atmosphere containing CH4, NH3, etc.
In 1953, S.L. Miller created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800°C and observed formation of amino acids.
Similar experiments by others produced sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats; analysis of meteorites also revealed similar compounds.
The first non-cellular forms of life could have originated about 3 billion years back, as giant molecules (RNA, protein, polysaccharides) that perhaps reproduced themselves.
nuggets.tip: Miller's flask: CH4 + H2 + NH3 + water vapour, 800°C, electric discharge → amino acids. Watch for 80°C or NH2 traps.

questions.why: Oparin was from Russia and Haldane from England; both proposed that life arose from pre-existing non-living organic molecules.
Miller used CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800°C with electric discharge. Options with CH3/NH4 or 600°C are wrong.
Miller observed amino acids in his spark-discharge flask. Sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats were reported in similar experiments by others.
NCERT: the first non-cellular forms of life could have originated 3 billion years back. Cellular forms came much later, about 2000 mya.
The primitive atmosphere was reducing: CH4, NH3, H2 and water vapour were present, but free oxygen was absent.

nuggets.title: Special creation and Darwin's voyage
lines: The theory of special creation has three connotations: all living organisms were created as such; diversity was always the same and will remain so; earth is about 4000 years old.
These ideas were strongly challenged in the 19th century, based on observations made during a sea voyage round the world in a sail ship called H.M.S. Beagle.
Charles Darwin concluded that existing living forms share similarities to varying degrees among themselves and with life forms that existed millions of years ago.
Many such life forms no longer exist; there were extinctions of different life forms, just as new forms of life arose at different periods of earth's history.
There has been gradual evolution of life forms; any population has built-in variation in characteristics.

questions.why: All three are NCERT's connotations of special creation: organisms created as such, diversity fixed forever, and earth about 4000 years old.
Both correct: Darwin sailed round the world on H.M.S. Beagle and concluded that existing life forms share similarities among themselves and with forms that lived millions of years ago.
All are conclusions in NCERT: life forms share similarities and common ancestors, new forms arose at different periods, and earth's geological history correlates with its biological history.
a, b and d are correct. (c) is wrong: Darwin's fitness is reproductive fitness. (e) is wrong: it was Alfred Wallace, not de Vries, who worked in the Malay Archipelago.

nuggets.title: Paleontological evidence: fossils
lines: Fossils are remains of hard parts of life forms found in rocks, and are evidence that evolution of life forms has occurred.
Rocks form sediments; a cross-section of earth's crust shows sediments arranged one over the other during the long history of earth.
Different-aged rock sediments contain fossils of different life forms which probably died during the formation of that particular sediment.
Some fossils resemble modern organisms; others represent extinct organisms (e.g., dinosaurs).
Fossils in different sedimentary layers indicate the geological period in which they existed; life forms varied over time and certain forms are restricted to certain geological time spans.
Hence new forms of life arose at different times in earth's history; all this is called paleontological evidence.

questions.why: NCERT defines fossils as remains of hard parts of life forms found in rocks; they are organic remains, not stuffed or laboratory-preserved animals.
A study of fossils in different sedimentary layers indicates the geological period in which they existed; it is not limited to extinct organisms.
All three are NCERT lines: layers indicate the geological period, fossils represent extinct organisms (dinosaurs), and life forms varied over time and are restricted to certain time spans.
'Diversity was the same since creation and will remain so' is special creation, contradicted by fossils, which show new forms arising at different times.
Rocks form sediments, and fossils are found in the sedimentary layers laid one over another during earth's history.

nuggets.title: Homologous organs and divergent evolution
lines: Whales, bats, cheetah and human (all mammals) share a similar pattern of forelimb bones: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges.
These forelimbs perform different functions but have similar anatomical structure: the same structure developed along different directions due to adaptations to different needs.
This is divergent evolution, and such structures are homologous; homology indicates common ancestry.
Other animal examples of homology are the heart and brain of vertebrates.
In plants, the thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendrils of Cucurbita represent homology.
nuggets.tip: Homology = same structure, different function → divergent. Analogy = different structure, same function → convergent.

questions.why: Eye of octopus vs mammals is analogy (convergent evolution). Brain, heart and forelimbs of bat, man and cheetah are homologous, i.e., divergent evolution.
Hearts and brains of vertebrates are homologous (common ancestry). Sweet potato/potato, butterfly/bird wings and penguin/dolphin flippers are analogous.
Homologous organs share the same basic anatomical plan, which indicates common ancestry; they arose by divergent evolution.
Thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita are NCERT's plant example of homologous organs: same origin, different functions.
Homologous organs have anatomical similarity but different functions (e.g., forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah, human). Same function with different structure describes analogous organs.

nuggets.title: Analogous organs and convergent evolution
lines: Analogous structures are not anatomically similar, though they perform similar functions.
Analogy results from convergent evolution: different structures evolving for the same function and hence having similarity.
Examples: wings of butterfly and of birds; eyes of the octopus and of mammals; flippers of penguins and dolphins.
Sweet potato (root modification) and potato (stem modification) are another example of analogy.
Similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms give clues to common ancestry (biochemical similarities).
nuggets.tip: Sweet potato = root, potato = stem: analogy, not homology.

questions.why: Flippers of penguins (birds) and dolphins (mammals) have different structures but the same function, which is convergent evolution.
Sweet potato (root) and potato (stem) differ in origin but both store food: analogy, produced by convergent evolution.
Analogous structures arise by convergent evolution: different structures evolve for the same function. Shared ancestry and divergent evolution produce homology.
Eyes of octopus and cat differ in structure but do the same job, so they are analogous organs produced by convergent evolution.
c, d, e are analogous (bird/butterfly wings, octopus/mammal eyes, penguin/dolphin flippers). Mammalian hearts are homologous, and (b) and (f) are plant examples, not animal.

nuggets.title: Natural selection: industrial melanism in moths
lines: In England, collections from the 1850s (before industrialisation) showed more white-winged moths on trees than dark-winged or melanised moths.
Collections from the same area in 1920 (after industrialisation) showed more dark-winged moths.
After industrialisation, tree trunks became dark from industrial smoke and soot, so white-winged moths could not camouflage and were picked out by predators; dark moths survived.
Before industrialisation, a thick growth of almost white lichens covered the trees, so white moths survived while dark ones were picked out; predators spot a moth against a contrasting background.
Lichens are industrial pollution indicators that do not grow in polluted areas; in rural areas without industrialisation, the count of melanic moths stayed low.
No variant is completely wiped out; the change in moth population is explained by natural selection.
nuggets.tip: Moths did not 'turn' dark from soot; pre-existing dark moths were selected. That is natural selection, not acquired inheritance.

questions.why: Dark moths already existed; on soot-darkened trunks they escaped predators and left more progeny. This is natural selection, not inheritance of an acquired dark colour.
White-winged moths were more common in the 1850s, before industrialisation, when white lichens covered tree trunks. After industrialisation (1920), dark moths dominated.
Before industrialisation, a thick growth of almost white lichens covered trees, so white moths were camouflaged. Lichens, not mycorrhizae, are NCERT's pollution indicators.
NCERT stresses that no variant is completely wiped out; only the proportions of white and dark moths changed. Predators do spot moths against a contrasting background.
In unpolluted rural areas, tree trunks stayed covered with white lichens, so melanic moths could not camouflage and were picked out by predators; their count stayed low.

nuggets.title: Evolution by anthropogenic action
lines: Excess use of herbicides, pesticides, etc., has resulted in selection of resistant varieties in a much shorter time scale.
The same is true for microbes against which we employ antibiotics, and for drugs used against eukaryotic organisms/cells; resistant forms appear in months or years, not centuries.
These are examples of evolution by anthropogenic action (human-caused changes in the environment).
Evolution is not a directed process in the sense of determinism; it is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutation in organisms.

questions.why: Herbicide-resistant weeds, drug-resistant eukaryotes and man-made dog breeds all result from human action. Darwin's finches arose by natural adaptive radiation on the Galapagos.
NCERT: anthropogenic evolution shows evolution is not directed in the sense of determinism and is a stochastic process based on chance events and chance mutations.
Antibiotic only selects resistant bacteria that already existed; resistance reflects pre-existing variation in the population, not adaptive radiation or divergent evolution.
Industrial melanism is seen in the moth Biston betularia, not in Darwin's finches; the finches are an example of adaptive radiation.

nuggets.title: Adaptive radiation: finches and marsupials
lines: On the Galapagos Islands, Darwin observed an amazing diversity of small black birds, later called Darwin's finches.
From the original seed-eating finches, others with altered beaks arose on the same island, becoming insectivorous and vegetarian finches.
Adaptive radiation is evolution of different species in a given geographical area, starting from a point and radiating to other areas of geography (habitats).
Australian marsupials are another example: different marsupials (e.g., numbat, spotted cuscus, flying phalanger, koala) evolved from an ancestral stock within the Australian island continent.
When more than one adaptive radiation appears in an isolated geographical area (representing different habitats), it can be called convergent evolution.
Placental mammals in Australia also show adaptive radiation, each resembling a marsupial counterpart (e.g., placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf).
nuggets.tip: Bobcat, lemur, anteater and mole are placental; numbat, cuscus, phalanger, koala, wombat are marsupials.

questions.why: Darwin's finches, which diversified from a seed-eating ancestor into forms with different beaks on the Galapagos, are NCERT's classic example of adaptive radiation.
NCERT: from the original seed-eating features, other finches with altered beaks arose, becoming insectivorous and vegetarian finches.
Numbat, spotted cuscus and flying phalanger are all Australian marsupials. Bobcat, mole, flying squirrel, lemur, anteater and wolf are placental mammals.
Darwin's finches, Australian marsupials and placental mammals all show adaptive radiation. The long-necked giraffe is Lamarck's use and disuse example, not adaptive radiation.
NCERT: when more than one adaptive radiation appears in an isolated geographical area, it can be called convergent evolution (e.g., Australian marsupials and placentals).

nuggets.title: Darwin's theory: natural selection and fitness
lines: The two key concepts of Darwin's theory of evolution are branching descent and natural selection.
Fitness, according to Darwin, refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness; the better fit leave more progeny and are selected by nature.
Fitness is the end result of the ability to adapt and get selected by nature; the 'survival of the fittest' is based on characteristics that are inherited.
Alfred Wallace, a naturalist who worked in the Malay Archipelago, reached similar conclusions around the same time.
The rate of appearance of new forms is linked to the life cycle or life span; fast-dividing microbes become millions within hours, so a better-adapted variant can soon dominate.
Darwinian variations are small and directional, and evolution for Darwin was gradual.
nuggets.tip: Darwin's fitness = reproductive fitness, not physical strength.

questions.why: Darwin's fitness refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness: those who leave more progeny are selected. Physical strength alone does not count.
Alfred Wallace was a naturalist who worked in the Malay Archipelago. The Galapagos Islands are linked to Darwin's finches.
Fitness depends on leaving more progeny. Microbes that divide fast and carry built-in variation (e.g., ability to use a feed component) multiply into millions in hours, so they are fittest.
All three are NCERT lines: fitness is based on inherited characteristics, Darwinian variations are small and directional, and fitness is the end result of the ability to adapt.
Both correct: Darwinian variations are small and directional, and evolution for Darwin was gradual, unlike de Vries's single-step saltation.

nuggets.title: Mechanism of evolution: Lamarck and de Vries
lines: Before Darwin, French naturalist Lamarck said evolution of life forms occurred but was driven by use and disuse of organs.
His example: giraffes, trying to forage leaves on tall trees, elongated their necks and passed this acquired character to progeny; nobody believes this conjecture any more.
Work of Hugo de Vries on evening primrose (Oenothera lamarckiana) brought forth the idea of mutations, large differences arising suddenly in a population.
De Vries believed it is mutation that causes evolution, not the minor heritable variations Darwin spoke of.
He called single-step large mutation saltation; mutations are random and directionless, while Darwinian variations are small and directional.
nuggets.tip: De Vries: Oenothera lamarckiana, mutation, saltation (single big step). Darwin: small, directional, gradual.

questions.why: Lamarck thought giraffe ancestors stretched their necks to reach leaves and passed the acquired long neck on. 'Longer-necked ones left more offspring' is Darwin's natural selection.
Lamarck, a French naturalist, said evolution was driven by use and disuse of organs. Darwin was English; de Vries was Dutch.
Hugo de Vries called single-step large mutation saltation and believed mutation, not minor variations, causes evolution.
De Vries proposed mutation theory from work on evening primrose, Oenothera lamarckiana. Pisum was Mendel's plant and Drosophila was Morgan's.
A is correct: de Vries said mutations cause speciation. B is wrong: mutations are sudden, single-step large changes (saltation), not slow ones.

nuggets.title: Hardy–Weinberg principle
lines: In a given population, the frequency of alleles of a gene (or locus) is supposed to stay fixed through generations.
Hardy–Weinberg principle: allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation.
The gene pool (total genes and their alleles in a population) remains constant, which is called genetic equilibrium; the sum of all allelic frequencies is 1.
If p and q are frequencies of alleles A and a, then AA = p2, aa = q2 and Aa = 2pq; so p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1, the binomial expansion of (p + q)2.
When measured frequency differs from the expected value, the difference (direction) indicates the extent of evolutionary change.
nuggets.tip: Given q² (recessive phenotype), take the square root to get q, then p = 1 − q and heterozygotes = 2pq.

questions.why: In p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1, homozygous AA = p2, aa = q2, and heterozygotes Aa = 2pq; pq alone misses the factor 2.
Heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48 = 48%. 36% is p2 (AA) and 16% is q2 (aa).
q2 = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6; heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48. Population size (800) does not change the frequency.
Hardy–Weinberg principle: allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation.
The gene pool is the total genes and their alleles in a population; its constancy is genetic equilibrium. It includes all alleles, not only dominant or recessive ones.

nuggets.title: Factors affecting equilibrium: gene flow, drift, founder effect
lines: Five factors affect Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection.
When a section of a population migrates to another place, gene frequencies change in both the original and the new population; if gene migration happens multiple times, there is gene flow.
If the same change in gene frequency occurs by chance, it is called genetic drift.
Sometimes the change in allele frequency is so different in the new sample that it becomes a different species; the original drifted population becomes founders, called the founder effect.
Disturbance of genetic equilibrium (change in allele frequency) is interpreted as resulting in evolution.
nuggets.tip: Five factors: gene flow, drift, mutation, recombination, natural selection. A 'constant gene pool' means equilibrium, not a factor.

questions.why: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium holds only without disturbing factors; frequent mutations change allele frequencies. A large, isolated, freely interbreeding population favours equilibrium.
Gene migration, genetic drift and genetic recombination are among the five factors that disturb equilibrium. A constant gene pool is the equilibrium itself.
The principle assumes random mating; if individuals mate selectively, genotype frequencies shift. No mutation, no migration and large size support equilibrium.
When a drifted population becomes founders of a new population, the effect is the founder effect, a result of genetic drift (chance change in allele frequency).
Both correct: gene flow changes allele frequencies in future generations, and NCERT says gene flow results when gene migration happens multiple times.

nuggets.title: Natural selection: stabilising, directional, disruptive
lines: Natural selection is a process in which heritable variations enabling better survival allow organisms to reproduce and leave a greater number of progeny.
Variation due to mutation, recombination, gene flow or genetic drift changes the frequency of genes and alleles in future generations.
Stabilisation: more individuals acquire the mean character value.
Directional change: more individuals acquire a value other than the mean character value.
Disruption: more individuals acquire peripheral character values at both ends of the distribution curve.
nuggets.tip: Mean favoured → stabilising; one side favoured → directional; both extremes favoured → disruptive.

questions.why: Average-weight babies (3–3.3 kg) survive best while both extremes die, so the mean is favoured: stabilising selection.
When more individuals acquire a character value other than the mean, the curve shifts one way: directional change. Mean favoured = stabilising.
Only extremely tall and extremely dwarf plants remain, with no intermediates, so both peripheral values are favoured: disruptive selection.
I, III and IV are correct. II is wrong: more individuals acquiring the mean value is stabilisation, while disruption favours both extremes.
Both are wrong. Disruptive selection favours both extremes, not one direction (that is directional), and favouring average individuals is stabilising selection.

nuggets.title: Brief account of evolution: water to land
lines: About 2000 mya, the first cellular forms of life appeared on earth; they were probably single cells, and all life forms were in water.
By about 500 mya, invertebrates were formed and active.
Jawless fish probably evolved around 350 mya; seaweeds and a few plants probably existed around 320 mya.
Fish with stout and strong fins could move on land and go back to water around 350 mya; these lobefins evolved into the first amphibians, ancestors of frogs and salamanders.
In 1938, a fish caught in South Africa turned out to be a Coelacanth, which was thought to be extinct.
Amphibians evolved into reptiles, which lay thick-shelled eggs that do not dry up in the sun, unlike those of amphibians.
nuggets.tip: Coelacanth: caught in 1938, in South Africa. Jawless fish: ~350 mya. Seaweeds: ~320 mya.

questions.why: Both correct: the first cellular life did not originate until about 2000 mya, probably as single cells, and all life forms were then in water.
Only I and IV are correct. Coelacanth was caught in 1938 (not 1983), seaweeds existed around 320 mya (not 500), and invertebrates were active by 500 mya (not 300).
Both correct per NCERT: amphibians evolved into reptiles, and fish with stout, strong fins could move on land and back to water about 350 mya.
In 1938, a fish caught in South Africa turned out to be a Coelacanth, a lobefin thought to be extinct.
The lobefins (like the Coelacanth), with stout, strong fins, evolved into the first amphibians that lived on both land and water.

nuggets.title: Reptiles, dinosaurs and mammals
lines: The first organisms to invade land were plants; they were widespread on land by the time animals invaded it.
Giant ferns (pteridophytes) were present but all fell and slowly formed coal deposits.
Around 200 mya, some land reptiles went back into water to evolve into fish-like reptiles (e.g., Ichthyosaurs); the land reptiles were the dinosaurs.
The biggest dinosaur in NCERT, Tyrannosaurus rex, was about 20 feet tall with huge, dagger-like teeth; about 65 mya, dinosaurs suddenly disappeared from earth.
The first mammals were like shrews; mammals were viviparous and protected their unborn young inside the mother's body.
Due to continental drift, Australia separated from other continents, so its pouched mammals survived through lack of competition from other mammals.
nuggets.tip: Ichthyosaurs ~200 mya; dinosaurs vanished ~65 mya. Do not swap these two numbers.

questions.why: Only II and IV are correct: plants invaded land first, and giant ferns formed coal. Dinosaurs vanished about 65 mya, Ichthyosaurs arose about 200 mya, and lobefins about 350 mya.
Ichthyosaurus: fish-like reptiles about 200 mya. Coelacanth: caught in South Africa in 1938. Giant pteridophytes: formed coal. Dinosaurs: disappeared about 65 mya.
NCERT names Tyrannosaurus rex as the biggest dinosaur, about 20 feet tall with dagger-like teeth. Answer NEET questions with this NCERT line.
NCERT: the first mammals were like shrews, and their fossils are small-sized. Ichthyosaurs were fish-like reptiles and lobefins were fish.
When Australia separated by continental drift, its pouched mammals survived because they faced no competition from other mammals.

nuggets.title: Early human ancestors: Dryopithecus to Homo erectus
lines: About 15 mya, primates called Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus existed; they were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees.
Ramapithecus was more man-like, while Dryopithecus was more ape-like.
Fossils of man-like bones found in Ethiopia and Tanzania reveal hominid features; 3–4 mya, man-like primates not taller than 4 feet walked upright in eastern Africa.
About 2 mya, Australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands; they hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit.
The first human-like being, the hominid, was Homo habilis; its brain capacity was 650–800 cc, and it probably did not eat meat.
Fossils discovered in Java in 1891 revealed Homo erectus about 1.5 mya, with a large brain of around 900 cc; it probably ate meat.
nuggets.tip: Ramapithecus = more man-like; Dryopithecus = more ape-like. Habilis did not eat meat; erectus probably did.

questions.why: Only I and II are correct. NCERT says Ramapithecus was more man-like and Dryopithecus more ape-like, the reverse of III and IV.
Australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands about 2 mya. The 15 mya date belongs to Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus.
Homo habilis had a brain capacity of 650–800 cc. 900 cc is H. erectus and 1400 cc is the Neanderthal man.
NCERT: Homo habilis probably did not eat meat. Cave painting is linked to about 18,000 years ago, and hides were used by Neanderthals.
All are correct: Homo erectus arose about 1.5 mya with a 900 cc brain, probably ate meat, and followed H. habilis in human evolution.

nuggets.title: Neanderthals to modern Homo sapiens
lines: The Neanderthal man, with brain size of 1400 cc, lived in near east and central Asian countries between 1,00,000–40,000 years back.
Neanderthals used hides to protect their body and buried their dead.
Homo sapiens arose in Africa, moved across continents and developed into distinct races.
During the ice age, between 75,000–10,000 years ago, modern Homo sapiens arose.
Pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago.
Agriculture came around 10,000 years back, and human settlements started.
nuggets.tip: Brain size: habilis 650–800 → erectus 900 → Neanderthal 1400 cc. Cave art 18,000; agriculture 10,000 years ago.

questions.why: The order from past to recent is H. habilis → H. erectus → H. neanderthalensis → H. sapiens, matching increasing brain size (650–800 → 900 → 1400 cc).
Neanderthals had a brain of about 1400 cc, not 900 cc (that is H. erectus). They lived 1,00,000–40,000 years back, used hides and buried their dead.
Modern Homo sapiens arose during the ice age between 75,000 and 10,000 years ago. 1.5 mya is H. erectus and 18,000 years is cave art.
NCERT: pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago. Agriculture came later, around 10,000 years back.
I, II and IV are correct. III is wrong because cave art (~18,000 years ago) is not linked to Java man, and V is wrong because H. erectus probably ate meat.

nuggets.title: Health: from humours to pathogens
lines: For a long time, health was considered a state of body and mind with a balance of certain 'humors', as asserted by early Greeks like Hippocrates and the Indian Ayurveda system.
Persons with 'black bile' were thought to belong to a hot personality and to have fevers.
William Harvey's discovery of blood circulation, and the demonstration of normal body temperature in persons with black bile using a thermometer, disproved the 'good humor' hypothesis.
Health is not simply 'absence of disease' or 'physical fitness'; it is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and healthy people are more efficient at work.
Disease-causing organisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, helminths, etc.) are pathogens; most parasites are therefore pathogens, as they harm the host by living in or on them.
Diseases spreading from an infected person to a healthy one are infectious (e.g., AIDS, common cold); among non-infectious diseases, cancer is a major cause of death.

questions.why: Only III is wrong: the humour theory linked 'black bile' (not brown bile) to a hot personality and fevers. I and II correctly describe Hippocrates and Ayurveda.
William Harvey's experimental discovery of blood circulation, together with thermometer readings, disproved the 'good humor' hypothesis. Jenner is linked to vaccination.
A thermometer showed normal body temperature in persons with 'black bile', contradicting the idea that they had hot personalities and fevers.
Only I and II are correct. Withdrawal syndrome involves anxiety and shakiness, not calmness; pathogens must adapt to the host; and the black-bile idea came from humour theory, not from Harvey.
All four are correct, so none is incorrect. Disease-causing organisms are pathogens, most parasites are pathogens, ringworm affects the skin, and HIV-infected cells survive while releasing virus.

nuggets.title: Typhoid
lines: Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium which causes typhoid fever in human beings.
The pathogens generally enter the small intestine through contaminated food and water and migrate to other organs through blood.
Symptoms: sustained high fever (39° to 40°C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite; intestinal perforation and death may occur in severe cases.
Typhoid fever is confirmed by the Widal test.
Mary Mallon, nicknamed Typhoid Mary, was a cook and a typhoid carrier who kept spreading typhoid for several years through the food she prepared.
nuggets.tip: Typhoid: Salmonella typhi → small intestine; confirmed by the Widal test. Temperature is 39–40°C, not °F.

questions.why: Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi and confirmed by the Widal test. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumonia, and the anthrone test is not used for typhoid.
S. typhi enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water, then migrates to other organs through blood.
All are NCERT symptoms of typhoid: sustained high fever (39–40°C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite.
Both are correct: Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary) was a cook who carried and spread typhoid, and Salmonella typhi is a bacterium (moneran) causing typhoid.
The Widal test confirms typhoid by detecting antibodies against Salmonella antigens. The Mantoux test is for tuberculosis.

nuggets.title: Pneumonia and other bacterial diseases
lines: Bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae cause pneumonia in humans, infecting the alveoli (air-filled sacs) of the lungs.
As a result, the alveoli get filled with fluid, causing severe problems in respiration.
Symptoms include fever, chills, cough and headache; in severe cases the lips and fingernails may turn gray to bluish in colour.
A healthy person acquires infection by inhaling droplets/aerosols released by an infected person, or even by sharing glasses and utensils with an infected person.
Dysentery, plague and diphtheria are some other bacterial diseases in man.
nuggets.tip: Pneumonia affects the alveoli (lungs); common cold affects the nose and respiratory passage, not the lungs.

questions.why: Pneumonia infects the alveoli, causing difficulty in breathing, fever, chills, cough and headache. Nasal congestion is common cold; high fever with constipation is typhoid.
