Both correct: in pneumonia, fluid fills the alveoli and disturbs gas transport, and in severe cases lips and fingernails turn gray to bluish.
Haemophilus influenzae (like Streptococcus pneumoniae) is an NCERT-named bacterium causing pneumonia.
NCERT: pneumonia spreads by inhaling droplets/aerosols from an infected person, or by sharing glasses and utensils with one, so both routes are correct.
Typhoid, diphtheria, cholera and tuberculosis are all caused by bacteria. NCERT lists dysentery, plague and diphtheria as other bacterial diseases.

nuggets.title: Common cold
lines: Many viruses also cause diseases in humans; rhinoviruses represent one such group, causing one of the most infectious human ailments, the common cold.
Rhinoviruses infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs.
Symptoms: nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache and tiredness, which usually last for 3–7 days.
Droplets from cough or sneezes of an infected person are either inhaled directly or transmitted through contaminated objects like pens, books, cups, doorknobs, computer keyboard or mouse.

questions.why: Rhinoviruses infect the nose and respiratory passage (upper respiratory tract) but not the lungs. Infection of alveoli is pneumonia.
NCERT: common cold symptoms usually last for 3–7 days.
Droplets from coughs or sneezes of an infected person do spread common cold, directly or via contaminated objects. The other three statements are NCERT facts.
Pneumonia infects the alveoli, while common cold affects the nose and respiratory passage, not the lungs. Pneumonia is bacterial and common cold is viral (rhinovirus).
Common cold is caused by a virus (rhinovirus); antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses.

nuggets.title: Malaria: Plasmodium species and haemozoin
lines: Plasmodium, a tiny protozoan, is responsible for malaria; different species are P. vivax, P. malariae and P. falciparum.
Malignant malaria, the most serious one and possibly fatal, is caused by Plasmodium falciparum.
Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites (infectious form) through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
The rupture of RBCs is associated with release of a toxic substance, haemozoin, responsible for chill and high fever recurring every three to four days.
nuggets.tip: Haemozoin comes from Plasmodium-infected RBCs, not WBCs. Fever recurs every 3–4 days, not hours.

questions.why: Malignant malaria, the most serious and possibly fatal form, is caused by Plasmodium falciparum. P. vivax and P. malariae cause milder forms.
Haemozoin is released when Plasmodium-infected RBCs rupture in malaria, causing chill and high fever recurring every 3–4 days.
Sporozoites do not multiply in blood; they first multiply in liver cells, then attack RBCs. The other options are correct NCERT facts.
NCERT names three malaria-causing species: P. vivax, P. malariae and P. falciparum.
Malaria is spread by the bite of an infected female Anopheles, not the male. Haemozoin, P. falciparum and sporozoite entry are correct statements.

nuggets.title: Malaria: life cycle of Plasmodium
lines: Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites; the parasites initially multiply asexually within the liver cells.
They then attack the red blood cells, multiplying asexually inside them and causing their rupture.
Inside RBCs, sexual stages called gametocytes develop.
When a female Anopheles bites an infected person, gametocytes enter the mosquito; fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's intestine (stomach).
Mature infective stages (sporozoites) escape from the intestine and migrate to the mosquito's salivary glands, ready to be injected with the next bite.
The malarial parasite requires two hosts, human and mosquito, to complete its life cycle.
nuggets.tip: Man gets sporozoites; the mosquito gets gametocytes. Fertilisation happens in the mosquito, not in man.

questions.why: Sporozoites are the mature infective stages that pass from the mosquito's salivary glands into man. Gametocytes go the other way, from man to mosquito.
Gametocytes develop in human RBCs. Sporozoites multiply asexually in the liver, the mosquito takes up gametocytes, and sporozoites (not gametocytes) are injected into man.
Gametocytes taken up by the female Anopheles fuse in the mosquito's gut (intestine/stomach); fertilisation never occurs in the human host.
In humans, Plasmodium first multiplies in liver cells and then in RBCs, where gametocytes form.
Malaria fever recurs every three to four days, not hours. The other statements on sporozoites, liver, RBCs and salivary glands are NCERT facts.

nuggets.title: Amoebiasis and ascariasis
lines: Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoan parasite in the large intestine of humans, causes amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery).
Symptoms of amoebiasis: constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, and stools with excess mucus and blood clots.
Houseflies act as mechanical carriers, transmitting the parasite from faeces of an infected person to food and food products, thereby contaminating them.
Ascaris, the common round worm, an intestinal parasite, causes ascariasis; symptoms include internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anemia and blockage of the intestinal passage.
Ascaris eggs are excreted with the faeces of infected persons and contaminate soil, water and plants; a healthy person is infected through contaminated water, vegetables and fruits.
nuggets.tip: Housefly: mechanical carrier of amoebiasis. Mosquito (female Culex/Anopheles): biological vector of filariasis/malaria.

questions.why: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite in the large intestine of humans. Salmonella (typhoid) enters through the small intestine.
All are amoebiasis symptoms in NCERT: constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, and stools with excess mucus and blood clots.
Houseflies are mechanical carriers of amoebiasis; female mosquitoes transmit filariasis.
Ascaris eggs passed in faeces contaminate soil, water and plants; a healthy person is infected by drinking water or eating food containing these eggs.
Haemophilus influenzae–pneumonia, Entamoeba histolytica–amoebiasis, Plasmodium falciparum–malignant malaria, Wuchereria bancrofti–elephantiasis.

nuggets.title: Filariasis and ringworm
lines: Wuchereria (W. bancrofti and W. malayi), the filarial worms, cause slow, chronic inflammation of the organs they live in for years, usually the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs.
The disease is called elephantiasis or filariasis; genital organs are also often affected, resulting in gross deformities.
The pathogens are transmitted to a healthy person through the bite of female mosquito vectors.
Many fungi belonging to Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton cause ringworms, one of the most common infectious diseases in man.
Ringworm shows dry, scaly lesions with intense itching on skin, nails and scalp; heat and moisture help the fungi grow, so they are common in skin folds like the groin or between the toes.
Ringworms are generally acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or even the comb of infected individuals.
nuggets.tip: Ringworm fungi: Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton. Filariasis worm: Wuchereria (a nematode).

questions.why: NCERT names two filarial worms, Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi, as causes of filariasis/elephantiasis.
Filarial worms are transmitted by the bite of female mosquito vectors, specifically Culex. Anopheles spreads malaria; Aedes spreads dengue and chikungunya.
Typhoid–bacteria, leishmaniasis–protozoa, ringworm–fungus (Microsporum, Trichophyton), filariasis–nematode (Wuchereria).
Ringworm fungi are generally acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or even the comb of infected persons, not by mosquito bites.
Both correct: heat and moisture help ringworm fungi grow, so infection is common in skin folds such as the groin or between the toes.

nuggets.title: Prevention and control of infectious diseases
lines: Personal hygiene (keeping the body clean, clean drinking water, food, vegetables, fruits) and public hygiene (proper disposal of waste and excreta, clean reservoirs) prevent many infectious diseases.
For air-borne diseases like pneumonia and common cold, close contact with infected persons or their belongings should be avoided.
For vector-borne diseases like malaria and filariasis, the most important measure is to control or eliminate the vectors and their breeding places.
Avoid stagnant water around homes, clean household coolers regularly, use mosquito nets, spray insecticides, and introduce fishes like Gambusia in ponds to feed on mosquito larvae.
Dengue and chikungunya are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, so these measures help control them too.
Vaccines and antibiotics have helped: smallpox is eradicated, while polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus have been controlled to a large extent.
nuggets.tip: Gambusia (a fish) eats mosquito larvae. Aedes spreads dengue and chikungunya.

questions.why: Statements i–iv are NCERT measures: no stagnant water, cleaning coolers, mosquito nets, and Gambusia to eat larvae. Spraying perfumes is not a control measure.
Dengue and chikungunya are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Anopheles transmits malaria and Culex transmits filariasis.
Gambusia is a bony fish (Osteichthyes) introduced in ponds to feed on mosquito larvae, which are arthropods.
Amoebiasis–use only sterilised food and water; diphtheria–DPT vaccine; malaria–Gambusia to eat larvae; dengue–Aedes vector.
III and IV are incorrect: chikungunya spreads by Aedes, not Anopheles, and the cancer biological response modifier is α-interferon, not α-1 antitrypsin.

nuggets.title: Innate immunity: four barriers
lines: Immunity is the overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system; it is of two types: innate and acquired.
Innate immunity is non-specific defence present at the time of birth, provided by four types of barriers.
Physical barriers: skin, and the mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts.
Physiological barriers: acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth and tears from the eyes.
Cellular barriers: leukocytes like PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes and natural killer (a type of lymphocyte) in blood, and macrophages in tissues, which phagocytose and destroy microbes.
Cytokine barriers: virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.
nuggets.tip: Mucus = physical; acid, saliva, tears = physiological; PMNL, NK, macrophages = cellular; interferons = cytokine.

questions.why: Interferons are proteins secreted by virus-infected host cells; they protect neighbouring non-infected cells from further viral infection (cytokine barrier).
Interferons are produced against viral infections, and measles is the only viral disease listed. Malaria is protozoan; tetanus and anthrax are bacterial.
II, IV, V are correct. I is wrong because mucus coating is a physical barrier, and III is wrong because acid, saliva and tears are physiological barriers.
Cellular barrier–PMNL; physiological–saliva; physical–mucus coating of epithelial lining; cytokine–virus-infected cell (secretes interferons).
Neutrophils, NK cells and macrophages form the innate cellular barrier. Helper T cells belong to acquired immunity.

nuggets.title: Acquired immunity: memory, B and T cells
lines: Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific and characterised by memory.
The first encounter with a pathogen produces a low-intensity primary response; a later encounter elicits a highly intensified secondary (anamnestic) response, owing to memory of the first.
Primary and secondary responses are carried out by B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes; B-cells produce proteins called antibodies into blood.
T-cells themselves do not secrete antibodies but help B-cells produce them; each antibody has four peptide chains, two small light and two longer heavy chains, hence H2L2.
Types of antibodies include IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG; because antibodies are found in blood, this response is called the humoral immune response.

The T-lymphocyte-mediated cell-mediated immune response (CMI) is responsible for graft rejection; tissue and blood group matching are essential before transplants, and immunosuppressants are taken lifelong.
nuggets.tip: Humoral = B cells + antibodies; CMI = T cells and graft rejection. Antibody = H2L2.

questions.why: Acquired immunity is specific and develops after exposure; non-specific defence present at birth is innate immunity. The primary and anamnestic response statements are correct.
Each antibody has two heavy (H) and two light (L) peptide chains, so it is represented as H2L2.
Only I is correct: T-cells do not secrete antibodies but help B-cells make them. II is wrong because there is no 'IgB'; NCERT lists IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG.
Humoral immunity is antibody-mediated, and antibodies are produced by B-lymphocytes. T-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity.
Graft rejection is due to the cell-mediated immune response (T-lymphocytes), which can tell 'self' from 'non-self'. Humoral (antibody) immunity is not responsible.

nuggets.title: Active and passive immunity
lines: When a host is exposed to antigens (living or dead microbes or other proteins), antibodies are produced in the host body: active immunity, which is slow and takes time.
Active immunity can be induced deliberately by injecting microbes in immunisation, or naturally when infectious organisms gain access during natural infection.
When ready-made antibodies are given directly to protect the body against foreign agents, it is passive immunity.
Yellowish colostrum, secreted in the initial days of lactation, has abundant IgA antibodies to protect the infant; the foetus also receives antibodies from the mother through the placenta.
For deadly microbes needing a quick response (e.g., tetanus), preformed antibodies or antitoxin are injected; in snakebite, the injection contains preformed antibodies against snake venom.
nuggets.tip: Colostrum = IgA; placenta passes IgG. Both are natural passive immunity.

questions.why: Giving preformed antibodies for a quick response (e.g., tetanus antitoxin) is passive immunisation; active immunity requires the body to make its own antibodies, which is slow.
Colostrum contains abundant IgA antibodies, which protect the newborn; this is natural passive immunity.
Both are true: colostrum has abundant IgA, and the foetus receives antibodies through the placenta. These are two separate routes, so the reason does not explain the assertion.
For deadly infections like tetanus that need a quick immune response, preformed antibodies or antitoxin are injected (passive immunisation).
Natural active–fighting infections; artificial passive–antiserum injection; artificial active–vaccination; natural passive–mother to foetus via placenta.

nuggets.title: Vaccination and immunisation
lines: Vaccination is based on the 'memory' of the immune system: antigenic proteins of a pathogen, or inactivated/weakened pathogens (vaccine), are introduced into the body.
Antibodies produced against these antigens neutralise the pathogenic agents during actual infection, and memory B- and T-cells recognise the pathogen quickly on later exposure.
Vaccination gives artificial active immunity, whereas injecting preformed antibodies (e.g., antitoxin, anti-venom) gives passive immunity.
Recombinant DNA technology allows large-scale production of antigenic polypeptides; e.g., hepatitis B vaccine is produced from yeast.

questions.why: Anti-venom gives ready-made antibodies (passive), while polio drops contain attenuated (weakened) pathogens that make the body produce its own antibodies (active).
Both correct: vaccines contain antigenic proteins or inactivated/weakened pathogens, and hepatitis B vaccine is produced from yeast by recombinant DNA technology.
Hepatitis B vaccine–yeast; preformed antibodies–against snake venom; colostrum–IgA; PMNL–neutrophils.
Vaccination induces artificial active immunity, because the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells. Natural infection gives natural active immunity.

nuggets.title: Allergy and autoimmunity
lines: The exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens present in the environment is called allergy; such substances are allergens (e.g., mites in dust, pollens, animal dander).
Antibodies produced against allergens are of the IgE type.
Allergy is due to release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from the mast cells; symptoms include sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing.
Drugs like anti-histamine, adrenalin and steroids quickly reduce the symptoms of allergy; modern lifestyle has lowered immunity and increased sensitivity to allergens.
When, due to genetic and other unknown reasons, the body attacks self-cells, it causes auto-immune disease, e.g., rheumatoid arthritis.
nuggets.tip: Histamine and serotonin cause allergy; anti-histamine, adrenalin and steroids treat it. Do not mix them up.

questions.why: Antibodies produced in allergy are of the IgE type. IgA is in colostrum and IgG crosses the placenta.

I, II and IV are true. III is wrong: allergy symptoms come from histamine and serotonin released by mast cells, while adrenalin and steroids are treatments. V is wrong: rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune.
II is wrong because that definition is of allergy, not autoimmunity. IV is wrong because modern lifestyle has lowered immunity. V is wrong because health is more than absence of disease.
When the body fails to tell its own (self) antigens from foreign ones and attacks self-cells, the result is autoimmunity, e.g., rheumatoid arthritis.
In autoimmune disease like rheumatoid arthritis, the body loses its ability to tell self from non-self (iv) and attacks self-cells (ii).

nuggets.title: Lymphoid organs and MALT
lines: Primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and thymus, where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes.

The bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced; bone marrow and thymus provide micro-environments for the development and maturation of T-lymphocytes.
The thymus is a lobed organ located near the heart beneath the breastbone; it is quite large at birth but keeps reducing in size with age.

After maturation, lymphocytes migrate to secondary lymphoid organs (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of small intestine, appendix) to interact with antigens and proliferate into effector cells.
The spleen is a large bean-shaped organ with mainly lymphocytes and phagocytes; it filters blood by trapping blood-borne microorganisms and holds a large reservoir of erythrocytes.
Lymphoid tissue within the lining of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts is MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue), about 50% of the lymphoid tissue in the human body.
nuggets.tip: Primary: bone marrow, thymus. Secondary: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix. MALT is about 50%.

questions.why: Both correct: bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ producing all blood cells including lymphocytes, and both bone marrow and thymus provide micro-environments for T-lymphocyte maturation.
The primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus. Lymph nodes, tonsils and Peyer's patches are secondary lymphoid organs.
Spleen, lymph nodes and Peyer's patches are secondary lymphoid organs where lymphocytes meet antigens. Thymus and bone marrow are primary organs.
All are NCERT functions of the spleen: it filters blood by trapping blood-borne microbes, contains mainly lymphocytes and phagocytes, and holds a large reservoir of erythrocytes.
MALT, the lymphoid tissue lining the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts, makes up about 50% of the lymphoid tissue in the human body.

nuggets.title: AIDS: transmission, diagnosis and prevention
lines: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is a deficiency of the immune system acquired during a lifetime; it was first reported in 1981, and 'syndrome' means a group of symptoms.
AIDS is caused by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), a member of the group of viruses called retroviruses, which have an envelope enclosing the RNA genome.
HIV spreads by sexual contact with an infected person, transfusion of contaminated blood, sharing infected needles, and from an infected mother to her child through the placenta.
There is a time-lag between infection and appearance of AIDS symptoms, from a few months to many years (usually 5–10 years).
A widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is ELISA (enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay); anti-retroviral drugs are only partially effective and can only prolong the life of the patient.
Prevention is the best option: NACO and NGOs ensure safe blood, disposable needles and syringes, free condoms, control of drug abuse, safe sex and regular check-ups.
nuggets.tip: Time-lag is usually 5–10 years. AIDS is diagnosed by ELISA; typhoid is diagnosed by the Widal test.

questions.why: AIDS was first reported in 1981, is diagnosed by ELISA, and is caused by HIV, a retrovirus. The time-lag before symptoms is usually 5–10 years.
HIV spreads through infected blood, needles, and mother to child, and sexual contact with an infected person. Contact with an uninfected person cannot transmit it.
NCERT: the time-lag between HIV infection and AIDS symptoms varies from a few months to many years (usually 5–10 years).
Both correct: AIDS was first reported in 1981, 'syndrome' means a group of symptoms, and infected macrophages keep producing virus, acting as an HIV factory.
All five are NCERT measures to combat AIDS: safe blood, disposable needles and syringes, free condoms, controlling drug abuse, and safe sex with regular check-ups.

nuggets.title: HIV: how it destroys immunity
lines: After entering the body, HIV enters macrophages, where its RNA genome replicates to form viral DNA with the help of the enzyme reverse transcriptase.
The viral DNA is incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs infected cells to produce virus particles; macrophages continue to produce virus and act as an HIV factory.
HIV also enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), where it replicates and produces progeny viruses, which attack other helper T-cells.
This repeats, leading to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes in the body of the infected person.
The person becomes immunodeficient and cannot fight infections by bacteria (especially Mycobacterium), viruses, fungi and parasites like Toxoplasma.
nuggets.tip: HIV factory = macrophages; HIV is killing helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA.

questions.why: A retrovirus introduces its RNA into the host cell; reverse transcriptase then copies it into viral DNA, which is incorporated into host DNA.
HIV replicates in helper T-lymphocytes (TH), producing progeny viruses that attack more TH cells. B-cells, basophils and eosinophils are not its targets.
In macrophages, HIV's RNA genome is copied into viral DNA by reverse transcriptase (RNA → DNA).
Infected macrophages keep producing virus and so act like an HIV factory.
With helper T-cells depleted, the patient cannot fight infections by Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and even parasites like Toxoplasma, so all are correct.

nuggets.title: Cancer: contact inhibition, tumours and metastasis
lines: In our body, cell growth and differentiation are highly controlled; cancer cells have broken down these regulatory mechanisms.
Normal cells show contact inhibition: contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth; cancer cells have lost this property.
Cancer cells keep dividing, giving rise to masses of cells called tumors.
Benign tumors normally remain confined to their original location, do not spread and cause little damage.
Malignant tumors are masses of proliferating neoplastic (tumor) cells that grow rapidly, invade and damage surrounding normal tissues, and starve normal cells by competing for nutrients.
Cells sloughed from malignant tumors reach distant sites through blood and start new tumors wherever they lodge; this property, metastasis, is the most feared property of malignant tumors.
nuggets.tip: Cancer cells have LOST contact inhibition. 'Shows contact inhibition' is the classic wrong option.

questions.why: Cancer cells have lost contact inhibition, so 'exhibit contact inhibition' is incorrect. They are metastatic, proliferate rapidly and arise from activated proto-oncogenes.
Malignant tumors grow rapidly and invade and damage surrounding normal tissues. Staying confined to one location is a feature of benign tumors.
Metastasis is the most feared property of malignant tumors: sloughed cells travel through blood and start new tumors wherever they lodge.
Both are wrong: I describes benign tumors (confined, little damage), and the mass of proliferating neoplastic cells in II describes malignant tumors.
Benign tumors remain confined to their original location and do not spread; malignant tumors invade and metastasise.

nuggets.title: Cancer: causes, detection and treatment
lines: Transformation of normal cells into cancerous neoplastic cells may be induced by physical, chemical or biological agents, called carcinogens.
Ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays and non-ionising UV cause DNA damage leading to neoplastic transformation; tobacco smoke chemicals are a major cause of lung cancer.
Cancer-causing viruses, oncogenic viruses, have viral oncogenes; cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto-oncogenes in normal cells can cause oncogenic transformation when activated.
Detection is based on biopsy and histopathological studies, blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in leukemias, and radiography (X-rays), CT and MRI for internal organs.
CT uses X-rays to make a three-dimensional image; MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations; antibodies against cancer-specific antigens are also used for detection.
Treatment: surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, in which biological response modifiers like α-interferon activate the immune system to destroy the tumor.
nuggets.tip: α-interferon = biological response modifier for cancer. Widal test is for typhoid, not cancer.

questions.why: Cancers of internal organs are detected by radiography, CT and MRI, so a and b are correct. The Widal test is for typhoid.
A and C are correct. Chemotherapy kills cancerous cells, the biological response modifier is α-interferon (not chemotherapy drugs), and leukaemia shows increased cell counts.
Biopsy–a piece of suspected tissue; oncogenic viruses–viral oncogenes; MRI–strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation; CT–X-rays for a 3-D image.
Both correct: any agent inducing cancer is a carcinogenic/oncogenic agent, and normal cells carry c-onc (proto-oncogenes) that can cause cancer when activated.
Proto-oncogenes (c-onc) are normal cellular genes which, when activated under certain conditions, lead to oncogenic transformation.

nuggets.title: Opioids: morphine and heroin
lines: Opioids are drugs which bind to specific opioid receptors present in our central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract.
Heroin, commonly called smack, is chemically diacetylmorphine, a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound.
Heroin is obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum.
Heroin is generally taken by snorting and injection; it is a depressant and slows down body functions.
Morphine is a very effective sedative and painkiller, useful in patients who have undergone surgery.
nuggets.tip: Heroin = acetylated morphine (not the reverse). Smack comes from poppy latex.

questions.why: Morphine is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant, Papaver somniferum. Cannabis gives cannabinoids and Erythroxylum gives cocaine.
Heroin (smack, diacetylmorphine) is made by acetylation of morphine.
I, II and IV are correct. III is not accepted because heroin is made by acetylating morphine; it is morphine that is extracted from poppy latex.
Opioids bind to specific opioid receptors present in both the central nervous system and the gastrointestinal tract.
Cocaine–Erythroxylum; heroin–Papaver somniferum; morphine–effective sedative in surgery; marijuana–Cannabis sativa.

nuggets.title: Cannabinoids, cocaine and hallucinogens
lines: Cannabinoids interact with cannabinoid receptors present principally in the brain; they are obtained from the inflorescences of Cannabis sativa.
Flower tops, leaves and resin of the cannabis plant are used to make marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja; these are generally taken by inhalation and oral ingestion.
Cannabinoids are known for their effects on the cardiovascular system, and these days they are being abused by some sportspersons.
Coca alkaloid or cocaine is obtained from the coca plant Erythroxylum coca, native to South America; it is usually snorted and is commonly called coke or crack.
Cocaine interferes with the transport of the neuro-transmitter dopamine; it is a potent stimulant producing euphoria and increased energy, and excessive doses cause hallucinations.
Other plants with hallucinogenic properties are Atropa belladonna and Datura.
nuggets.tip: Smack → Papaver; coke/crack → Erythroxylum; marijuana → Cannabis. Cocaine blocks dopamine transport.

questions.why: Cocaine interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine, producing euphoria and increased energy.
A is wrong: heroin is obtained by acetylation of morphine, not the reverse. B is correct: cannabinoids affect the cardiovascular system.
Smack (heroin) comes from Papaver somniferum, and crack (cocaine) comes from Erythroxylum coca.
Heroin–slows down body functions; marijuana–effect on cardiovascular system; cocaine–interferes with dopamine transport; morphine–painkiller.
Datura–hallucinogen; cocaine–Erythroxylum coca; opioids–Papaver somniferum; cannabinoids–Cannabis sativa.

nuggets.title: Adolescence, addiction and effects of drug abuse
lines: Adolescence is the period between 12–18 years of age; curiosity, need for adventure and excitement, and experimentation are common reasons for drug and alcohol use.
Addiction is psychological attachment to effects like euphoria; dependence is the body's tendency to show withdrawal syndrome when the regular dose is abruptly stopped.
Withdrawal is characterised by anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating; dependence leads patients to ignore all social norms to get sufficient funds for drugs.
Excessive doses may cause coma and death; those who take drugs intravenously are more likely to get AIDS and hepatitis B, and chronic use damages the nervous system and liver (cirrhosis).
Anabolic steroids in females cause masculinisation, increased aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, abnormal menstrual cycles and excessive hair growth on the face and body.
Prevention: avoid undue peer pressure, education and counselling, seeking help from parents and peers, watching for danger signs, and professional and medical help.
nuggets.tip: Withdrawal syndrome: anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating. Never calmness.

questions.why: In females, anabolic steroids cause masculinisation (male-like features), along with aggressiveness, mood swings and abnormal menstrual cycles. Cirrhosis is linked to alcohol.
Withdrawal syndrome shows anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating; calmness is not a feature.
Both correct: dependence makes people ignore social norms to fund drugs, and excessive doses can cause coma and death from respiratory failure, heart failure or cerebral haemorrhage.
Both correct: intravenous drug users risk AIDS and hepatitis B, and chronic drug and alcohol use damages the nervous system and liver (cirrhosis).
All four are NCERT measures for preventing drug and alcohol abuse: no undue pressure, education and counselling, help from parents and peers, and professional help.

nuggets.title: Curd and lactic acid bacteria
lines: Microbes such as Lactobacillus, commonly called lactic acid bacteria (LAB), grow in milk and convert it to curd.
During growth, LAB produce acids that coagulate and partially digest the milk proteins.
A small amount of curd added to fresh milk acts as the inoculum or starter, which contains millions of LAB.
LAB improve the nutritional quality of curd by increasing vitamin B12.
In our stomach, LAB play a very beneficial role in checking disease-causing microbes.
nuggets.tip: Curd raises vitamin B<sub>12</sub>, not vitamin C or D.

questions.why: Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB) such as Lactobacillus convert milk to curd. Acetic acid bacteria (Acetobacter) make vinegar, not curd.
Lactobacillus (a LAB) grows in milk and produces acids that coagulate milk proteins to form curd. Acetobacter makes acetic acid.
NCERT: LAB improve the nutritional quality of curd by increasing vitamin B12.
In our stomach LAB play a beneficial role in checking disease-causing microbes; they do not regulate HCl secretion.

i and iii match NCERT (acids coagulate and partly digest milk proteins; vitamin B12 rises). ii is false because the starter with millions of LAB is what converts milk to curd, so only 'i and iii' fits.

nuggets.title: Dough, toddy and cheese
lines: The dough used for dosa and idli is fermented by bacteria; its puffed-up appearance is due to CO2 gas.
Dough for bread is fermented using baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).
Toddy, a traditional drink of parts of southern India, is made by fermenting sap from palms.
Microbes also ferment fish, soyabean and bamboo shoots to make foods; cheese types differ in texture, flavour and taste because of the microbes used.
Large holes in Swiss cheese are due to much CO2 made by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii.
Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it.
nuggets.tip: Swiss cheese = bacterium (CO<sub>2</sub>); Roquefort cheese = fungus.

questions.why: The dough looks puffed-up because of CO2 released by fermenting microbes.
Toddy is made by fermentation of sap from palm trees, not by aerobic respiration.
Propionibacterium sharmanii is a bacterium (kingdom Monera); its CO2 makes the large holes in Swiss cheese.
Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it. Bacteria (Propionibacterium) are linked to Swiss cheese.
I is wrong: dosa/idli dough is fermented by bacteria. III is wrong: Swiss cheese holes are due to CO2, not methane. II and IV are correct.

nuggets.title: Fermented beverages and fermentors
lines: Microbes are grown in very large vessels called fermentors for industrial production of beverages, antibiotics and other products.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the yeast used for bread, is called brewer's yeast when used to ferment malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol.
Wine and beer are produced without distillation.
Whisky, brandy and rum are produced by distillation of the fermented broth.
nuggets.tip: Not distilled: wine and beer. Distilled: whisky, brandy, rum.

questions.why: Industrial-scale growth of microbes for alcohol and antibiotics is done in very large vessels called fermentors.
Brewer's yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae; the same species is baker's yeast. Penicillium notatum gives penicillin.
Whisky, brandy and rum come from distillation of the fermented broth. Wine and beer are made without distillation.
Wine (like beer) is produced without distillation; whisky, rum and brandy are distilled.
Beer is a non-distilled beverage made by yeast fermentation. Rum, whisky and brandy are all distilled.

nuggets.title: Antibiotics: penicillin
lines: Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by some microbes that can kill or retard the growth of other (disease-causing) microbes.
Penicillin was the first antibiotic discovered, by Alexander Fleming, by chance.
Fleming, working on Staphylococci bacteria, saw a mould in an unwashed culture plate around which the bacteria could not grow; the mould was Penicillium notatum.
Its full potential as an effective antibiotic was established by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey; penicillin treated wounded soldiers in World War II.
Fleming, Chain and Florey received the Nobel Prize in 1945.
Antibiotics help treat deadly diseases such as plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy.
nuggets.tip: Fleming discovered penicillin; Chain and Florey established its full potential.

questions.why: Fleming was working on Staphylococci; the mould that stopped their growth was Penicillium notatum. Saccharomyces is yeast.
Fleming worked on a bacterium (Staphylococcus); the chemical was named Penicillin after the mould Penicillium notatum.
Ernest Chain and Howard Florey established the full potential of penicillin as an effective antibiotic. Streptokinase is unrelated.
Fleming, Chain and Florey shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for penicillin. Norman Borlaug is linked to the Green Revolution.
NCERT lists plague, whooping cough (kali khansi), diphtheria (gal ghontu) and leprosy (kusht rog) as diseases treated with antibiotics, so all of these is correct.

nuggets.title: Organic acids and ethanol from microbes
lines: The fungus Aspergillus niger is used for commercial production of citric acid.
The bacterium Acetobacter aceti produces acetic acid.
Clostridium butylicum (a bacterium) produces butyric acid.
Lactobacillus (a bacterium) produces lactic acid.
Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is used for commercial production of ethanol.
nuggets.tip: Citric acid comes from a fungus (Aspergillus); acetic, butyric and lactic acids come from bacteria.

questions.why: Aspergillus niger: citric acid; Acetobacter aceti: acetic acid; Clostridium butylicum: butyric acid; Lactobacillus: lactic acid. So A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q.
The fungus Aspergillus (A. niger) is NCERT's producer of citric acid.
C. butylicum: butyric acid; S. cerevisiae: ethanol; Trichoderma polysporum: cyclosporin A; Streptococcus: streptokinase. So A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q.
Lactobacillus: curd; S. cerevisiae: bread; A. niger: citric acid; Acetobacter aceti: acetic acid. Cheese is the distractor.
Only i (A. niger, fungus, citric acid) and iv (Streptococcus, bacterium, clot buster) are right. Saccharomyces is a fungus, not an alga; Lactobacillus does not make penicillin.

nuggets.title: Microbial enzymes: lipases, pectinases, streptokinase
lines: Lipases are used in detergent formulations and help remove oily stains from laundry.
Bottled fruit juices are clearer than home-made ones because they are clarified using pectinases and proteases.
Streptokinase is produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering.
Streptokinase is used as a 'clot buster' to remove clots from blood vessels of patients who have had myocardial infarction (heart attack).
nuggets.tip: Lipase = oily stains; pectinase/protease = clear juice; streptokinase = clot buster.

questions.why: Lipases are used in detergent formulations to remove oily stains. Juice clarification uses pectinases; clot busting uses streptokinase.
Bottled juices are clarified by pectinases (and proteases). Lipases act on fats and are used in detergents.
Streptokinase is made by Streptococcus, is used as a clot buster after myocardial infarction. Staphylococci were Fleming's bacteria.
Streptokinase acts as a clot buster, dissolving clots in blood vessels after myocardial infarction. Lowering cholesterol is the role of statins.
Streptokinase from Streptococcus is used for removing clots from blood vessels. Curd and ethanol come from LAB and yeast.

nuggets.title: Cyclosporin A and statins
lines: Cyclosporin A, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients, is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum.
Statins, produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus, are commercialised as blood-cholesterol lowering agents.
Statins act by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol.
Bioactive molecules from microbes thus include streptokinase (clot buster), cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant) and statins (cholesterol lowering).
nuggets.tip: Trichoderma polysporum is a fungus (cyclosporin A); Monascus purpureus is a yeast (statins).

questions.why: Cyclosporin A comes from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum. C. butylicum makes butyric acid; A. niger, citric acid.
NCERT names Trichoderma polysporum as the source of the immunosuppressant cyclosporin A; the other Trichoderma species are distractors.
Statins are produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus, not by a bacterium or protist.
Statins competitively inhibit the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol, lowering blood cholesterol.
Cyclosporin A: immunosuppressant; streptokinase: clot buster; statins: cholesterol lowering; penicillin: antibiotic. So A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q.

nuggets.title: Sewage and its primary treatment
lines: Municipal waste-water is called sewage; it contains large amounts of organic matter and microbes, many of them pathogenic.
Sewage is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) to make it less polluting before discharge into natural water bodies.
Primary treatment is the physical removal of particles from sewage through filtration and sedimentation.
Floating debris is removed by sequential filtration; grit (soil and small pebbles) is removed by sedimentation.
All settled solids form the primary sludge, and the supernatant forms the effluent, which goes for secondary treatment.
nuggets.tip: Primary treatment is physical (no microbes); secondary treatment is biological.

questions.why: Sewage contains large amounts of organic matter and microbes, many of which are pathogenic.
In primary treatment, grit (soil and small pebbles) is removed by sedimentation; floating debris is removed by filtration.
Settled solids form the primary sludge and the supernatant forms the effluent.
Primary treatment is physical: filtration and sedimentation. Aerobic and anaerobic microbial steps belong to secondary treatment and sludge digestion.
Primary treatment physically removes particles (debris, grit, settleable solids) from sewage. Secondary treatment is biological.

nuggets.title: Secondary (biological) treatment and BOD
lines: The primary effluent is passed into large aeration tanks, where it is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped in.
This lets useful aerobic microbes grow rapidly into flocs: masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments forming mesh-like structures.
The microbes consume the major part of the organic matter in the effluent, significantly reducing its BOD.
BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria.
The greater the BOD of waste water, the more is its polluting potential.
nuggets.tip: BOD measures oxygen consumed, not released. High BOD = more polluted.

questions.why: Flocs are masses of aerobic bacteria associated with fungal filaments. Anaerobic bacteria act later in sludge digesters.
Flocs are mesh-like structures of bacteria associated with fungal filaments, formed in aeration tanks. Primary sludge is the settled solid of primary treatment.
Only II is correct. Statement I is wrong because BOD is the oxygen consumed, not released, when organic matter in 1 L of water is oxidised by bacteria.
Higher BOD means more organic matter and more pollution, so the sample with the highest BOD, 6 mg/L, is the most polluted.
Secondary treatment matters because its microbes consume most organic matter and reduce the BOD of sewage. Debris removal is primary treatment.

nuggets.title: Activated sludge, sludge digesters and river action plans
lines: Once BOD is reduced significantly, the effluent goes to a settling tank where bacterial flocs sediment; this sediment is activated sludge.
A small part of the activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank to serve as the inoculum.
The major part is pumped into large tanks called anaerobic sludge digesters, where anaerobic bacteria digest the bacteria and fungi in the sludge.
During this digestion, bacteria produce biogas, a mixture of methane, hydrogen sulphide and CO2.
The effluent from secondary treatment is generally released into natural water bodies like rivers and streams.
The Ministry of Environment and Forests initiated the Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan to save these rivers from pollution.
nuggets.tip: Flocs are allowed to settle only after BOD has dropped, not when it rises.

questions.why: Bacterial flocs sedimented in the settling tank after BOD reduction form the activated sludge. Primary sludge comes from primary treatment.
The major part of the sludge is pumped into large tanks called anaerobic sludge digesters.
Activated sludge is pumped into the anaerobic sludge digester, where anaerobic bacteria digest its bacteria and fungi.
Biogas from sludge digesters is a mixture of methane, hydrogen sulphide and CO2; it is produced anaerobically, so no O2.
I is wrong (cyclosporin A is from Trichoderma polysporum), III is wrong (flocs settle once BOD is reduced), V is wrong (Methanobacterium is in anaerobic sludge). II, IV and VI are correct.

nuggets.title: Methanogens
lines: Biogas is a mixture of gases (containing predominantly methane) produced by microbial activity and used as fuel.
Certain bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material produce large amounts of methane along with CO2 and H2; they are called methanogens.
One such methanogen is Methanobacterium.
Methanogens are commonly found in the anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment.
They are also present in the rumen of cattle, where they help break down the cellulose in the cattle's food.
nuggets.tip: Methanogens: rumen, not omasum or abomasum; anaerobic, not aerobic sludge.

questions.why: Methanogens (archaebacteria such as Methanobacterium) produce biogas from the dung of ruminants.
Methanogens belong to Archaebacteria; they are not eubacteria, mycoplasma or cyanobacteria.
Methanobacterium lives in the rumen of cattle and helps break down cellulose. Rhizobium lives in root nodules.
NCERT places methanogens in marshy areas, the rumen of cattle and anaerobic sludge. Hot thermal vents are not listed as their home, so II, III and IV is correct.
I is wrong: methanogens grow anaerobically. V is wrong: they live in the rumen, not the omasum. II, III and IV are correct.

nuggets.title: Biogas plant (gobar gas)
lines: Cattle excreta (dung), rich in methanogens, is used to generate biogas, commonly called gobar gas.
A biogas plant has a concrete tank (10–15 feet deep) where bio-wastes are collected and a slurry of dung is fed.
A floating cover over the slurry rises as gas is produced; an outlet pipe supplies the gas to nearby houses.
The spent slurry is removed through another outlet and may be used as fertiliser.
Biogas technology in India was developed mainly by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).
nuggets.tip: Tank depth is 10–15 feet; developers are IARI and KVIC.

questions.why: Biogas technology in India was developed mainly by IARI and KVIC, not by oil or gas companies.
Biogas (gobar gas) is predominantly methane.
The spent slurry from a biogas plant is removed and may be used as fertiliser.
Both are wrong: cellulosic material is in the rumen (not abomasum), and the biogas tank is 10–15 feet deep (not 15–25).
IV is wrong: cyanobacteria are autotrophic prokaryotes. I, II (IARI and KVIC), III (10–15 ft concrete tank) and V are correct.

nuggets.title: Biocontrol: the organic-farming approach
lines: Biocontrol is the use of biological methods for controlling plant diseases and pests.
Chemical insecticides and pesticides are toxic and harmful to humans and animals and pollute soil and ground water; weedicides can also harm the environment.
An organic farmer creates a system where insects called pests are not eradicated but kept at manageable levels by a complex system of checks and balances.
Biological farming requires familiarity with field life forms, predators and pests, their life cycles, feeding patterns and preferred habitats.
Ladybird beetles control aphids, and dragonflies control mosquitoes.
nuggets.tip: Ladybird eats aphids; dragonfly eats mosquitoes. Do not swap them.

questions.why: Both are NCERT lines: biocontrol uses biological methods against plant diseases and pests, and Trichoderma species are effective against several plant pathogens.
Ladybird beetles get rid of aphids and dragonflies get rid of mosquitoes; option 3 swaps them.
B. thuringiensis controls caterpillars, ladybird controls aphids and dragonflies control mosquitoes: A-P, B-R, C-Q.
NCERT says biological farming means knowing the field's life forms, predators and pests, life cycles, feeding patterns and habitats, so all three are correct.
Biocontrol aims to reduce dependence on synthetic pesticides, so the statement that it increases their use is incorrect.

nuggets.title: Microbial biocontrol: Bt, Trichoderma, baculoviruses
lines: The bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is used to control butterfly caterpillars.
Bt is sold as dried spores in sachets; mixed with water and sprayed on plants such as brassicas and fruit trees, they are eaten by insect larvae, whose gut releases the toxin.
Trichoderma species are free-living fungi, very common in root ecosystems, and are effective biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens.
Baculoviruses are pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods; most used as biocontrol agents belong to the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus.
Baculoviruses are species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticides with no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects, so they suit IPM in ecologically sensitive areas.
nuggets.tip: Trichoderma fights plant pathogens, not insects; Bt targets caterpillars.

questions.why: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is the microbial biocontrol agent for butterfly caterpillars; the other Bacillus names are distractors.
Trichoderma (fungus), baculovirus and Bacillus thuringiensis are all biocontrol agents. Oscillatoria, Rhizobium, Nostoc and Azospirillum are biofertilisers.
Trichoderma is a free-living fungus used against several plant pathogens. Anabaena is a biofertiliser and Lactobacillus makes curd.
Bt is available as dried spores that are sprayed on plants and eaten by insect larvae, in whose gut the toxin is released.
Both are true: baculoviruses are narrow-spectrum, species-specific insecticides, ideal for IPM in ecologically sensitive areas.

nuggets.title: Biofertilisers: nitrogen-fixing bacteria
lines: Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil; their main sources are bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria.
Root nodules of leguminous plants are formed by the symbiotic association of Rhizobium, which fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
Bacteria that are free-living in the soil, such as Azospirillum and Azotobacter, also fix atmospheric nitrogen.
Pressure to cut chemical fertiliser use has encouraged organic farming with biofertilisers.
nuggets.tip: Rhizobium = symbiotic; Azotobacter and Azospirillum = free-living.

questions.why: Azospirillum: free-living; Rhizobium: symbiotic bacterium; Oscillatoria: BGA (cyanobacterium); Glomus: fungus. So A-S, B-R, C-P, D-Q.
Rhizobium forms symbiotic root nodules in legumes. Azotobacter, Clostridium and Beijerinckia are free-living.
Soyabean is a legume, so its biofertiliser is the nodule-forming symbiont Rhizobium.
Biofertilisers include blue-green algae, Rhizobium and other N2-fixing bacteria. Lichens and Saccharomyces are not biofertilisers in NCERT.

nuggets.title: Biofertilisers: mycorrhiza and cyanobacteria
lines: Fungi form symbiotic associations with plants called mycorrhiza; many members of the genus Glomus form mycorrhiza.
The fungal symbiont absorbs phosphorus from the soil and passes it to the plant.
Plants with mycorrhiza show resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, and an overall increase in growth and development.
Cyanobacteria are autotrophic microbes widely found in aquatic and terrestrial environments; many fix atmospheric nitrogen, e.g. Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria.
In paddy fields, cyanobacteria serve as an important biofertiliser and also add organic matter to the soil, increasing its fertility.
nuggets.tip: Mycorrhiza mainly supplies phosphorus; it is mutualism, not commensalism.

questions.why: II is wrong: mycorrhiza is a mutualistic symbiosis, not commensalism. I, III (Glomus), IV and V match NCERT.
Many members of the genus Glomus (a fungus) form mycorrhiza. Nostoc is a cyanobacterium.
NCERT lists all four benefits: resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, phosphorus absorption, and better growth.
Rhizobium is a symbiotic bacterium, not a free-living cyanobacterium. Anabaena, Nostoc and Aulosira are N2-fixing cyanobacteria.
Volvox is a green alga and cannot fix nitrogen. Azotobacter, Oscillatoria, Anabaena and Nostoc are all N2 fixers.

nuggets.title: Biotechnology: definition, core techniques, first rDNA
lines: The EFB (European Federation of Biotechnology) definition covers both traditional and modern molecular biotechnology: integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof and molecular analogues for products and services.
Modern biotechnology rests on two core techniques: genetic engineering (altering the chemistry of genetic material and introducing it into host organisms) and bioprocess engineering.
Bioprocess engineering maintains sterile (microbial contamination-free) conditions so that only the desired microbe or eukaryotic cell grows in large quantities.
Genetic modification needs three basic steps: identify DNA with desirable genes, introduce it into the host, and maintain it in the host and transfer it to progeny.
The first recombinant DNA linked an antibiotic-resistance gene with a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium; Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer did this in 1972.
When transferred into Escherichia coli, the recombinant DNA replicated using the host's DNA polymerase; making multiple identical copies of a template DNA is called cloning.
nuggets.tip: Cohen and Boyer: 1972. Enzymes restricting phage growth in E. coli: 1963. Hind II: five years later.

questions.why: The EFB definition explicitly encompasses both the traditional view and modern molecular biotechnology, so 'Both (1) and (2)' is correct.
NCERT names genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering as the two core techniques that gave birth to modern biotechnology; HGP and bioinformatics came later.
Genetic engineering alters the chemistry of genetic material (Q), bioprocess engineering keeps sterile conditions so only the desired microbe grows (R), and sexual reproduction permits variation (P).
The first recombinant DNA was made by Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer in 1972; 1963 is when the two phage-restricting enzymes of E. coli were isolated.

Only III and IV are true: an antibiotic-resistance gene from a Salmonella typhimurium plasmid was moved into E. coli. It was 1972 (not 1970), the names are Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer, and the DNA did replicate in E. coli.

nuggets.title: Restriction enzymes: discovery and naming
lines: In 1963, two enzymes responsible for restricting the growth of bacteriophage in Escherichia coli were isolated: one added methyl groups to DNA, the other cut DNA.
The DNA-cutting one was called a restriction endonuclease; these enzymes protect bacteria by restricting the growth of invading phages.
Five years later Hind II, the first restriction endonuclease, was isolated; it always cuts DNA at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs.
Today more than 900 restriction enzymes have been isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria, each recognising a different recognition sequence.
In EcoRI, 'E' is the genus Escherichia, 'co' the species coli, 'R' the strain RY 13, and the Roman numeral 'I' the order of isolation from that strain.
nuggets.tip: Name code: Genus (1 letter) + species (2 letters) + strain + Roman numeral of discovery order.

questions.why: Restriction endonucleases restrict the growth of bacteriophages, i.e. they are a bacterial defence against viruses; they are not used for protein synthesis or reproduction.
NCERT: Hind II always cuts DNA at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs, its recognition sequence.
In EcoRI, 'E' is the genus Escherichia and 'co' is the species coli; 'R' is the strain RY 13.
Cohen and Boyer made rDNA in 1972 (S), phage-restricting enzymes were isolated in 1963 (R), Hind II five years later in 1968 (P), and EcoRI comes from strain RY 13 (Q).
More than 900 restriction enzymes have been isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria; 230 is the number of strains, not enzymes.

nuggets.title: Restriction enzymes: palindromes, sticky ends and ligase
lines: Restriction enzymes are nucleases: exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA, while endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA.
Each restriction endonuclease inspects the length of DNA, binds at its specific recognition sequence and cuts each of the two strands at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones.
Each one recognises a specific palindromic nucleotide sequence: the base sequence reads the same on the two strands when read in the same 5'→3' orientation (EcoRI: 5'-GAATTC-3' / 3'-CTTAAG-5').
They cut a little away from the centre of the palindrome but between the same two bases on opposite strands, leaving single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends.
Sticky ends form hydrogen bonds with complementary cut counterparts, and this stickiness facilitates the action of DNA ligase, which joins the fragments.
Cutting the vector and source DNA with the same restriction enzyme gives the same kind of sticky ends, which ligase joins end-to-end to make recombinant DNA.
nuggets.tip: EcoRI cuts between G and A on both strands, leaving AATT overhangs.

questions.why: A restriction endonuclease cuts both strands at the sugar-phosphate backbone, not just one, so option 2 is the incorrect statement; the other three are NCERT facts.
EcoRI recognises 5'-GAATTC-3' / 3'-CTTAAG-5', which reads the same on both strands in the 5'→3' direction; option 2 just writes the strands in reverse order.
Both statements are correct: the enzyme recognises a palindromic sequence and cuts a little away from its centre, between the same two bases on opposite strands.
EcoRI cuts away from the centre of the palindrome, leaving single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends; EcoRV-type cutting at the centre gives blunt ends.
Fragments cut by the same restriction enzyme have matching sticky ends, which DNA ligase joins; EcoRI cuts DNA and Taq polymerase is used in PCR, not for joining.

nuggets.title: Agarose gel electrophoresis and elution
lines: Restriction digestion produces DNA fragments, which are separated by gel electrophoresis.
DNA is negatively charged, so in an electric field the fragments move towards the anode through a matrix, most commonly agarose.
Agarose is a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds; its sieving effect separates fragments by size, so the smaller the fragment, the farther it moves.
Separated DNA is seen only after staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV radiation, which shows bright orange bands (pure DNA is not visible in visible light).
Cutting the separated bands out of the gel and extracting the DNA from the gel piece is called elution; the purified fragments are then used to build recombinant DNA.
nuggets.tip: Wells sit at the cathode end, so the smallest fragments end up farthest from the wells, near the anode.

questions.why: Smaller fragments move farther towards the anode, so the claim that they stay close to the cathode is wrong. DNA moves towards the anode through agarose and resolves by size.
Agarose gel sieves DNA, so the smaller the fragment, the farther it moves; all DNA is negatively charged, so charge does not separate the fragments.
Ethidium bromide-stained DNA shows up as bright orange bands under UV light.
Elution means cutting the separated DNA bands out of the agarose gel and extracting the DNA from the gel piece; making bands visible is the job of EtBr staining and UV light.
Both are correct: eluted fragments are used to build recombinant DNA, and smaller fragments travel farther towards the anode while larger ones stay near the wells.

nuggets.title: Cloning vector features: ori and selectable marker
lines: Plasmids and bacteriophages can replicate inside bacterial cells independently of chromosomal DNA; phages, being many per cell, give very high copy numbers of their genome.
Some plasmids have only one or two copies per cell, while others have 15–100 copies per cell or more.
Ori is the sequence where replication starts; any DNA linked to it can replicate in the host, and ori also controls the copy number of the linked DNA.
A selectable marker helps identify and eliminate non-transformants and selectively permits the growth of transformants.
Transformation introduces a piece of DNA into a host bacterium; genes for resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin are useful markers because normal E. coli lacks them.
nuggets.tip: The marker selects TRANSFORMANTS (cells with the vector), not recombinants. Telling recombinants apart needs insertional inactivation.

questions.why: The origin of replication (ori) starts replication and controls the copy number of the linked DNA; palindromes are recognition sites for restriction enzymes.
A selectable marker identifies and eliminates non-transformants while selectively letting transformants grow; option 3 reverses this.
An antibiotic-resistance gene in the vector lets only cells that took up the vector survive, so it selects transformed cells.
On ampicillin medium only cells carrying the ampR recombinant DNA survive, so transformants grow and non-transformants die.
Both are NCERT lines: bacteriophages have very high copy numbers because there are many per cell, and plasmids range from 1–2 to 15–100 copies per cell or more.

nuggets.title: Cloning sites, pBR322 and insertional inactivation
lines: To link alien DNA, a vector needs very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the restriction enzymes used; more sites cut the vector into several fragments and complicate cloning.
In E. coli vector pBR322, rop codes for proteins involved in plasmid replication; it carries ampR and tetR genes, ori and several restriction sites.
In pBR322, BamHI and SalI sites lie in the tetracycline-resistance gene, and PstI and PvuI sites lie in the ampicillin-resistance gene.
Foreign DNA ligated at the BamHI site inactivates tetR; recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline, while non-recombinants grow on both.
In the alternative method, inserting DNA into the β-galactosidase coding sequence inactivates the enzyme (insertional inactivation).
With a chromogenic substrate, colonies without an insert turn blue, while recombinant colonies stay colourless.
nuggets.tip: Blue colonies = no insert (non-recombinant); white/colourless colonies = recombinant.

questions.why: In pBR322, rop codes for the proteins involved in plasmid replication; ori is where replication starts and the markers are ampR and tetR.
A vector should have very few, preferably single, recognition sites; two or more sites cut the vector into several fragments and complicate gene cloning.
PstI cuts inside ampR, so inserting a gene there causes insertional inactivation and the plasmid can no longer give ampicillin resistance.
Colonies with an insert have an inactivated β-galactosidase and give no colour, so they are the recombinants. Blue colonies have no insert, which makes A wrong and B right.
Both are correct: an insert at BamHI inactivates tetR, so recombinants grow on ampicillin but not tetracycline, while non-recombinants keep both genes and grow on both.

nuggets.title: Vectors for plants and animals
lines: Pathogens have learned to transfer their genes into plant and animal cells, and these delivery mechanisms are used to carry genes of interest.
Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants, delivers a piece of DNA called T-DNA that transforms normal plant cells into a tumour.
The Ti plasmid (tumour-inducing plasmid) of A. tumefaciens has been modified into a cloning vector that no longer causes disease but still delivers genes into many plants.
In animals, retroviruses can transform normal cells into cancerous cells; disarmed retroviruses are used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.
nuggets.tip: Agrobacterium infects dicots (not cereals) and is a plant pathogen, not a root symbiont.

questions.why: Ti stands for tumour-inducing: the Ti plasmid's T-DNA turns normal plant cells into tumour cells.
The Ti plasmid has been modified to be non-pathogenic while still delivering genes, so 'always pathogenic without exception' is wrong. The other options are true of Agrobacterium.
The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens was disarmed into a cloning vector that still delivers genes into many plants; the other genus names are distractors.
Insertional inactivation involves the β-galactosidase gene (Q), A. tumefaciens is a pathogen of several dicots (R), and retroviruses turn normal cells cancerous (P).
Statement A is wrong because A. tumefaciens is popular as a dicot pathogen that delivers T-DNA, not as a root associate of cereals. Statement B is right: retroviruses can make normal cells cancerous.

nuggets.title: Making hosts competent to take up DNA
lines: DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass through cell membranes, so bacterial cells must first be made competent.
Treating bacteria with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium increases the efficiency with which DNA enters through pores in the cell wall.
Recombinant DNA is taken up when cells are incubated with it on ice, briefly given a heat shock at 42°C, and then put back on ice.
In micro-injection, recombinant DNA is injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell.
In biolistics (gene gun), suited to plants, cells are bombarded with high-velocity microparticles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA.
A disarmed pathogen vector lets it infect the cell and transfer the recombinant DNA into the host.
nuggets.tip: Microinjection = animal cell nucleus; biolistics = plant cells; heat shock with Ca<sup>2+</sup> = bacteria.

questions.why: Elution is extracting DNA bands from agarose gel, not a transfer method. Biolistics, disarmed pathogen vectors and micro-injection all introduce DNA into host cells.
In biolistics, cells are bombarded with high-velocity microparticles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA.
Only I is correct: ice, a 42°C heat shock, then ice again. In micro-injection the DNA goes directly into the nucleus of the animal cell, not the cytoplasm.
Both are correct: DNA is hydrophilic and therefore cannot pass through cell membranes, which is why cells must be made competent.
Biolistics suits plant hosts (R), micro-injection is used for animal cells (P), and heat shock with calcium makes bacteria competent (Q).

nuggets.title: Isolating pure DNA
lines: DNA is enclosed within membranes, so the cell is broken open to release DNA along with RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and lipids.
Cell walls are broken with lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plant cells) and chitinase (fungus).
RNA is removed with ribonuclease, proteins with protease, and other molecules by appropriate treatments.
Purified DNA finally precipitates out on adding chilled ethanol and is seen as a collection of fine threads in the suspension.
Restriction digestion is done by incubating purified DNA with the enzyme under optimal conditions, and agarose gel electrophoresis checks how far the digestion has progressed.
nuggets.tip: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, so they need chitinase. Restriction enzymes are not used to isolate DNA.

questions.why: After cell-wall breakage and enzyme treatments, chilled ethanol precipitates the purified DNA as fine threads; RNA and proteins have already been removed by RNase and protease.
Lysozyme breaks bacterial walls (S), cellulase plant walls (R), chitinase fungal walls (P), ribonuclease removes RNA (T) and protease removes proteins (Q).
Both are correct: chilled ethanol precipitates purified DNA as fine threads, and a bioreactor cultures large volumes of living cells.
A is correct because chitinase is needed for fungal cells. B is wrong because the fungal cell wall is made of chitin, not cellulose.
Both are NCERT lines: digestion is done by incubating purified DNA with the enzyme under optimal conditions, and agarose gel electrophoresis checks its progress.

nuggets.title: PCR: amplifying the gene of interest
lines: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) makes multiple copies of a gene (DNA of interest) in vitro using two sets of primers and a DNA polymerase.
Primers are small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of the template DNA.
Each cycle has three steps in order: denaturation (strands separate at high temperature), annealing (primers bind) and extension by DNA polymerase.
A thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus (Taq polymerase) stays active during the high-temperature denaturation step.
Repeated cycles amplify the DNA segment roughly a billion times; the amplified fragment can then be ligated with a vector for cloning.
nuggets.tip: Cycle order: Denature → Anneal → Extend. Copies double every cycle (2<sup>n</sup>).

questions.why: Each PCR cycle runs denaturation → annealing → extension: strands separate, primers bind, then the polymerase extends them.
High temperature is needed to separate the DNA strands, so without it denaturation, the first step, fails, and annealing and extension cannot follow.
Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus is thermostable; it stays active through the high-temperature denaturation steps of PCR.
Primers are small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of the template DNA, so the options calling them non-complementary or restriction sites are wrong.
Each PCR cycle doubles the DNA, so after n cycles one template gives 2n copies; this is how amplification reaches about a billion times.

nuggets.title: rDNA steps, gene expression and recombinant protein
lines: rDNA technology runs: isolate DNA → cut it with restriction endonucleases → isolate the desired fragment → amplify it (PCR) → ligate it into a vector → insert it into the host → culture the host → extract the product.
Alien DNA without an ori may get integrated into the host genome and then multiply and be inherited along with the host DNA.
Expressing the cloned gene under appropriate conditions is the ultimate aim, so the target protein can be produced on a large scale.
A protein-encoding gene expressed in a heterologous host gives a recombinant protein.
In a continuous culture system, used medium is drained out and fresh medium added, keeping cells in their physiologically most active log phase and giving larger biomass and higher yields.

questions.why: Order: cut DNA with restriction enzyme → isolate the desired fragment → amplify it by PCR → insert the rDNA into the host, i.e. B, C, D, A.
Isolate the desired fragment (iii) → amplify it (ii) → ligate it into the vector (iv) → insert the rDNA into the host (v) → extract the product (i).
Alien DNA without an ori cannot replicate on its own, but it may integrate into the host genome and then multiply and be inherited with the host DNA (B and C).
Any protein-encoding gene expressed in a heterologous host is called a recombinant protein.
A continuous culture system drains used medium and adds fresh medium, keeping cells in the log phase. This gives larger biomass and higher yield than a flask or a closed tank.

nuggets.title: Bioreactors and downstream processing
lines: Large volumes of recombinant product need bioreactors, where 100–1000 litres of culture can be processed.
A bioreactor provides optimal growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen) for converting raw materials into specific products.
The most commonly used stirred-tank bioreactor is usually cylindrical with a curved base; its stirrer mixes the contents and makes oxygen available throughout.
Air can be bubbled through the reactor (sparged stirred-tank); a bioreactor has agitator, oxygen-delivery, foam-control, temperature-control and pH-control systems and sampling ports.
Downstream processing means separation and purification of the product, followed by formulation with suitable preservatives; drugs undergo clinical trials.
Strict quality control testing is required, and downstream processing and quality control vary from product to product.
nuggets.tip: Downstream processing = separation + purification (+ formulation). Gene expression is an upstream step.

questions.why: The stirrer in a stirred-tank bioreactor mixes the contents evenly and ensures oxygen availability throughout the vessel.
Downstream processing is separation and purification of the product followed by formulation with preservatives. Expression of the gene happens before this, inside the host.
NCERT lists all six as bioreactor components: agitator, oxygen delivery, foam control, temperature control, pH control systems and sampling ports.
Bioreactors process large volumes (100–1000 L), not small ones, so i is wrong. They provide optimal conditions (ii), and a sparged stirred-tank bioreactor bubbles air through (iii).
Both are correct: every product needs strict quality control testing, and downstream processing and quality control vary from product to product.

nuggets.title: Biotechnology: scope and three routes to more food
lines: Biotechnology deals with industrial-scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using genetically modified microbes, fungi, plants and animals.
Its applications include therapeutics, diagnostics, GM crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production.
Three critical research areas: providing the best catalyst (improved organism or pure enzyme), creating optimal conditions for it to act, and downstream processing.
Three options for increasing food production: agro-chemical based agriculture, organic agriculture and genetically engineered crop-based agriculture.
The Green Revolution tripled the food supply, yet it was not enough for the growing human population.
Agrochemicals are often too expensive for farmers in the developing world, and yields from existing varieties cannot be raised much further by conventional breeding.

questions.why: Both: NCERT says biotechnology deals with industrial-scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using GM microbes, fungi, plants and animals. Conventional hybridisation is plant breeding, not biotechnology.
All of them: NCERT lists therapeutics, diagnostics, GM crops, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production as applications of biotechnology.
All of the above: the three critical research areas are the best catalyst, optimal conditions for the catalyst to act, and downstream processing to purify the product.

Both 1 and 2: the three options are agro-chemical based agriculture, organic agriculture and genetically engineered crop-based agriculture. Simply pouring in more agrochemicals is not one of the routes NCERT names.
A-Q, B-R, C-P: the Green Revolution tripled the food supply; biotechnology research aims to provide the best catalyst; RNAi was used to make tobacco resistant to a nematode.

nuggets.title: GMOs and the advantages of GM plants
lines: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called genetically modified organisms (GMO).
GM has made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat).
Pest-resistant GM crops reduce reliance on chemical pesticides; GM also helps reduce post-harvest losses.
GM plants use minerals more efficiently, which prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility.
GM enhances the nutritional value of food, e.g. Golden rice, i.e. Vitamin 'A' enriched rice.
GM has also produced tailor-made plants that supply alternative resources to industries: starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals.
nuggets.tip: GM crops REDUCE post-harvest losses and INCREASE mineral-use efficiency. Options that say the opposite are the wrong ones.

questions.why: Organisms whose genes have been altered by manipulation are genetically modified organisms. 'Recombinant' or 'hybrid' are not the NCERT term.
All of the above: GM crops are more tolerant to abiotic stresses, reduce post-harvest losses and help maximise yield.
The incorrect statement is decreased mineral-use efficiency. GM plants use minerals more efficiently, which prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility.
Increasing post-harvest losses is not an advantage. GM crops reduce post-harvest losses, reduce pesticide use, enhance nutrition and improve mineral-use efficiency.
Golden rice is Vitamin 'A' enriched rice, so it can help fight vitamin A deficiency, which causes night blindness. The other options are not vitamin A crops.

nuggets.title: Bt toxin: source and how it kills insects
lines: Bt toxin is produced by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt). Its gene, cloned and expressed in plants, makes them resistant to insects, so they work as a bio-pesticide.
Some strains kill certain insects: lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).
B. thuringiensis forms protein crystals during a particular phase of its growth; these contain a toxic insecticidal protein.
The toxin does not kill the Bacillus because it exists there as an inactive protoxin.
In the insect gut the alkaline pH solubilises the crystals, and the protoxin is converted into the active toxin.
The active toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores that cause cell swelling and lysis, and finally the death of the insect.
nuggets.tip: Protoxin is activated by ALKALINE pH of the insect gut, not acidic. This is a favourite NEET trap.

questions.why: Alkaline pH of the insect gut solubilises the crystals and activates the protoxin. 'Acidic pH' is the classic wrong option.
Alkaline pH of gut: once the bollworm ingests the inactive protoxin, the alkaline gut solubilises the crystals and converts the protoxin into the active Bt toxin.
The inactive protoxin is converted into active form in the insect gut. Inside the Bacillus it stays inactive, which is why it does not kill the bacterium.
A true, B false: Bt toxins are coded by cry genes such as cryIAc, but the protoxin is activated by the alkaline pH of the insect gut, not acidic pH.
Tapeworm is a flatworm, not an insect. Bt proteins kill certain insects such as the lepidopteran tobacco budworm, armyworm and cotton bollworm.

nuggets.title: cry genes and Bt crops
lines: The Bt toxin is coded by a gene named cry; there are a number of such genes.
Proteins encoded by cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms; the protein of cryIAb controls corn borer.
Bt toxins are insect-group specific, so the choice of genes depends on the crop and the targeted pest.
Examples of crops expressing Bt toxin genes are Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato and soybean.
Pest-resistant Bt crops reduce the need for chemical insecticides.
nuggets.tip: cryIAb (single 'A', single 'b') = corn borer; cryIAc and cryIIAb = cotton bollworm.

questions.why: cryIAc (with cryIIAb) codes for proteins that control the cotton bollworm. Corn borer is controlled by the cryIAb protein.
A-R, B-S, C-P, D-Q: α-1-antitrypsin treats emphysema; cryIAb controls corn borer; cryIAc controls cotton bollworm; enzyme replacement therapy treats ADA deficiency.
