Corn borer and cotton bollworm, respectively: the cryIAb protein controls corn borer, while cryIIAb (with cryIAc) controls cotton bollworm.
High yield and resistance to bollworms: Bt cotton expresses cry genes such as cryIAc and cryIIAb, whose proteins kill bollworms (lepidopterans), not dipterans, beetles or aphids.

I, III, IV, V: the toxin creates pores in midgut cells; it is insect-group specific; cryIAc/cryIIAb control bollworm and cryIAb controls corn borer. II is wrong because abiotic-stress tolerance is not a Bt effect.

nuggets.title: RNA interference: the principle
lines: RNA interference (RNAi) takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence.
RNAi silences a specific mRNA: a complementary dsRNA molecule binds to the mRNA and prevents its translation.
The complementary RNA may come from infection by viruses with RNA genomes, or from mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.
The nematode Meloidogyne incognita infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield.
A novel strategy based on RNAi was adopted to prevent this infestation.
nuggets.tip: RNAi blocks translation of mRNA, not transcription. It occurs in eukaryotes, not prokaryotes.

questions.why: In RNAi the complementary dsRNA binds the specific mRNA and prevents its translation. Transcription still happens; the mRNA is silenced afterwards.
Silencing happens because of a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the specific mRNA.
RNA viruses and transposons that replicate via an RNA intermediate are the source of complementary RNA that silences mRNA in RNAi.
A incorrect, B correct: tRNA and rRNA do interact with mRNA during translation, and RNAi does occur in all eukaryotes as a method of cellular defence.
Assertion correct, Reason incorrect: RNAi is a cellular defence in eukaryotes, but it silences a specific mRNA, not tRNA.

nuggets.title: RNAi: nematode-resistant tobacco
lines: Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host (tobacco) plant.
The DNA was introduced so that it produced both sense and anti-sense RNA in the host cells.
Being complementary, the two RNAs formed a dsRNA that initiated RNAi and silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode.
The parasite could not survive in a transgenic host expressing the specific interfering RNA, so the transgenic plant was protected from it.

questions.why: The introduced DNA produced both sense and anti-sense RNA in host cells. Being complementary, they formed the dsRNA that triggers RNAi.
mRNA silencing (RNAi) was used to make tobacco resistant to the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita. Bollworm resistance comes from Bt cry genes instead.
dsRNA formed from sense and anti-sense RNA silences the nematode mRNA. The technique is RNA interference (RNAi).
Option 3: Agrobacterium vectors carried nematode-specific genes into the plant; the dsRNA silenced the nematode's mRNA; the transgenic plant was protected from M. incognita.
Both correct, Reason explains: Meloidogyne incognita infects tobacco roots, which is why yield is greatly reduced.

nuggets.title: Recombinant therapeutics and why human insulin
lines: Recombinant DNA technology allows mass production of safe and more effective therapeutic drugs.
Recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses, as is common with similar products from non-human sources.
About 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use worldwide; 12 of these are currently marketed in India.
Insulin for diabetes was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.
Insulin from an animal source caused some patients to develop allergy or other reactions to the foreign protein.
nuggets.tip: Numbers: 30 approved worldwide, 12 marketed in India.

questions.why: Recombinant therapeutics such as human insulin do not induce unwanted immunological responses, unlike insulin from non-human sources such as cattle.
Only A: about 30 recombinant therapeutics are approved worldwide, but only 12 (not 21) are marketed in India.
I, III: rDNA gives safer and more effective drugs, and 30 are approved with 12 marketed in India. II is wrong because recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immune responses.
Insulin was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.
Insulin was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs. It is a protein, so it is not given orally; animal insulin can cause allergy; GM E. coli does make it.

nuggets.title: Insulin structure and Eli Lilly's method
lines: Mature insulin has two short polypeptide chains, chain A and chain B, linked together by disulphide bridges.
In mammals including humans, insulin is synthesised as a prohormone (pro-insulin) that contains an extra stretch called the C peptide.
The C peptide is removed during maturation and is absent in mature insulin; assembling insulin into its mature form was the main challenge for rDNA production.
In 1983, Eli Lilly, an American company, prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains and introduced them in plasmids of E. coli.
The A and B chains were produced separately, extracted, and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin.
nuggets.tip: Only A and B chains were made in E. coli. The C peptide was never produced, so 'A, B and C produced' is a trap.

questions.why: The A and B chains of insulin are linked by disulphide bridges. Hydrogen bonds or phosphodiester bonds do not link them.
Incorrect: the A and B chains are linked by disulphide bridges, not hydrogen bonds. The other statements (C-peptide in pro-insulin, production in E. coli) are correct.
The C-peptide is removed during maturation of pro-insulin, so mature insulin has only the A and B chains.
1, 3, 4: the C-peptide is absent from mature insulin, is present in pro-insulin, and A and B are joined by disulphide bridges. rDNA insulin was made from A and B chains only, so it has no C-peptide.
Assertion correct, Reason incorrect: human insulin is made in bacteria, but only the A and B chains were produced. No C chain was made.

nuggets.title: Gene therapy and ADA deficiency
lines: Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo.
Genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease; a normal gene is delivered to compensate for the non-functional gene.
The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
The ADA enzyme is crucial for the immune system to function.
ADA deficiency is caused by deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase.
nuggets.tip: 1990, 4-year-old girl, ADA. Do not mix it up with 1983 (Eli Lilly insulin) or 1997 (Rosie).

questions.why: A collection of methods to correct a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo is gene therapy.
In 1990 a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency received the first clinical gene therapy.
Adenosine deaminase, 1990: the first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency. 1983 is the year Eli Lilly made insulin.
ADA is crucial for the immune system, so its deficiency causes dysfunction of the immune system.
A incorrect, B correct: ADA deficiency is caused by deletion of the ADA gene, not by excess synthesis; it does affect the immune system.

nuggets.title: Treating ADA deficiency
lines: In some children ADA deficiency can be cured by bone marrow transplantation; in others by enzyme replacement therapy (injection of functional ADA).
Neither of these approaches is completely curative.
In gene therapy, lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture outside the body.
A functional ADA cDNA is introduced into these lymphocytes using a retroviral vector, and they are returned to the patient.
These cells are not immortal, so the patient needs periodic infusion of genetically engineered lymphocytes.
Introducing the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA into cells at early embryonic stages could be a permanent cure.

questions.why: Bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy treat ADA deficiency, but neither is completely curative.
Periodic infusion is needed because genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal. They die and must be replaced.
Incorrect: the patient does require periodic infusion of engineered lymphocytes, because these cells are not immortal.
A permanent cure is possible only by introducing the gene from ADA-producing marrow cells into cells at early embryonic stages. Lymphocyte infusion and ERT are temporary.
Only III: a permanent cure needs the gene from ADA-producing marrow cells introduced at early embryonic stages. Lymphocyte infusion and enzyme replacement are not permanent.

nuggets.title: Molecular diagnosis: why early, and PCR
lines: Effective treatment requires early diagnosis and understanding of the disease's pathophysiology.
Conventional methods such as serum and urine analysis cannot detect disease early.
Recombinant DNA technology, PCR and ELISA are techniques that serve the purpose of early diagnosis.
A pathogen is normally suspected only after it produces symptoms, and by then its concentration in the body is already very high.
PCR amplifies nucleic acid, so very low concentrations of a bacterium or virus can be detected.
PCR is now routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and gene mutations in suspected cancer patients, and to identify many other genetic disorders.

questions.why: Serum and urine analysis are conventional methods that cannot detect disease early. rDNA technology, PCR and ELISA can.
PCR amplifies the pathogen's nucleic acid, so very low concentrations of bacteria or viruses can be detected. ELISA detects antigens or antibodies instead.
All of the above: PCR is routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients, gene mutations in suspected cancer patients and many other genetic disorders.
I, II and IV: PCR detects HIV and cancer mutations and identifies genetic disorders. III is wrong because the probe has no complementarity with the mutated gene, and it is a probe method, not PCR.
i, ii and iii: rDNA technology, PCR and ELISA serve early diagnosis. Conventional serum and urine analysis cannot.

nuggets.title: Probes, autoradiography and ELISA
lines: A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule is called a probe.
The probe is allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, followed by detection using autoradiography.
A clone with a mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film, because the probe has no complementarity with the mutated gene.
ELISA is based on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction.
With ELISA, infection is detected by the presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins, etc.) or of antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.
nuggets.tip: Autoradiography: the mutated gene is the clone that does NOT show up on the film.

questions.why: A single strand of DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule is a probe.
The mutated gene does not appear on the film because the probe has no complementarity with it, so it cannot hybridise.
ELISA is based on antigen-antibody interaction. PCR amplifies DNA, and gel electrophoresis separates DNA by size.
Both correct: ELISA works on antigen-antibody interaction and can detect either the pathogen's antigens or the antibodies made against it.
A-R, B-P, C-Q: ELISA works on antigen-antibody reaction; PCR amplifies nucleic acid; a probe is ssDNA or ssRNA tagged with a radioactive molecule.

nuggets.title: Transgenic animals: definition, physiology and disease models
lines: Animals whose DNA is manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are called transgenic animals.
Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, but over 95% of all existing transgenic animals are mice.
They are designed to study how genes are regulated and how they affect normal functions of the body and its development.
One example is the study of complex factors involved in growth such as insulin-like growth factor: genes that alter the formation of such a factor reveal its biological role.
Transgenic models exist for many human diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's.
These models increase understanding of how genes contribute to disease and allow investigation of new treatments.

questions.why: Over 95% of all existing transgenic animals are mice.
NCERT's example for studying growth factors with transgenic animals is insulin-like growth factor.
i, ii, iii, v: transgenic models exist for Alzheimer's, cystic fibrosis, cancer and rheumatoid arthritis. PKU and emphysema are linked to biological products, not disease models.
Genes that alter the formation of a particular factor are introduced, and the resulting changes show the biological role of that factor in the body.
All of these: disease models increase understanding of how genes contribute to disease, allow new treatments to be investigated, and exist for Alzheimer's and cystic fibrosis.

nuggets.title: Transgenic animals: products, Rosie and safety testing
lines: Transgenic animals that make useful biological products are created by introducing the portion of DNA (genes) that codes for that product.
Human protein α-1-antitrypsin, made by transgenic animals, is used to treat emphysema; similar attempts are being made for phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis.
In 1997 the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre).
Rosie's milk contained human alpha-lactalbumin and was nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow milk.
Transgenic mice are being developed to test the safety of polio vaccine; if reliable, they could replace monkeys for testing vaccine batches.
In chemical safety (toxicity) testing, animals carry genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances, so results come in less time.
nuggets.tip: Rosie = alpha-lactalbumin (milk). α-1-antitrypsin = emphysema. Do not swap them.

questions.why: Human α-1-antitrypsin, used to treat emphysema, is obtained from a transgenic animal.
Rosie produced human protein-enriched milk at 2.4 g per litre (grams per litre, not per millilitre).
Both correct: ELISA works on antigen-antibody interaction, and Rosie's milk with human alpha-lactalbumin is nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.
Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of polio vaccine before it is used on humans. Rosie's milk was not high-fat milk for ghee.
Only I: transgenic mice test polio vaccine safety, and they could replace monkeys, not gorillas.

nuggets.title: Ethical issues: GEAC and biopatents
lines: Genetic modification can have unpredictable results when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem, so the Indian Government set up the GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee).
GEAC makes decisions on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services.
There is public anger over patents granted for products and technologies that use genetic materials and plants long identified and used by farmers and indigenous people.
In 1997 an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office; the 'new' variety was derived from Indian farmers' varieties.
There are an estimated 2,00,000 varieties of rice in India alone, and 27 documented varieties of Basmati are grown in India.
Turmeric and neem are other Indian plants that have been patented, or that others have tried to patent.
nuggets.tip: Basmati: 27 documented varieties; India has about 2,00,000 rice varieties in total.

questions.why: The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services.
GEAC assesses the safety of introducing GM organisms for public use. NCERT expands it as Genetic Engineering Approval Committee; the official body is now named Appraisal Committee.
Basmati: in 1997 an American company got patent rights on a Basmati variety derived from Indian farmers' varieties.
27, India: 27 documented varieties of Basmati are grown in India. About 2,00,000 is the estimate for all rice varieties in India.
Incorrect: India has an estimated 2,00,000 rice varieties, not 20,000. Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge.

nuggets.title: Biopiracy and the Indian Patents Bill
lines: Biopiracy is the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned, and without compensatory payment.
Most industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge.
Developing and underdeveloped nations are rich in biodiversity and in traditional knowledge related to bio-resources.
Traditional knowledge about bio-resources can be exploited to develop modern applications and save time, effort and expenditure during commercialisation.
The Indian Parliament cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, which covers patent terms, emergency provisions and research and development initiative.

questions.why: Use of bio-resources by multinational companies without authorisation from the concerned country and its people is biopiracy.
All of the above: biopiracy is the unauthorised exploitation of bio-resources and of traditional knowledge about them, without compensatory payment.
Both 1 and 2: the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill covers patent terms, emergency provisions and research and development initiative.
Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. The Basmati patent went to an American company, not the US Government.
A-Q, B-R, C-P: GEAC decides the validity of GM research; biopiracy is illegal use of bio-resources; the Indian Patents Bill covers patent terms and emergency provisions.

nuggets.title: Ecology and what a population is
lines: Ecology studies the interactions among organisms and between the organism and its physical (abiotic) environment.
Ecology is concerned with four levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities and biomes.
Ramdeo Misra is revered as the Father of Ecology in India.
A population is a group of individuals of a species that live in a well-defined geographical area, share or compete for similar resources, and potentially interbreed.
Interbreeding implies sexual reproduction, but a group produced even by asexual reproduction is generally treated as a population for ecological studies.
Examples: cormorants in a wetland, rats in an abandoned dwelling, teakwood trees in a forest tract, bacteria in a culture plate, lotus plants in a pond.

questions.why: Ecology deals with four levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities and biomes.
Ramdeo Misra is revered as the Father of Ecology in India.
A and B only: a population is made of individuals of the same species living in a well-defined geographical area. Density and dispersion are not constant; they keep changing.
For ecological studies, individuals from both asexual and sexual reproduction count as a population, even though 'interbreeding' implies sexual reproduction.
All of them: cormorants in a wetland, rats in an abandoned dwelling, teakwood trees, bacteria in a culture plate and lotus plants in a pond are all NCERT examples of populations.

nuggets.title: Population attributes: birth rate, death rate, sex ratio
lines: Population ecology is important because it links ecology to population genetics and evolution.
A population has attributes that an individual lacks: an individual has births and deaths, but a population has birth rates and death rates.
Rates are expressed per capita: if 20 lotus plants last year gave 8 new plants, the birth rate is 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.
If 4 of 40 fruit flies in a laboratory population died during a week, the death rate is 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week.
An individual is either male or female, but a population has a sex ratio, e.g. 60% females and 40% males.
nuggets.tip: Rate = change / initial number. Always divide by the starting population, not the final one.

questions.why: Population ecology matters because it links ecology to population genetics and evolution.
Birth rate = 8 new plants / 20 existing plants = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.
Death rate = 8 dead / 80 flies = 0.1 individuals per Drosophila per week. Do not answer 10; rates are per capita.
Species interaction is not an attribute of one population; it happens between populations. Natality, mortality and sex ratio are population attributes.
Both correct: a population has attributes an individual lacks, and an individual is male or female while a population has a sex ratio.

nuggets.title: Age distribution and age pyramids
lines: A population at any given time is made of individuals of different ages.
Plotting the age distribution (percent individuals of a given age or age group) gives an age pyramid.
Age groups are pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive; human age pyramids show males and females in one combined diagram.
The shape of the pyramid shows growth status: expanding (triangular) for a growing population, bell-shaped for a stable one and urn-shaped for a declining one.
nuggets.tip: Triangle = growing, Bell = stable, Urn = declining.

questions.why: In a growing population, pre-reproductive individuals outnumber reproductive ones, which gives the broad-based triangular pyramid.
A-P, B-R, C-Q: growing = triangular (expanding), stable = bell-shaped, declining = urn-shaped.
An urn-shaped pyramid has a narrow base (few pre-reproductive individuals), so it denotes a declining population.

A-Q, B-P, C-R, D-S: logistic growth happens with limited resources and exponential growth with unlimited ones; an expanding pyramid has the most pre-reproductives; a stable one has pre-reproductive about equal to reproductive.
A population at any given time is composed of individuals of different ages, which is why age distribution can be plotted.

nuggets.title: Population size and how density is measured
lines: Population size is technically called population density (N), and it need not be measured only in numbers.
Size can be under 10 (Siberian cranes at Bharatpur wetlands in a year) or run into millions (Chlamydomonas in a pond).
Total number is the most appropriate measure, but where one huge banyan tree sits among 200 Parthenium plants, percent cover or biomass is more meaningful.
When absolute numbers are not needed, relative density works, e.g. the number of fish caught per trap shows fish density in a lake.
Density can also be estimated indirectly: the tiger census in national parks relies on pug marks and fecal pellets.

questions.why: Siberian cranes at Bharatpur (under 10 in a year) and Chlamydomonas in a pond (millions) are NCERT's two extremes of population size.
Population size is technically called population density (N).
A single huge banyan tree cannot be fairly compared with 200 Parthenium plants by number, so biomass or percent cover is used.
Fish caught per trap is a relative density: it shows fish abundance in a lake without counting every fish.
The tiger census uses pug marks and fecal pellets, an indirect estimate that does not require seeing the tigers.

nuggets.title: Population growth: B, D, I and E
lines: Population density changes with food availability, predation pressure and adverse weather.
Natality is the number of births during a given period and mortality the number of deaths; immigration adds individuals from elsewhere and emigration removes those who leave.
Natality and immigration increase population density; mortality and emigration decrease it.
N<sub>t+1</sub> = N<sub>t</sub> + [(B + I) − (D + E)].
Births and deaths are normally the most important factors; when a new habitat is just being colonised, immigration may contribute more than birth rates.

questions.why: Nt+1 = Nt + [(B + I) − (D + E)]: births and immigrants add to the population, deaths and emigrants subtract.
Natality and immigration both add individuals, so they increase population density.
When a new habitat is just being colonised, immigration may contribute more to growth than birth rates.
All of the above: population size changes with food availability, predation pressure and adverse weather.

nuggets.title: Exponential growth
lines: With unlimited resources, each species can fully realise its innate potential to grow in number, as Darwin observed.
Growth is then exponential: dN/dt = (b − d) × N; putting r = b − d gives dN/dt = rN.
r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, an important parameter for assessing biotic or abiotic effects on population growth.
Sample r values: Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12; for India's population in 1981, r was 0.0205.
Integral form: Nt = N0 ert, where e is the base of natural logarithms (2.71828); N plotted against time gives a J-shaped curve.
Any species growing exponentially with unlimited resources can reach enormous densities quickly; Darwin showed this even for a slow-growing animal like the elephant.
nuggets.tip: r values in order: Norway rat 0.015 < human 1981 0.0205 < flour beetle 0.12.

questions.why: In dN/dt = rN, r = b − d is the intrinsic rate of natural increase.
NCERT values: Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12, Indian population (1981) 0.0205.
In Nt = N0ert, e is the base of natural logarithms (2.71828).
Only I: exponential growth can quickly reach enormous densities, but Darwin's example of a slow-growing animal was the elephant, not the tiger.
II and IV are wrong: the human r for 1981 is 0.0205 (not 0.0170), and the Norway rat's r is 0.015 (not 0.15). The flour beetle's 0.12 is correct.

nuggets.title: Logistic growth and carrying capacity
lines: No population in nature has unlimited resources, so individuals compete for limited resources and the 'fittest' survives and reproduces.
A habitat can support only a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible: the carrying capacity (K).
With limited resources, growth shows a lag phase, then acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when density reaches K.
N plotted against time gives a sigmoid curve; this is Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth: dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K].
Because resources become limiting sooner or later, the logistic model is considered more realistic than the exponential one.
nuggets.tip: At N = K the factor (K − N)/K becomes 0, so growth stops: this is the asymptote.

questions.why: In the logistic equation, K is the carrying capacity, the maximum number the habitat's resources can support. r is the intrinsic rate.
Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth is dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K].
With limited resources: lag → acceleration → deceleration → asymptote, which gives the sigmoid curve.
The asymptote is reached when N = K: (K − N)/K becomes zero, so dN/dt = 0.
II, III, IV: r is the intrinsic rate; no natural population has unlimited resources; limited resources give lag, acceleration, deceleration and asymptote. I is wrong: the integral form is Nt = N0ert.

nuggets.title: Life history variation
lines: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness (high r value), in the habitat where they live.
Under a given set of selection pressures, organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy.
Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime (Pacific salmon fish, bamboo); others breed many times (most birds and mammals).
Some produce a large number of small offspring (oysters, pelagic fishes); others a small number of large offspring (birds, mammals).
Life history traits have evolved in relation to the constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat.

questions.why: Populations evolve to maximise reproductive fitness, which is also called Darwinian fitness.
Darwinian fitness corresponds to a high r value, the intrinsic rate of natural increase.
A-P, B-R, C-Q: Pacific salmon breed only once; most birds and mammals breed many times; oysters produce many small offspring.
A-Q, B-R, C-S, D-P: salmon breed once; Nt = N0ert is exponential growth; oysters produce many small offspring; dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K is Verhulst-Pearl.
I, II, III, V are correct NCERT examples. IV is wrong: fig's mutualistic partner is a wasp, not a bumblebee.

nuggets.title: Population interactions: the +, −, 0 code
lines: No species lives alone: even a plant needs soil microbes to break down organic matter and return inorganic nutrients, and animals for pollination.
Interspecific interactions can be beneficial (+), detrimental (−) or neutral (0) to one or both species.
Mutualism (+,+) benefits both; competition (−,−) harms both; in predation and parasitism (+,−) only one species benefits.
Commensalism (+,0): one benefits and the other is unaffected; amensalism (−,0): one is harmed and the other is unaffected.
Predation, parasitism and commensalism share one feature: the interacting species live closely together.
nuggets.tip: Competition is the only (−,−) interaction; amensalism is (−,0).

questions.why: ++ is mutualism, −− is competition and +0 is commensalism.
A-S, B-P, C-Q, D-R: mutualism (+,+), commensalism (+,0), amensalism (−,0), parasitism (+,−).
Predation is (+,−): the predator benefits and the prey is harmed. Commensalism is (+,0) and competition is (−,−).
Amensalism is A (−), B (0): one species is harmed while the other is unaffected.
Predation, parasitism and commensalism need close living. In competition the species may simply share a resource without living together.

nuggets.title: Predation: energy transfer and control of prey
lines: Predation is nature's way of transferring the energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels.
A tiger eating a deer and a sparrow eating seed are both predation; herbivores are not very different from predators.
Predators keep prey populations under control; an exotic species becomes invasive and spreads fast because the invaded land lacks its natural predators.
The prickly pear cactus, introduced into Australia in the early 1920s, spread over millions of hectares of rangeland until a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) was introduced.
Biological control methods in agricultural pest control are based on the ability of the predator to regulate the prey population.

questions.why: All of them: tiger and deer, a sparrow eating seed and herbivores eating plants are all predation in NCERT's broad sense.
Exotic species become invasive because the invaded land lacks their natural predators, which would otherwise keep their numbers in check.
A correct, B incorrect: a cactus-feeding moth did control the prickly pear, but it was introduced into Australia in the early 1920s, not the 1930s.
The invasive prickly pear in Australia was brought under control by a cactus-feeding predator, a moth.
Biological pest control relies on the predator's ability to regulate the prey population, so it is based on predation.

nuggets.title: Predators maintain diversity and are 'prudent'
lines: Predators help maintain species diversity in a community by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.
The starfish Pisaster is an important predator in the rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific Coast.
When all starfish were removed from an enclosed intertidal area, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year due to interspecific competition.
A predator that is too efficient and overexploits its prey may drive the prey extinct, and the predator would follow; so predators in nature are 'prudent'.

questions.why: Predators maintain diversity by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.
Removing Pisaster led to the extinction of more than 10 species of invertebrates within a year.
II, interspecific competition: without the starfish to keep prey numbers down, the invertebrate prey species competed among themselves, and the weaker ones went extinct.
Predators are 'prudent' because they do not overexploit their prey. Over-efficient predators could wipe out the prey and then themselves.
Predation is (+,−). 'Both species negatively impacted' describes competition, not predation.

nuggets.title: Prey defences: camouflage, poison, thorns, chemicals
lines: Prey species have evolved defences against predators: some insects and frogs are cryptically coloured (camouflaged).
The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its bird predator because of a chemical it acquires by feeding on a poisonous weed in its caterpillar stage.
For plants, herbivores are predators; nearly 25% of all insects are phytophagous (feed on plant sap and other plant parts).
Plants cannot run away, so thorns (Acacia, cactus) are the most common morphological defence.
Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats never browse on it.
Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are chemicals plants produce as defences against grazers and browsers.
nuggets.tip: Calotropis makes cardiac glycosides (a chemical), not glycosidase (an enzyme).

questions.why: Both true, and B explains A: the Monarch caterpillar feeds on a poisonous weed, and the chemical it acquires makes the butterfly distasteful to its predators.
A-S, B-P, C-Q, D-R: Calotropis makes cardiac glycosides; Pisaster preys on invertebrates; the Monarch is distasteful; frogs are cryptically coloured.
Nearly 25% of all insects are phytophagous, feeding on plant sap and other plant parts.
Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats avoid it. 'Glycosidase' would be an enzyme.
II only: nicotine, caffeine, quinine and strychnine are made by plants as defences against grazers and browsers. Human use is incidental.

nuggets.title: Competition: what it really means
lines: Darwin was convinced that interspecific competition is a potent force in organic evolution.
Competition is not only between closely related species: totally unrelated species can compete, e.g. flamingoes and resident fishes for zooplankton in South American lakes.
Resources need not be limiting: in interference competition, one species' feeding efficiency is reduced by the interfering and inhibitory presence of another, even when resources are abundant.
Competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured by its 'r') is significantly lower in the presence of another species.
The Abingdon tortoise in the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, apparently due to the goats' greater browsing efficiency.

questions.why: Only II: Darwin stressed interspecific (not intraspecific) competition; and 'closely related species, limiting resources' is not entirely true.
Flamingoes and resident fishes both lose by sharing zooplankton, so this is competition (−,−). It also shows that unrelated species can compete.
When feeding efficiency drops because of another species' inhibitory presence, even with abundant resources, it is interference competition.
Competition is defined as a process where the fitness (r) of one species is significantly lower in the presence of another.
The Abingdon tortoise became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, because the goats browsed more efficiently.

nuggets.title: Competitive release, Gause and resource partitioning
lines: Competitive release: a species restricted to a small area by a superior competitor expands its range dramatically when the competitor is experimentally removed.
In Connell's field experiments on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller Chthamalus.
In general, herbivores and plants appear to be more adversely affected by competition than carnivores.
Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the inferior one is eventually eliminated.
Competing species may evolve ways to coexist, such as resource partitioning: MacArthur's five closely related warbler species on one tree avoided competition through different foraging behaviour.
nuggets.tip: Connell = barnacles (Balanus beats Chthamalus); MacArthur = warblers (resource partitioning).

questions.why: Balanus, the superior barnacle, excludes Chthamalus from the intertidal zone. This is competition, and removing Balanus showed competitive release.
A correct, B false: Gause's principle is stated correctly, but it is herbivores and plants, not carnivores, that are more adversely affected by competition.
A incorrect, B correct: Gause's principle is about species competing for the same resources, not different ones; elimination of the inferior competitor may hold when resources are limiting.
Competing species may evolve resource partitioning to coexist, for example by feeding at different times or in different patterns.
MacArthur's five warbler species on one tree coexisted through behavioural differences in foraging, which is resource partitioning.

nuggets.title: Parasitism: adaptations and effects on the host
lines: Parasitism evolved in many taxonomic groups, from plants to higher vertebrates, because it ensures free lodging and meals.
Many parasites are host-specific, so host and parasite tend to co-evolve.
Parasite adaptations: loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs or suckers to cling to the host, loss of digestive system, and high reproductive capacity.
The human liver fluke (a trematode) needs two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish; the malarial parasite needs a vector (mosquito) to spread.
Most parasites harm the host: they reduce its survival, growth, reproduction and population density, and may make it physically weak and more vulnerable to predation.
nuggets.tip: Liver fluke = trematode (flatworm), not a nematode. Its intermediate hosts are a snail and a fish.

questions.why: Absence of adhesive organs is not an adaptation. Parasites have adhesive organs or suckers to cling to the host.
The human liver fluke depends on two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish, to complete its life cycle.
All five are NCERT facts: host specificity, parasitism in many groups, the trematode liver fluke with two intermediate hosts, and harm to the host's survival, growth, reproduction and density.
Incorrect: parasites make the host more vulnerable to predation by making it physically weak, not physically better.
II and III: parasitism ensures free lodging and meals, and the female mosquito is not considered a parasite. I is wrong: the liver fluke is a trematode, not a nematode.

nuggets.title: Ectoparasites, endoparasites and brood parasitism
lines: Ectoparasites feed on the external surface of the host: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, and copepods on many marine fish.
Cuscuta, a parasitic plant on hedge plants, has lost its chlorophyll and leaves during evolution and takes its nutrition from the host.
The female mosquito is not considered a parasite, although it needs our blood for reproduction.
Endoparasites live inside the host at different sites; their life cycles are more complex because of extreme specialisation, with simplified anatomy and high reproductive potential.
In brood parasitism, the parasitic bird (cuckoo or koel) lays its eggs in the host's (crow's) nest and lets the host incubate them.
The parasite's eggs have evolved to resemble the host's eggs in size and colour, so the host is less likely to detect and eject them.
nuggets.tip: Cuscuta lost chlorophyll and leaves, but it still has a stem. Koel/cuckoo is the parasite; the crow is the host.

questions.why: During evolution Cuscuta lost its chlorophyll and leaves, so it depends on the host plant for nutrition.
Only II: the female mosquito is not considered a parasite. I is wrong because copepods on marine fish are ectoparasites.
Only III: endoparasite life cycles are complex due to extreme specialisation. Cuscuta lacks chlorophyll, the liver fluke needs two hosts, and the parasite's eggs mimic the host's.
Both true: the parasitic bird lays eggs in the host's nest, and its eggs have evolved to resemble the host's eggs in size and colour.
A correct, B incorrect: the eggs do mimic the host's, but the koel is the parasite and the crow is the host.

nuggets.title: Commensalism and amensalism
lines: Commensalism is an interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither benefited nor harmed.
Examples: an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch, and barnacles growing on the back of a whale.
The cattle egret forages close to grazing cattle; the cattle stir up insects from the vegetation, which the egrets then catch.
Clown fish living among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone get protection from predators; the anemone does not appear to gain anything.
Amensalism is an interaction in which one species is harmed and the other is unaffected.
nuggets.tip: Clown fish and sea anemone is commensalism, not mutualism.

questions.why: Orchid and mango tree is commensalism: the epiphytic orchid benefits and the mango is unaffected. Fig-wasp is mutualism and cuckoo-crow is parasitism.
An epiphyte on a mango branch is commensalism (+,0): the orchid gets support and the tree is unaffected.
Tapeworm and man is parasitism (+,−), not commensalism. Clown fish-anemone, orchid-mango and egret-cattle are NCERT commensalism examples.
III and IV are incorrect: the clown fish-anemone association is commensalism, not amensalism, and the female mosquito is not considered a parasite.
One species harmed and the other unaffected is amensalism (−,0).

nuggets.title: Mutualism: lichens, mycorrhizae, plant-animal rewards
lines: Mutualism confers benefits on both interacting species.
Lichens are an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria.
Mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and roots of higher plants: the fungi help absorb essential nutrients from soil, and the plant gives them energy-yielding carbohydrates.
Plants need animals to pollinate flowers and disperse seeds, and they reward them with pollen and nectar (pollinators) or juicy, nutritious fruits (seed dispersers).
Mutually beneficial plant-pollinator systems must be safeguarded against 'cheaters', for example insects that steal nectar without pollinating.

questions.why: Both: lichens are a mutualism between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria.
Mycorrhizae are mutualism: the fungus helps the root absorb nutrients, and the plant supplies carbohydrates.
Cattle egret and grazing cattle is commensalism, not mutualism. Lichens, mycorrhizae and plant-pollinator relations are all mutualism.
Both correct: plants need animals for pollination and seed dispersal, and they reward pollinators with pollen and nectar.
Mycorrhizae are fungi associated with the roots of higher plants, so both angiosperms and gymnosperms qualify.

nuggets.title: Co-evolution: fig-wasp and Ophrys-bee
lines: Plant-pollinator mutualisms show co-evolution: the plant's and the animal's evolution are linked.
Many fig species have a tight one-to-one relationship with their pollinator species of wasp; a fig can be pollinated only by its partner wasp species.
The female wasp uses the fruit as an egg-laying (oviposition) site and pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites.
In return, the fig offers the wasp some of its developing seeds as food for the developing wasp larvae.
The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys uses 'sexual deceit': one petal looks uncannily like a female bee in size, colour and markings, and the male bee pseudocopulates with it, picking up pollen.
If the female bee's colour patterns change even slightly, pollination success falls unless the orchid flower co-evolves to keep the resemblance.

questions.why: Both: the female wasp uses the fig fruit as an oviposition site, and the developing seeds feed its larvae.
Fig trees and their pollinator wasp species show a tight one-to-one relationship, which is NCERT's classic example of co-evolution.
In the Mediterranean orchid Ophrys, one petal resembles the female bee in size, colour and markings.
Male bees pseudocopulate with the bee-like petal of the orchid (Ophrys) and transfer its pollen.
A wasp pollinating a fig flower is mutualism: the fig gets pollinated and the wasp gets a breeding site and food for its larvae.

nuggets.title: Ecosystem: the functional unit of nature
lines: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with the surrounding physical environment.
Ecosystems vary greatly in size, from a small pond to a large forest or a sea.
Many ecologists regard the entire biosphere as a global ecosystem, a composite of all local ecosystems on Earth.
Two basic categories: terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary).
Crop fields and an aquarium are man-made ecosystems.

questions.why: Ecosystem: the functional unit where organisms interact with each other and with the physical environment. A community lacks the abiotic part; biosphere is the global sum of ecosystems.
NCERT gives crop fields and an aquarium as man-made ecosystems. A desert is a natural terrestrial ecosystem.
Grassland is terrestrial (A-Q), estuary is aquatic (B-R) and an aquarium is man-made (C-P).
I, III, IV and VI are NCERT lines. II is wrong: the structural features are species composition and stratification, not productivity. V describes stratification, not species composition.
A is correct (functional unit of nature). B is wrong: crop fields and an aquarium are man-made ecosystems.

nuggets.title: Ecosystem structure: species composition and stratification
lines: Interaction of biotic and abiotic components results in a physical structure characteristic of each type of ecosystem.
Identification and enumeration of plant and animal species of an ecosystem gives its species composition.
Stratification is the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels.
In a forest, trees occupy the top vertical layer, shrubs the second, and herbs and grasses the bottom layers.
Components function as a unit in productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.
nuggets.tip: Enumerating species = species composition; vertical layering = stratification. Examiners swap the two.

questions.why: Statement I is the NCERT line. Statement II is wrong because listing and counting species gives species composition, not stratification.
Stratification is the vertical distribution of species occupying different levels (trees, shrubs, herbs). Option 1 describes species composition.
Vertical distribution of species at different levels in a community is stratification, e.g. trees above shrubs above herbs in a forest.
A is wrong: stratification is vertical, not horizontal distribution. B is the NCERT forest example (trees, shrubs, herbs and grasses).
Productivity, energy flow and decomposition are functional aspects. Stratification is a structural feature of an ecosystem.

nuggets.title: Pond ecosystem: a self-sustaining model
lines: In a pond, the abiotic component is water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances and the rich soil deposit at the bottom.
Solar input, the cycle of temperature, day-length and other climatic conditions regulate the rate of function of the whole pond.
Autotrophs: phytoplankton, some algae and the floating, submerged and marginal plants at the edges.
Consumers: zooplankton and free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms; decomposers (fungi, bacteria, flagellates) are abundant at the bottom.
A pond shows all functions: autotrophs fix inorganic matter using solar energy, heterotrophs consume them, and decomposition with mineralisation returns nutrients.
Energy moves upward to higher trophic levels and is dissipated to the environment as heat.
nuggets.tip: Phytoplankton = producers; zooplankton = consumers. Decomposers are abundant at the bottom, not the surface.

questions.why: Pond autotrophs are phytoplankton, some algae and floating, submerged and marginal plants, so both 1 and 3. Zooplankton are consumers.
All four are pond abiotic factors in NCERT: dissolved substances, bottom soil deposit, solar input and temperature cycle, day-length and climate.
Zooplankton are consumers (A-Q), bacteria and flagellates are decomposers (B-P), phytoplankton are autotrophs (C-R).
The Assertion lists pond autotrophs correctly. The Reason is wrong: decomposers are abundant at the bottom of the pond, not the surface.
Both are wrong because the roles are swapped: phytoplankton are autotrophs and zooplankton are consumers.

nuggets.title: Primary production and productivity
lines: Primary production is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis.
Primary production is expressed in terms of weight (g m<sup>-2</sup>) or energy (kcal m<sup>-2</sup>).
The rate of biomass production is called productivity.
Productivity is expressed in g m<sup>-2</sup> yr<sup>-1</sup> or (kcal m<sup>-2</sup>) yr<sup>-1</sup>, so different ecosystems can be compared.
Primary productivity is divided into gross (GPP) and net (NPP) primary productivity.
nuggets.tip: Production has no time unit (g m<sup>-2</sup>); productivity is a rate, so it carries yr<sup>-1</sup>.

questions.why: Both statements are NCERT: primary production is organic matter made per unit area over time by plants in photosynthesis, expressed as g m<sup>-2</sup> or kcal m<sup>-2</sup>. Plants make organic, not inorganic, matter.
The rate of biomass production is called productivity.
Productivity is a rate per unit area, so it is expressed as g m<sup>-2</sup> yr<sup>-1</sup> or (kcal m<sup>-2</sup>) yr<sup>-1</sup>. kcal m<sup>-2</sup> alone has no time unit.
Productivity is a rate, so its unit needs area and time: (kcal m-2) yr-1. g m-2 and kcal m-2 lack time; m-3 is a volume unit.
A is wrong: production is per unit area (m-2), not volume (m-3). B is correct: g m-2 yr-1 or (kcal m-2) yr-1 lets ecosystems be compared.

nuggets.title: GPP, NPP and secondary productivity
lines: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis.
A considerable amount of GPP is used by plants in respiration.
GPP minus respiration losses (R) is net primary productivity: GPP − R = NPP.
NPP is the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers).
Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.
nuggets.tip: GPP is always more than NPP. R = respiration loss of the plants themselves.

questions.why: The rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis is GPP. NPP is what remains after respiration losses are subtracted.
In GPP − R = NPP, R is the respiration loss of the producers.
NPP (GPP minus respiration) is the biomass available for consumption by herbivores and decomposers. GPP includes the part plants burn in respiration.
Since NPP = GPP − R and R is always used, GPP is always more than NPP.
A deer is a consumer, and new organic matter formed by consumers is secondary productivity. Primary productivity is by producers.

nuggets.title: What controls primary productivity
lines: Primary productivity depends on the plant species inhabiting an area.
It also depends on environmental factors, availability of nutrients and the photosynthetic capacity of plants, so it varies between ecosystems.
The annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter.
Despite occupying about 70 per cent of the surface, the oceans produce only about 55 billion tons.
nuggets.tip: 170 billion tons for the biosphere, only 55 billion tons from oceans. Not million, not kilogram.

questions.why: Primary productivity depends on nutrient availability and on the photosynthetic capacity of plants, so both. Respiration reduces NPP but is not listed as a controlling factor.
NCERT lists plant species, environmental factors, nutrients and photosynthetic capacity. Predation is not one of them.
Both are wrong: NPP varies between ecosystems because it depends on plant species, environmental factors, nutrients and photosynthetic capacity.
Biosphere NPP is about 170 billion tons (dry weight). Oceans cover about 70% of the surface but give only 55 billion tons.
The annual NPP of the biosphere is about 170 billion tons of organic matter (dry weight). 55 billion tons is the oceans' share.

nuggets.title: Decomposition: detritus, fragmentation, leaching, catabolism
lines: Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like CO2, water and nutrients; this is decomposition.
Detritus (dead plant remains like leaves, bark, flowers and dead animal remains including faecal matter) is the raw material of decomposition.
Steps of decomposition: fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.
Fragmentation: detritivores such as the earthworm break detritus into smaller particles.
Leaching: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances.
nuggets.tip: Earthworm = fragmentation (not catabolism). Detritus is the input, not the product, of decomposition.

questions.why: Breaking detritus into smaller particles by detritivores like the earthworm is fragmentation. Catabolism is enzymatic degradation by microbes.
Detritivores breaking detritus into small particles is fragmentation. Humification makes humus; catabolism is enzyme action by bacteria and fungi.
Water-soluble inorganic nutrients moving down into the soil horizon and precipitating as unavailable salts is leaching.
The earthworm is a detritivore that fragments detritus and loosens soil, which is why it is called the farmer's friend.
Both are NCERT definitions: leaching takes soluble nutrients down as unavailable salts, and catabolism is enzymatic degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances.

nuggets.title: Humification and mineralisation
lines: Fragmentation, leaching and catabolism operate simultaneously on the detritus.
Humification leads to accumulation of a dark coloured amorphous substance called humus.
Humus is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes at an extremely slow rate.
Being colloidal in nature, humus serves as a reservoir of nutrients.
Mineralisation: humus is further degraded by some microbes and inorganic nutrients are released.
nuggets.tip: Humus decomposes extremely slowly. Mineralisation releases inorganic nutrients from humus.

questions.why: Accumulation of a dark coloured amorphous substance (humus) is humification. Mineralisation is the later release of inorganic nutrients from humus.
Both are NCERT: humus is highly resistant to microbes and decomposes extremely slowly, and being colloidal it acts as a reservoir of nutrients.
In mineralisation, humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients.
NCERT order: fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation. Humification comes before mineralisation because mineralisation acts on humus.
I, II and III are correct. IV is wrong because the detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter. V is wrong because earthworms carry out fragmentation, not catabolism.

nuggets.title: Factors affecting rate of decomposition
lines: Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process.
The rate of decomposition is controlled by the chemical composition of detritus and climatic factors.
Decomposition is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker if rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars.
Temperature and soil moisture regulate decomposition through their effects on soil microbes; a warm and moist environment favours it.
Low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition, resulting in build-up of organic material.
nuggets.tip: Lignin/chitin slow it; nitrogen/sugars speed it. Cold + no oxygen = organic matter piles up.

questions.why: Statement I is correct: microbes degrade detritus into simpler substances. Statement II is wrong: lignin and chitin make decomposition slower, not faster.
Decomposition is delayed when detritus is rich in lignin and chitin. Sugars, nitrogen, aeration and warm moist conditions all speed it up.
Both are NCERT lines: lignin and chitin slow decomposition while nitrogen and sugars speed it, and low temperature with anaerobiosis causes organic matter to build up.
The Assertion is correct. The Reason is wrong: microbes do not work effectively at low temperature, which is exactly why decomposition is inhibited.
II is wrong (low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit), V is wrong (composition and climate control the rate), VI is wrong (lignin and chitin slow it). I, III and IV are correct.

nuggets.title: Energy flow: sun, PAR and the second law
lines: Except for the deep sea hydro-thermal ecosystem, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth.
Of the incident solar radiation, less than 50 per cent is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).
Plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the PAR, and this small amount sustains the entire living world.
Energy flows unidirectionally from the sun to producers and then to consumers.
Ecosystems are not exempt from the second law of thermodynamics; they need a constant supply of energy to counteract increasing disorderliness.
nuggets.tip: 2–10% is of PAR, not of total sunlight. The exception to solar energy is the deep sea hydro-thermal ecosystem.

questions.why: NCERT says the sun is the only energy source for all ecosystems except the deep sea hydro-thermal ecosystem, which runs on chemical energy.
A is wrong: the deep sea hydro-thermal ecosystem is the exception to solar energy. B is correct: less than 50% of incident radiation is PAR.
Plants capture only 2–10 per cent of PAR, yet this small amount sustains the entire living world.
The incorrect statement is that plants capture about 10% of the sunlight falling on leaves. NCERT says plants capture 2–10% of PAR. The other statements are correct.
A is correct: energy flows one way, from the sun to producers to consumers. B is wrong: ecosystems are not exempt from the second law of thermodynamics.

nuggets.title: Producers, consumers and trophic levels
lines: Producers trap solar energy as chemical bond energy; in terrestrial ecosystems the major producers are herbaceous and woody plants.
In aquatic ecosystems, primary producers are phytoplankton, algae and higher plants.
All animals depend on plants for food, directly or indirectly; they are consumers (heterotrophs).
Herbivores are primary consumers (second trophic level); carnivores eating herbivores are secondary consumers (third trophic level).
A species may occupy more than one trophic level at the same time: a sparrow eating seeds is a primary consumer, but eating worms it is a secondary consumer.
nuggets.tip: Trophic level counts from producers = T1. Primary consumer = T2, not T1.

questions.why: Both are NCERT: herbaceous and woody plants are the main terrestrial producers, and phytoplankton, algae and higher plants are the aquatic producers.
Green plants that convert solar energy into chemical bond energy are both producers and autotrophs.
Grass is T1 (C-S), rabbit T2 (B-R), crow T3 (D-P) and vulture T4 (A-Q).
II (secondary consumers: birds, fishes, wolf at T3) and III (primary consumers: zooplankton, grasshopper, cow at T2) are correct. I and IV put the wrong organisms at T4.
A sparrow is a primary consumer when it eats seeds and fruits, and a secondary consumer when it eats worms and insects, so it occupies two levels at once.

nuggets.title: Grazing food chain, detritus food chain and food web
lines: The grazing food chain (GFC) begins with producers at the first trophic level.
The detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter; death of an organism is the beginning of the detritus food chain.
Decomposers (saprotrophs), mainly fungi and bacteria, secrete digestive enzymes to break down detritus and meet their energy and nutrient needs.
In an aquatic ecosystem GFC is the major conduit for energy flow; in a terrestrial ecosystem a much larger fraction flows through DFC.
DFC may be connected to GFC at some levels, and the natural interconnection of food chains makes a food web.
nuggets.tip: Aquatic = GFC dominant; terrestrial = DFC carries the larger fraction of energy.

questions.why: The incorrect statement reverses NCERT: GFC is the major conduit in aquatic ecosystems, while in terrestrial ecosystems more energy flows through DFC.
NCERT: in an aquatic ecosystem the GFC is the major conduit for energy flow. So saying DFC is the major conduit there is incorrect.
Both are NCERT: some DFC organisms are prey to GFC animals, so the chains connect, and the natural interconnection of food chains forms a food web.
DFC begins with dead organic matter because its decomposers (bacteria, fungi) get energy and nutrients by degrading detritus. So the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.
Death of an organism is the beginning of the detritus food chain or web, since dead organic matter is its starting point.

nuggets.title: Standing crop and the 10 per cent law
lines: Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time called the standing crop.
Standing crop is measured as the mass of living organisms (biomass) or their number in a unit area.
Biomass measured as dry weight is more accurate.
Energy decreases at successive trophic levels; no energy trapped in an organism remains in it forever.
10 per cent law: only 10% of energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower trophic level.
nuggets.tip: 10% passes from the lower to the higher level. 'From the higher level' is a classic wrong option.

questions.why: The mass of living material at a trophic level at a particular time is the standing crop. Standing state refers to nutrients in the soil.
A is wrong: the term is standing crop, not floating crop. B is correct: it is measured as biomass or number per unit area.
Biomass measured as dry weight is more accurate, because water content in fresh weight varies.
With 10% passed at each step: plant 20 J, mice 2 J, snake 0.2 J, peacock 0.02 J.
The Assertion is correct. The Reason is wrong: 10% of energy passes to each level from the lower trophic level, not from the higher one.

nuggets.title: Ecological pyramids: number, biomass, energy
lines: The base of each pyramid represents producers (first trophic level) and the apex represents the tertiary or top-level consumer.
The three pyramids usually studied are the pyramid of number, of biomass and of energy.
Any calculation of energy content, biomass or number must include all organisms at that trophic level.
In most ecosystems, such as a grassland, all three pyramids are upright.
The pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted, because some energy is always lost as heat at each step.

questions.why: The pyramid of energy is always upright with a broad base, since energy is lost at each step. So 'it is inverted in shape' is incorrect.
Energy is lost as heat at every transfer, so the pyramid of energy can never be inverted. Number and biomass pyramids can be.
Both are NCERT: the three pyramids are number, biomass and energy, and an organism may occupy more than one trophic level simultaneously.
The incorrect statement is that the energy pyramid may sometimes be inverted. NCERT says it is always upright. The other three are NCERT lines.
These are g/m2 values (biomass) falling from producers (763) to secondary consumers (2.6), so this is an upright pyramid of biomass.

nuggets.title: Inverted pyramids and limitations of pyramids
lines: The pyramid of biomass in the sea is generally inverted, because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton.
Ecological pyramids do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels.
They assume a simple food chain, something that almost never exists in nature, and do not accommodate a food web.
Saprophytes are not given any place in ecological pyramids, even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem.
nuggets.tip: Saprophytes are left out of pyramids even though they play a vital role, not because they are unimportant.

questions.why: The pyramid of biomass in the sea is generally inverted because fish biomass far exceeds phytoplankton biomass. Grassland number and forest biomass pyramids are upright.
Both are true, but the inversion is due to fish biomass exceeding phytoplankton biomass. Phytoplankton outnumbering fishes does not explain a biomass pyramid.
a, b and d are NCERT limitations. c is wrong: pyramids give saprophytes no place.
All three are limitations listed by NCERT: species at two or more trophic levels are ignored, a simple chain is assumed, and saprophytes get no place.
Both are wrong. Pyramids do not account for a species at two or more levels, and saprophytes are left out even though they play a vital role.

nuggets.title: Biodiversity and genetic diversity
lines: There are more than 20,000 species of ants, 3,00,000 species of beetles, 28,000 species of fishes and nearly 20,000 species of orchids.
Biodiversity, the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation, is a term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson.
Genetic diversity: a single species may show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range.
Rauwolfia vomitoria from different Himalayan ranges varies in the potency and concentration of the active chemical reserpine.
India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.
nuggets.tip: 50,000 is rice, 1,000 is mango. Examiners swap them.

questions.why: A matches NCERT (20,000 orchids, 3,00,000 beetles, 28,000 fishes). B is wrong because Edward Wilson was a sociobiologist, not a sociophysicist.
Edward Wilson popularised the term biodiversity for the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation.
Variation within one species (Rauwolfia vomitoria) across Himalayan ranges, in the potency and concentration of reserpine, is genetic diversity.
India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.
Varieties of indigenous cows are variation within one species, which is genetic diversity, like the rice strains and mango varieties of India.

nuggets.title: Species diversity and ecological diversity
lines: Species diversity is the diversity at the species level, e.g. the Western Ghats have greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.
Ecological diversity is diversity at the ecosystem level.
India, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.
The diversity of plants and animals is not uniform throughout the world but shows a rather uneven distribution.
nuggets.tip: Western Ghats have more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats. Do not reverse this.

questions.why: Comparing the number of amphibian species in two regions (Western vs Eastern Ghats) is species diversity.
A is wrong: the variable chemical in Rauwolfia vomitoria is reserpine. B is correct: the Western Ghats have greater amphibian diversity than the Eastern Ghats.
II (India has greater ecosystem diversity than Norway) and III (Wilson's definition) are correct. I reverses the Ghats, and IV is wrong because reserpine comes from Rauwolfia.
I, II and III are correct. IV is wrong because species diversity generally decreases, not increases, with altitude.

nuggets.title: How many species: global estimates
lines: According to the IUCN (2004), slightly more than 1.5 million plant and animal species have been described so far.
Robert May places global species diversity at about 7 million.
More than 70 per cent of all recorded species are animals; plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) are no more than 22 per cent.
Among animals, insects are the most species-rich group, more than 70 per cent of the total: 7 of every 10 animals are insects.
Fungi species outnumber the combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.
Conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species, so their diversity is poorly known.
nuggets.tip: Robert May's 7 million is a global figure, not India's.

questions.why: Robert May estimated global species diversity at about 7 million. About 1.5 million is the number described so far.
Insects are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70% of all animals (7 of every 10 animals).
NCERT notes that fungi species outnumber the combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.
A is wrong: May's 7 million is a global estimate, not India's. B is correct: insects are more than 70% of animal species.
A is wrong: fungi are more than fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals combined. B is correct: conventional taxonomy cannot identify microbes.

nuggets.title: India's share of biodiversity
lines: India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, but its share of global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent.
India is one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world.
Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many animals have been recorded from India.
Applying May's estimate, more than 1,00,000 plant species and more than 3,00,000 animal species are yet to be discovered in India.
nuggets.tip: 2.4% of the land, 8.1% of the species. Plants about 45,000; animals twice that.

questions.why: India has only 2.4% of the world's land area, yet 8.1% of global species diversity.
India's share of global species diversity is about 8.1%, which is why it is a mega diversity country. 2.4% is its land share.
Land area 2.4% (A-Q), species diversity 8.1% (B-P) and about 45,000 plant species (C-R).
By May's estimate, India has more than 1,00,000 plant and more than 3,00,000 animal species still to be discovered and described.
A is correct: India is one of the 12 mega diversity countries. B is wrong: India has about 45,000 plant species and twice, not triple, as many animals.

nuggets.title: Latitudinal gradient in diversity
lines: Species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles; tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species.
Colombia, near the equator, has nearly 1,400 bird species; New York (41° N) has 105 and Greenland (71° N) only 56.
India, with much of its land in tropical latitudes, has more than 1,200 species of birds.
A tropical forest in Ecuador has up to 10 times as many vascular plant species as an equal-area temperate forest in the Midwest of the USA.
The tropical Amazonian rain forest in South America has the greatest biodiversity on Earth.
nuggets.tip: Bird counts: Colombia 1,400, India 1,200+, New York 105, Greenland 56.

questions.why: Species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles, so the tropics are richest.
New York at 41° N has 105 bird species and Greenland at 71° N only 56, showing the fall in diversity with latitude.
Both are NCERT figures: Greenland has 56 bird species and Colombia, near the equator, nearly 1,400.
A is correct (India has more than 1,200 bird species). B is wrong: an Ecuador forest has up to 10 times, not 12 times, the vascular plants of a Midwest USA forest.
The tropical Amazonian rain forest in South America has the greatest biodiversity on Earth.

nuggets.title: Why the tropics are so rich
lines: Speciation is generally a function of time: temperate regions had frequent glaciations, while tropical latitudes stayed undisturbed for millions of years.
Tropical environments are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable.
Constant environments promote niche specialisation and lead to greater species diversity.
More solar energy is available in the tropics, which contributes to higher productivity and, indirectly, to greater diversity.
The Amazon is home to more than 40,000 plants, 3,000 fishes, 1,300 birds, 427 mammals, 427 amphibians, 378 reptiles and over 1,25,000 invertebrates.
nuggets.tip: Glaciations happened in temperate regions, not the tropics. Tropical environments are less seasonal, not more.

questions.why: A, C, D and E are the NCERT reasons. B is wrong because tropical environments are less seasonal.
A relatively constant tropical environment promotes niche specialisation and leads to greater species diversity.
Only IV is incorrect: tropical latitudes stayed undisturbed for millions of years, while temperate regions had frequent glaciations.
Both are NCERT: speciation is a function of time, and constant environments promote niche specialisation and greater species diversity.
A is correct: rain forests may hold at least two million undiscovered insect species. B is wrong: it was temperate regions that had glaciations and the tropics that stayed undisturbed.

nuggets.title: Species–area relationship
lines: German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed that species richness increases with explored area, but only up to a limit.
For many taxa (angiosperms, birds, bats, freshwater fishes), the species–area relation is a rectangular hyperbola.
On a logarithmic scale it is a straight line: log S = log C + Z log A (S species richness, A area, Z slope or regression coefficient, C Y-intercept).
Z values usually lie between 0.1 and 0.2, regardless of taxonomic group or region.
For very large areas like entire continents the slope is steeper (Z = 0.6 to 1.2); for frugivorous birds and mammals across continents Z = 1.15.
nuggets.tip: Small area: Z 0.1–0.2. Continents: Z 0.6–1.2. Rectangular hyperbola on a normal scale, straight line on a log scale.

questions.why: Alexander von Humboldt first described the species–area relationship: species richness rises with explored area, up to a limit.
On a log scale the relation is log S = log C + Z log A, a straight line with slope Z. The other options drop or misplace terms.
Plotted on a normal scale, species richness against area is a rectangular hyperbola. It becomes a straight line only on a log scale.
Z (the slope) typically lies between 0.1 and 0.2, regardless of taxonomic group or region. Steeper values (0.6–1.2) are for whole continents.
Both are NCERT: for entire continents Z is 0.6 to 1.2, and for frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents the slope is 1.15.

nuggets.title: Species diversity and ecosystem stability
lines: For many decades ecologists believed that communities with more species tend to be more stable than those with fewer species.
A stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year.
It must be resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances and resistant to invasions by alien species.
David Tilman's long-term outdoor plot experiments: plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass.
Tilman also showed that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.
nuggets.tip: Tilman = outdoor plots, stability and productivity. Ehrlich = rivet popper. Humboldt = species–area.

questions.why: Tilman found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, which indicates stability.
Tilman showed both: diversity contributed to higher productivity, and species-rich plots varied less in total biomass from year to year.
Only II is correct. I and III reverse Tilman's result (more species means less variation), and IV is wrong because more diversity means more productivity.
A is wrong: ecologists believed species-rich communities are more stable. B is correct: a stable community shows little year-to-year variation in productivity.
David Tilman's long-term outdoor plot experiments gave a tentative answer that species-rich communities are more stable.

nuggets.title: Rivet popper hypothesis
lines: Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich proposed the rivet popper hypothesis to explain the role of each species.
The ecosystem is compared to an airplane, and all species to the rivets joining its parts.
Losing a few rivets (species) may not affect flight safety at first, but as more are lost the plane becomes dangerously weak.
Which rivet is lost also matters: losing rivets on the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is a more serious threat than losing a few on the seats.

questions.why: The rivet popper hypothesis was given by the Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich.
A is wrong: Paul Ehrlich was a Stanford ecologist, not a physiologist. B is correct: Earth's biological wealth is declining because of human activities.
The rivet popper hypothesis belongs to Paul Ehrlich, not David Tilman, who did the outdoor plot experiments. The other three pairs are correct.
Robert May gave the 7 million estimate (A-R), Humboldt the species–area relation (B-P), Ehrlich the rivet popper hypothesis (C-S) and Tilman the outdoor plots (D-Q).
Both are wrong because the names are swapped: Humboldt was the German naturalist and geographer, and Ehrlich the Stanford ecologist.

nuggets.title: Loss of biodiversity: recent extinctions
lines: Human colonisation of tropical Pacific islands is said to have led to the extinction of more than 2,000 species of native birds.
The IUCN Red List (2004) documents 784 extinctions in the last 500 years: 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants.
Recent extinctions: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia) and Steller's sea cow (Russia).
Three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian) have also become extinct.
The last twenty years alone have seen the disappearance of 27 species.
nuggets.tip: Dodo-Mauritius, Quagga-Africa, Thylacine-Australia, Steller's sea cow-Russia.

questions.why: Red List (2004) extinctions in the last 500 years: 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants (784 in all).
Steller's sea cow is from Russia, not North America. Dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa) and thylacine (Australia) are correctly matched.
The three extinct tiger subspecies are Bali, Javan and Caspian. The Sumatran, Siberian and Bengal tigers survive.
The last twenty years alone have witnessed the disappearance of 27 species.
Colonisation of tropical Pacific islands by humans led to the extinction of more than 2,000 species of native birds. The other figures are Red List counts.

nuggets.title: Threatened groups, sixth extinction and consequences
lines: Extinctions across taxa are not random; amphibians appear more vulnerable to extinction.
Presently 12% of birds, 23% of mammals, 32% of amphibians and 31% of gymnosperms face the threat of extinction.
There were five past mass extinctions; the ongoing sixth extinction is 100–1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and humans are responsible.
If this trend continues, nearly half of all species on Earth might be wiped out within the next 100 years.
Loss of biodiversity causes a decline in plant production, lowered resistance to perturbations like drought, and greater variability in productivity, water use and pest and disease cycles.
nuggets.tip: Threat %: birds 12, mammals 23, gymnosperms 31, amphibians 32.

questions.why: NCERT figures for species facing the threat of extinction: birds 12%, mammals 23%, amphibians 32%, gymnosperms 31%.
Both are NCERT: amphibians are more vulnerable, and 12% of birds, 23% of mammals and 32% of amphibians face the threat of extinction.
