The current sixth extinction is 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and human activities are responsible.
Biodiversity loss causes a decline in plant production (II), lowered resistance to perturbations like drought (III) and increased variability in ecosystem processes (I). IV reverses III.
A is correct: there were five past mass extinctions. B is wrong: the 100–1,000 times faster rate is due to human activities.

nuggets.title: Evil Quartet I: habitat loss and fragmentation
lines: The four major causes of biodiversity loss are called 'The Evil Quartet'.
Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.
Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14% of Earth's land surface; now they cover no more than 6%.
The Amazon rain forest, the 'lungs of the planet', is being cleared for soya beans or for grasslands to raise beef cattle.
Fragmentation affects mammals and birds needing large territories and animals with migratory habits, leading to population declines.
nuggets.tip: Rain forest cover: 14% before, no more than 6% now.

questions.why: Of the Evil Quartet, habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause driving species to extinction.
The Evil Quartet is habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions, so A, B and D. Mutation and migration are not in it.
A is wrong: rain forests once covered more than 14% of land and now cover no more than 6%. B is correct: the Amazon is the 'lungs of the planet'.
The Amazon rain forest is being cleared to grow soya beans or to make grasslands for beef cattle.
Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause of extinction. Over-exploitation and alien invasions are also causes, but less important.

nuggets.title: Evil Quartet II: over-exploitation and alien species
lines: Over-exploitation: when 'need' turns to 'greed', natural resources are over-exploited.
Many extinctions in the last 500 years, such as Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon, were due to over-exploitation by humans.
Alien species invasions: the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria (East Africa) led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
Invasive weeds such as carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eicchornia) threaten native species.
Illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture threatens indigenous catfishes in our rivers.
nuggets.tip: Lake Victoria is in East Africa. Parthenium is carrot grass, not Lantana.

questions.why: The passenger pigeon, like Steller's sea cow, became extinct due to over-exploitation by humans.
The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria caused the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish. The African catfish threatens Indian rivers instead.
A is correct. B is wrong because Lake Victoria is in East Africa, not West Africa. The rest of B (Nile perch, 200+ cichlids) is NCERT.
Steller's sea cow is extinct, through over-exploitation. Parthenium is an alien weed, the African catfish does threaten native catfish, and carrot grass is Parthenium.
Lantana, Eichhornia and the African catfish are all alien invasive species in India, so they are neither native nor threatened.

nuggets.title: Evil Quartet III: co-extinctions
lines: Co-extinction: when a species becomes extinct, plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct.
When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets the same fate.
In a coevolved plant–pollinator mutualism, extinction of one invariably leads to extinction of the other.
Habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions together make up the Evil Quartet.

questions.why: Both are NCERT co-extinction lines: obligately associated species die out with the host, e.g. a host fish's unique parasites.
Extinction of species associated in an obligatory way when their partner disappears is co-extinction.

Rain forests shrinking from 14% to 6% is habitat loss (A-R), 'need turns to greed' is over-exploitation (B-P), cichlid loss is alien invasion (C-S), and loss of a pollinator causes co-extinction (D-Q).
Habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien invasions and co-extinction are the Evil Quartet, the causes of biodiversity loss.

nuggets.title: Why conserve biodiversity
lines: Reasons for conservation are grouped as narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical.
Narrowly utilitarian: food, firewood, fibre, construction material and industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicines.
More than 25% of drugs sold worldwide come from plants, and 25,000 plant species are used in traditional medicines; bioprospecting could bring enormous benefits to biodiversity-rich nations.
Broadly utilitarian: ecosystem services such as oxygen (the Amazon produces about 20% of Earth's oxygen), pollination and aesthetic pleasure.
Ethical: every species has an intrinsic value, and we have a moral duty to pass on our biological legacy in good order.
nuggets.tip: Drugs and products = narrow. Oxygen, pollination and aesthetics = broad. Intrinsic value = ethical.

questions.why: Food, medicine and industrial products are narrowly utilitarian (A-R), ecosystem services are broadly utilitarian (B-P), and intrinsic value is the ethical argument (C-Q).
Direct economic benefits such as drugs and traditional medicines are a narrowly utilitarian reason for conservation.
Oxygen, pollination and aesthetic pleasure are ecosystem services, so they are broadly utilitarian. Industrial products, bioprospecting, drugs, fibre and firewood are narrowly utilitarian.
Food, drugs and fibre are direct products, so three are narrowly utilitarian. Oxygen and flood or erosion control are broadly utilitarian services.
A is the NCERT definition of bioprospecting. B is wrong: biodiversity-rich nations can expect to reap enormous benefits, not losses.

nuggets.title: In situ conservation: biodiversity hotspots
lines: In in situ (on site) conservation the whole ecosystem is protected, so its biodiversity at all levels is protected.
Hotspots are regions with very high species richness and a high degree of endemism.
Initially 25 hotspots were identified, and 9 more were added, making 34 worldwide.
India's three hotspots are the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and the Himalaya.
All hotspots together cover less than 2% of Earth's land area; their strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30%.
nuggets.tip: 34 hotspots, under 2% of land, about 30% fewer extinctions. India has 3, not 4.

questions.why: There are 34 biodiversity hotspots: 25 identified first and 9 added later.
Strict protection of biodiversity hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30%.
Hotspots are defined by high species richness, high endemism and threat to habitats. A large number of exotic species is not one of their features.
II, III, IV and V are NCERT facts. I is wrong: useful genes are not found only in hotspots.
The incorrect statement says hotspots have few or no threatened species. Hotspots are defined by high richness and endemism and are under threat.

nuggets.title: Protected areas and sacred groves
lines: Ecologically unique, biodiversity-rich regions are protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries.
India now has 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries.
Sacred groves are traditionally protected forest patches where all trees and wildlife are venerated and given total protection.
Sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), Western Ghats (Karnataka, Maharashtra) and Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar (MP).
In Meghalaya, sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.
nuggets.tip: 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, 448 sanctuaries.

questions.why: India has 14 biosphere reserves (A-Q), 90 national parks (B-R) and 448 wildlife sanctuaries (C-P).
NCERT lists sacred groves in all three: Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar.
I, II, IV, V and VI are correct. III is wrong because Sarguja and Bastar are in Madhya Pradesh, not Mizoram.
A botanical garden protects plants away from their natural habitat, so it is ex situ. Biosphere reserves, sanctuaries and sacred groves are in situ.
Both are wrong. India has three hotspots (A lists three regions but calls them four), and it has 448 wildlife sanctuaries, not 484.

nuggets.title: Ex situ conservation
lines: In ex situ (off site) conservation, threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and protected in special settings.
Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose.
Gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods by cryopreservation.
Eggs can be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture.
Seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks.
nuggets.tip: Hotspots, national parks, sanctuaries and sacred groves are in situ. Zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and cryopreservation are ex situ.

questions.why: Wildlife safari parks, like zoos and botanical gardens, are ex situ. Hotspots, the Amazon and the Himalaya protect species in their natural habitat.
Cryopreservation of gametes in viable and fertile condition is an advanced ex situ conservation method.
A national park protects species in their natural habitat, so it is in situ. Micropropagation, cryopreservation and IVF are ex situ.
Field gene banks, seed banks and botanical gardens are ex situ methods. Shifting cultivation is a farming practice, not a conservation method.
A national park is in situ and a botanical garden is ex situ. The other options swap the categories.

nuggets.title: International efforts for conservation
lines: Biodiversity knows no political boundaries, so conservation is a collective responsibility of all nations.
The historic Convention on Biological Diversity, 'The Earth Summit', was held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.
It called on all nations to take measures to conserve biodiversity and to use its benefits sustainably.
The World Summit on Sustainable Development was held in 2002 in Johannesburg, South Africa.
There, 190 countries pledged to achieve a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.
nuggets.tip: Rio 1992 = Earth Summit (CBD). Johannesburg 2002 = World Summit; target year 2010.

questions.why: The 1992 Rio Earth Summit called on nations to take measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable use of its benefits.
The Earth Summit (Convention on Biological Diversity) was held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992. 2002 was the Johannesburg World Summit.
The historic Convention on Biological Diversity is known as the Earth Summit (Rio, 1992). The Kyoto and Montreal Protocols deal with climate and the ozone layer.
The World Summit was in Johannesburg (A-R), the Earth Summit in Rio (B-P), zoological parks are ex situ (C-Q) and hotspots are in situ (D-S).
The World Summit on Sustainable Development (2002) was held in Johannesburg, South Africa.
